school-c11-biology-b.title: Class 11 Biology — Part B (Ch 11 to Revision & Practice)
school-c11-biology-b.description: All 19 chapters of Class 11 Biology, chapter by chapter: diversity, structure, cell biology, plant physiology and human physiology, with solved questions, quizzes, chapter tests and a revision course.

courses.title: Ch 11 · Photosynthesis in Higher Plants
courses.summary: Classic experiments, the site of photosynthesis, pigments, the light reactions (photosystems, Z scheme, photolysis, chemiosmosis), the Calvin cycle, the C4 pathway, photorespiration and limiting factors.
outcomes: Learners can describe the key experiments that revealed photosynthesis
Learners can explain the light reactions, cyclic and non-cyclic photophosphorylation and chemiosmosis
Learners can describe the Calvin cycle and its ATP/NADPH needs
Learners can compare C3 and C4 plants and explain photorespiration and limiting factors

lessons.title: Early experiments and the site of photosynthesis

story.title: The candle, the mouse and the mint

scenes.text: In 1770, Joseph Priestley found that a candle went out in a closed jar — but burned on if a mint plant was inside.
Plants restore the air that burning and breathing use up. That 'air' was later named oxygen.

steps.title: Milestones
steps.body:
- **Joseph Priestley (1770):** plants restore air (bell jar, candle, mouse, mint). He discovered oxygen in 1774.
- **Jan Ingenhousz:** only **green parts** in **sunlight** restore air (bubbles around aquatic plants in light).
- **Julius von Sachs (1854):** green substance (chlorophyll) is in special bodies (chloroplasts); **glucose** is made and usually stored as **starch**.
- **T.W. Engelmann:** split light with a prism onto the alga *Cladophora* with aerobic bacteria; bacteria gathered in **blue and red** light → first **action spectrum**.
- **Cornelius van Niel:** using purple and green sulphur bacteria showed photosynthesis is light-dependent reduction of CO₂ by hydrogen from a donor; in green plants **O₂ comes from H₂O**, not CO₂.

Overall: **6CO₂ + 12H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6H₂O + 6O₂** (light, chlorophyll).

steps.title: Where it happens
steps.body: In the **mesophyll** cells of leaves, inside **chloroplasts**. Membranes (grana thylakoids) trap light and make ATP and NADPH — the **light reactions**; the **stroma** uses them to fix CO₂ into sugar — the **biosynthetic (carbon) reactions** (often called 'dark' reactions, though they need light products).

steps.title: Solved question 1
steps.body: How did van Niel's work show that O₂ comes from water? Sulphur bacteria use H₂S and release sulphur, not oxygen; by analogy green plants split H₂O and release O₂ — later confirmed with radioisotopes.

steps.title: Solved question 2
steps.body: Half-leaf experiment: a leaf partly enclosed with KOH (absorbs CO₂) shows starch only in the exposed half → CO₂ is needed for photosynthesis.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying O₂ comes from CO₂.
- Thinking 'dark reactions' happen only at night.
- Crediting Ingenhousz with discovering oxygen (it was Priestley).

events.text: Ingenhousz: green parts in sunlight needed
Sachs: glucose formed and stored as starch
van Niel: O₂ comes from the hydrogen donor (water)
Calvin traces the carbon pathway with ¹⁴C

quiz.q: Engelmann's experiment showed maximum photosynthesis in
quiz.why: Engelmann used Cladophora and bacteria and found that the bacteria gathered at the blue and red regions, where photosynthesis is highest. Chlorophyll absorbs these lights best.

quiz.q: Oxygen released in photosynthesis comes from
quiz.why: The oxygen released in photosynthesis comes from water, which is split in the light reaction. van Niel showed this, and it is not from CO₂.
Sachs showed that glucose is made in the green parts of leaves and stored as starch, which he tested with iodine. It did not show the production of protein or fat.
The light reactions need chlorophyll and photosystems, which are on the thylakoid membranes of the grana. The dark reactions occur in the stroma.

options: a candle, a mouse and mint in a bell jar
quiz.why: Priestley (1770) put a candle, then a mouse, in a bell jar with a mint plant. The plant kept the air fit for the candle to burn and the mouse to live, which showed plants restore air.

sources: NCERT Class 11 Biology (Photosynthesis in Higher Plants)

lessons.title: Pigments and the light reactions

scenes.text: Chlorophyll absorbs red and blue light strongly but reflects green.
Absorbed light energy drives two photosystems that split water and make ATP and NADPH.

steps.title: Pigments
steps.body: Paper chromatography of leaf pigments shows: **chlorophyll a** (bright or blue-green; the chief pigment), **chlorophyll b** (yellow-green), **xanthophylls** (yellow), **carotenoids** (yellow to yellow-orange). Accessory pigments widen the range of usable wavelengths and protect chlorophyll a from photo-oxidation. Absorption peaks in **blue and red** regions.

steps.title: Photosystems, Z scheme and photolysis
steps.body:
- Light-harvesting complexes (antennae) funnel energy to a reaction centre chlorophyll a: **PS I** has **P700**, **PS II** has **P680** (absorption peaks in nm). PS II was discovered after PS I but acts first.
- **Non-cyclic (Z scheme):** PS II absorbs light → excited electrons pass down an electron transport chain (cytochromes) → PS I → further excited → reduce **NADP⁺ to NADPH + H⁺**.
- **Photolysis of water** at PS II (inner side of thylakoid membrane): 2H₂O → 4H⁺ + O₂ + 4e⁻; replaces PS II's electrons; associated with Mn and Cl.
- **Cyclic photophosphorylation:** only PS I; electrons cycle back; **ATP only** (no NADPH, no O₂); occurs in **stroma lamellae** (which lack PS II and NADP reductase) or when only light beyond 680 nm is available.
- **Chemiosmosis:** protons accumulate in the **lumen** (from water splitting, from H⁺ pumped by the electron carrier, and as H⁺ is removed in the stroma for NADPH formation) → gradient → protons flow back through **ATP synthase** (CF₀ channel in the membrane, CF₁ headpiece facing the stroma) → **ATP**.

steps.title: Solved question 1
steps.body: Products of non-cyclic photophosphorylation? **ATP, NADPH and O₂**. Cyclic gives **ATP** only.

steps.title: Solved question 2
steps.body: Where do protons accumulate during the light reaction? Inside the **thylakoid lumen**, making it acidic relative to the stroma.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying PS I has P680 (it has P700).
- Thinking cyclic photophosphorylation releases O₂.
- Placing the CF₁ part inside the lumen (it faces the stroma, where ATP forms).

pairs: Splitting of water at PS II

quiz.why: Chlorophyll a is the chief pigment, because it is in the reaction centres of both photosystems. The other pigments pass energy to it as accessory pigments.

options: PS II side by water splitting
quiz.why: Oxygen comes from the splitting of water (photolysis) associated with PS II, on the inner side of the thylakoid. The Calvin cycle in the stroma does not release O₂.
NADPH forms in non-cyclic photophosphorylation, where electrons pass from PS II to PS I and are finally taken by NADP⁺. Cyclic flow makes only ATP.
Stroma lamellae have only PS I and ATP synthase, and lack PS II and NADP reductase. So only cyclic electron flow can occur there, with no NADPH or oxygen.

quiz.q: ATP synthesis in chloroplasts is explained by
quiz.why: The chemiosmotic hypothesis explains ATP synthesis: a proton gradient builds up across the thylakoid membrane, and protons flowing through ATP synthase drive ATP production.

sources: NCERT Class 11 Biology (Photosynthesis in Higher Plants)

lessons.title: The Calvin cycle (C3 pathway)

scenes.text: Melvin Calvin fed algae with radioactive ¹⁴CO₂ and stopped the reaction after seconds.
The first labelled compound was a 3-carbon acid — 3-PGA — so this route is called the C3 pathway.

steps.title: Three stages
steps.body:
1. **Carboxylation:** CO₂ + **RuBP** (ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate, 5C) → 2 molecules of **3-phosphoglyceric acid (3-PGA)**, catalysed by **RuBisCO** (RuBP carboxylase-oxygenase). This is the most crucial step.
2. **Reduction:** 3-PGA → triose phosphate (glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate) using **ATP and NADPH**; some is used to make glucose.
3. **Regeneration:** RuBP is re-formed using ATP, so the cycle continues.

**Cost:** to fix **1 CO₂** → **3 ATP + 2 NADPH**. To make **1 glucose** (6 CO₂) → **6 turns, 18 ATP + 12 NADPH**.

steps.title: Solved question 1
steps.body: How many ATP and NADPH are needed for one glucose? 6 turns × (3 ATP + 2 NADPH) = **18 ATP and 12 NADPH**.

steps.title: Solved question 2
steps.body: Why does the light reaction make more ATP than NADPH? The Calvin cycle needs ATP:NADPH in a 3:2 ratio; cyclic photophosphorylation supplies extra ATP.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling RuBP the first stable product (the first stable product is 3-PGA in C3 plants).
- Saying the Calvin cycle happens in grana (it is in the stroma).
- Writing 12 ATP instead of 18 for one glucose.

steps.title: Remember
steps.body: C3 = first product 3-carbon (PGA); C4 = first product 4-carbon (OAA).

activity.prompt: How many ATP molecules are needed by the Calvin cycle to make 2 molecules of glucose?

quiz.q: The CO₂ acceptor in the Calvin cycle is
quiz.why: The acceptor of CO₂ in the Calvin cycle is RuBP (ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate), a 5-carbon sugar. OAA and PEP are linked to C4 pathway.

quiz.q: The first stable product of the C3 cycle is
quiz.why: The first stable product of the C3 (Calvin) cycle is 3-phosphoglyceric acid (3-PGA), a 3-carbon compound, hence the name C3. OAA is the first stable product in C4 plants.
RuBisCO catalyses the carboxylation of RuBP, where CO₂ is added to RuBP to give two molecules of 3-PGA. This is the carbon fixation step.

quiz.q: For fixing one CO₂, the cycle uses
quiz.why: For each CO₂ fixed, the Calvin cycle uses 3 ATP and 2 NADPH. For one glucose (6 CO₂) that is 18 ATP and 12 NADPH.
Melvin Calvin used radioactive ¹⁴C (as ¹⁴CO₂) to trace the path of carbon in the dark reactions. ¹⁵N, ³²P and ¹⁸O are tracers for other studies.

sources: NCERT Class 11 Biology (Photosynthesis in Higher Plants)

lessons.title: C4 pathway, photorespiration and limiting factors

scenes.text: On hot, dry, bright days, maize and sugarcane keep growing strongly while wheat and rice slow down.
Maize uses the C4 trick to concentrate CO₂ and avoid wasteful photorespiration.

steps.title: C4 pathway (Hatch–Slack)
steps.body:
- C4 plants (maize, sorghum, sugarcane) adapted to dry tropical regions; tolerate high temperature and light intensity.
- **Kranz anatomy:** large **bundle sheath** cells around vascular bundles, with many chloroplasts, thick walls impervious to gas exchange, no intercellular spaces.
- In **mesophyll** cells: **PEP** (phosphoenolpyruvate, 3C) + CO₂ → **oxaloacetic acid (OAA, 4C)** by **PEP carboxylase (PEPcase)** (mesophyll lacks RuBisCO).
- OAA → malic or aspartic acid → moves to **bundle sheath** → decarboxylated → CO₂ enters the **Calvin cycle** (bundle sheath has RuBisCO but lacks PEPcase); the 3C acid returns to mesophyll to regenerate PEP.

steps.title: Photorespiration and limiting factors
steps.body:
- **Photorespiration:** RuBisCO can bind **O₂** instead of CO₂ (high O₂/low CO₂, high temperature): RuBP + O₂ → 1 PGA + **phosphoglycolate**; uses ATP, **no sugar, no ATP or NADPH made** — wasteful. Absent in C4 plants because CO₂ is concentrated around RuBisCO in bundle sheath cells.
- **Blackman's law of limiting factors (1905):** when a process depends on several factors, its rate is set by the factor nearest its minimal value.
- **Light:** linear rise at low intensity; saturation at about 10% of full sunlight (except shade plants); very high light can damage chlorophyll.
- **CO₂:** the major limiting factor (about 0.03–0.04% of air); increasing to about 0.05% raises photosynthesis; C4 plants saturate at about 360 µL/L; C3 plants respond up to about 450 µL/L — used in greenhouse crops like tomato and bell pepper.
- **Temperature:** dark reactions are enzymatic; C4 plants have higher optima.
- **Water:** stress closes stomata (less CO₂) and wilts leaves.

steps.title: Solved question 1
steps.body: Why do C4 plants show higher productivity? They concentrate CO₂ around RuBisCO, so photorespiration is negligible and photosynthesis continues at high temperature and light.

steps.title: Solved question 2
steps.body: A greenhouse raises CO₂ for tomatoes. Why does yield increase? C3 plants are CO₂-limited at normal levels; extra CO₂ raises photosynthesis.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying C4 plants do not use the Calvin cycle (they do, in bundle sheath cells).
- Calling PEPcase the enzyme in bundle sheath cells.
- Saying photorespiration produces ATP.

quiz.q: The primary CO₂ acceptor in C4 plants is
quiz.why: In C4 plants the primary acceptor of CO₂ is PEP (phosphoenolpyruvate), a 3-carbon compound, in the mesophyll cells. It forms OAA, which is a 4-carbon compound.

options: large bundle sheath cells around veins
quiz.why: Kranz anatomy means large bundle sheath cells that surround the vascular bundles in a wreath-like ring, as in C4 plants. They hold the Calvin cycle.
RuBisCO can also bind oxygen, as well as CO₂, and this oxygenase activity starts photorespiration. It is present in C3 plants, and PEP carboxylase is a different enzyme.

quiz.q: The law of limiting factors was given by
quiz.why: Blackman's law of limiting factors (1905) says that when several factors affect a process, the one in shortest supply controls the rate. Hatch and Slack worked out the C4 pathway.
Sorghum is a tropical grass and a C4 plant. Potato, rice and wheat are C3 plants.

sources: NCERT Class 11 Biology (Photosynthesis in Higher Plants)

questions.q: Photosynthesis takes place in
questions.why: Photosynthesis takes place in chloroplasts, which have the chlorophyll. Mitochondria are for respiration and ribosomes make proteins.

questions.q: Oxygen in photosynthesis comes from
questions.why: The oxygen given off in photosynthesis comes from the splitting of water (photolysis), not from CO₂ or glucose.

questions.q: First stable product of the Calvin cycle is
questions.why: The first stable product of the Calvin cycle is 3-PGA, a three-carbon compound, so it is called the C3 pathway. Glucose is a later product.

questions.q: Reaction centre of PS I is
questions.why: The reaction centre of PS I is P700, named because it absorbs best at 700 nm. PS II has P680.

questions.q: C4 plants include
questions.why: Maize and sugarcane are C4 plants, which are tropical grasses with Kranz anatomy. Potato, tomato, pea, bean, wheat and rice are C3.

questions.q: Splitting of water is associated with
questions.why: Water splitting (photolysis) is linked to PS II, on the inner side of the thylakoid membrane. It supplies electrons, protons and oxygen.

questions.q: Assertion: Cyclic photophosphorylation does not release oxygen. Reason: PS II is not involved in cyclic electron flow.
options: Both true and R explains A
Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true and R explains A. Oxygen comes from water splitting by PS II. Cyclic flow uses only PS I, so no water is split and no oxygen is released.

questions.q: Number of ATP and NADPH for one glucose by Calvin cycle
questions.why: For one glucose, six CO₂ are fixed, which means six turns of the cycle. Each turn needs 3 ATP and 2 NADPH, so 18 ATP and 12 NADPH in all.

questions.q: PEP carboxylase is found in
options: bundle sheath cells of C4 plants
questions.why: PEP carboxylase is the enzyme for the first CO₂ fixation in C4 plants, and it is in the mesophyll cells. The bundle sheath cells have RuBisCO and the Calvin cycle.

questions.q: Protons accumulate in the ___ during light reactions
questions.why: During the light reactions, protons pile up in the thylakoid lumen as water is split and electrons are carried across. This gradient drives ATP synthase.

questions.q: Case: A greenhouse grower raises CO₂ from 0.04% to near 0.1% for tomatoes. Yield rises because
options: CO₂ was a limiting factor for these C3 plants
questions.why: CO₂ at 0.04% is below what C3 plants like tomato can use, so CO₂ limits photosynthesis. Raising it to about 0.1% increases the rate, and photorespiration falls rather than rises.

questions.q: Case: In an experiment with ¹⁸O-labelled water, the labelled oxygen appears in
questions.why: Photosynthesis splits water, so the oxygen from H₂¹⁸O is released as ¹⁸O₂. The CO₂ and glucose do not get this label, because their oxygen comes from CO₂.

questions.q: Photorespiration is absent in C4 plants because
options: CO₂ is concentrated around RuBisCO in bundle sheath cells
questions.why: C4 plants fix CO₂ first in mesophyll cells and pass it to bundle sheath cells, where CO₂ builds up around RuBisCO. High CO₂ stops RuBisCO from binding O₂, so photorespiration is almost absent.

questions.q: In photorespiration, the products from RuBP and O₂ are
questions.why: When RuBisCO binds O₂ instead of CO₂ (oxygenase action), RuBP gives one molecule of 3-PGA and one of phosphoglycolate. In carboxylation, it gives two PGA.

questions.q: Engelmann's experiment used
questions.why: Engelmann put the alga Cladophora with aerobic bacteria under a prism-split light. The bacteria gathered where oxygen was released most, at the blue and red parts, which gave the action spectrum.

questions.q: Which statement is incorrect?
options: Calvin cycle occurs in the stroma
RuBisCO is the most abundant enzyme
Calvin cycle occurs only in C3 plants
questions.why: The incorrect statement is that the Calvin cycle occurs only in C3 plants. C4 plants also run the Calvin cycle, in the bundle sheath cells, after the C4 pathway delivers CO₂.

questions.q: The ATP synthase of chloroplasts: protons move from
options: lumen to stroma through CF₀, and ATP forms at CF₁ on the stroma side
questions.why: Protons collect in the thylakoid lumen and flow down their gradient back to the stroma through the CF₀ channel of ATP synthase. This drives ATP formation at the CF₁ part, on the stroma side.

courses.title: Ch 12 · Respiration in Plants
courses.summary: How plants release energy: glycolysis, fermentation, aerobic respiration (link reaction, Krebs cycle, electron transport and oxidative phosphorylation), the respiratory balance sheet, the amphibolic pathway and respiratory quotient.
outcomes: Learners can describe glycolysis and its energy yield
Learners can explain alcoholic and lactic acid fermentation
Learners can describe the link reaction, Krebs cycle and the electron transport system
Learners can calculate ATP yield and respiratory quotients and explain the amphibolic pathway

lessons.title: Do plants breathe? Glycolysis

scenes.text: A flask of germinating seeds becomes warm and its air loses oxygen.
Seeds respire like animals — breaking down food to release energy as ATP and heat.

steps.title: Respiration in plants
steps.body:
Plants have no specialised respiratory organs; **stomata** and **lenticels** exchange gases; each part meets its own needs; most living cells are near the surface; large trunks have mostly dead interior cells.

C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + energy. Energy is released stepwise and trapped as **ATP** — the energy currency.

steps.title: Glycolysis (EMP pathway)
steps.body:
Named after **Embden, Meyerhof and Parnas**. Occurs in the **cytoplasm** of all living organisms; the only respiratory process in anaerobes.
- Glucose → glucose-6-phosphate (hexokinase; **ATP used**) → fructose-6-phosphate → fructose-1,6-bisphosphate (**ATP used**) → two triose phosphates (DHAP and PGAL/G3P).
- PGAL → 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate (BPGA) with **NADH** formed.
- BPGA → 3-PGA (**ATP formed**, substrate-level); PEP → **pyruvic acid** (**ATP formed**).
- **Net per glucose:** 2 pyruvate + **2 ATP (net)** + **2 NADH**. (4 ATP made, 2 used.)
- In plants, glucose comes from sucrose (split by invertase into glucose and fructose) or from starch.

steps.title: Solved question 1
steps.body: Net ATP from glycolysis? 4 ATP produced − 2 ATP used = **2 ATP** (plus 2 NADH).

steps.title: Solved question 2
steps.body: Where does glycolysis occur, and does it need oxygen? In the **cytoplasm**; it does **not** need oxygen.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Placing glycolysis in mitochondria.
- Saying glycolysis produces CO₂ (no CO₂ is released).
- Forgetting that two ATP are invested at the start.

items: It splits into two triose phosphates
PGAL is oxidised to BPGA with NADH formed
BPGA → 3-PGA → PEP → pyruvic acid with ATP formed

quiz.why: Glycolysis takes place in the cytoplasm of the cell, and it is the same in all organisms. It does not need oxygen or mitochondria.

quiz.q: Net ATP gain from glycolysis of one glucose is
quiz.why: Glycolysis uses 2 ATP and makes 4 ATP, so the net gain is 4 − 2 = 2 ATP per glucose. The larger numbers (36 or 38) are for complete aerobic respiration.
Glycolysis breaks a glucose (6 C) into two molecules of pyruvic acid (3 C each). Acetyl CoA and citric acid come in later steps.
The glycolysis pathway is named EMP after Embden, Meyerhof and Parnas, the scientists who worked out its steps.

quiz.q: Gases are exchanged in plants through
quiz.why: Plants have no special breathing organs. Gases are exchanged by diffusion through stomata in leaves and lenticels in woody stems.

sources: NCERT Class 11 Biology (Respiration in Plants)

lessons.title: Fermentation

scenes.text: Bread rises and idli batter puffs up overnight; after a sprint, legs ache.
Yeast makes CO₂ and alcohol; overworked muscles make lactic acid — both are ways of using pyruvate without oxygen.

steps.title: Anaerobic routes
steps.body:
- **Alcoholic fermentation (yeast):** pyruvic acid → acetaldehyde + CO₂ (**pyruvic acid decarboxylase**) → **ethanol** (**alcohol dehydrogenase**, using NADH).
- **Lactic acid fermentation** (some bacteria; animal muscle during vigorous exercise when O₂ is short): pyruvic acid → **lactic acid** (**lactate dehydrogenase**, using NADH).
- In both, NADH + H⁺ is reoxidised to NAD⁺ so glycolysis can continue.
- Energy: less than **7%** of the energy in glucose is released, and not all is trapped as ATP; products are toxic (yeasts die at about **13% alcohol**). Hence aerobic respiration evolved as the main route for most organisms.

steps.title: Solved question 1
steps.body: Why does a sprinter's muscle ache? With insufficient O₂, pyruvate is reduced to lactic acid, which accumulates.

steps.title: Solved question 2
steps.body: Why can't a yeast culture make spirit stronger than about 13% alcohol by fermentation alone? Yeast is poisoned by ethanol at about that concentration.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying lactic acid fermentation releases CO₂ (it does not).
- Thinking fermentation yields lots of ATP — only the 2 ATP of glycolysis.
- Forgetting the role of NAD⁺ regeneration.

quiz.why: In alcoholic fermentation, as in yeast, pyruvic acid is changed to ethanol and CO₂. Lactic acid is the product in muscle (lactic fermentation).

quiz.q: Enzyme converting pyruvate to lactic acid is
quiz.why: Lactate dehydrogenase converts pyruvate to lactic acid using NADH. Alcohol dehydrogenase works in alcohol fermentation, and hexokinase acts early in glycolysis.
Fermentation only partly breaks down glucose, so it releases less than 7% of the energy in glucose. The rest stays in ethanol or lactic acid.
Yeasts poison themselves when alcohol reaches about 13%, so fermented drinks like wine stop at about this level. Higher levels need distilling.
Fermentation changes NADH back to NAD⁺, which glycolysis needs so it can keep running without oxygen. It does not make oxygen, glucose or much ATP.

sources: NCERT Class 11 Biology (Respiration in Plants)

lessons.title: Aerobic respiration: link reaction, Krebs cycle and ETS

scenes.text: In a muscle cell's mitochondria, pyruvate is completely burned to CO₂ and water.
Most ATP comes from the electron transport system on the inner membrane.

steps.title: Link reaction and Krebs cycle
steps.body:
- Pyruvate enters the **mitochondrial matrix**: **oxidative decarboxylation** by the **pyruvate dehydrogenase** complex (needs NAD⁺ and coenzyme A, Mg²⁺) → **acetyl CoA** + CO₂ + NADH. Two pyruvates → 2 NADH.
- **Krebs (TCA/citric acid) cycle** (Hans Krebs): acetyl CoA (2C) + **oxaloacetic acid (OAA, 4C)** + H₂O → **citric acid (6C)** (citrate synthase) → isocitrate → two successive **decarboxylations** → α-ketoglutaric acid → succinyl CoA → succinic acid (**substrate-level GTP/ATP**) → … → malic acid → OAA regenerated.
- Per **pyruvate** in the matrix (including link reaction): 3 CO₂ formed; **4 NADH, 1 FADH₂, 1 ATP (GTP)**. Per glucose, double this.

steps.title: Electron transport system and oxidative phosphorylation
steps.body:
On the **inner mitochondrial membrane**:
- **Complex I** (NADH dehydrogenase) accepts electrons from NADH → **ubiquinone**.
- **Complex II** receives electrons from **FADH₂** (succinate dehydrogenase) → ubiquinone.
- Ubiquinol → **Complex III** (cytochrome bc₁) → **cytochrome c** (small mobile protein on the outer surface of the inner membrane) → **Complex IV** (cytochrome c oxidase: cytochromes a and a₃ and two copper centres) → **O₂**, the final acceptor, forming **water**.
- Energy pumps protons into the intermembrane space; they flow back through **Complex V (ATP synthase: F₀ channel + F₁ headpiece)** → ATP. This is **oxidative phosphorylation**, explained by chemiosmosis.
- Yield (textbook values): **1 NADH → 3 ATP, 1 FADH₂ → 2 ATP**.

steps.title: Solved question 1: balance sheet
steps.body:
Per glucose (assuming NADH from glycolysis gives 3 ATP each):
- Glycolysis: 2 ATP + 2 NADH (6 ATP) = 8
- Link reaction: 2 NADH = 6
- Krebs: 2 ATP + 6 NADH (18) + 2 FADH₂ (4) = 24
- **Total = 38 ATP** (theoretical; real values are lower and vary).

steps.title: Solved question 2
steps.body: Role of oxygen? It is the **final electron acceptor** at Complex IV; without it the chain stops and NADH cannot be reoxidised.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the Krebs cycle occurs on cristae (it is in the matrix; succinate dehydrogenase is the exception, on the inner membrane).
- Writing that OAA is 6-carbon (it is 4C; citric acid is 6C).
- Assuming the 38 ATP figure is always achieved in a living cell.

activity.prompt: Using textbook values (NADH = 3 ATP, FADH₂ = 2 ATP), how many ATP come from the Krebs cycle and link reaction for ONE pyruvate (4 NADH, 1 FADH₂, 1 GTP)?

quiz.q: The link reaction converts pyruvate to
quiz.why: In the link reaction, pyruvate is changed to acetyl CoA by oxidative decarboxylation, releasing CO₂ and NADH. Acetyl CoA then enters the Krebs cycle.

quiz.q: The first product of the Krebs cycle is
quiz.why: Acetyl CoA joins OAA to form citric acid, a six-carbon compound, which is the first product of the Krebs cycle. OAA is the starting compound.

quiz.q: The final electron acceptor in aerobic respiration is
quiz.why: Oxygen is the final acceptor of electrons at the end of the electron transport chain, and it combines with protons to form water. That is why oxygen is needed for aerobic respiration.
Complex IV is cytochrome c oxidase, which has cytochromes a and a₃ and copper. It passes electrons to oxygen. Complex II is succinate dehydrogenase and Complex I is NADH dehydrogenase.

quiz.q: Theoretical net ATP per glucose in aerobic respiration (textbook) is
quiz.why: By the textbook count, complete aerobic respiration of one glucose gives a net of 38 ATP. Real cells may get fewer, but the textbook balance sheet gives 38.
ATP synthase is Complex V of the respiratory chain, with an F₀ channel in the membrane and F₁ headpiece. It makes ATP from the proton gradient.

sources: NCERT Class 11 Biology (Respiration in Plants)

lessons.title: Amphibolic pathway and respiratory quotient

scenes.text: In long races, athletes burn more fat once sugar stores fall.
Fats and proteins enter the same respiratory pathway at different points — and they use oxygen differently.

steps.title: Amphibolic pathway
steps.body:
Respiration is not only **catabolic**: its intermediates are withdrawn to build other molecules (**anabolic**). Hence it is **amphibolic**.
- **Fats** → glycerol (→ PGAL) + fatty acids (→ **acetyl CoA**).
- **Proteins** → amino acids → deaminated → enter at pyruvate, acetyl CoA or Krebs intermediates.
- The reverse routes (e.g. acetyl CoA → fatty acids) are used for synthesis.

steps.title: Respiratory quotient (RQ)
steps.body:
**RQ = volume of CO₂ evolved / volume of O₂ consumed.**
- **Carbohydrates:** C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → RQ = **1.0**.
- **Fats:** e.g. tripalmitin 2(C₅₁H₉₈O₆) + 145 O₂ → 102 CO₂ + 98 H₂O → RQ = 102/145 = **0.7**.
- **Proteins:** about **0.9**.
- Organic acids (rich in oxygen) can give RQ > 1; anaerobic respiration gives a very high or infinite RQ (CO₂ without O₂ use).

steps.title: Solved question 1
steps.body: A seed has RQ 0.7 during germination. What is it respiring? **Fats** (e.g. castor, groundnut seeds).

steps.title: Solved question 2
steps.body: Why is RQ for fats less than 1? Fats are poor in oxygen, so more O₂ is consumed per CO₂ released.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing RQ as O₂/CO₂ (it is CO₂/O₂).
- Thinking respiration is only catabolic.
- Saying proteins have RQ 1.

activity.prompt: Calculate the RQ of tripalmitin: 102 CO₂ produced for 145 O₂ consumed (2 decimal places).

quiz.why: The RQ is CO₂ released divided by O₂ used. For carbohydrates, equal volumes are used and released, so RQ = 1.
Fats have little oxygen in them, so more O₂ is needed to burn them than the CO₂ released. The RQ is therefore less than 1, about 0.7.
Fats are broken into fatty acids, which are oxidised (β-oxidation) to acetyl CoA. This then enters the Krebs cycle.

quiz.q: Respiration is called amphibolic because it
quiz.why: Respiration is amphibolic because it breaks down substances to release energy and also gives intermediates used to build fats, proteins and other compounds.
In anaerobic respiration CO₂ is released but no O₂ is used. Dividing by zero gives an RQ that is infinite.

sources: NCERT Class 11 Biology (Respiration in Plants)

questions.q: Glycolysis takes place in
questions.why: Glycolysis happens in the cytoplasm in all living organisms. It does not need chloroplasts, mitochondria or the nucleus.

questions.q: The end product of glycolysis is
questions.why: The end product of glycolysis is pyruvic acid, a three-carbon compound. Acetyl CoA is formed from it later.

questions.q: Final electron acceptor in ETS is
questions.why: Oxygen is the last electron acceptor in the electron transport system, and it forms water. NAD, FAD and ubiquinone pass electrons along earlier.

questions.q: RQ of glucose is
questions.why: For glucose, 6 CO₂ are given out for 6 O₂ used, so RQ = 6/6 = 1. Fats give about 0.7 and proteins about 0.9.

questions.q: Krebs cycle takes place in the
questions.why: The Krebs cycle enzymes are in the mitochondrial matrix. Glycolysis is in the cytoplasm and the electron transport is on the inner membrane.

questions.q: Yeast fermentation produces
questions.why: Yeast fermentation changes pyruvic acid into ethanol and CO₂. Lactic acid is formed in muscle, and oxygen is not a product.

questions.q: Assertion: Respiration is an amphibolic pathway. Reason: Its intermediates are also used to synthesise fats and proteins.
options: Both true and R explains A
Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true and R explains A. Respiratory intermediates are used to make fats, proteins and other compounds, so the pathway is both catabolic and anabolic, which is amphibolic.

questions.q: Number of CO₂ molecules released per glucose in aerobic respiration (link reaction + Krebs) is
questions.why: The link reaction gives 1 CO₂ per pyruvate, so 2 per glucose. Each turn of the Krebs cycle gives 2 CO₂, so 4 for two turns. Total = 2 + 4 = 6 CO₂.

questions.q: Number of NADH formed per glucose in the Krebs cycle alone is
questions.why: Each Krebs turn makes 3 NADH, and one glucose gives two turns. So 3 × 2 = 6 NADH.

questions.q: Cytochrome c is
options: a small mobile protein on the outer surface of the inner membrane
questions.why: Cytochrome c is a small, mobile protein on the outer side of the inner mitochondrial membrane. It carries electrons from Complex III to Complex IV.

questions.q: Case: Germinating castor seeds show RQ of 0.7. They are mainly respiring
questions.why: An RQ of 0.7 shows that more oxygen is used than CO₂ released, as happens when fats are burned. Castor seeds are rich in oil (fat), so fats are the substrate.

questions.q: Case: A student's muscles cramp after a 400 m sprint. The cause is accumulation of
questions.why: In a hard sprint the muscle cells get too little oxygen, so pyruvic acid is changed to lactic acid by anaerobic glycolysis. The build-up of lactic acid causes the cramps.

questions.q: Using NADH = 3 ATP and FADH₂ = 2 ATP, ATP from oxidative phosphorylation of NADH and FADH₂ formed in two Krebs cycles is
questions.why: Two Krebs turns give 6 NADH and 2 FADH₂. So ATP = 6 × 3 + 2 × 2 = 18 + 4 = 22.

questions.q: The enzyme complex for oxidative decarboxylation of pyruvate is
questions.why: The pyruvate dehydrogenase complex does oxidative decarboxylation of pyruvate to acetyl CoA, the link reaction. Lactate dehydrogenase and pyruvate decarboxylase work in fermentation.

questions.q: Succinate dehydrogenase passes electrons via FADH₂ to
questions.why: Succinate dehydrogenase is Complex II. It passes electrons from FADH₂ to ubiquinone, not through Complex I, and then they move on to Complex III.

questions.q: Which is correct about fermentation?
options: It releases less than 7% of glucose energy
questions.why: Fermentation is partial breakdown of glucose, so it releases less than 7% of the energy. It does not need oxygen, does not give 38 ATP and happens in the cytoplasm.

questions.q: ATP made by substrate-level phosphorylation per glucose in glycolysis + Krebs cycle is
options: 6 (4 in glycolysis + 2 in Krebs), net 4 after the 2 used
questions.why: Substrate-level phosphorylation gives 4 ATP in glycolysis (2 used, so net 2) and 2 ATP in the Krebs cycle (one per turn). So the gross total is 6 and the net is 4.

questions.q: RQ of a protein diet is about
questions.why: The RQ of proteins is about 0.9, in between that of fats (0.7) and carbohydrates (1.0).

courses.title: Ch 13 · Plant Growth and Development
courses.summary: Growth and its phases and rates, differentiation, dedifferentiation and redifferentiation, developmental plasticity, and the five classes of plant growth regulators with their discovery and uses.
outcomes: Learners can describe the phases and measurement of growth and the sigmoid growth curve
Learners can distinguish arithmetic and geometric growth and absolute vs relative growth rate
Learners can explain differentiation, dedifferentiation, redifferentiation and plasticity
Learners can describe the discovery and physiological effects of auxins, gibberellins, cytokinins, ethylene and ABA

lessons.title: Growth: phases, rates and curves

scenes.text: Priya measures her bean plant every day: slow at first, then a growth spurt, then it levels off.
Plotted on a graph, her numbers make an S-shaped (sigmoid) curve.

steps.title: Growth in plants
steps.body:
**Growth** is an irreversible permanent increase in size of an organ, its parts or a cell. Plants show **indeterminate** growth throughout life because of **meristems** (open form of growth). Root and shoot apical meristems → primary growth (length); lateral meristems (vascular cambium, cork cambium) → secondary growth (girth) in dicots and gymnosperms.
- **Measured** as increase in fresh/dry weight, length, area, volume, cell number. E.g. a single maize root apical meristem can produce more than 17,500 new cells per hour; a watermelon cell may increase in size by up to 3,50,000 times.
- **Phases:** **meristematic** (dense protoplasm, large nucleus, thin cellulose walls, many plasmodesmata), **elongation** (vacuolation, cell enlargement, new wall deposition), **maturation** (cells reach maximal size in wall thickening and protoplasm).

steps.title: Growth rates
steps.body:
- **Arithmetic growth:** only one daughter cell keeps dividing; e.g. a root elongating at a constant rate: **Lₜ = L₀ + rt** (straight line).
- **Geometric growth:** both daughter cells divide; initial **lag**, then rapid **log/exponential** phase, then **stationary** phase when nutrients limit — **sigmoid (S) curve**: **W₁ = W₀ e^(rt)** (r = relative growth rate, a measure of efficiency index).
- **Absolute growth rate:** total growth per unit time. **Relative growth rate:** growth per unit time per unit initial size.

steps.title: Solved question 1: relative growth rate
steps.body:
Leaf A grows from 5 cm² to 10 cm² in a day; leaf B grows from 50 cm² to 55 cm².

- Absolute growth: both 5 cm²/day.
- Relative growth: A = 5/5 = **100%**, B = 5/50 = **10%**. A is growing far faster relative to its size.

steps.title: Solved question 2: arithmetic growth
steps.body: A root 2 cm long grows 0.5 cm per day. After 6 days: Lₜ = 2 + 0.5 × 6 = **5 cm**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling growth reversible (swelling of a dry seed in water is not true growth until cells divide/enlarge).
- Mixing absolute and relative growth rates.
- Thinking the sigmoid curve is arithmetic (it is typical of geometric growth limited by resources).

activity.prompt: A leaf grows from 4 cm² to 6 cm² in one day. What is its relative growth rate in percent per day?

quiz.q: Plants grow throughout life because of
quiz.why: Plants grow throughout life because they have meristems, regions of cells that keep dividing. This is called open growth.
Lₜ = L₀ + rt means length increases by a constant amount in each unit of time. This is arithmetic (linear) growth.
The S-shaped (sigmoid) growth curve has a lag phase, then a log (exponential) phase, and then a stationary phase when growth slows.

quiz.q: Cells in the meristematic phase have
quiz.why: Cells in the meristematic phase divide actively. They have dense protoplasm, large nuclei and thin walls. Large vacuoles and thick walls appear later.

quiz.q: Relative growth rate compares growth with
quiz.why: Relative growth rate is growth per unit of initial size. So a small leaf that doubles has a higher relative rate than a big leaf that adds the same amount.

sources: NCERT Class 11 Biology (Plant Growth and Development)

lessons.title: Differentiation, development and plasticity

story.title: Making a whole plant from a leaf bit

scenes.text: In tissue culture, a tiny piece of carrot tissue forms a callus and then a whole new plant.
Mature cells regain the power to divide — dedifferentiation — and then redifferentiate.

steps.title: Key terms
steps.body:
- **Differentiation:** cells from meristems mature to perform specific functions, with structural changes in walls and protoplasm, e.g. tracheary elements lose protoplasm and develop strong lignified walls.
- **Dedifferentiation:** living differentiated cells regain the capacity to divide, e.g. **interfascicular cambium** and **cork cambium** form from fully differentiated parenchyma.
- **Redifferentiation:** cells from such meristems lose the ability to divide again and mature for specific functions (e.g. secondary xylem and phloem).
- **Development:** all changes in an organism's life cycle from seed germination to senescence.
- **Plasticity:** ability to follow different pathways in response to environment or life phase, e.g. **heterophylly** — different leaf shapes in juvenile and adult plants of **cotton, coriander, larkspur**; in **buttercup**, leaves under water differ from those in air (environmental heterophylly).

steps.title: Solved question 1
steps.body: Is the formation of cork cambium from cortical cells differentiation or dedifferentiation? **Dedifferentiation** — mature cells regain the ability to divide.

steps.title: Solved question 2
steps.body: Why is the leaf shape of buttercup in water different from that in air? It shows **plasticity** — the environment changes the developmental pathway.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing dedifferentiation (regaining division) and redifferentiation (losing it again).
- Thinking development and growth are the same (development includes differentiation and the whole life cycle).

pairs: Meristem cells mature for specific roles
Mature cells regain the power to divide
Cells from a new meristem mature again
Different leaf shapes on the same plant
All changes in the life cycle

quiz.q: Formation of interfascicular cambium is an example of
quiz.why: Interfascicular cambium forms when mature parenchyma cells between the bundles regain the ability to divide. This is dedifferentiation.

quiz.q: Heterophylly due to age is seen in
quiz.why: Cotton, coriander and larkspur have different leaf shapes in the young (juvenile) and adult stages. This is heterophylly due to age.
Tracheary elements (xylem) lose their protoplasm as they mature, and become dead hollow tubes. This helps them carry water.

quiz.q: Buttercup leaves differ in air and water because of
quiz.why: Buttercup makes different leaf shapes in air and in water, because the plant can change its form with the environment. This ability is plasticity.

quiz.q: Secondary xylem formed by cambium is an example of
quiz.why: Cells made by dedifferentiated cambium divide and then mature again into secondary xylem. This loss of division ability and maturing again is redifferentiation.

sources: NCERT Class 11 Biology (Plant Growth and Development)

lessons.title: Plant growth regulators I: auxins, gibberellins, cytokinins

scenes.text: Japanese farmers noticed rice seedlings that grew absurdly tall and fell over — the 'foolish seedling' (bakanae) disease.
E. Kurosawa traced it to a fungus, Gibberella fujikuroi, which makes gibberellins.

steps.title: Auxins
steps.body:
- Discovery: **Charles and Francis Darwin** — coleoptiles of canary grass bend towards light (**phototropism**); the tip sends a signal. **F.W. Went** isolated auxin from oat coleoptile tips.
- Natural: **IAA**, IBA; synthetic: **NAA**, **2,4-D**.
- Effects/uses: initiate **rooting** in stem cuttings; promote flowering (pineapple); prevent premature fruit and leaf drop but promote abscission of older parts; **apical dominance** (removal of shoot tip → lateral buds grow; used in tea plantations and hedge-making); **parthenocarpy** (tomato); **weedicide** — 2,4-D kills dicot weeds without affecting mature monocots (lawns); xylem differentiation; cell division.

steps.title: Gibberellins and cytokinins
steps.body:
- **Gibberellins:** more than **100** found (GA₁, GA₂, GA₃ …); **GA₃** first discovered and most studied; acidic. Effects: **stem elongation**; increase **grape stalk length**; elongate and improve **apple shape**; delay senescence (fruits stay longer on trees); spraying **sugarcane** increases stem length and yield by as much as **20 tonnes per acre**; speed **malting** in brewing; hasten maturity and early seed production in conifers; promote **bolting** (internode elongation before flowering) in beet, cabbage and rosette plants.
- **Cytokinins:** **F. Skoog** and co-workers found **kinetin** (a modified adenine) from autoclaved herring sperm DNA; natural **zeatin** from corn kernels and coconut milk. Effects: **cytokinesis** (cell division); new leaves, chloroplasts in leaves, lateral shoot growth and adventitious shoots; help **overcome apical dominance**; promote nutrient mobilisation and **delay leaf senescence**.

steps.title: Solved question 1
steps.body: A tea planter wants bushy plants. What should he do? Remove the shoot tips (decapitation) — this removes apical dominance caused by auxin and lateral buds grow.

steps.title: Solved question 2
steps.body: Which PGR would you spray to increase sugarcane yield? **Gibberellins** — they elongate the stem, adding up to about 20 tonnes per acre.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying 2,4-D kills monocot weeds (it targets dicots).
- Crediting gibberellin discovery to Went (it was Kurosawa).
- Saying cytokinins cause apical dominance (they help overcome it).

activity.prompt: Match the PGR with its effect.

quiz.q: Bakanae disease of rice is caused by a fungus producing
quiz.why: Bakanae (foolish seedling) disease of rice is caused by the fungus Gibberella fujikuroi, which makes gibberellins. They make the plants grow unusually tall.
Skoog and co-workers first isolated kinetin from autoclaved herring sperm DNA. It is a cytokinin that promotes cell division.
Auxin made at the shoot tip flows down and stops the growth of lateral buds. This is apical dominance. Cutting the tip removes it, so side branches grow.
Gibberellins cause bolting, where the internodes of a rosette plant elongate rapidly before flowering, as in cabbage and beet.
Zeatin is a natural cytokinin, first found in maize kernels. Ethephon is an ethylene source, and 2,4-D and NAA are synthetic auxins.

sources: NCERT Class 11 Biology (Plant Growth and Development)

lessons.title: Plant growth regulators II: ethylene and abscisic acid

scenes.text: A trader puts unripe bananas in a closed room with a few ripe ones; they ripen faster.
Ripe fruit gives off ethylene gas, which speeds ripening of the others.

steps.title: Ethylene
steps.body:
- Gaseous PGR; H.H. Cousins confirmed that ripened oranges released a volatile substance that hastened ripening of stored unripe bananas — later identified as ethylene.
- Produced in large amounts by tissues undergoing **senescence** and by **ripening fruits**.
- Effects: **horizontal growth of seedlings, swelling of the axis and apical hook** in dicot seedlings (triple response); senescence and **abscission** of leaves and flowers; **fruit ripening** — increases respiration rate (**respiratory climacteric**); breaks seed and bud dormancy (sprouting of potato tubers); promotes rapid internode/petiole elongation in deep-water rice; promotes root growth and root hairs; induces flowering and synchronises fruit set in **pineapple**; induces flowering in mango; promotes female flowers in cucumbers.
- **Ethephon** (a source) hastens fruit ripening in tomatoes and apples and thinning of cotton, cherry, walnut.

steps.title: Abscisic acid (ABA)
steps.body:
- Discovered in the 1960s as three inhibitors: inhibitor-B, abscission II and dormin — later shown to be the same: **ABA**.
- General **growth inhibitor** and inhibitor of plant metabolism; inhibits seed germination; **stimulates closure of stomata**; increases tolerance to stresses — the **stress hormone**; induces **seed dormancy**, helping seeds withstand desiccation; mostly **antagonistic to GAs**.

PGRs often act together, interacting synergistically or antagonistically, e.g. dormancy, abscission, senescence, apical dominance.

steps.title: Solved question 1
steps.body: Which PGR would you use to ripen tomatoes quickly? **Ethephon** (releases ethylene).

steps.title: Solved question 2
steps.body: During drought, which hormone closes stomata? **Abscisic acid (ABA)**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling ethylene a liquid.
- Thinking ABA promotes seed germination (it inhibits it; GA promotes it).
- Forgetting that ethylene promotes female flowers in cucumber.

steps.title: On the farm
steps.body: Auxins for cuttings and weed control, GA for grapes and sugarcane, cytokinins for tissue culture shoots, ethylene/ethephon for ripening and pineapple flowering, ABA research for drought-tolerant crops.

quiz.why: Ethylene is the only gaseous plant growth regulator. IAA, GA₃ and ABA are not gases.
Abscisic acid (ABA) is the stress hormone. It helps plants cope with stress such as drought, by closing stomata.
Ethephon breaks down to release ethylene, which hastens ripening of fruits like tomato and apple.
ABA mostly acts against gibberellins. GA promotes germination and growth, while ABA keeps seeds dormant and slows growth.
A rise in respiration during ripening of some fruits is the respiratory climacteric. It is linked to ethylene, so it goes with fruit ripening.

sources: NCERT Class 11 Biology (Plant Growth and Development)

questions.q: Growth in plants is
questions.why: Plant growth is indeterminate (open) because meristems keep adding new cells throughout life. Animal growth is usually determinate.

questions.q: The first gibberellin discovered and most studied is
questions.why: GA₃ (gibberellic acid) was the first gibberellin discovered and is the best studied. Over a hundred gibberellins are now known.

questions.q: Which PGR is a gas?
questions.why: Ethylene is the gaseous plant growth regulator. Auxin, cytokinin and ABA are not gases.

questions.q: Synthetic auxins include
questions.why: NAA and 2,4-D are synthetic (man-made) auxins. IAA and IBA are natural auxins, and zeatin and kinetin are cytokinins.

questions.q: Stomatal closure is induced by
questions.why: ABA makes the stomata close during water stress, which saves water. Auxin, GA and cytokinin do not cause this closure.

questions.q: Kinetin is a modified form of
questions.why: Kinetin is a modified form of adenine, a purine base. Cytokinins are adenine derivatives.

questions.q: Assertion: Removal of the shoot apex promotes lateral branching. Reason: The shoot tip produces auxin that inhibits lateral buds.
options: Both true and R explains A
Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true and R explains A. Auxin from the shoot tip stops lateral buds from growing, so cutting off the apex removes it and side branches grow.

questions.q: The S-shaped growth curve is typical of
questions.why: The S-shaped curve comes from geometric (exponential) growth that is limited by resources. It has a lag, log and stationary phase. Arithmetic growth is a straight line.

questions.q: Phototropism of coleoptiles was first studied by
questions.why: Charles and Francis Darwin studied phototropism in canary grass coleoptiles and saw that the tip senses light and sends a signal to bend the shoot.

questions.q: Which hormone increases sugarcane yield?
questions.why: Gibberellin sprayed on sugarcane makes stems longer, so it increases the amount of sugar and the yield. 2,4-D and ethylene do not do this.

questions.q: Case: A farmer wants seedless tomatoes. He sprays
questions.why: Spraying auxin on unpollinated flowers makes fruits form without fertilisation (parthenocarpy), so the tomatoes are seedless.

questions.q: Case: A florist keeps cut flowers fresh longer by applying a hormone that delays senescence. It is
questions.why: Cytokinins delay senescence (ageing) by slowing the breakdown of chlorophyll and proteins, so cut flowers stay fresh longer. Ethylene and ABA speed up ageing.

questions.q: Leaf A: 2 → 4 cm²; leaf B: 20 → 24 cm² in a day. Which statement is correct?
options: A has greater relative growth rate; B has greater absolute growth
B has greater relative growth rate
questions.why: Leaf A grew by 2 cm² from 2, which is 100% relative growth. Leaf B grew by 4 cm² from 20, which is 20% relative growth. B has the larger absolute growth (4 against 2).

questions.q: Cork cambium arising from cortical cells shows
questions.why: Cork cambium forms when mature cortical cells begin dividing again. Differentiated cells regaining the ability to divide is dedifferentiation.

questions.q: Which pair is incorrectly matched?
questions.why: ABA does not promote seed germination. It keeps seeds dormant and inhibits germination, which is the opposite of what GA does.

questions.q: Heterophylly in larkspur is due to
options: different phases of life (juvenile vs mature)
questions.why: In larkspur the juvenile and mature plant make leaves of different shapes. This is heterophylly due to the plant's age, a type of developmental plasticity.

questions.q: Arithmetic growth equation: a root 1.5 cm long grows 0.25 cm/day. Length after 10 days?
questions.why: For arithmetic growth, Lₜ = L₀ + rt = 1.5 + 0.25 × 10 = 1.5 + 2.5 = 4 cm.

questions.q: Which combination is used to overcome apical dominance and to produce many shoots from callus in tissue culture?
questions.why: In tissue culture, a high cytokinin to auxin ratio makes shoot buds form from callus and overcomes apical dominance. A high auxin ratio favours roots instead.

courses.title: Ch 14 · Breathing and Exchange of Gases
courses.summary: Respiratory organs across animals, the human respiratory system, the mechanism of breathing and lung volumes, gas exchange by partial pressures, transport of O₂ and CO₂, regulation of breathing and common disorders.
outcomes: Learners can trace the path of air in the human respiratory system
Learners can explain inspiration, expiration and respiratory volumes and capacities
Learners can explain gas exchange using partial pressures
Learners can describe O₂ and CO₂ transport, the regulation of breathing and common disorders

lessons.title: Respiratory organs and the human respiratory system

scenes.text: A fish uses gills, an earthworm its moist skin, a grasshopper tiny tubes, and you — lungs.
Each organ matches its habitat. In humans, air travels a long, protected path before reaching the alveoli.

steps.title: Across animals
steps.body:
- Simple diffusion over the body surface: sponges, coelenterates, flatworms.
- **Moist cuticle/skin:** earthworms.
- **Tracheal tubes:** insects.
- **Gills (branchial respiration):** most aquatic arthropods and molluscs; fishes.
- **Lungs (pulmonary respiration):** terrestrial vertebrates; amphibians (frogs) also use moist skin (cutaneous).

steps.title: Human respiratory system
steps.body:
External **nostrils** → **nasal chamber** → **pharynx** (common passage for food and air) → **larynx** (cartilaginous **sound box**; the **epiglottis** covers the glottis during swallowing) → **trachea** (straight tube to mid-thoracic cavity; divides at the level of the **5th thoracic vertebra** into right and left primary **bronchi**) → secondary and tertiary bronchi → **bronchioles** → very thin, irregular-walled, vascularised bag-like **alveoli**.
- Trachea, bronchi and initial bronchioles are supported by incomplete cartilaginous rings.
- **Lungs** are covered by a double-layered **pleura** with **pleural fluid** (reduces friction).
- **Conducting part** (nostrils to terminal bronchioles): transports, cleans, humidifies and warms air. **Respiratory/exchange part**: alveoli and their ducts — site of diffusion.
- Lungs lie in the air-tight **thoracic chamber**: vertebral column dorsally, sternum ventrally, ribs laterally, dome-shaped **diaphragm** below.

steps.title: Solved question 1
steps.body: Why don't we choke on food normally? The **epiglottis**, a cartilaginous flap, closes the glottis during swallowing.

steps.title: Solved question 2
steps.body: Why is the thoracic chamber kept air-tight? So that changes in its volume change the pressure in the lungs — essential for breathing.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the trachea divides at the 5th cervical vertebra (it is thoracic).
- Calling the pharynx a part of only the respiratory tract (it is shared with digestion).
- Placing gas exchange in the bronchi.

activity.prompt: Order the path of inhaled air.

quiz.why: Insects breathe through a network of tracheal tubes that carry air straight to the tissues. They do not have lungs or gills.
The larynx is the sound box, since it contains the vocal cords. The trachea is the windpipe and the pharynx is the throat.
Gas exchange takes place in the alveoli, which have very thin walls and many capillaries. The trachea and bronchi only carry air.
The lungs are covered by a double-layered pleura, with pleural fluid between the layers that reduces friction. The pericardium covers the heart.

quiz.q: The epiglottis prevents food from entering the
quiz.why: The epiglottis is a flap of tissue that covers the glottis (opening to the larynx) while swallowing, so food goes down the oesophagus and not into the windpipe.

sources: NCERT Class 11 Biology (Breathing and Exchange of Gases)

lessons.title: Mechanism of breathing and lung volumes

scenes.text: A doctor asks Kiran to blow as hard as she can into a spirometer after a deep breath.
The reading — her vital capacity — tells how well her lungs are working.

steps.title: Inspiration and expiration
steps.body:
Breathing works by creating a pressure gradient between the lungs and the atmosphere.
- **Inspiration:** **diaphragm contracts** (flattens) → thoracic volume increases in the antero-posterior axis; **external intercostal muscles contract** → ribs and sternum lift → volume increases in the dorso-ventral axis. Pulmonary volume increases, **intra-pulmonary pressure falls below atmospheric** → air rushes in.
- **Expiration:** diaphragm and intercostals **relax** → thoracic and pulmonary volume decrease → intra-pulmonary pressure rises slightly above atmospheric → air is expelled.
- Additional abdominal muscles help in forced breathing.
- A healthy adult breathes **12–16 times per minute**. A **spirometer** measures volumes.

steps.title: Volumes and capacities (approximate, healthy adult)
steps.body:
- **Tidal volume (TV):** about **500 mL** (≈ 6000–8000 mL per minute)
- **Inspiratory reserve volume (IRV):** 2500–3000 mL
- **Expiratory reserve volume (ERV):** 1000–1100 mL
- **Residual volume (RV):** 1100–1200 mL (cannot be expelled)
- **Inspiratory capacity** = TV + IRV
- **Expiratory capacity** = TV + ERV
- **Functional residual capacity** = ERV + RV
- **Vital capacity** = ERV + TV + IRV
- **Total lung capacity** = VC + RV

steps.title: Solved question 2
steps.body: Minute ventilation with TV 500 mL at 14 breaths/min = 500 × 14 = **7000 mL/min**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the diaphragm relaxes during inspiration.
- Including RV in vital capacity.
- Thinking air is 'sucked' by the lungs themselves — it is the pressure gradient.

activity.prompt: TV = 500 mL, IRV = 3000 mL, ERV = 1100 mL. What is the vital capacity in mL?

quiz.why: In inspiration the diaphragm contracts and flattens, which increases the volume of the thoracic cavity. Air then flows in.

quiz.q: Volume of air remaining after forcible expiration is
quiz.why: The volume of air still left in the lungs after a forced expiration is the residual volume (RV). It cannot be breathed out.
Vital capacity is the maximum air one can breathe out after a deepest breath in. It equals ERV + TV + IRV. Residual volume is not included.

quiz.q: Normal breathing rate of an adult is
quiz.why: An adult at rest breathes about 12 to 16 times a minute. Infants and exercise raise the rate.
Functional residual capacity is the air left in the lungs after a normal expiration. It equals the expiratory reserve volume plus residual volume (ERV + RV).

sources: NCERT Class 11 Biology (Breathing and Exchange of Gases)

lessons.title: Exchange of gases

scenes.text: At high altitude, climbers feel breathless though they breathe faster.
The partial pressure of oxygen in the air is lower, so less O₂ diffuses into the blood.

steps.title: Partial pressures (mm Hg)
steps.body:
Gas exchange happens by **simple diffusion**, driven by partial pressure (p) gradients, solubility and membrane thickness.

| | pO₂ | pCO₂ |
- Atmospheric air: 159 | 0.3
- Alveoli: 104 | 40
- Deoxygenated blood: 40 | 45
- Oxygenated blood: 95 | 40
- Tissues: 40 | 45

O₂ moves alveoli → blood → tissues; CO₂ moves tissues → blood → alveoli. CO₂ is **20–25 times more soluble** than O₂, so much more CO₂ can diffuse per unit difference in partial pressure.

steps.title: The diffusion membrane
steps.body: Three layers: the thin **squamous epithelium of alveoli**, the **endothelium of alveolar capillaries**, and the **basement substance** between them. Its total thickness is much less than a millimetre — ideal for diffusion. Alveoli are the **primary sites** of exchange; some exchange also occurs between blood and tissues.

steps.title: Solved question 1
steps.body: Why does O₂ enter blood in the lungs? pO₂ in alveoli (104 mm Hg) is higher than in deoxygenated blood (40 mm Hg).

steps.title: Solved question 2
steps.body: Why can CO₂ diffuse quickly despite a small gradient (45 → 40)? Its solubility is 20–25 times higher than O₂.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking gas exchange uses active transport (it is diffusion).
- Mixing up pO₂ of alveoli (104) and oxygenated blood (95).
- Forgetting the three layers of the diffusion membrane.

activity.prompt: Match the site with its pO₂ (mm Hg).

quiz.q: Gas exchange in the alveoli is by
quiz.why: Gas exchange in the alveoli is by simple diffusion, as O₂ and CO₂ move from higher to lower partial pressure. No energy is used.

quiz.q: pCO₂ in deoxygenated blood is about
quiz.why: The pCO₂ of deoxygenated blood is about 45 mm Hg, higher than the 40 mm Hg of the alveoli, so CO₂ diffuses out into the alveoli.

quiz.q: CO₂ is about how many times more soluble than O₂?
quiz.why: CO₂ is about 20 to 25 times more soluble in water than O₂. So it diffuses across the membrane well even with a small pressure difference.

quiz.q: Which is not part of the diffusion membrane?
quiz.why: The diffusion membrane has three layers: the alveolar epithelium, the capillary endothelium and the basement substance between them. Cartilage rings are in the airways, not here.

quiz.q: pO₂ of alveolar air is about
quiz.why: The pO₂ of alveolar air is about 104 mm Hg. It is lower than the 159 mm Hg of the atmosphere because the air mixes with air already in the lungs.

sources: NCERT Class 11 Biology (Breathing and Exchange of Gases)

lessons.title: Transport of gases, regulation and disorders

story.title: Car exhaust in a closed garage

scenes.text: Running a car in a closed garage is deadly even without visible smoke.
Carbon monoxide binds haemoglobin far more strongly than oxygen, blocking O₂ transport. Understanding transport explains why.

steps.title: Transport of O₂ and CO₂
steps.body:
- **O₂:** about **97%** carried by **haemoglobin** in RBCs as **oxyhaemoglobin** (each Hb binds up to 4 O₂); **3%** dissolved in plasma. Binding depends mainly on pO₂; also pCO₂, H⁺ and temperature. The **oxygen dissociation curve** is **sigmoid**. In alveoli (high pO₂, low pCO₂, less H⁺, lower temperature) oxyhaemoglobin forms; in tissues (low pO₂, high pCO₂, high H⁺, higher temperature) O₂ dissociates. Every **100 mL of oxygenated blood delivers about 5 mL of O₂** to tissues under normal conditions.
- **CO₂:** about **20–25%** as **carbamino-haemoglobin**, about **70%** as **bicarbonate**, about **7%** dissolved in plasma. RBCs have high **carbonic anhydrase**: CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃ ⇌ HCO₃⁻ + H⁺. Every **100 mL of deoxygenated blood delivers about 4 mL of CO₂** to the alveoli.

steps.title: Regulation and disorders
steps.body:
- **Respiratory rhythm centre** in the **medulla**; **pneumotaxic centre** in the **pons** moderates it (can shorten inspiration and alter rate). A **chemosensitive area** next to the rhythm centre responds to **CO₂ and H⁺**; receptors in the **aortic arch** and **carotid artery** also sense CO₂/H⁺ changes. The role of O₂ in regulation is quite insignificant.
- **Asthma:** difficulty in breathing with wheezing due to inflammation of bronchi and bronchioles.
- **Emphysema:** chronic disorder; alveolar walls damaged → less respiratory surface; **cigarette smoking** is a major cause.
- **Occupational respiratory disorders:** long exposure to dust (grinding, stone-breaking, silica, asbestos) → inflammation → **fibrosis** (proliferation of fibrous tissue) → serious lung damage; workers should wear protective masks.

General education, not medical advice: see a doctor for persistent breathlessness, wheezing or chest pain; emergency help in India: **112**.

steps.title: Solved question 1
steps.body: Which form carries most CO₂? **Bicarbonate (~70%)**, formed in RBCs by carbonic anhydrase.

steps.title: Solved question 2
steps.body: Why does exercise increase breathing? Muscles produce more CO₂ and H⁺; chemoreceptors detect this and the rhythm centre increases rate and depth.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying most CO₂ travels as carbamino-haemoglobin.
- Claiming O₂ is the main chemical regulator of breathing (CO₂ and H⁺ are).
- Placing the pneumotaxic centre in the medulla (it is in the pons).

activity.prompt: Conditions in the alveoli or in tissues?

quiz.q: About what percentage of O₂ is carried by haemoglobin?
quiz.why: About 97% of the O₂ in blood is carried by haemoglobin in red blood cells. The remaining 3% is dissolved in plasma.
Carbonic anhydrase, which speeds the reaction of CO₂ and water to make carbonic acid, is abundant in red blood cells (RBCs).

quiz.q: The pneumotaxic centre is located in the
quiz.why: The pneumotaxic centre is in the pons region of the brain. It moderates the rhythm centre in the medulla by reducing the duration of inspiration.
In emphysema the walls of the alveoli are damaged, so the surface area for gas exchange is reduced. It is often caused by smoking.
The oxygen dissociation curve is sigmoid (S-shaped), because haemoglobin binds O₂ in a way that makes later binding easier.

quiz.q: 100 mL of oxygenated blood delivers about ___ mL O₂ to tissues
quiz.why: Under normal conditions 100 mL of oxygenated blood gives about 5 mL of O₂ to the tissues. The rest stays bound to haemoglobin in the returning blood.

sources: NCERT Class 11 Biology (Breathing and Exchange of Gases)

questions.q: The respiratory organ of earthworm is its
questions.why: The earthworm breathes through its moist skin (cutaneous respiration). It has no lungs, gills or tracheae.

questions.q: Tidal volume of a healthy adult is about
questions.why: Tidal volume is the air breathed in or out in a normal breath. For a healthy adult it is about 500 mL.

questions.q: Breathing rhythm centre lies in the
questions.why: The main rhythm centre for breathing is in the medulla oblongata of the brain stem. The pons has the pneumotaxic centre that moderates it.

questions.q: The trachea divides into bronchi at the level of the
questions.why: The trachea divides into left and right bronchi at about the level of the 5th thoracic vertebra, in the middle of the chest cavity.

questions.q: During inspiration, intra-pulmonary pressure is
questions.why: In inspiration the lung volume increases, so the pressure inside the lungs falls below atmospheric pressure. Air then rushes in.

questions.q: About 70% of CO₂ is transported as
questions.why: About 70% of CO₂ travels as bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻), formed in the RBCs with carbonic anhydrase. About 20 to 25% is carbamino-haemoglobin and 7% is dissolved.

questions.q: Assertion: The pressure gradient for CO₂ is small, yet CO₂ diffuses efficiently. Reason: CO₂ is 20–25 times more soluble than O₂.
options: Both true and R explains A
Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true and R explains A. The pressure gradient of CO₂ is small, but CO₂ is 20 to 25 times more soluble than O₂, which makes up for it.

questions.q: Total lung capacity equals
questions.why: Total lung capacity is the air in the lungs after the deepest breath in. It equals vital capacity plus residual volume (VC + RV).

questions.q: Which factor favours formation of oxyhaemoglobin?
questions.why: Oxyhaemoglobin forms where pO₂ is high and pCO₂, H⁺ and temperature are low. This is the case in the alveoli.

questions.q: The respiratory centre is most sensitive to changes in
questions.why: The chemosensitive area of the respiratory centre is highly sensitive to CO₂ and H⁺ concentration. A rise in these increases the breathing rate. O₂ has a smaller role.

questions.q: Case: A stone-quarry worker develops progressive breathlessness; X-ray shows lung fibrosis. The likely cause is
questions.why: Long exposure to dust such as silica in quarries and mines causes fibrosis of the lungs, with breathlessness. This is an occupational lung disorder.

questions.q: Case: A person's TV = 500, IRV = 2500, ERV = 1000 and RV = 1200 mL. Inspiratory capacity is
questions.why: Inspiratory capacity is the total air that can be breathed in after a normal expiration. It equals TV + IRV = 500 + 2500 = 3000 mL.

questions.q: For the same person, functional residual capacity is
questions.why: Functional residual capacity = ERV + RV = 1000 + 1200 = 2200 mL.

questions.q: pO₂ and pCO₂ of tissues are roughly
questions.why: In the tissues pO₂ is about 40 mm Hg and pCO₂ about 45 mm Hg. This makes O₂ move from the blood into the tissues and CO₂ move into the blood.

questions.q: Every 100 mL of deoxygenated blood delivers about ___ of CO₂ to the alveoli
questions.why: Each 100 mL of deoxygenated blood delivers about 4 mL of CO₂ to the alveoli. This is the normal value.

questions.q: Which statement is incorrect?
options: The pneumotaxic centre is in the medulla
Alveoli are the primary site of exchange
questions.why: The pneumotaxic centre is in the pons, not the medulla, so that statement is incorrect. The other three statements are correct.

questions.q: If a person breathes 15 times per minute with TV 500 mL, minute volume is
questions.why: Minute volume = tidal volume × breaths per minute = 500 mL × 15 = 7500 mL = 7.5 L.

courses.title: Ch 15 · Body Fluids and Circulation
courses.summary: Blood plasma and formed elements, blood groups and clotting, lymph, circulatory pathways in animals, the human heart and its conducting system, the cardiac cycle, ECG, double circulation, regulation and disorders.
outcomes: Learners can describe plasma proteins and the formed elements of blood with counts and functions
Learners can explain ABO and Rh blood groups and the clotting cascade
Learners can describe the structure of the human heart and its conducting system
Learners can explain the cardiac cycle, heart sounds, ECG and double circulation

lessons.title: Blood: plasma and formed elements

scenes.text: Ravi's blood report lists haemoglobin 14 g/dL, RBC 5.1 million/mm³, WBC 7,200/mm³ and platelets 2.5 lakh/mm³.
Each number describes a different component of blood — a fluid connective tissue.

steps.title: Plasma (≈ 55%)
steps.body: Straw-coloured, viscous fluid: **90–92% water**, **6–8% proteins** — **fibrinogen** (clotting), **globulins** (defence), **albumins** (osmotic balance); small amounts of minerals (Na⁺, Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺, HCO₃⁻, Cl⁻), glucose, amino acids, lipids. Factors for clotting are in plasma in inactive form. **Serum** = plasma without clotting factors.

steps.title: Formed elements (≈ 45%)
steps.body:
- **RBCs (erythrocytes):** most abundant; **5–5.5 million/mm³** in a healthy adult; formed in **red bone marrow**; biconcave, **no nucleus** in most mammals; contain **haemoglobin** (12–16 g per 100 mL); lifespan about **120 days**; destroyed in the **spleen** ('graveyard of RBCs').
- **WBCs (leucocytes):** nucleated, colourless, **6000–8000/mm³**, short-lived.
  - Granulocytes: **neutrophils** (most abundant, **60–65%**, phagocytic), **eosinophils** (2–3%, resist infections, allergic reactions), **basophils** (least, secrete histamine, serotonin, heparin; inflammation).
  - Agranulocytes: **lymphocytes** (20–25%; **B and T** forms; immunity), **monocytes** (6–8%; phagocytic).
- **Platelets (thrombocytes):** fragments of **megakaryocytes** in bone marrow; **1.5–3.5 lakh/mm³**; release factors for coagulation; low count → bleeding disorders.

steps.title: Solved question 1
steps.body: Which WBC is most abundant and what does it do? **Neutrophils** (60–65%) — phagocytose foreign organisms.

steps.title: Solved question 2
steps.body: Why do mature mammalian RBCs lack a nucleus? It leaves more space for haemoglobin and gives the biconcave shape for efficient gas exchange.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling lymphocytes the most abundant WBC.
- Saying platelets are complete cells (they are cell fragments).
- Confusing plasma with serum.

activity.prompt: Match the blood component to its role.

quiz.q: Normal RBC count in a healthy adult is
quiz.why: A healthy adult has about 5 to 5.5 million RBCs per mm³ of blood. They are the most abundant cells in blood.

quiz.q: Lifespan of human RBCs is about
quiz.why: Human RBCs live about 120 days and are then destroyed in the spleen, which is called the graveyard of RBCs.
Platelets (thrombocytes) are pieces of the cytoplasm of megakaryocytes in the bone marrow. They help in blood clotting.
Plasma forms about 55% of blood, and the formed elements (RBCs, WBCs and platelets) make up the other 45%.
Eosinophils (2 to 3% of WBCs) take part in allergic reactions and fight parasites. Neutrophils and monocytes engulf germs.

sources: NCERT Class 11 Biology (Body Fluids and Circulation)

lessons.title: Blood groups and coagulation

scenes.text: An accident victim needs blood urgently and her group is unknown.
Doctors may give O negative red cells — why? Because those cells carry no A, B or Rh antigens.

steps.title: ABO and Rh
steps.body:
- **ABO grouping** depends on antigens **A and B** on RBCs; plasma has natural antibodies.
  - Group A: antigen A, antibody anti-B; donors A, O.
  - Group B: antigen B, antibody anti-A; donors B, O.
  - Group AB: antigens A and B, no antibodies; donors AB, A, B, O → **universal recipient**.
  - Group O: no antigens, antibodies anti-A and anti-B; donor O only → **universal donor**.
- **Rh factor:** an antigen (first found in Rhesus monkeys); ~80% of humans are **Rh⁺**. An **Rh⁻** person exposed to Rh⁺ blood forms antibodies.
- **Erythroblastosis foetalis:** Rh⁻ mother, Rh⁺ foetus. First pregnancy usually safe (placenta separates the bloods), but mother may be exposed at delivery and form antibodies; in a later Rh⁺ pregnancy her antibodies can destroy foetal RBCs → severe anaemia and jaundice. Prevented by giving the mother **anti-Rh antibodies** immediately after the first delivery.

steps.title: Coagulation
steps.body: Injury → platelets and damaged tissues release factors → a cascade forms **thrombokinase** → converts inactive **prothrombin** to **thrombin** → thrombin converts soluble **fibrinogen** to insoluble **fibrin** threads → network traps formed elements → **clot**. **Calcium ions** are essential. A clot looks dark reddish-brown.

steps.title: Solved question 1
steps.body: Can a group B person receive group AB blood? **No** — AB red cells carry antigen A, which reacts with the recipient's anti-A antibodies.

steps.title: Solved question 2
steps.body: Why is a citrate solution added to stored blood? It binds **Ca²⁺**, preventing clotting.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling AB the universal donor.
- Saying erythroblastosis affects the first pregnancy typically.
- Reversing thrombin and prothrombin.

buckets: Can donate to group A recipient
Cannot donate to group A recipient

quiz.q: The universal donor blood group is
quiz.why: Group O RBCs have neither A nor B antigens, so they do not set off a reaction in the recipient. That makes O the universal donor.
Group AB has both A and B antigens on RBCs and no anti-A or anti-B antibodies in plasma. So AB can receive from all groups and is the universal recipient.
Thrombin is an enzyme that converts soluble fibrinogen into insoluble fibrin threads. Fibrin makes the clot.

quiz.q: An ion essential for clotting is
quiz.why: Calcium ions (Ca²⁺) are required for several steps in blood clotting. Na⁺, K⁺ and Cl⁻ are not clotting factors.

options: an Rh⁺ mother carries an Rh⁻ foetus
an Rh⁻ mother carries an Rh⁺ foetus (later pregnancy)
quiz.why: Erythroblastosis foetalis happens when an Rh⁻ mother carries an Rh⁺ foetus. Her body makes anti-Rh antibodies, which in a later pregnancy can destroy the RBCs of the baby.

sources: NCERT Class 11 Biology (Body Fluids and Circulation)

lessons.title: Lymph, circulatory pathways and the human heart

scenes.text: A heart taken out for transplant can keep beating for a while in the right solution.
It has its own pacemaker — the sino-atrial node — so it is 'myogenic'.

steps.title: Lymph and pathways
steps.body:
- **Lymph (tissue fluid):** as blood passes capillaries, some water and small solutes leave; this fluid lacks large proteins and most formed elements; collected by lymphatic vessels and drained into major veins. Contains **lymphocytes**; carries **fats absorbed through lacteals** in intestinal villi.
- **Open circulation** (arthropods, molluscs) vs **closed** (annelids, chordates).
- Hearts: **fishes 2 chambers** (single circulation); **amphibians and reptiles (except crocodiles) 3 chambers** — mixed blood in the ventricle (**incomplete double circulation**); **crocodiles, birds, mammals 4 chambers** — **double circulation**.

steps.title: Human heart
steps.body:
- Mesodermal; in the thoracic cavity between the lungs, slightly tilted left; about the size of a clenched fist; protected by a double-walled **pericardium** with pericardial fluid.
- Four chambers: two thin-walled **atria**, two thick-walled **ventricles**; inter-atrial septum, inter-ventricular septum, atrio-ventricular septum.
- Valves: **tricuspid** (right atrium–right ventricle), **bicuspid/mitral** (left atrium–left ventricle), **semilunar valves** at the openings of the pulmonary artery and aorta; valves allow one-way flow.
- **Nodal tissue:** **SAN** (right upper corner of right atrium) → **AVN** (lower left corner of right atrium near the AV septum) → **bundle of His** (AV bundle) → right and left bundle branches → **Purkinje fibres**. SAN generates the most action potentials (**70–75/min**) → **pacemaker**.

steps.title: Solved question 1
steps.body: Why is circulation in frogs called incomplete double circulation? Oxygenated and deoxygenated blood mix in the single ventricle.

steps.title: Solved question 2
steps.body: Why is the left ventricle wall thicker? It pumps blood to the whole body (systemic circulation) at high pressure.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Placing the tricuspid valve on the left side.
- Saying the AVN is the pacemaker.
- Saying lymph contains RBCs.

activity.prompt: Order the conducting system of the heart.

quiz.q: The pacemaker of the heart is the
quiz.why: The sinoatrial node (SAN) is the pacemaker of the heart. It starts the impulse for each beat, about 70 to 75 per minute.
The bicuspid (mitral) valve is between the left atrium and the left ventricle. The tricuspid valve is on the right side.
Amphibians have a three-chambered heart with two atria and one ventricle. Fishes have two chambers, and birds and mammals have four.

quiz.q: Fats from the intestine are absorbed into
quiz.why: Fats are absorbed into the lacteals, the lymph vessels inside the villi, and travel by the lymph. Other nutrients go into blood capillaries.
Crocodiles are an exception among reptiles, as they have a four-chambered heart. Most reptiles have three chambers.

sources: NCERT Class 11 Biology (Body Fluids and Circulation)

lessons.title: Cardiac cycle, ECG, double circulation and disorders

scenes.text: In the hospital, a monitor draws a repeating wave: a small bump, a sharp spike, a broad hump.
P, QRS and T waves tell doctors how the heart's electrical activity is going.

steps.title: Cardiac cycle
steps.body:
Sequence of events in one heartbeat (systole = contraction, diastole = relaxation): joint diastole → SAN fires → **atrial systole** (adds ~30% more blood to ventricles) → **ventricular systole** (AV valves close; semilunar valves open; blood to pulmonary artery and aorta) → **ventricular diastole** (semilunar valves close; AV valves open).
- Heart rate ~**72 beats/min**, so one cycle ≈ **0.8 s**.
- **Stroke volume** ≈ **70 mL**; **cardiac output** = stroke volume × heart rate ≈ **5000 mL (5 L) per minute**; athletes have higher output.
