- **Heart sounds:** **'lub'** — closure of tricuspid and bicuspid valves; **'dub'** — closure of semilunar valves.

steps.title: ECG, double circulation, regulation, disorders
steps.body:
- **ECG:** **P wave** = atrial depolarisation (atrial contraction); **QRS complex** = ventricular depolarisation (ventricular contraction); **T wave** = ventricular repolarisation (return to normal). Counting QRS complexes in a time gives heart rate.
- **Double circulation:** **pulmonary** (right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary veins → left atrium) and **systemic** (left ventricle → aorta → tissues → veins → venae cavae → right atrium). **Hepatic portal system** carries blood from the intestine to the liver; **coronary circulation** supplies heart muscle.
- **Regulation:** heart is **myogenic**; a centre in the **medulla oblongata** moderates it via the ANS — **sympathetic** nerves increase rate, strength and output; **parasympathetic** (vagus) decrease them; adrenal medullary hormones increase output.
- **Disorders:** **hypertension** (persistently ≥ 140/90 mm Hg; normal ~120/80); **coronary artery disease/atherosclerosis** (deposits of Ca, fat, cholesterol, fibrous tissue narrow arteries); **angina** (chest pain when not enough O₂ reaches heart muscle); **heart failure** (heart cannot pump enough blood; congestion of lungs); **cardiac arrest** (heart stops beating); **heart attack** (heart muscle damaged by sudden lack of blood supply).

General education, not medical advice. Chest pain with sweating or breathlessness is an emergency — call **112**.

steps.title: Solved question 1
steps.body: Find cardiac output for stroke volume 70 mL and heart rate 75/min. 70 × 75 = **5250 mL/min ≈ 5.25 L/min**.

steps.title: Solved question 2
steps.body: What does the QRS complex represent? **Depolarisation of the ventricles**, which triggers ventricular contraction.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying 'lub' is semilunar valve closure (it is AV valve closure).
- Saying the T wave shows atrial repolarisation (it is ventricular repolarisation).
- Mixing heart attack (muscle damage) with cardiac arrest (heart stops).

activity.prompt: Stroke volume is 70 mL and heart rate is 72 beats/min. What is the cardiac output in mL per minute?

quiz.q: The 'lub' sound is due to closure of
quiz.why: The first heart sound 'lub' is caused by the closure of the tricuspid and bicuspid valves at the start of ventricular systole. The second sound 'dub' is from the semilunar valves.

quiz.q: Duration of one cardiac cycle at 72 beats/min is about
quiz.why: The cardiac cycle lasts 60 seconds ÷ heart rate. At 72 beats per minute, that is 60/72 ≈ 0.8 seconds.
The P wave in an ECG shows the electrical excitation (depolarisation) of the atria. The QRS complex shows the ventricles and the T wave shows their return to normal.
Sympathetic nerves raise the heart rate and the strength of contraction, as in fight or flight. Parasympathetic stimulation slows the heart.

quiz.q: Blood pressure of 140/90 mm Hg or higher persistently indicates
quiz.why: Normal blood pressure is about 120/80 mm Hg. A persistent reading of 140/90 or higher is called hypertension (high blood pressure).

quiz.q: Blood from the intestine reaches the liver through the
quiz.why: Blood from the intestine goes to the liver through the hepatic portal vein, which forms the hepatic portal system.

sources: NCERT Class 11 Biology (Body Fluids and Circulation)

questions.q: Most abundant plasma protein group for osmotic balance is
questions.why: Albumins are the most abundant plasma proteins and they help keep the osmotic balance of blood. Globulins fight infection and fibrinogen helps in clotting.

questions.q: Universal recipient blood group is
questions.why: AB is the universal recipient, as its RBCs have both antigens but the plasma has no anti-A or anti-B antibodies.

questions.q: Pacemaker of the human heart is
questions.why: The SAN is the pacemaker of the human heart, because it starts the electrical impulse that makes the heart beat.

questions.q: Normal WBC count is
questions.why: The normal WBC (leucocyte) count is about 6000 to 8000 per mm³. RBCs are in millions and platelets in lakhs per mm³.

questions.q: Mammals and birds have
questions.why: Birds and mammals have a four-chambered heart, so oxygenated and deoxygenated blood do not mix. This gives complete double circulation.

questions.q: The T wave of an ECG represents
questions.why: The T wave of an ECG shows the return of the ventricles to their normal (resting) state, which is ventricular repolarisation. The QRS complex is ventricular depolarisation.

questions.q: Assertion: Group O individuals are universal donors. Reason: Their RBCs lack A and B antigens.
options: Both true and R explains A
Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true and R explains A. Group O RBCs have no A or B antigens, so they do not react with the antibodies of the recipient, making O a universal donor.

questions.q: Cardiac output in a resting adult is about
questions.why: Cardiac output = stroke volume × heart rate = about 70 mL × 72 per minute ≈ 5000 mL = 5 L per minute in a resting adult.

questions.q: Which is correctly matched?
questions.why: Basophils release histamine and heparin, which are involved in inflammation. Haemoglobin is in RBCs, and antibodies come from lymphocytes.

questions.q: Ventricular systole begins with
questions.why: Ventricular systole begins as the AV valves close, which causes the first sound 'lub'. Then the ventricular pressure rises and opens the semilunar valves.

questions.q: Case: An Rh⁻ woman's second baby (Rh⁺) shows severe anaemia and jaundice at birth. The condition is
questions.why: A second Rh⁺ baby of an Rh⁻ mother, with severe anaemia and jaundice, shows erythroblastosis foetalis. The mother's anti-Rh antibodies from the first pregnancy attack the baby's RBCs.

questions.q: Case: A patient feels chest pain on climbing stairs that eases with rest. The most likely condition is
questions.why: Chest pain on effort that eases with rest is angina. The heart muscle does not get enough oxygen when the demand rises.

questions.q: Stroke volume 80 mL, heart rate 65/min. Cardiac output is
questions.why: Cardiac output = stroke volume × heart rate = 80 × 65 = 5200 mL = 5.2 L per minute.

questions.q: In fish, blood passes through the heart
questions.why: Fish have a two-chambered heart and blood passes through it only once in a complete circuit. This is single circulation.

questions.q: The correct sequence in clotting is
options: thrombokinase → prothrombin to thrombin → fibrinogen to fibrin
questions.why: Injury releases thrombokinase, which converts prothrombin into thrombin. Thrombin then converts fibrinogen to fibrin, which forms the clot.

questions.q: Atrial systole adds about what share of ventricular filling?
questions.why: Most of the ventricular filling (about 70%) is passive, as blood flows in while the atria are relaxed. Atrial systole adds about 30%.

questions.q: Which statement is incorrect?
options: Lymph contains large numbers of RBCs
questions.why: Lymph has lymphocytes but very few other blood cells, and it has no large numbers of RBCs. The other statements are correct.

questions.q: If heart rate rises to 90/min, the cardiac cycle lasts about
questions.why: Cardiac cycle time = 60 ÷ heart rate = 60/90 ≈ 0.67 seconds. A faster heart rate shortens the cycle.

courses.title: Ch 16 · Excretory Products and their Elimination
courses.summary: Ammonotelism, ureotelism and uricotelism, excretory organs across animals, the human kidney and nephron, urine formation, counter-current mechanism, hormonal regulation, micturition, other excretory organs and kidney disorders.
outcomes: Learners can classify animals by their main nitrogenous waste and excretory organs
Learners can describe kidney and nephron structure
Learners can explain filtration, reabsorption, secretion and the counter-current mechanism
Learners can explain regulation by ADH, RAAS and ANF and describe common disorders and treatments

lessons.title: Modes of excretion and excretory organs

scenes.text: Bird droppings have a white paste — that is uric acid.
Birds save water by making nearly insoluble uric acid; fish simply let ammonia diffuse into water.

steps.title: Nitrogenous wastes
steps.body:
- **Ammonotelism** (ammonia; most toxic, needs much water; excreted by diffusion across body surfaces/gills as NH₄⁺): many **bony fishes, aquatic amphibians, aquatic insects**.
- **Ureotelism** (urea; made in the **liver** from ammonia; less toxic): **mammals, many terrestrial amphibians, marine fishes**. Some urea is retained in the kidney matrix of some animals for osmolarity.
- **Uricotelism** (uric acid as pellet or paste; minimum water loss): **reptiles, birds, land snails, insects**.

steps.title: Excretory structures
steps.body:
- **Protonephridia/flame cells:** Platyhelminthes (*Planaria*), rotifers, some annelids, the cephalochordate *Amphioxus* — mainly osmoregulation.
- **Nephridia:** earthworms and other annelids — remove nitrogenous wastes and maintain fluid and ionic balance.
- **Malpighian tubules:** most insects including cockroaches.
- **Antennal glands (green glands):** crustaceans such as prawns.
- **Kidneys:** vertebrates.

steps.title: Solved question 1
steps.body: Why are terrestrial animals mostly ureotelic or uricotelic? Ammonia needs much water to dilute; land animals conserve water by converting it to less toxic urea or uric acid.

steps.title: Solved question 2
steps.body: Excretory organ of prawn? **Antennal (green) glands**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling birds ureotelic.
- Saying marine fishes are ammonotelic (they are ureotelic).
- Mixing nephridia (annelids) with Malpighian tubules (insects).

quiz.why: Bony fishes excrete ammonia, which is very toxic but dissolves in the water around them. This is called ammonotelic excretion. Mammals excrete urea and birds and reptiles excrete uric acid.
Urea is made in the liver through the ornithine cycle, from ammonia. It then goes in the blood to the kidneys for removal.

quiz.q: Flame cells are excretory structures of
quiz.why: Flame cells (protonephridia) are the excretory and osmoregulatory structures of flatworms such as Planaria. Earthworms use nephridia and cockroaches use Malpighian tubules.
Birds and reptiles excrete uric acid, a semi-solid waste that saves water. They are uricotelic. Bony fishes excrete ammonia and mammals excrete urea.
Green glands (antennal glands) are the excretory organs of crustaceans such as prawns. Insects use Malpighian tubules and earthworms use nephridia.

sources: NCERT Class 11 Biology (Excretory Products and their Elimination)

lessons.title: The human excretory system and nephron

scenes.text: Each of your kidneys is about the size of a fist and filters your entire blood volume many times a day.
Inside each are about a million tiny units — nephrons.

steps.title: Kidneys and associated organs
steps.body:
A pair of **kidneys**, a pair of **ureters**, a **urinary bladder** and a **urethra**.
- Kidneys: reddish-brown, bean-shaped, between the levels of the **last thoracic and third lumbar vertebra**, close to the dorsal inner wall of the abdominal cavity. Each adult kidney is about 10–12 cm long, 5–7 cm wide, 2–3 cm thick and weighs **120–170 g**.
- The inner concave **hilum** admits the ureter, blood vessels and nerves; inside is the funnel-shaped **renal pelvis** with **calyces**.
- Outer **cortex**, inner **medulla** divided into **medullary pyramids**; cortex extends between pyramids as **renal columns (columns of Bertini)**.

steps.title: The nephron
steps.body:
About **one million** nephrons per kidney. Each has a **glomerulus** (capillary tuft from the **afferent arteriole**, leaving as the narrower **efferent arteriole**) and a **renal tubule**:
- **Bowman's capsule** (double-walled cup around the glomerulus) — together with the glomerulus = **Malpighian body (renal corpuscle)**.
- **Proximal convoluted tubule (PCT)** → **Henle's loop** (descending and ascending limbs; hairpin) → **distal convoluted tubule (DCT)** → **collecting duct** (many nephrons) → renal pelvis.
- Malpighian corpuscle, PCT and DCT lie in the cortex; the loop dips into the medulla.
- **Cortical nephrons** (most): short loops, little medullary penetration. **Juxtamedullary nephrons:** very long loops deep into the medulla.
- The efferent arteriole forms the **peritubular capillaries**; a minute vessel parallel to Henle's loop forms the U-shaped **vasa recta** (absent or reduced in cortical nephrons).

steps.title: Solved question 1
steps.body: Why is the efferent arteriole narrower than the afferent? It keeps the glomerular blood pressure high, driving filtration.

steps.title: Solved question 2
steps.body: Which nephrons help concentrate urine most? **Juxtamedullary nephrons** with long loops and vasa recta.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Placing Henle's loop entirely in the cortex.
- Calling the collecting duct part of a single nephron (it collects from many).
- Saying the medulla extends between pyramids (it is cortex — columns of Bertini).

activity.prompt: Order the parts of a nephron through which filtrate flows.

quiz.q: Each kidney has about how many nephrons?
quiz.why: Each human kidney has about one million nephrons, the functional units.
The Malpighian body (renal corpuscle) is made of the glomerulus, a knot of capillaries, and the Bowman's capsule around it.

quiz.q: Columns of Bertini are extensions of the
quiz.why: The columns of Bertini are extensions of the renal cortex that dip between the medullary pyramids. They are also called renal columns.
The vasa recta is a thin capillary loop that runs parallel to the loop of Henle in juxtamedullary nephrons. It helps keep the medullary gradient.

quiz.q: Kidneys lie between the levels of
options: last thoracic and third lumbar vertebrae
quiz.why: The kidneys lie against the dorsal abdominal wall, between the levels of the last thoracic and third lumbar vertebrae.

sources: NCERT Class 11 Biology (Excretory Products and their Elimination)

lessons.title: Urine formation and the counter-current mechanism

scenes.text: Your kidneys filter about 180 litres of fluid every day — yet you pass only about 1.5 litres of urine.
About 99% of the filtrate is reabsorbed. The nephron is a master recycler.

steps.title: Filtration, reabsorption, secretion
steps.body:
- **Glomerular filtration (ultrafiltration):** kidneys receive about **1100–1200 mL of blood per minute** (≈ 1/5 of cardiac output). Blood is filtered through three layers — glomerular endothelium, epithelium of Bowman's capsule (**podocytes** with **filtration slits/slit pores**) and the basement membrane between. Nearly everything except proteins passes. **GFR ≈ 125 mL/min ≈ 180 L/day**.
- **Reabsorption** (~99% of filtrate): active (glucose, amino acids, Na⁺) and passive (nitrogenous wastes, water).
- **Tubular secretion:** H⁺, K⁺ and ammonia are secreted into the filtrate — maintains ionic and acid–base balance.

steps.title: Segment by segment
steps.body:
- **PCT:** simple cuboidal **brush-border** epithelium; reabsorbs nearly all essential nutrients and **70–80% of electrolytes and water**; secretes H⁺, ammonia, K⁺; absorbs HCO₃⁻ — maintains pH.
- **Descending limb of Henle's loop:** **permeable to water**, almost impermeable to electrolytes → filtrate becomes concentrated.
- **Ascending limb:** **impermeable to water**, but electrolytes are transported actively or passively → filtrate gets diluted.
- **DCT:** conditional reabsorption of Na⁺ and water; reabsorbs HCO₃⁻; selective secretion of H⁺, K⁺, NH₃.
- **Collecting duct:** reabsorbs large amounts of water to make urine concentrated; lets small amounts of **urea** pass into the medullary interstitium; secretes H⁺/K⁺.

**Counter-current mechanism:** opposite flows in the two limbs of Henle's loop and in the two limbs of the vasa recta, with **NaCl** (from the ascending limb, exchanged with the vasa recta) and **urea** (from the collecting duct), maintain an increasing osmolarity in the medullary interstitium — from **300 mOsmol/L in the cortex to about 1200 mOsmol/L in the inner medulla**. Water then leaves the collecting duct easily → concentrated urine. Human kidneys can make urine nearly **four times** as concentrated as the initial filtrate.

steps.title: Solved question 1
steps.body: If GFR is 125 mL/min, how much filtrate forms per day? 125 × 60 × 24 = 180,000 mL = **180 L**.

steps.title: Solved question 2
steps.body: Why is the ascending limb important though it absorbs no water? It pumps out NaCl, building the medullary gradient that the collecting duct uses to reabsorb water.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Swapping the permeabilities of the two limbs of Henle's loop.
- Saying proteins appear in normal filtrate.
- Thinking only NaCl builds the gradient (urea contributes too).

activity.prompt: GFR is 120 mL/min. How many litres of filtrate are formed in a day? (Round to the nearest whole number.)

quiz.q: Normal GFR in a healthy person is about
quiz.why: The glomerular filtration rate (GFR) in a healthy person is about 125 mL per minute, which is about 180 litres a day.

quiz.q: The descending limb of Henle's loop is
quiz.why: The descending limb of Henle's loop is permeable to water but almost impermeable to electrolytes. Water leaves, so the filtrate gets more concentrated as it goes down.

quiz.q: Most reabsorption of nutrients occurs in the
quiz.why: The PCT, with a brush border of microvilli, reabsorbs most nutrients, such as glucose and amino acids, along with much of the water and salts.

quiz.q: Osmolarity of inner medulla interstitium is about
quiz.why: The interstitial fluid of the inner medulla has an osmolarity of about 1200 mOsmol per litre, compared with 300 in the cortex. This gradient helps make concentrated urine.
Podocytes are special cells of the inner layer of Bowman's capsule. They have filtration slits that let small molecules pass but hold back large proteins.

quiz.q: Urea enters the medullary interstitium from the
quiz.why: Urea passes from the collecting duct into the medullary interstitium, and adds to the osmotic gradient there. The PCT does not contribute in the same way.

sources: NCERT Class 11 Biology (Excretory Products and their Elimination)

lessons.title: Regulation, micturition, other organs and disorders

scenes.text: After playing cricket for hours in the heat, Arjun's urine is dark and small in volume.
His body released ADH to save water. Hormones fine-tune what the kidneys keep and what they lose.

steps.title: Regulation of kidney function
steps.body:
- **ADH (vasopressin):** osmoreceptors sense excess loss of fluid → **hypothalamus** → **neurohypophysis** releases ADH → water reabsorption from the later parts of the tubule increases → less urine (diuresis prevented). ADH also constricts blood vessels, raising blood pressure and GFR.
- **RAAS:** fall in glomerular blood flow/pressure/GFR → **JGA** (juxtaglomerular apparatus, where the DCT touches the afferent arteriole) releases **renin** → angiotensinogen → **angiotensin I** → **angiotensin II** (a powerful vasoconstrictor; raises BP and GFR) → stimulates the adrenal cortex to release **aldosterone** → Na⁺ and water reabsorption in distal parts → BP and GFR rise.
- **ANF (atrial natriuretic factor):** released by heart atria when blood flow increases; causes **vasodilation**, lowers BP — a check on RAAS.

steps.title: Micturition, other excretory organs, disorders
steps.body:
- **Micturition:** bladder fills → stretch receptors → CNS → motor signals → bladder smooth muscle contracts, urethral sphincter relaxes → urine released (**micturition reflex**). An adult passes **1–1.5 L** of urine per day; light yellow, slightly **acidic (pH ≈ 6.0)**, characteristic odour; about **25–30 g urea** excreted daily. Glucose (**glycosuria**) and ketone bodies (**ketonuria**) in urine suggest **diabetes mellitus**.
- **Other organs:** **lungs** remove CO₂ (~200 mL/min) and water; **liver** secretes bile with **bilirubin, biliverdin**, cholesterol, degraded steroid hormones, vitamins and drugs; **skin** — sweat (NaCl, small amounts of urea, lactic acid) mainly for cooling, and sebum (sterols, hydrocarbons, waxes); saliva removes small amounts of nitrogenous wastes.
- **Disorders:** **uremia** (urea accumulates in blood; can cause kidney failure) → **haemodialysis** (blood from an artery passes through a **dialyser** with a cellophane tube in dialysing fluid without nitrogenous wastes; **heparin** as anticoagulant, **antiheparin** added back) → **kidney transplantation** (preferably from a close relative to reduce rejection); **renal calculi** (kidney stones: insoluble crystallised salts, e.g. oxalates); **glomerulonephritis** (inflammation of glomeruli).

General education, not medical advice: see a doctor for blood in urine, severe flank pain or very low urine output.

steps.title: Solved question 1
steps.body: A drop in blood pressure activates which system? **RAAS** — renin from the JGA → angiotensin II → aldosterone → BP and GFR increase.

steps.title: Solved question 2
steps.body: Why is heparin added during haemodialysis? To prevent blood clotting in the dialyser; antiheparin is added before blood returns to the body.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying ADH increases urine output (it decreases it).
- Placing the JGA at the PCT (it is where DCT contacts the afferent arteriole).
- Thinking ANF works with RAAS (it opposes it).

quiz.why: ADH is made in the hypothalamus and released from the neurohypophysis (posterior pituitary). It helps the kidney retain water.
Aldosterone is a hormone of the adrenal cortex. It is released when angiotensin II acts, and it makes the tubules reabsorb Na⁺ and water.

quiz.q: Daily urea excretion in an adult is about
quiz.why: An adult excretes about 25 to 30 g of urea in a day. The other values are too small or too large.
Kidney stones are masses of crystallised salts such as calcium oxalate, formed in the kidney. They are called renal calculi.

quiz.q: Bilirubin and biliverdin are excreted by the
quiz.why: Bilirubin and biliverdin are bile pigments made when RBCs are broken down. The liver removes them in bile. They do not leave through the skin or lungs.
Normal urine is slightly acidic, with pH about 6.0. Extremely acidic or alkaline values would be abnormal.

sources: NCERT Class 11 Biology (Excretory Products and their Elimination)

questions.q: Humans are
questions.why: Humans are ureotelic, meaning they excrete urea made in the liver as the main nitrogenous waste. Uric acid is for birds and reptiles, and ammonia for bony fishes.

questions.q: The functional unit of the kidney is the
questions.why: The nephron is the structural and functional unit of the kidney. Each kidney has about a million nephrons.

questions.q: Excretory organs of cockroach are
questions.why: Insects such as the cockroach excrete wastes with Malpighian tubules. Flame cells are in flatworms, nephridia in earthworms and green glands in prawns.

questions.q: Glomerular filtrate per day in an adult is about
questions.why: At a GFR of 125 mL per minute, the daily filtrate is 125 × 60 × 24 ≈ 180,000 mL = 180 L.

questions.q: Ascending limb of Henle's loop is
questions.why: The ascending limb of Henle's loop is impermeable to water but allows transport of electrolytes. So the filtrate gets diluted as it moves up.

questions.q: Hormone that reduces urine output is
questions.why: ADH (antidiuretic hormone) makes the kidney reabsorb more water, so less urine is passed. ANF does the opposite.

questions.q: Assertion: Juxtamedullary nephrons help produce concentrated urine. Reason: They have long Henle's loops and vasa recta deep in the medulla.
options: Both true and R explains A
Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true and R explains A. Juxtamedullary nephrons have long loops of Henle and vasa recta going deep in the medulla, which makes the counter-current gradient needed for concentrated urine.

questions.q: Juxtaglomerular apparatus is formed where
options: the collecting duct meets the pelvis
questions.why: The juxtaglomerular apparatus (JGA) is formed where the distal convoluted tubule touches the afferent arteriole near the glomerulus. It releases renin when blood pressure falls.

questions.q: Which substance is secreted into the filtrate by tubular cells?
questions.why: Tubular cells secrete H⁺, K⁺ and ammonia into the filtrate, which helps keep the ionic balance and pH of body fluids. Glucose, RBCs and proteins are not secreted.

questions.q: About 70–80% of electrolytes and water are reabsorbed in the
questions.why: The proximal convoluted tubule reabsorbs about 70 to 80% of the electrolytes and water, which is more than any other part of the nephron.

questions.q: Case: A patient's urine shows glucose and ketone bodies. The likely condition is
questions.why: Glucose in urine (glycosuria) and ketone bodies (ketonuria) are typical signs of diabetes mellitus, where insulin is low or ineffective.

questions.q: Case: In a patient with failed kidneys, blood is passed through a cellophane tube in a fluid lacking nitrogenous wastes. The procedure is
questions.why: In haemodialysis, a patient's blood passes through a cellophane tube bathed in a fluid without nitrogenous wastes. Wastes diffuse out, and the cleaned blood goes back. The machine is the artificial kidney.

questions.q: The medullary gradient is maintained mainly by
questions.why: The medullary gradient is kept by NaCl and urea, through the counter-current mechanism of Henle's loop and vasa recta.

questions.q: Angiotensin II
options: raises blood pressure and stimulates aldosterone release
questions.why: Angiotensin II is a strong vasoconstrictor, so it raises blood pressure, and it stimulates the adrenal cortex to release aldosterone. It is not released by the heart.

questions.q: Kidneys receive about what fraction of cardiac output?
questions.why: The kidneys get about 1100 to 1200 mL of blood per minute, which is about one-fifth of the cardiac output.

questions.q: ANF is secreted by the
questions.why: ANF (atrial natriuretic factor) is released by the atria of the heart when blood pressure rises. It makes blood vessels widen and lowers blood pressure.

questions.q: If GFR = 125 mL/min and urine output = 1.5 L/day, the percentage of filtrate reabsorbed is closest to
questions.why: Filtrate is 125 mL/min × 1440 min ≈ 180 L per day. Urine is 1.5 L, so only about 0.8% is excreted and about 99% is reabsorbed.

questions.q: Which statement is incorrect?
questions.why: The incorrect statement is that marine fishes are ammonotelic. Marine fishes are ureotelic, as they keep urea to balance the salt in sea water. Freshwater bony fishes excrete ammonia.

courses.title: Ch 17 · Locomotion and Movement
courses.summary: Types of movement, skeletal muscle structure, contractile proteins and the sliding filament theory, the human skeleton bone by bone, joints, and disorders of muscles and bones.
outcomes: Learners can describe amoeboid, ciliary and muscular movement
Learners can describe sarcomere structure and the proteins actin and myosin
Learners can explain the sliding filament mechanism of contraction
Learners can list the bones of the axial and appendicular skeleton and classify joints
Learners can describe common muscular and skeletal disorders

lessons.title: Types of movement and muscle

scenes.text: When you get a splinter, white blood cells crawl out of capillaries towards it.
They move like Amoeba — using pseudopodia. Movement happens from cells to whole bodies.

steps.title: Types of movement
steps.body:
Movement is a significant feature of living beings; **locomotion** is movement that changes location (walking, swimming, flying).
- **Amoeboid:** specialised cells like **macrophages and leucocytes** in blood; pseudopodia formed by protoplasm streaming, with microfilaments involved.
- **Ciliary:** most internal tubular organs lined by ciliated epithelium; coordinated cilia in the **trachea** remove dust and foreign particles; passage of **ova through the female reproductive tract**.
- **Muscular:** limbs, jaws, tongue etc., used for locomotion and other movements; requires coordinated activity of muscular, skeletal and neural systems.

steps.title: Muscle
steps.body:
Muscle is a specialised tissue of **mesodermal origin**; about **40–50%** of adult human body weight. Properties: excitability, contractility, extensibility, elasticity.
- **Skeletal** (striated, voluntary; attached to bones),
- **Visceral/smooth** (non-striated, involuntary; walls of hollow organs like the alimentary canal and reproductive tract),
- **Cardiac** (striated, involuntary; branched).

steps.title: Solved question 1
steps.body: Which movement helps remove dust from the windpipe? **Ciliary movement** of the tracheal epithelium.

steps.title: Solved question 2
steps.body: Why is smooth muscle called visceral? It lines the inner walls of hollow visceral organs.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking all movements are locomotion.
- Calling smooth muscle striated.
- Forgetting that muscle is mesodermal.

items.text: Ova moving in the fallopian tube

quiz.why: Leucocytes such as macrophages and neutrophils move by amoeboid movement, using pseudopodia formed by the flow of cytoplasm. Skeletal muscle and neurons do not move this way.

quiz.q: Muscle forms about ___ of adult body weight
quiz.why: Muscles make up about 40 to 50 percent of the adult human body weight.

quiz.q: Ciliary movement helps pass ova through the
quiz.why: Cilia lining the fallopian tube beat to help move the ovum along the female reproductive tract.
Muscles develop from the mesoderm, the middle germ layer of the embryo. Ectoderm gives skin and nerves, and endoderm gives the gut lining.
Locomotion is a voluntary movement that changes the position of the whole body or place, like walking, running or swimming. A change in shape alone is a movement, not locomotion.

sources: NCERT Class 11 Biology (Locomotion and Movement)

lessons.title: Structure of skeletal muscle and contractile proteins

scenes.text: Under a microscope, skeletal muscle fibres show alternating light and dark bands.
These stripes come from a precise arrangement of two proteins — actin and myosin.

steps.title: Organisation
steps.body:
Each skeletal muscle has bundles called **fascicles** held by **fascia** (collagenous connective tissue). Each fascicle has many **muscle fibres**, each lined by the **sarcolemma**, with cytoplasm called **sarcoplasm** containing many nuclei (**syncytium**). The ER is the **sarcoplasmic reticulum** — the **store of Ca²⁺**.
- Fibres contain parallel **myofibrils** with alternate **light (I band, isotropic; actin)** and **dark (A band, anisotropic; myosin)** bands.
- Each I band is bisected by an elastic **Z line**; thin filaments are attached to it. The **M line** holds thick filaments in the middle of the A band. The central part of the A band not overlapped by thin filaments is the **H zone**.
- **Sarcomere** = segment between two successive Z lines — the functional unit of contraction.

steps.title: Actin and myosin
steps.body:
- **Thin (actin) filament:** two **F-actin** strands helically wound, each a polymer of monomeric **G-actin**; two filaments of **tropomyosin** run along; **troponin** at regular intervals masks the active myosin-binding sites on actin in the resting state.
- **Thick (myosin) filament:** polymer of **meromyosins**; each has a globular **head** with a short arm (**heavy meromyosin, HMM**) and a tail (**light meromyosin, LMM**). The head–arm projects outward as a **cross arm**; the head is an **active ATPase** and has binding sites for ATP and actin.

steps.title: Solved question 1
steps.body: Which band contains only actin? The **I band** (light band).

steps.title: Solved question 2
steps.body: Name the Ca²⁺ store of a muscle fibre. The **sarcoplasmic reticulum**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the A band contains only myosin (thin filaments overlap it except in the H zone).
- Calling the sarcomere the region between two M lines.
- Mixing troponin (masks binding sites) with tropomyosin (runs along filament).

pairs: Bisects I band; anchors thin filaments
Central A band without thin filament overlap

quiz.q: The functional unit of contraction is the
quiz.why: The sarcomere, the part of a myofibril between two Z lines, is the functional unit of contraction in muscle.
Calcium ions are stored in the sarcoplasmic reticulum (the modified ER of muscle) and released when the muscle fibre is stimulated.

options: masks the active sites on actin
quiz.why: In resting muscle troponin, together with tropomyosin, covers the active sites on actin so myosin cannot bind. Calcium removes this block.
Heavy meromyosin (HMM) is the part of the myosin molecule that makes the head and the short arm (cross arm). Light meromyosin is the tail.

quiz.q: Each F-actin is a polymer of
quiz.why: Each F-actin filament is a polymer of many globular G-actin monomers, which are arranged in two strands twisted around each other.

sources: NCERT Class 11 Biology (Locomotion and Movement)

lessons.title: Sliding filament mechanism

scenes.text: When Neha lifts a bucket of water, her biceps shortens — but no protein filament itself gets shorter.
Thin filaments slide over thick ones. That is the sliding filament theory.

steps.title: Steps of contraction
steps.body:
1. A signal from the CNS via a **motor neuron** reaches the **neuromuscular junction (motor end plate)**; a motor neuron with the fibres it supplies is a **motor unit**.
2. **Acetylcholine** is released → generates an action potential in the sarcolemma.
3. It spreads through the fibre → **Ca²⁺ released** from the sarcoplasmic reticulum into the sarcoplasm.
4. Ca²⁺ binds a **troponin** subunit on actin → active sites on actin are unmasked.
5. Using energy from **ATP hydrolysis**, the myosin head binds the exposed site → **cross bridge**.
6. The cross bridge pulls the actin filament towards the centre of the A band; Z lines are pulled inward → **sarcomere shortens** (contraction).
7. ADP and Pᵢ released; a new ATP binds → cross bridge breaks; ATP hydrolysed → cycle repeats while Ca²⁺ remains.
8. **Relaxation:** Ca²⁺ is pumped back into the SR → actin sites masked again → Z lines return.

During contraction **the I bands shorten (and H zone narrows), while the A band length stays the same**.

steps.title: Fatigue and fibre types
steps.body:
Repeated activation → anaerobic breakdown of glycogen → **lactic acid** accumulation → **fatigue**.
- **Red fibres:** high **myoglobin** (red O₂-storing pigment), many mitochondria → **aerobic** muscles.
- **White fibres:** little myoglobin, few mitochondria, but high sarcoplasmic reticulum → depend on anaerobic processes.

steps.title: Solved question 1
steps.body: What happens to band lengths in contraction? I band shortens; H zone shortens/disappears; **A band remains constant**; sarcomere shortens.

steps.title: Solved question 2
steps.body: Why does muscle stay contracted in rigor after death? No ATP to detach myosin heads from actin.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the A band shortens.
- Saying Ca²⁺ binds myosin (it binds troponin).
- Thinking ATP is needed only for contraction (also for detachment and Ca²⁺ pumping).

activity.prompt: Order the events of muscle contraction.
items: Motor neuron releases acetylcholine at the motor end plate
Action potential spreads over the sarcolemma
Ca²⁺ is released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum
Ca²⁺ binds troponin and exposes active sites on actin
Myosin heads form cross bridges and pull actin inward

quiz.q: The neurotransmitter at the neuromuscular junction is
quiz.why: Acetylcholine is the neurotransmitter released by motor neurons at the neuromuscular junction. It triggers the muscle impulse.

quiz.q: During contraction, which band remains the same length?
quiz.why: In contraction the thin filaments slide over the thick ones, so the I band and H zone get shorter. The A band, made by myosin, keeps the same length.
Ca²⁺ binds to troponin, which moves tropomyosin and uncovers the active sites on actin. Then myosin heads can bind and the muscle contracts.

quiz.q: Red muscle fibres are rich in
quiz.why: Red fibres have a lot of myoglobin and many mitochondria, so they work by aerobic respiration and can keep going for a long time.

quiz.q: Muscle fatigue is due to accumulation of
quiz.why: With repeated activity, muscle uses oxygen faster than it is supplied, so it makes lactic acid by anaerobic glycolysis. Its build-up causes fatigue.

sources: NCERT Class 11 Biology (Locomotion and Movement)

lessons.title: The human skeleton

scenes.text: A biology teacher challenges: 'You have 206 bones — can you name where they all are?'
Divide them into the axial skeleton (80) and appendicular skeleton (126) and it becomes easy.

steps.title: Axial skeleton (80 bones)
steps.body:
- **Skull (22):** **cranial 8** + **facial 14**; plus **hyoid** (1, U-shaped, base of buccal cavity) and **ear ossicles** (malleus, incus, stapes in each ear = 6). Skull joins the vertebral column through **two occipital condyles** (**dicondylic** skull).
- **Vertebral column (26):** **cervical 7**, **thoracic 12**, **lumbar 5**, **sacral 1 (fused)**, **coccygeal 1 (fused)**. The first vertebra is the **atlas**, which articulates with the occipital condyles. The column protects the spinal cord, supports the head and gives attachment to ribs and back muscles.
- **Sternum (1)** — flat bone on the ventral midline.
- **Ribs:** **12 pairs**. 1st–7th pairs: **true ribs** (attached dorsally to thoracic vertebrae and ventrally to sternum by hyaline cartilage); 8th–10th: **false/vertebrochondral ribs** (join the 7th rib's cartilage); 11th–12th: **floating ribs** (not connected ventrally). Thoracic vertebrae, ribs and sternum form the **rib cage**.

steps.title: Appendicular skeleton (126 bones)
steps.body:
- Each **limb** has **30** bones.
  - **Forelimb:** humerus, radius, ulna, **carpals 8**, **metacarpals 5**, **phalanges 14**.
  - **Hind limb:** **femur** (the longest bone), tibia, fibula, **tarsals 7**, **metatarsals 5**, **phalanges 14**; **patella** (knee cap).
- **Pectoral girdle** (each half): **clavicle** (collar bone) and **scapula** (flat triangular bone with a ridge, the spine, ending in the **acromion**; the **glenoid cavity** articulates with the head of the humerus — shoulder joint).
- **Pelvic girdle:** two **coxal bones**, each formed by fusion of **ilium, ischium and pubis**; at their fusion is the **acetabulum** for the femur head; the two halves meet ventrally at the **pubic symphysis**.

steps.title: Solved question 1
steps.body: Count the bones of one hand and arm: humerus 1 + radius 1 + ulna 1 + carpals 8 + metacarpals 5 + phalanges 14 = **30**.

steps.title: Solved question 2
steps.body: Total vertebrae in an adult: 7 + 12 + 5 + 1 + 1 = **26**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Counting 33 vertebrae for adults (that is before fusion; adults have 26 bones).
- Saying floating ribs join the sternum.
- Putting the patella in the forelimb.

quiz.q: Total number of bones in the adult human skeleton is
quiz.why: An adult human skeleton has 206 bones: 80 in the axial skeleton and 126 in the appendicular skeleton.
The femur, the thigh bone, is the longest bone in the body. The humerus, radius and tibia are shorter.
The 11th and 12th pairs of ribs are floating ribs, because they are not joined to the sternum at the front, and stay free ventrally.
Each hip bone is formed by the ilium, ischium and pubis fused together. At their junction is a cavity called the acetabulum, where the head of the femur fits.
The first cervical vertebra is the atlas. It articulates with the occipital condyles of the skull. The second is the axis.

quiz.q: The glenoid cavity is part of the
quiz.why: The glenoid cavity is the socket in the scapula where the head of the humerus fits, making the shoulder joint. The pelvis has the acetabulum.

sources: NCERT Class 11 Biology (Locomotion and Movement)

lessons.title: Joints and disorders

scenes.text: Ammi's knees ache and creak each morning; the doctor talks of arthritis.
Joints let bones move — and when they are inflamed, every step hurts.

steps.title: Joints
steps.body:
Joints are points of contact between bones, or bones and cartilages; essential for movement.
- **Fibrous joints:** no movement; dense fibrous tissue — **sutures** of the skull.
- **Cartilaginous joints:** bones joined by cartilage, limited movement — between **adjacent vertebrae**.
- **Synovial joints:** fluid-filled **synovial cavity** between articulating surfaces; considerable movement:
  - **Ball and socket:** humerus and pectoral girdle (and hip)
  - **Hinge:** knee
  - **Pivot:** atlas and axis
  - **Gliding:** between carpals
  - **Saddle:** carpal and metacarpal of the thumb

steps.title: Disorders
steps.body:
- **Myasthenia gravis:** autoimmune disorder affecting the **neuromuscular junction** → fatigue, weakening and paralysis of skeletal muscle.
- **Muscular dystrophy:** progressive degeneration of skeletal muscle, mostly due to a **genetic** disorder.
- **Tetany:** rapid spasms (wild contractions) due to **low Ca²⁺** in body fluid.
- **Arthritis:** inflammation of joints.
- **Osteoporosis:** age-related; decreased bone mass, increased fractures; **decreased oestrogen** levels are a common cause.
- **Gout:** inflammation of joints due to accumulation of **uric acid crystals**.

General education, not medical advice: persistent joint pain, swelling or muscle weakness should be checked by a doctor.

steps.title: Solved question 1
steps.body: Type of joint between atlas and axis? **Pivot joint** — lets the head rotate.

steps.title: Solved question 2
steps.body: Why are post-menopausal women at higher risk of osteoporosis? Falling **oestrogen** levels reduce bone mass.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling skull sutures synovial.
- Saying the knee is a ball-and-socket joint (it is a hinge).
- Linking gout to calcium (it is uric acid).

activity.prompt: Match the joint to its example.

quiz.why: Joints between adjacent vertebrae are cartilaginous, with cartilage discs between them. They allow only limited movement.
Tetany is rapid spasms of muscles caused by a low level of Ca²⁺ in body fluids. It is not an autoimmune or hormonal disorder in this sense.
Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune disorder that affects the neuromuscular junction. It causes weakness and fatigue of skeletal muscle.
Gout is caused by uric acid crystals that collect in the joints, causing inflammation and pain. It is not caused by bacteria.
The knee is a hinge joint that moves in one plane, bending and straightening. The shoulder is a ball and socket joint.

sources: NCERT Class 11 Biology (Locomotion and Movement)

questions.q: Amoeboid movement is seen in
questions.why: Macrophages and some other WBCs show amoeboid movement through pseudopodia. Cardiac and skeletal muscles contract differently, and sperm swim by a tail.

questions.q: The number of bones in the human skull (cranial + facial) is
questions.why: The human skull has 22 bones: 8 cranial and 14 facial bones.

questions.q: The functional unit of a myofibril is the
questions.why: The sarcomere, between two successive Z lines, is the functional unit of a myofibril. Each has A and I bands.

questions.q: Number of thoracic vertebrae is
questions.why: The human vertebral column has 12 thoracic vertebrae, which are joined to the ribs. There are 7 cervical and 5 lumbar vertebrae.

questions.q: The dark band of a myofibril is the
questions.why: The dark A band (anisotropic band) of a myofibril contains myosin and part of the actin. The light I band has only actin.

questions.q: Pivot joint is found between
questions.why: The pivot joint between the atlas and the axis lets the head rotate from side to side. Humerus and scapula form a ball-and-socket joint.

questions.q: Assertion: During muscle contraction the A band does not shorten. Reason: Thin filaments slide over thick filaments without the filaments changing length.
options: Both true and R explains A
Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true and R explains A. By the sliding filament theory, thin filaments slide over thick ones without changing length, so the A band stays the same.

questions.q: The vertebrochondral ribs are the
questions.why: Ribs 8th, 9th and 10th pairs are vertebrochondral (false) ribs, as they join the 7th rib's cartilage instead of the sternum directly. The first seven are true ribs and the last two are floating.

questions.q: Which protein masks the active sites of actin at rest?
questions.why: Troponin, a regulatory protein in the thin filament, covers the active sites on actin at rest. Calcium binding to it exposes these sites.

questions.q: Muscles that depend mainly on aerobic metabolism are
questions.why: Red fibres have plenty of myoglobin and mitochondria, so they depend mainly on aerobic metabolism. White fibres use more anaerobic energy.

questions.q: Case: A runner develops cramps and fatigue at the end of a race. The main cause is
questions.why: At the end of a race the muscles have used a lot of energy faster than oxygen can arrive, so lactic acid builds up by anaerobic glycolysis, causing cramps and fatigue.

questions.q: Case: An elderly woman suffers frequent fractures after minor falls; tests show reduced bone mass. The condition is
questions.why: Frequent fractures with reduced bone mass in an older woman are signs of osteoporosis, an age-related loss of bone linked to falling oestrogen levels.

questions.q: Number of bones in one hind limb including the patella is
questions.why: One hind limb: femur 1 + tibia and fibula 2 + tarsals 7 + metatarsals 5 + phalanges 14 + patella 1 = 30 bones.

questions.q: The bones forming each coxal bone are
questions.why: Each coxal (hip) bone is made of three bones, the ilium, ischium and pubis, which are fused. The clavicle and scapula form the pectoral girdle.

questions.q: The head of the myosin acts as
questions.why: The head of myosin has ATPase activity and binding sites for actin and ATP. It uses ATP energy to pull the actin filaments.

questions.q: In the axial skeleton, the number of ear ossicles (both ears) is
questions.why: Each middle ear has 3 ossicles (malleus, incus and stapes), so two ears have 6 in all.

questions.q: Which correctly describes changes during contraction?
options: I band and H zone shorten; A band unchanged
A band shortens; I band unchanged
questions.why: In contraction, the thin filaments slide inward, so the I band and H zone become shorter. The A band stays the same length since the myosin filaments do not shorten.

questions.q: Total bones in the appendicular skeleton = limbs + girdles. With 30 per limb, 2 per pectoral half, and 1 coxal per pelvic half, the total is
questions.why: Appendicular skeleton = 4 limbs × 30 = 120, plus pectoral girdle (2 × 2 = 4) and pelvic girdle (2 coxal bones). So 120 + 4 + 2 = 126.

courses.title: Ch 18 · Neural Control and Coordination
courses.summary: Organisation of the neural system, the neuron, resting and action potentials, synaptic transmission, and the structure and functions of the human brain.
outcomes: Learners can describe the organisation of the human neural system
Learners can describe neuron types and myelinated fibres
Learners can explain resting potential and the generation and conduction of a nerve impulse
Learners can compare electrical and chemical synapses and describe the parts and functions of the brain

lessons.title: The neural system and the neuron

scenes.text: Kabir touches a hot pan and pulls his hand back before he even feels the pain.
Messages race along neurons — the cells of the neural system — in a fraction of a second.

steps.title: Organisation
steps.body:
- Lower invertebrates: simple; e.g. *Hydra* has a network of neurons. Insects: brain plus ganglia and neural tissues. Vertebrates: more developed.
- Human neural system: **central neural system (CNS)** — brain and spinal cord (site of information processing and control) — and **peripheral neural system (PNS)** — all nerves associated with the CNS.
- PNS fibres: **afferent** (tissues/organs → CNS) and **efferent** (CNS → tissues/organs).
- PNS divisions: **somatic** (CNS → skeletal muscles) and **autonomic** (CNS → involuntary organs and smooth muscles). Autonomic is further **sympathetic** and **parasympathetic**. The **visceral** nervous system is the part of the PNS with nerves, fibres, ganglia and plexuses linking CNS to viscera.

steps.title: The neuron
steps.body:
Microscopic structural and functional unit: **cell body** (cytoplasm with organelles and **Nissl's granules**), **dendrites** (short, branched; carry impulses **towards** the cell body; contain Nissl's granules), **axon** (long fibre; distal end branches into terminals with **synaptic knobs** containing **synaptic vesicles** of neurotransmitters; carries impulses **away** from the cell body).
- **Multipolar** (one axon, two or more dendrites; **cerebral cortex**), **bipolar** (one axon, one dendrite; **retina**), **unipolar** (cell body with one axon only; usually in the **embryonic stage**).
- **Myelinated** fibres: enveloped by **Schwann cells** forming a myelin sheath; gaps are **nodes of Ranvier**; found in spinal and cranial nerves. **Non-myelinated** fibres: Schwann cell does not form a myelin sheath; common in autonomic and somatic neural systems.

steps.title: Solved question 1
steps.body: Which neurons are found in the retina? **Bipolar neurons**.

steps.title: Solved question 2
steps.body: Direction of impulse in a dendrite? **Towards** the cell body.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying axons carry impulses towards the cell body.
- Calling Nissl's granules part of the axon.
- Mixing afferent (sensory, towards CNS) with efferent (motor, from CNS).

quiz.why: The central nervous system (CNS) is the brain and spinal cord. Nerves and ganglia belong to the peripheral nervous system.
Nissl's granules are clusters of ribosomes found in the cell body and dendrites of a neuron. They make proteins.

quiz.q: Unipolar neurons are usually found in
quiz.why: Unipolar neurons, which have a cell body with just one process, are usually found in the embryonic stage. Adult neurons are mostly multipolar or bipolar.
The autonomic neural system controls the involuntary organs and smooth muscles, such as the heart, gut and glands. Voluntary skeletal muscles are under the somatic system.
Hydra has a simple nerve net, a network of neurons spread through the body, with no brain or cord.

sources: NCERT Class 11 Biology (Neural Control and Coordination)

lessons.title: Generation and conduction of a nerve impulse

scenes.text: A resting neuron is like a charged battery: negative inside, positive outside.
When stimulated, a wave of charge reversal travels along it — the nerve impulse.

steps.title: Resting potential
steps.body:
Neurons are **excitable** because their membranes are **polarised**.
- At rest, the axonal membrane is more permeable to **K⁺** and nearly impermeable to **Na⁺** (and to negatively charged proteins inside).
- **Axoplasm** has high K⁺ and negatively charged proteins and low Na⁺; **outside** fluid has low K⁺, high Na⁺ — a concentration gradient.
- **Sodium–potassium pump** actively transports **3 Na⁺ out for 2 K⁺ in**.
- Result: outer surface **positive**, inner surface **negative** → the membrane is **polarised**; the potential difference is the **resting potential**.

steps.title: Action potential and conduction
steps.body:
- A stimulus at site A makes the membrane **freely permeable to Na⁺** → rapid **influx of Na⁺** → the membrane reverses polarity: outside **negative**, inside **positive** → **depolarised**. This electrical potential difference is the **action potential** = the **nerve impulse**.
- Just ahead (site B) the membrane is still polarised (outside positive); current flows inside from A to B and outside from B to A, so polarity reverses at B too — the impulse moves along the axon.
- The rise in Na⁺ permeability is short-lived; it is quickly followed by a rise in **K⁺ permeability** → **K⁺ diffuses out** → **repolarisation**; the fibre becomes ready for further stimulation.
- In myelinated fibres the impulse jumps from node to node (**saltatory conduction**) — much faster.

steps.title: Solved question 1
steps.body: Which ion causes depolarisation? **Na⁺ influx**.

steps.title: Solved question 2
steps.body: Which ion movement restores the resting state? **K⁺ efflux** (outward diffusion) → repolarisation; the Na⁺–K⁺ pump then maintains gradients.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the inside is positive at rest.
- Reversing the pump ratio (it is 3 Na⁺ out : 2 K⁺ in).
- Saying K⁺ entry causes repolarisation (K⁺ leaves).

activity.prompt: Order the events of a nerve impulse at one site.
items: Membrane polarised: outside positive, inside negative
Na⁺ rushes in and the membrane depolarises
Action potential spreads to the next site
K⁺ diffuses out and the membrane repolarises

quiz.why: The sodium–potassium pump uses ATP to push 3 Na⁺ out of the neuron while bringing 2 K⁺ in. This is active transport and it keeps the resting potential.

quiz.q: At rest the inside of the axon is
quiz.why: At rest the axon is polarised, with the inside negative and the outside positive. This difference in charge is the resting potential, kept by the Na⁺–K⁺ pump and K⁺ leak channels.
When a neuron is stimulated, Na⁺ channels open and Na⁺ rushes in, so the inside becomes positive. This reverses the polarity and is depolarisation.
After depolarisation Na⁺ channels close and K⁺ channels open, so K⁺ moves out. This brings the inside back to negative, which is repolarisation.

quiz.q: At rest the axonal membrane is more permeable to
quiz.why: At rest the membrane is much more permeable to K⁺ than Na⁺ because of K⁺ leak channels. K⁺ moves out, and this helps make the inside negative.

sources: NCERT Class 11 Biology (Neural Control and Coordination)

lessons.title: Transmission at synapses

scenes.text: In a relay race, the baton is handed over at a narrow gap between runners.
At a synapse, the 'baton' is usually a chemical — a neurotransmitter crossing a tiny cleft.

steps.title: Synapse
steps.body:
A **synapse** is formed by the membranes of a **pre-synaptic** neuron and a **post-synaptic** neuron, which may or may not be separated by a gap called the **synaptic cleft**.
- **Electrical synapses:** membranes very close; current flows directly from one neuron to the next; transmission is **faster** but such synapses are **rare** in our system.
- **Chemical synapses:** separated by a fluid-filled synaptic cleft; **neurotransmitters** carry the signal. Impulse arrives at the axon terminal → **synaptic vesicles** move to the membrane, fuse and release neurotransmitters into the cleft → neurotransmitters bind **specific receptors** on the post-synaptic membrane → **ion channels open** → a new potential is generated in the post-synaptic neuron, which may be **excitatory** or **inhibitory**.

steps.title: Solved question 1
steps.body: Why is transmission one-way at a chemical synapse? Neurotransmitter is stored and released only from the pre-synaptic terminal; receptors are only on the post-synaptic membrane.

steps.title: Solved question 2
steps.body: Name a common neurotransmitter. **Acetylcholine** (also at neuromuscular junctions).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying electrical synapses are the most common in humans.
- Thinking neurotransmitters enter the post-synaptic neuron — they bind receptors on its membrane.
- Assuming every post-synaptic potential is excitatory.

statements.s: Electrical synapses are faster than chemical synapses.
Electrical synapses are common in the human neural system.
Neurotransmitters are stored in synaptic vesicles.
A post-synaptic potential can be inhibitory.
statements.why: Depends on the transmitter and receptor.

statements.s: The synaptic cleft is absent in chemical synapses.

options: synaptic vesicles of the pre-synaptic terminal
quiz.why: Neurotransmitters are stored in synaptic vesicles at the axon terminal of the pre-synaptic neuron. When the impulse arrives, the vesicles fuse with the membrane and release them by exocytosis.

quiz.q: The gap between neurons at a chemical synapse is the
quiz.why: At a chemical synapse the pre- and post-synaptic membranes are separated by a fluid-filled space called the synaptic cleft. The transmitter diffuses across it.
Neurotransmitters bind to specific receptors on the post-synaptic membrane, which opens ion channels and starts a new potential. They do not enter the nucleus or mitochondria.
At electrical synapses the membranes of the two neurons are very close and current flows directly, so transmission is fast. But they are rare in humans, where chemical synapses are common.

quiz.q: Transmission at a chemical synapse is
quiz.why: Transmission at a chemical synapse is one-way, from the pre-synaptic to the post-synaptic neuron, because the transmitter is only released on the pre-synaptic side.

sources: NCERT Class 11 Biology (Neural Control and Coordination)

lessons.title: The human brain

scenes.text: After a minor head injury, a doctor checks Riya's balance, speech and breathing — each tests a different part of the brain.
The forebrain, midbrain and hindbrain each have their own jobs.

steps.title: Protection and forebrain
steps.body:
The brain is the central information-processing organ and 'command and control system'. It is protected by the **skull** and three **cranial meninges**: outer **dura mater**, thin middle **arachnoid**, inner **pia mater** (in contact with brain tissue).
- **Forebrain:** **cerebrum**, **thalamus**, **hypothalamus**.
  - Cerebrum: major part; a deep cleft divides it into left and right **cerebral hemispheres** connected by the **corpus callosum** (a tract of nerve fibres). The outer **cerebral cortex** (grey matter, with prominent folds) has **motor areas, sensory areas** and large **association areas** (responsible for intersensory associations, memory and communication). Inner part = **white matter** (myelinated tracts).
  - **Thalamus:** major coordinating centre for sensory and motor signalling.
  - **Hypothalamus** (at the base of the thalamus): centres for **body temperature, urge for eating and drinking**; contains **neurosecretory cells** that secrete hypothalamic hormones.
  - **Limbic system** (inner parts of cerebral hemispheres with **amygdala** and **hippocampus**): with the hypothalamus regulates sexual behaviour and expression of emotional reactions (excitement, pleasure, rage, fear) and motivation.

steps.title: Midbrain and hindbrain
steps.body:
- **Midbrain:** between thalamus/hypothalamus and pons; the **cerebral aqueduct** passes through; dorsal portion has four round swellings — **corpora quadrigemina**.
- **Hindbrain:** **pons** (fibre tracts linking different brain regions), **cerebellum** (very convoluted surface for more neurons; balance and coordination) and **medulla** (connected to the spinal cord; centres controlling **respiration, cardiovascular reflexes and gastric secretions**).
- **Brain stem** = midbrain + pons + medulla oblongata; connects brain and spinal cord.

Tip: a **reflex action** is an involuntary response to a peripheral stimulus through a pathway involving the CNS (often the spinal cord) — e.g. the knee-jerk; see your edition for how much detail is required.

steps.title: Solved question 1
steps.body: Damage to which part affects balance? The **cerebellum**.

steps.title: Solved question 2
steps.body: Which part controls breathing and heart reflexes? The **medulla oblongata**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Placing the hypothalamus in the hindbrain.
- Saying the pia mater is the outermost meninx (it is innermost).
- Confusing corpus callosum (joins hemispheres) with corpora quadrigemina (midbrain).

quiz.q: The two cerebral hemispheres are connected by the
quiz.why: The two cerebral hemispheres are joined by a thick band of nerve fibres called the corpus callosum. The medulla and pons belong to the brain stem.

quiz.q: The centre for body temperature, hunger and thirst is the
quiz.why: The hypothalamus contains centres that control body temperature, hunger and thirst. It also makes hormones, and it helps keep the internal conditions steady.
The brain has three coverings (meninges). The pia mater is the innermost and is in contact with the brain. The dura mater is the outermost, and the arachnoid is the middle layer.
The brain stem is the midbrain, pons and medulla oblongata. It joins the brain to the spinal cord. The cerebrum and cerebellum are not part of it.

quiz.q: Respiration and cardiovascular reflexes are controlled by the
quiz.why: The medulla oblongata has centres for respiration, cardiovascular reflexes and gastric secretions. These are vital functions that go on without our control.

quiz.q: Emotions are regulated by the limbic system together with the
quiz.why: The limbic system works together with the hypothalamus to control emotions such as fear and anger, and also motivation. It includes the amygdala and hippocampus.

sources: NCERT Class 11 Biology (Neural Control and Coordination)

questions.q: The structural and functional unit of the neural system is the
questions.why: The neuron, or nerve cell, is the structural and functional unit of the neural system. The alveolus is of the lung, the nephron of the kidney and the sarcomere of muscle.

questions.q: The outermost covering of the brain is the
questions.why: The dura mater is the tough, outermost meninx of the brain. Then comes the arachnoid in the middle and the pia mater, which is the innermost.

questions.q: Bipolar neurons are found in the
questions.why: Bipolar neurons have one axon and one dendrite and are found in the retina of the eye. Multipolar neurons are in the cerebral cortex.

questions.q: Balance and coordination are controlled by the
questions.why: The cerebellum, in the hindbrain, controls balance, posture and coordination of voluntary movements. Hunger is a hypothalamus function and breathing is controlled by the medulla.

questions.q: At resting potential the outside of the axon membrane is
questions.why: At resting potential the outer surface of the axon membrane is positively charged and the inner side is negatively charged. This is the polarised state.

questions.q: Myelin sheath is formed by
questions.why: The myelin sheath around many axons in the peripheral nervous system is formed by Schwann cells. In the CNS, oligodendrocytes do this.

questions.q: Assertion: Myelinated fibres conduct impulses faster. Reason: Impulses jump from one node of Ranvier to the next.
options: Both true and R explains A
Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true and R explains A. In myelinated fibres the impulse jumps from one node of Ranvier to the next (saltatory conduction), which is much faster than a continuous wave.

questions.q: Depolarisation results from
questions.why: Depolarisation is caused by a rapid influx of Na⁺ through opened Na⁺ channels. The membrane becomes positive inside. K⁺ efflux causes repolarisation instead.

questions.q: The corpora quadrigemina are part of the
questions.why: The corpora quadrigemina are four round swellings on the dorsal side of the midbrain. They are related to vision and hearing reflexes.

questions.q: Which is not part of the brain stem?
questions.why: The brain stem is made of the midbrain, pons and medulla. The cerebellum lies behind it, so it is not part of the brain stem.

questions.q: Case: After a stroke, a patient cannot regulate body temperature and shows abnormal hunger. The most likely affected area is the
questions.why: The hypothalamus has centres for temperature and hunger regulation. Damage there would cause loss of temperature control and abnormal hunger. The cerebellum is for balance and the medulla for breathing.

questions.q: Case: A drug blocks receptors on the post-synaptic membrane. Transmission at chemical synapses will
questions.why: At a chemical synapse the transmitter has to bind to receptors on the post-synaptic membrane to open channels. If the receptors are blocked, it cannot bind, so transmission fails.

questions.q: The Na⁺–K⁺ pump is an example of
questions.why: The Na⁺–K⁺ pump moves ions against their concentration gradients using ATP. That is active transport, unlike diffusion and osmosis.

questions.q: Association areas of the cerebral cortex are responsible for
questions.why: Association areas of the cerebral cortex are neither motor nor sensory. They deal with complex functions such as intersensory associations, memory and communication.

questions.q: Which division of the PNS conducts impulses from the CNS to skeletal muscles?
questions.why: The somatic neural system carries impulses from the CNS to skeletal muscles, which are voluntary. The autonomic system works on involuntary organs and smooth muscles.

questions.q: During repolarisation, which statement is correct?
options: K⁺ permeability increases and K⁺ moves out
questions.why: During repolarisation, K⁺ channels become more permeable and K⁺ moves out of the axon. This makes the inside negative again. Na⁺ entry has stopped by then.

questions.q: Which pair is correctly matched?
options: Medulla — respiration and gastric secretion centres
questions.why: The medulla has centres for respiration, cardiovascular reflexes and gastric secretion, so that pair is correct. Pons helps in breathing, the cerebellum is for balance and the hypothalamus controls hunger.

courses.title: Ch 19 · Chemical Coordination and Integration
courses.summary: Endocrine glands and hormones: hypothalamus, pituitary, pineal, thyroid, parathyroid, thymus, adrenal, pancreas and gonads; hormones of the heart, kidney and gut; and how hormones act.
outcomes: Learners can define hormones and locate the major endocrine glands
Learners can list the hormones of the hypothalamus and pituitary with their actions and disorders
Learners can describe thyroid, parathyroid, thymus, adrenal, pancreatic and gonadal hormones
Learners can explain mechanisms of hormone action through membrane and intracellular receptors

lessons.title: Hormones, hypothalamus and pituitary

story.title: The tallest man in the village

scenes.text: A boy in Ramesh's village keeps growing far taller than anyone else.
Doctors find excess growth hormone from his pituitary — a pea-sized gland that controls many others.

steps.title: Hormones and the hypothalamus
steps.body:
**Hormones** are non-nutrient chemicals that act as intercellular messengers and are produced in **trace amounts**. Endocrine glands lack ducts (ductless).
- The **hypothalamus** (base of the forebrain) has groups of **neurosecretory cells (nuclei)**. Its hormones are **releasing hormones** (stimulate pituitary secretion, e.g. **GnRH** stimulates gonadotrophin synthesis and release) and **inhibiting hormones** (e.g. **somatostatin** inhibits growth hormone release).
- They reach the anterior pituitary through a **portal circulatory system**; the posterior pituitary is directly under neural regulation of the hypothalamus.

steps.title: Pituitary
steps.body:
Located in the **sella turcica** (bony cavity), attached to the hypothalamus by a stalk.
- **Adenohypophysis:** **pars distalis** ('anterior pituitary') secretes **GH, prolactin (PRL), TSH, ACTH, LH, FSH**; **pars intermedia** secretes **MSH** (almost merged with pars distalis in humans).
- **Neurohypophysis (pars nervosa, posterior pituitary):** **stores and releases oxytocin and vasopressin**, which are actually made by the hypothalamus.
- Actions: **GH** — growth; **over-secretion** in childhood → **gigantism**; in adults (especially middle age) → **acromegaly** (severe disfigurement, especially of the face); **low secretion** → **pituitary dwarfism**. **PRL** — growth of mammary glands, milk formation. **TSH** — thyroid hormone synthesis. **ACTH** — glucocorticoid synthesis by the adrenal cortex. **LH and FSH** (gonadotrophins) — in males LH stimulates androgens, FSH (with androgens) spermatogenesis; in females LH induces **ovulation** and maintains the corpus luteum, FSH stimulates follicle growth. **MSH** — melanocytes, skin pigmentation. **Oxytocin** — contraction of smooth muscle: uterus at childbirth, milk ejection. **Vasopressin (ADH)** — water and electrolyte reabsorption in the distal tubules; deficiency → **diabetes insipidus** (excess dilute urine, dehydration).

steps.title: Solved question 1
steps.body: An adult develops enlarged jaw and hands years after growth stopped. Which hormone and disorder? Excess **GH** → **acromegaly**.

steps.title: Solved question 2
steps.body: Which hormones does the posterior pituitary release but not make? **Oxytocin and vasopressin** — synthesised in the hypothalamus.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the posterior pituitary synthesises oxytocin.
- Mixing diabetes insipidus (ADH) with diabetes mellitus (insulin).
- Calling somatostatin a releasing hormone.

activity.prompt: Match the hormone to its effect.

quiz.why: Somatostatin from the hypothalamus is an inhibiting hormone. It stops the pituitary from releasing growth hormone. Releasing hormones do the opposite.

quiz.q: Over-secretion of GH in adults causes
quiz.why: Too much growth hormone in adults, after the growth plates have closed, thickens bones of the face and hands and feet. This is acromegaly. In children it causes gigantism.

quiz.q: Diabetes insipidus results from deficiency of
quiz.why: Diabetes insipidus is caused by too little ADH (vasopressin). The kidneys cannot conserve water and the person passes a large amount of dilute urine.
The pituitary gland lies in a bony cavity of the skull called the sella turcica. It is joined to the hypothalamus by a stalk.
Melanocyte-stimulating hormone (MSH) is released by the pars intermedia of the pituitary. It acts on melanocytes of the skin, which make pigment.

sources: NCERT Class 11 Biology (Chemical Coordination and Integration)

lessons.title: Pineal, thyroid, parathyroid and thymus

scenes.text: Packets of salt in India say 'iodised'. Before this, goitre was common in some hilly regions.
The butterfly-shaped thyroid needs iodine to make its hormones.

steps.title: Pineal and thyroid
steps.body:
- **Pineal gland** (dorsal forebrain): **melatonin** — regulates the **24-hour (diurnal) rhythm** (sleep–wake cycle, body temperature); also influences metabolism, pigmentation, menstrual cycle and defence capability.
- **Thyroid:** two lobes on either side of the trachea, connected by the **isthmus**; made of **follicles** and stromal tissue. Follicular cells make **thyroxine (T₄, tetraiodothyronine)** and **T₃ (triiodothyronine)**; **iodine** is essential.
  - Iodine deficiency → **hypothyroidism** and **goitre** (enlarged thyroid).
  - Hypothyroidism during pregnancy → defective development of the baby: **stunted growth (cretinism), mental retardation**, low IQ, abnormal skin, deaf-mutism. In adult women it may cause an irregular menstrual cycle.
  - **Hyperthyroidism** (e.g. due to cancer or nodules) → adverse effects on physiology; **exophthalmic goitre (Graves' disease)** — enlarged thyroid, protruding eyeballs, increased basal metabolic rate, weight loss.
  - Thyroid hormones regulate **basal metabolic rate**, RBC formation, metabolism of carbohydrates, proteins and fats, water–electrolyte balance.
  - Thyroid also secretes **thyrocalcitonin (TCT)**, a protein hormone that regulates (lowers) blood calcium.

steps.title: Parathyroid and thymus
steps.body:
- **Parathyroid glands:** four, on the back side of the thyroid (one pair in each lobe); secrete **parathyroid hormone (PTH)**, a peptide that **increases blood Ca²⁺** (hypercalcaemic) — stimulates bone resorption (demineralisation), Ca²⁺ reabsorption by renal tubules and absorption from digested food. PTH and TCT together regulate Ca²⁺ balance.
- **Thymus:** lobular structure between the lungs behind the sternum on the ventral side of the aorta; major role in **immunity**; secretes **thymosins**, which help differentiate **T-lymphocytes** (cell-mediated immunity) and promote antibody production (humoral immunity). The thymus **degenerates in old people**, lowering immune responses.

steps.title: Solved question 1
steps.body: Blood Ca²⁺ falls. Which hormone rises? **PTH** — it raises Ca²⁺ by bone resorption and renal reabsorption.

steps.title: Solved question 2
steps.body: Why is iodised salt recommended? Iodine is needed to make T₃ and T₄; deficiency causes goitre and, in pregnancy, cretinism.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying TCT raises blood calcium (PTH raises it; TCT lowers it).
- Saying the thymus grows larger with age (it degenerates).
- Calling melatonin a thyroid hormone.

quiz.why: Melatonin from the pineal gland regulates the 24-hour (diurnal) rhythm of the body, such as the sleep–wake cycle. It also affects body temperature and pigmentation.
Parathyroid hormone (PTH) raises blood Ca²⁺ levels, so it is hypercalcaemic. Thyrocalcitonin does the opposite.

quiz.q: Exophthalmic goitre is a form of
quiz.why: Exophthalmic goitre (Graves' disease) is a form of hyperthyroidism, with enlarged thyroid and bulging eyes. Hypothyroidism has opposite effects.
Thymosins from the thymus help in the differentiation of T-lymphocytes, which give cell-mediated immunity. They do not act on RBCs, platelets or neurons.
Iodine is needed to make thyroid hormones. Without it the thyroid enlarges as it works harder, causing goitre. Tetany, diabetes and acromegaly have other causes.

sources: NCERT Class 11 Biology (Chemical Coordination and Integration)

lessons.title: Adrenal, pancreas and gonads

scenes.text: Just before her board exam, Sneha's heart pounds and her palms sweat.
Adrenaline from her adrenal medulla is preparing her body for 'fight or flight'.

steps.title: Adrenal glands
steps.body:
One on the anterior part of each kidney; central **adrenal medulla** and outer **adrenal cortex**.
- **Medulla:** **adrenaline (epinephrine)** and **noradrenaline (norepinephrine)** — **catecholamines**, released rapidly in stress and emergencies — **emergency hormones / hormones of fight or flight**. Effects: alertness, pupil dilation, piloerection, sweating, increased heartbeat, strength of heart contraction and rate of respiration; glycogen breakdown (raises blood glucose); breakdown of lipids and proteins.
- **Cortex:** three layers — **zona reticularis** (inner), **zona fasciculata** (middle), **zona glomerulosa** (outer). Hormones are **corticoids**: **glucocorticoids** (main: **cortisol**) — carbohydrate metabolism, gluconeogenesis, lipolysis, proteolysis; anti-inflammatory; suppress immune response; stimulate RBC production. **Mineralocorticoids** (main: **aldosterone**) — reabsorption of Na⁺ and water, excretion of K⁺ and phosphate; maintain electrolytes, body fluid volume, osmotic pressure and BP. Small amounts of **androgenic steroids** (growth of axial, pubic and facial hair during puberty).
- Under-production of cortex hormones → **Addison's disease** (altered carbohydrate metabolism, acute weakness and fatigue).

steps.title: Pancreas and gonads
steps.body:
- **Pancreas:** a composite gland (exocrine and endocrine). Endocrine part = **islets of Langerhans** (about 1–2 million, 1–2% of pancreatic tissue). **α-cells** secrete **glucagon** (peptide; acts on liver cells → glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis → **hyperglycaemia**; reduces cellular glucose uptake). **β-cells** secrete **insulin** (peptide; acts on liver and adipocytes → enhanced glucose uptake and use, glycogenesis → **hypoglycaemia**). Prolonged hyperglycaemia → **diabetes mellitus** (loss of glucose in urine, formation of harmful ketone bodies); treated with insulin therapy.
- **Testis:** **Leydig (interstitial) cells** produce **androgens**, mainly **testosterone** — development, maturation and functions of male accessory sex organs, muscular growth, facial and axillary hair, aggressiveness, low pitch voice; role in spermatogenesis; anabolic effects on protein and carbohydrate metabolism.
- **Ovary:** **estrogen** (from growing **ovarian follicles**) — growth of female secondary sex organs, follicles, mammary gland development, female secondary sex characters (e.g. high-pitched voice) and sexual behaviour. **Progesterone** (from the **corpus luteum**) — supports pregnancy; acts on mammary glands to form alveoli (sac-like structures storing milk) and milk secretion.

steps.title: Solved question 1
steps.body: Which pancreatic cells release glucagon, and what is its effect? **α-cells**; it raises blood glucose (hyperglycaemic).

steps.title: Solved question 2
steps.body: Which adrenal hormone helps conserve sodium? **Aldosterone** from the zona glomerulosa.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying insulin is made by α-cells.
- Placing aldosterone in the adrenal medulla.
- Saying the corpus luteum secretes mainly estrogen (its key hormone is progesterone).

quiz.q: Emergency hormones are secreted by the
quiz.why: The adrenal medulla secretes adrenaline and noradrenaline, called emergency or fight-or-flight hormones. They raise alertness, heart rate and breathing.

quiz.q: Addison's disease results from under-production of
quiz.why: Addison's disease is caused by too little of the hormones of the adrenal cortex, such as cortisol and aldosterone. It leads to weakness and low blood pressure.
The β-cells of the islets of Langerhans in the pancreas secrete insulin, which lowers blood glucose (hypoglycaemic). α-cells make glucagon.
Leydig (interstitial) cells of the testis secrete androgens, mainly testosterone. Insulin comes from the pancreas.
Aldosterone from the zona glomerulosa of the adrenal cortex is the main mineralocorticoid. It helps retain Na⁺ and water. Cortisol is a glucocorticoid.
Oestrogen is made mainly by the growing ovarian follicles. Leydig cells make androgens. The corpus luteum mainly makes progesterone.

sources: NCERT Class 11 Biology (Chemical Coordination and Integration)

lessons.title: Hormones of heart, kidney and gut; mechanism of action

scenes.text: The heart, kidneys and stomach are not 'glands' — yet they also make hormones.
And every hormone works only on cells that carry its specific receptor.

steps.title: Other hormone sources
steps.body:
- **Heart (atrial wall):** **atrial natriuretic factor (ANF)** — when BP rises, it causes dilation of blood vessels, reducing BP.
- **Kidney (juxtaglomerular cells):** **erythropoietin** — stimulates **erythropoiesis** (RBC formation).
- **Gastro-intestinal tract:** **gastrin** (stimulates gastric glands to secrete HCl and pepsinogen), **secretin** (acts on exocrine pancreas — water and bicarbonate secretion), **cholecystokinin (CCK)** (acts on pancreas and gall bladder — pancreatic enzymes and bile juice), **gastric inhibitory peptide (GIP)** (inhibits gastric secretion and motility).
- Several non-endocrine tissues secrete **growth factors** essential for normal growth and repair.

steps.title: How hormones act
steps.body:
Hormones bind specific **hormone receptors** in target tissues, forming a **hormone–receptor complex** that causes biochemical changes.
- **Membrane-bound receptors** (for hormones that do not enter cells: **protein/peptide** hormones and amino-acid derivatives like **epinephrine**) → generate **second messengers** (e.g. **cyclic AMP, IP₃, Ca²⁺**) → regulate cellular metabolism.
