- **Intracellular (mostly nuclear) receptors** (for hormones that enter cells: **steroid hormones** and **iodothyronines**) → interact with the genome → regulate **gene expression** or chromosome function → physiological and developmental effects.
- Chemical classes: **peptide/polypeptide/protein** (insulin, glucagon, pituitary and hypothalamic hormones), **steroids** (cortisol, testosterone, estradiol, progesterone), **iodothyronines** (thyroid hormones), **amino-acid derivatives** (epinephrine).

steps.title: Solved question 1
steps.body: Why can steroid hormones act on nuclear receptors? They are lipid-soluble and cross the plasma membrane.

steps.title: Solved question 2
steps.body: Which hormone stimulates RBC formation and where is it made? **Erythropoietin**, from juxtaglomerular cells of the kidney.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying insulin enters the cell to act on DNA (it acts via membrane receptors).
- Mixing secretin (bicarbonate) and CCK (enzymes and bile).
- Calling ANF a hormone that raises BP (it lowers it).

quiz.why: Erythropoietin, which stimulates RBC formation, is made by the juxtaglomerular cells of the kidney when oxygen levels are low.
Atrial natriuretic factor (ANF) is made by the atrial wall of the heart. It dilates blood vessels and lowers blood pressure.
Gastrin acts on the gastric glands and makes them secrete HCl and pepsinogen. Bicarbonate is stimulated by secretin.
Steroid hormones are lipid-soluble, so they cross the cell membrane and bind to intracellular receptors. The complex then changes gene expression.
Cyclic AMP is a second messenger. It carries the signal inside the cell after a peptide hormone binds its receptor on the surface. Steroid hormones like testosterone work differently.
Cholecystokinin (CCK) acts on the pancreas to release enzymes and on the gall bladder to release bile. It is made by the gut wall.

sources: NCERT Class 11 Biology (Chemical Coordination and Integration)

questions.q: Hormones are produced in
questions.why: Hormones are produced in very small (trace) amounts and still have large effects on their target tissues.

questions.q: Insulin is secreted by
questions.why: Insulin is made by the β-cells of the islets of Langerhans in the pancreas. α-cells make glucagon.

questions.q: The 'fight or flight' hormone is
questions.why: Adrenaline from the adrenal medulla is the fight-or-flight hormone, as it prepares the body to face stress. Insulin and prolactin have other roles.

questions.q: Goitre is caused by deficiency of
questions.why: Goitre is an enlarged thyroid caused by a lack of iodine in the diet, which is needed to make thyroid hormones.

questions.q: Oxytocin acts on
options: smooth muscles of uterus and mammary glands
questions.why: Oxytocin acts on the smooth muscles of the uterus, to cause strong contractions during childbirth, and on the mammary glands for milk ejection.

questions.q: The hormone that lowers blood calcium is
questions.why: Thyrocalcitonin (TCT) from the thyroid lowers blood calcium. PTH raises it.

questions.q: Assertion: The posterior pituitary is not a true endocrine gland in terms of synthesis. Reason: Oxytocin and vasopressin are synthesised in the hypothalamus and only stored there.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
Both true and R explains A
questions.why: Both are true and R explains A. Oxytocin and vasopressin are made in the hypothalamus and only stored and released from the posterior pituitary, so it is not a true gland of synthesis.

questions.q: Gigantism is due to
questions.why: Gigantism is caused by too much growth hormone in childhood, before the growth plates close. In adults the same excess causes acromegaly.

questions.q: Glucocorticoids are produced by the
questions.why: Glucocorticoids such as cortisol are made in the zona fasciculata, the middle layer of the adrenal cortex. Aldosterone comes from the zona glomerulosa.

questions.q: Which hormone acts through cyclic AMP?
questions.why: Glucagon is a peptide hormone and cannot cross the membrane, so it binds a surface receptor and acts through cyclic AMP. Steroid and thyroid hormones act inside the cell.

questions.q: Case: A pregnant woman with severe iodine deficiency is at risk that her baby will show
questions.why: Severe iodine deficiency in pregnancy lowers thyroid hormone in the baby and causes cretinism, with stunted growth and mental retardation. Acromegaly and Graves' disease are different.

questions.q: Case: A patient has persistently high blood glucose, glucose and ketone bodies in urine. The hormone deficient is
questions.why: High blood glucose with glucose and ketone bodies in the urine are signs of diabetes mellitus, caused by too little insulin or its action.

questions.q: Case: A patient passes large volumes of dilute urine and is always thirsty, but blood glucose is normal. The likely cause is deficiency of
questions.why: Large volumes of dilute urine with thirst and normal blood glucose point to diabetes insipidus, caused by too little ADH (vasopressin). In diabetes mellitus the glucose would be high.

questions.q: Secretin acts on the exocrine pancreas to secrete
questions.why: Secretin acts on the exocrine pancreas to release water and bicarbonate ions, which neutralise the acid from the stomach. Insulin comes from endocrine cells.

questions.q: PTH raises blood Ca²⁺ by
options: bone resorption, renal reabsorption and intestinal absorption
questions.why: PTH raises blood calcium by promoting bone resorption, increasing reabsorption in the kidney and increasing absorption in the intestine (with vitamin D).

questions.q: Which pair is incorrectly matched?
questions.why: Thymosins come from the thymus, which shrinks with age, not from the pineal gland. The other pairs are correct.

questions.q: Hormones that bind intracellular receptors and regulate gene expression include
questions.why: Steroids and iodothyronines (thyroid hormones) are lipid-soluble, so they bind to intracellular receptors and affect gene expression. FSH, LH, insulin, glucagon and adrenaline use membrane receptors.

questions.q: LH surge in females mainly causes
questions.why: A sudden surge of LH in the middle of the cycle makes the mature follicle burst and release the egg. This is ovulation.

courses.title: Revision & Practice · Class 11 Biology
courses.summary: Quick-revision sheets for all 19 chapters, high-yield facts and numbers, diagram checklists, answer-writing strategy and two mixed mock papers.

Learners can draw and label key diagrams from memory

lessons.title: Revision sheet I: diversity and structure (Ch 1–7)

scenes.text: Isha revises the night before with one page per unit, written in her own words.
Short, sharp, high-yield — and she tests herself instead of just reading.

steps.title: Living world and classification
steps.body:
- Defining features: metabolism, cellular organisation, consciousness.
- Hierarchy: species → genus → family → order → class → phylum/division → kingdom.
- Whittaker 1969: Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae, Animalia.
- Archaebacteria: halophiles, thermoacidophiles, methanogens. Viroids: Diener 1971 (free RNA). Lichens: pollution indicators.

steps.title: Plants and animals
steps.body:
- Algae pigments/foods: green (chl a, b; starch), brown (chl a, c, fucoxanthin; laminarin, mannitol), red (chl a, d, phycoerythrin; floridean starch).
- Bryophytes: gametophyte dominant. Pteridophytes: first vascular; heterospory in Selaginella, Salvinia. Gymnosperms: naked seeds. Angiosperms: double fertilisation, triploid endosperm.
- Animal criteria: organisation, symmetry, germ layers, coelom, segmentation, notochord.
- Largest phylum Arthropoda; second Mollusca; water vascular system in echinoderms; crocodile 4-chambered heart; platypus lays eggs.

steps.title: Morphology, anatomy, animal tissues
steps.body:
- Placentation: marginal (pea), axile (tomato), parietal (mustard), free central (Dianthus), basal (sunflower).
- Fabaceae % ⚥ K(5) C1+2+(2) A(9)+1 G1; Solanaceae ⊕ ⚥ K(5) C(5) A5 G(2); Liliaceae ⊕ ⚥ P(3+3) A3+3 G(3).
- Dicot root 2–4 xylem; monocot root polyarch + large pith; dicot stem ring of open bundles; monocot stem scattered closed bundles.
- Epithelia: squamous (alveoli), cuboidal (PCT), columnar (gut), ciliated (fallopian tube), compound (pharynx). Tendon: muscle–bone; ligament: bone–bone.
- Cockroach: 13-chambered heart, Malpighian tubules, 10 pairs spiracles. Frog: 3-chambered heart, ureotelic, 10 pairs cranial nerves.

steps.title: High-risk confusions
steps.body: - Taxonomy vs systematics; Gram +/− ; thorn (stem) vs spine (leaf); diploblastic coelenterates; pseudocoelomate Aschelminthes; exarch roots vs endarch stems.

quiz.q: The second largest animal phylum is
quiz.why: Mollusca is the second largest animal phylum, after Arthropoda.
A monocot root has radial bundles with polyarch xylem (more than six) and a large pith, as in maize. A dicot root has 2 to 4 xylem and little pith.
Fucoxanthin is the brown pigment of brown algae (Phaeophyceae), which gives them their colour. Mosses, green algae and red algae have other pigments.

quiz.q: Dense regular tissue joining bone to bone is
quiz.why: Ligaments are dense regular connective tissue that join bone to bone. Tendons join muscle to bone.

quiz.q: Which is uricotelic and has a 4-chambered heart?
quiz.why: Birds excrete uric acid (uricotelic) and have a four-chambered heart. Lizards are uricotelic but have a three-chambered heart. Frogs and fishes are not uricotelic.

sources: NCERT Class 11 Biology (Revision & Practice · Class 11 Biology)

lessons.title: Revision sheet II: cell biology, plant and human physiology (Ch 8–19)

scenes.text: NEET and board papers love numbers: 70S, 9+2, 18 ATP, 180 L, 0.8 s, 206 bones…
A list of high-yield numbers, revised daily for a week, sticks for good.

steps.title: Cell, biomolecules, division
steps.body:
- Ribosomes: prokaryote 70S (50S + 30S), eukaryote 80S (60S + 40S). Axoneme 9 + 2; centriole 9 triplets.
- Fluid mosaic model 1972. Endomembrane: ER, Golgi, lysosome, vacuole.
- B-DNA: 10 bp/turn, pitch 3.4 nm, 0.34 nm/bp. Most abundant protein: RuBisCO (biosphere), collagen (animals).
- Enzyme classes: oxidoreductases, transferases, hydrolases, lyases, isomerases, ligases. Malonate inhibits succinic dehydrogenase.
- S phase: DNA 2C → 4C. Prophase I: leptotene → zygotene (synapsis) → pachytene (crossing over) → diplotene (chiasmata) → diakinesis (terminalisation).

steps.title: Plant physiology
steps.body:
- Light reaction: PS II P680 (water splitting, O₂), PS I P700; cyclic → ATP only.
- Calvin cycle: RuBP + CO₂ → 2 PGA (RuBisCO); 1 glucose needs 18 ATP + 12 NADPH.
- C4: PEP + CO₂ → OAA (PEPcase, mesophyll); Kranz anatomy; no photorespiration.
- Glycolysis net 2 ATP + 2 NADH; aerobic total 38 ATP (textbook); RQ carbohydrate 1, fat 0.7, protein 0.9.
- PGRs: auxin (apical dominance, rooting, 2,4-D), GA (bolting, grapes, sugarcane), cytokinin (cell division, delay senescence), ethylene (ripening, pineapple flowering), ABA (stomatal closure, dormancy).

steps.title: Human physiology
steps.body:
- Lung volumes: TV 500 mL, IRV 2500–3000, ERV 1000–1100, RV 1100–1200 mL; VC = TV + IRV + ERV.
- O₂: 97% by Hb; CO₂: ~70% as bicarbonate. Rhythm centre: medulla; pneumotaxic: pons.
- Blood: RBC 5–5.5 million/mm³ (120 days); WBC 6000–8000; neutrophils 60–65%; platelets 1.5–3.5 lakh/mm³.
- Heart: SAN pacemaker 70–75/min; cycle 0.8 s; stroke volume 70 mL; cardiac output ≈ 5 L/min; P, QRS, T waves.
- Kidney: GFR 125 mL/min = 180 L/day; ~99% reabsorbed; medulla gradient 300 → 1200 mOsmol/L; ADH, RAAS, ANF.
- Skeleton: 206 bones (80 axial + 126 appendicular); 12 pairs of ribs; 26 vertebrae.
- Nerve: 3 Na⁺ out / 2 K⁺ in; Na⁺ influx → depolarisation; K⁺ efflux → repolarisation.
- Hormones: GH (gigantism/acromegaly/dwarfism), ADH (diabetes insipidus), insulin (diabetes mellitus), PTH (↑Ca²⁺), TCT (↓Ca²⁺), aldosterone (Na⁺ retention).

steps.title: High-risk confusions
steps.body: - Diabetes insipidus vs mellitus · prophase I sub-stages order · A band constant in contraction · descending vs ascending limb permeability · lub (AV valves) vs dub (semilunar).

activity.prompt: Match the number to the fact.

quiz.why: Crossing over takes place in pachytene of prophase I, between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes, helped by the enzyme recombinase.

quiz.q: The 'dub' heart sound is due to closure of
quiz.why: The second heart sound 'dub' is caused by closing of the semilunar valves at the end of ventricular systole. The 'lub' is from the AV valves.

quiz.q: Hormone deficient in diabetes insipidus is
quiz.why: Diabetes insipidus is caused by a lack of ADH (vasopressin), so the kidneys pass large amounts of dilute urine. Insulin deficiency causes diabetes mellitus.

quiz.q: First stable product in C4 plants is
quiz.why: In C4 plants the first stable product is oxaloacetic acid (OAA), a four-carbon compound, so they are called C4. PGA is the first product in C3 plants.
Neutrophils are the most abundant WBCs, making up about 60 to 65% of them. They engulf germs by phagocytosis.

sources: NCERT Class 11 Biology (Revision & Practice · Class 11 Biology)

lessons.title: Exam strategy, diagrams and answer writing

scenes.text: Amit always skipped diagrams. His teacher showed him that a labelled sketch earns marks even when words fall short.
Biology rewards clear diagrams, precise terms and well-structured answers.

steps.title: Diagrams to practise
steps.body:
- Prokaryotic cell; plant and animal cell; mitochondrion and chloroplast
- Stages of mitosis; prophase I sub-stages
- T.S. of dicot and monocot root and stem; dorsiventral leaf
- Z scheme; Calvin cycle outline; C4 pathway
- Human respiratory system; heart (sectional view) with conducting system
- Nephron with blood vessels; sarcomere; neuron; human brain (sagittal)
- Flower of Fabaceae/Solanaceae with floral formula

steps.title: Answer writing
steps.body:
- Start with a one-line definition using the exact term.
- Use points, not paragraphs; underline key words.
- For 'differentiate', use a two-column table with matching criteria.
- For assertion–reason, judge each statement separately first, then the link.
- For case-based questions, underline data in the case before answering.

steps.title: Worked assertion–reason
steps.body:
A: Lichens are good pollution indicators. R: Lichens do not grow in polluted areas.
- A true; R true; R explains why they indicate pollution → **both true, R explains A**.

steps.title: Worked case question
steps.body: Case: A plant's leaves show Kranz anatomy and it grows well in heat. Q: What enzyme first fixes CO₂ in its mesophyll? → **PEP carboxylase** (C4 plant).

steps.title: Avoid
steps.body: - Vague words ('stuff', 'thing'); wrong spellings of scientific names; unlabelled or unclear diagrams; mixing up similar terms.

items: I can draw and label 10 key diagrams from memory
I revised my high-yield numbers list today
I solved one full mock paper in time
I know the floral formulae of Fabaceae, Solanaceae and Liliaceae
I can explain sliding filament theory step by step

quiz.q: In assertion–reason questions you should first
quiz.why: In assertion–reason questions, first judge each statement on its own as true or false. Then check if the reason explains the assertion.

quiz.q: For 'differentiate between' questions, the best format is
options: a two-column table with matching criteria
quiz.why: For 'differentiate between' questions, a two-column table with the same points compared on each row gives a clear comparison and earns marks.

quiz.q: A labelled diagram in an answer
options: can earn marks and clarify the answer
quiz.why: A neat, labelled diagram shows understanding and can earn marks in biology. It also makes the answer clearer.

quiz.q: Scientific names in an answer should be
quiz.why: Scientific names follow convention: they are italicised in print and underlined separately (genus and species) when handwritten.
In a case-based question, underline the data given first, because the answer must use it. A general definition alone will not answer the case.

sources: NCERT Class 11 Biology (Revision & Practice · Class 11 Biology)

questions.q: Mock 1 · Q1. Five-kingdom classification was proposed by
questions.why: R.H. Whittaker proposed the five-kingdom classification in 1969. Linnaeus gave binomial nomenclature, and Mendel and Darwin worked on heredity and evolution.

questions.q: Mock 1 · Q2. Agar is obtained from
questions.why: Agar comes from red algae such as Gelidium and Gracilaria. Laminaria is a brown alga, Spirogyra a green alga and Funaria a moss.

questions.q: Mock 1 · Q3. Twisted aestivation is seen in
questions.why: Twisted aestivation, where each petal overlaps the next in one direction, is seen in china rose. Cassia has imbricate, pea has vexillary and Calotropis has valvate aestivation.

questions.q: Mock 1 · Q4. Casparian strips occur in the
questions.why: Casparian strips are suberin bands in the walls of the endodermis of roots. They force water to pass through the cells.

questions.q: Mock 1 · Q5. Which is an ascomycete?
questions.why: Neurospora is an ascomycete (sac fungus). Puccinia and Agaricus are basidiomycetes and Albugo is a phycomycete.

questions.q: Mock 1 · Q6. Assertion: Crocodiles have a four-chambered heart. Reason: Crocodiles are mammals.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
Both true and R explains A
questions.why: The assertion is true, as crocodiles have a four-chambered heart. The reason is false because crocodiles are reptiles, not mammals. So A is true and R is false.

questions.q: Mock 1 · Q7. Number of ATP needed in the Calvin cycle to fix 6 CO₂ is
questions.why: The Calvin cycle needs 3 ATP per CO₂ fixed. For 6 CO₂ that is 3 × 6 = 18 ATP (and 12 NADPH).

questions.q: Mock 1 · Q8. Synapsis occurs in
questions.why: Synapsis, the pairing of homologous chromosomes, occurs in zygotene of meiotic prophase I.

questions.q: Mock 1 · Q9. Case: A seedling grown in the dark shows a horizontal growth habit, swollen axis and apical hook. The hormone is
questions.why: A dark-grown seedling with horizontal growth, a swollen axis and an apical hook shows the triple response, which is caused by ethylene.

questions.q: Mock 1 · Q10. Using NADH = 3 and FADH₂ = 2 ATP, the ATP from oxidative phosphorylation of one acetyl CoA in the Krebs cycle is
questions.why: 3 NADH × 3 = 9 + 1 FADH₂ × 2 = 2 → 11 (plus 1 GTP by substrate level = 12 in total).

questions.q: Mock 2 · Q1. The pacemaker of the heart is
questions.why: The SAN (sinoatrial node) is the pacemaker of the heart. It starts the impulse for each heartbeat.

questions.q: Mock 2 · Q2. Uricotelic animals include
questions.why: Birds are uricotelic, excreting uric acid to save water. Humans are ureotelic, frogs ureotelic and bony fishes ammonotelic.

questions.q: Mock 2 · Q3. Vital capacity equals
questions.why: Vital capacity is the maximum air one can breathe out after a deepest inspiration. It equals TV + IRV + ERV, and excludes residual volume.

questions.q: Mock 2 · Q4. Floating ribs are the
questions.why: The 11th and 12th pairs of ribs are floating ribs because they are not attached to the sternum at the front.

questions.q: Mock 2 · Q5. Depolarisation of an axon is due to
questions.why: Depolarisation of an axon is due to the rapid influx of Na⁺ through opened channels. K⁺ efflux makes repolarisation.

questions.q: Mock 2 · Q6. Assertion: ADH reduces urine volume. Reason: ADH increases water reabsorption in the distal parts of the tubule.
options: Both true and R explains A
Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true and R explains A. ADH makes the distal part of the tubule reabsorb more water, so less urine is passed.

questions.q: Mock 2 · Q7. The hormone that raises blood calcium is
questions.why: PTH (parathyroid hormone) raises blood calcium. TCT lowers it. Insulin and glucagon control blood sugar.

questions.q: Mock 2 · Q8. Case: A patient's ECG shows an enlarged gap before each QRS complex after the P wave. The delay most likely involves conduction at the
questions.why: The PR interval, from the P wave to the QRS, reflects the time taken for the impulse to pass the AV node. A longer gap suggests delayed conduction there.

questions.q: Mock 2 · Q9. GFR is 125 mL/min and urine output is 1.5 L/day. Approximate % of filtrate reabsorbed:
questions.why: Filtrate per day is about 180 L (125 mL/min × 1440). Urine is 1.5 L, so about 0.8% leaves and about 99% is reabsorbed.

questions.q: Mock 2 · Q10. Stroke volume 75 mL and heart rate 80/min give a cardiac output of
questions.why: Cardiac output = stroke volume × heart rate = 75 mL × 80 = 6000 mL = 6.0 L per minute.

school-c11-business-a.title: Class 11 Business Studies (Part A)
school-c11-business-a.description: All chapters of Class 11 Business Studies: business and commerce, forms of organisation, services, ethics, finance, small business and trade, explained with Indian cases.

courses.title: Ch 1 · Business, Trade and Commerce
courses.summary: History of trade in India, meaning and features of business, business vs profession vs employment, industry and commerce, objectives, business risk and basic factors in starting a business.
outcomes: Learners can describe India’s historical trade and indigenous banking
Learners can distinguish business, profession and employment
Learners can classify industries and auxiliaries to trade
Learners can explain multiple objectives and causes of business risk

lessons.title: Trade and commerce in India’s history

scenes.text: Two thousand years ago, ships from Indian ports carried pepper, cotton and gems westward.
Caravans on land routes linked Indian towns to Central Asia and China.
India was one of the world’s great trading regions long before modern companies.

steps.title: Ancient and medieval trade
steps.body:
- The **Indus Valley (Harappan) civilisation** traded with Mesopotamia; standard weights and seals suggest organised trade.
- Land routes such as the **Silk Route** linked India with China, Central Asia and the Mediterranean; sea routes linked Indian ports with Arabia, East Africa and South-East Asia.
- Exports included spices (pepper), cotton and silk textiles, indigo, precious stones, ivory and sandalwood; imports included horses, gold, silver and some luxury goods.

steps.title: Trading centres and ports
steps.body: Important centres included Pataliputra, Taxila, Mathura, Varanasi, Ujjain, Kanchi and Madurai. Ports included **Bharuch (Broach)** on the west coast, **Kaveripattinam** (Puhar) in the south and **Tamralipti** in the east. Later, Surat and Calicut became major ports.

steps.title: Indigenous banking and credit
steps.body: Merchants used **hundis** — written orders to pay, like early bills of exchange — and *chitthis* for transfers. Bankers (shroffs, seths) accepted deposits, gave loans and financed long-distance trade. Merchant guilds (shrenis) set rules for members and settled disputes.

steps.title: Solved example 1: Why was India a trading power?
steps.body:
- Step 1: Rich resources (cotton, spices).
- Step 2: Skilled artisans and textiles valued abroad.
- Step 3: Long coastline and ports + land routes.
- Step 4: Credit instruments (hundi) and guilds reduced risk → long-distance trade grew.

steps.title: Solved example 2: Hundi in action
steps.body: A Surat merchant buys cloth from a Varanasi weaver. Instead of carrying coins on a risky road, he gives a hundi drawn on a banker in Varanasi who pays the weaver. Money moves by trust and paper, like a modern cheque.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying trade in India began with the British — it is thousands of years older.
- Calling a hundi a coin; it is a credit instrument.
- Mixing up ports and inland centres in answers.

pairs: Land trade route to China and Central Asia

quiz.why: A hundi was a written credit instrument used in ancient and medieval India, like a bill of exchange. It let merchants send money without carrying coins.
Bharuch (Broach) was an important port on the west coast, used for overseas trade. Tamralipti was on the east coast, and Pataliputra and Mathura are inland cities.
In ancient India merchant guilds, which looked after the interests of traders and craftsmen, were called shrenis.

quiz.q: A major ancient Indian export was…
quiz.why: Ancient India exported items such as spices (pepper), cotton and silk textiles. Tea and horses were not major exports of that time.
Archaeological finds, such as Harappan seals in Mesopotamian sites, show that the Harappans traded with Mesopotamia.

sources: NCERT Business Studies Class 11 — topic reference

lessons.title: Business: concept and characteristics

scenes.text: Raju runs a tea stall; his sister is a doctor; his father works as a bank clerk.
All three earn money — are all three “business”?
Economic activities come in three kinds.

steps.title: Economic vs non-economic activities
steps.body: **Economic activities** are done to earn a living (business, profession, employment). **Non-economic activities** are done for love, religion, social service (a mother cooking for her family, volunteering).

steps.title: Meaning and characteristics of business
steps.body:
**Business** is an economic activity involving the regular production and/or sale of goods and services with the aim of earning profit by satisfying human needs.

- Economic activity
- Production or procurement of goods and services
- Sale or exchange for value
- **Regularity** of dealings (a one-time sale of your old phone is not business)
- Profit as the main objective
- Uncertainty of returns
- Element of risk

steps.title: Business, profession and employment
steps.body:
- *Mode of establishment*: business — entrepreneur’s decision and legal formalities; profession — membership of a professional body and a certificate of practice; employment — appointment letter.
- *Nature of work*: goods/services to the public; personalised expert service; work as per contract.
- *Qualification*: none compulsory; prescribed qualification; as required by employer.
- *Reward*: profit; professional fee; salary/wages.
- *Capital*: as per need; limited; none.
- *Risk*: high; low; little or none.
- *Code of conduct*: none fixed; professional code; service rules.
- *Transfer of interest*: possible; not possible; not possible.

steps.title: Solved example 1: Classify
steps.body: (a) A chartered accountant auditing firms → *profession*. (b) A software engineer at a company → *employment*. (c) A person running a mobile shop → *business*. (d) A person selling her old bicycle once → *not business* (no regularity).

steps.title: Solved example 2: Is it risky?
steps.body: A mango trader buys stock in May. Rain spoils part of it and prices fall. His income is uncertain — showing **risk and uncertainty of return**, a feature of business but not of employment.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling any money-earning activity a business.
- Forgetting regularity as a characteristic.
- Saying professionals earn “profit” — they earn fees.

options: A mother cooking for her family
quiz.why: A mother cooking for her family acts out of love and duty, not for money, so it is non-economic. A factory job, a shop and a doctor's practice are done to earn income.

quiz.q: Regular dealings are a feature of…
quiz.why: Business involves regular dealings in goods or services. A one-off sale is not a business activity.
A professional such as a doctor or lawyer earns a fee for services. Employees earn wages or salary and businesses earn profit.

quiz.q: Transfer of interest is possible in…
quiz.why: A business can be sold or transferred to another person, so transfer of interest is possible. A profession and a job cannot be transferred this way.
Business has the highest risk, since returns are uncertain and losses are possible. A job and a profession have a more steady income.

lessons.title: Classification of business activities: industry and commerce

story.title: From iron ore to your doorstep

scenes.text: Iron ore is mined in Odisha.
A steel plant turns it into sheets; a factory makes a cycle.
Transport, warehouses, banks, insurance and shops bring the cycle to you.

steps.title: Industry
steps.body:
**Industry** produces or processes goods.

- **Primary**: *extractive* (mining, fishing, hunting, lumbering) and *genetic* (rearing and reproducing plants/animals — nurseries, poultry, cattle breeding, fish hatcheries).
- **Secondary**: *manufacturing* — analytical (oil refinery separates petrol, diesel), synthetical (cement from several materials), processing (sugar, paper), assembling (cars, TVs); and *construction* (roads, dams, buildings).
- **Tertiary (service)**: support services — transport, banking, insurance, warehousing, communication, advertising.

steps.title: Commerce = Trade + Auxiliaries to trade
steps.body:
Commerce removes hindrances between producer and consumer.

- **Trade**: buying and selling. *Internal* (wholesale, retail) and *external* (import, export, entrepot — import for re-export).
- **Auxiliaries**: transport (hindrance of place), banking and finance (finance), insurance (risk), warehousing (time — storage), advertising (information), communication.

steps.title: Solved example 1: Classify
steps.body: (a) Coal mining → primary, extractive. (b) Poultry farm → primary, genetic. (c) Petroleum refinery → secondary, analytical. (d) Car plant → secondary, assembling. (e) Courier company → tertiary (auxiliary — transport/communication).

steps.title: Solved example 2: Which hindrance is removed?
steps.body: Rice harvested in October is sold throughout the year → *warehousing* removes the hindrance of **time**. Kashmiri apples reach Chennai → *transport* removes the hindrance of **place**. A shopkeeper buys on credit from a bank loan → *banking* removes the hindrance of **finance**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling poultry “extractive” — it is genetic (reproduction).
- Treating commerce as only trade; auxiliaries are part of commerce.
- Confusing entrepot with export.

quiz.q: Oil refining is an example of…
quiz.why: Oil refining separates one raw material (crude oil) into many products like petrol and diesel. That makes it an analytical industry.
Warehousing stores goods until they are needed. It removes the hindrance of time between production and use.
Entrepot trade is import of goods for re-export to other countries. It is not for use in the home country.
Cattle breeding raises animals by reproduction, so it is a genetic industry. Mining and fishing are extractive.
Insurance covers the risk of loss from fire, accident or death. So it removes the hindrance of risk.

lessons.title: Objectives of business and business risk

scenes.text: A pharma company makes a large profit by overcharging for a life-saving drug.
Customers and the government react; its reputation collapses.
Businesses need multiple objectives.

steps.title: Role of profit
steps.body: Profit is the excess of revenue over cost. It is needed for: survival, growth and expansion, efficiency signal, reward for risk, and building reputation. But profit cannot be the *only* objective.

steps.title: Multiple objectives (key result areas)
steps.body:
- **Market standing**: position relative to competitors.
- **Innovation**: new ideas, products and methods.
- **Productivity**: output per input; efficiency.
- **Physical and financial resources**: acquire and use them well.
- **Earning profits**: adequate returns.
- **Manager performance and development**.
- **Worker performance and attitude**.
- **Social responsibility**: duties to society.

steps.title: Business risk
steps.body:
**Business risk** is the possibility of inadequate profit or loss due to uncertainties.

- Nature: arises from uncertainty; essential part of every business; degree depends on nature and size; profit is the reward for risk.
- **Causes**: natural (flood, earthquake, pandemic); human (theft, strikes, carelessness, dishonesty of employees); economic (fall in demand, price changes, competition, technology change); other (political changes, war, equipment failure).

steps.title: Solved example 1: Identify the objective
steps.body: A firm spends on R&D to launch an electric scooter → *innovation*. It trains supervisors → *manager performance and development*. It plants trees and runs a clinic for villagers → *social responsibility*.

steps.title: Solved example 2: Identify the cause of risk
steps.body: (a) Cyclone destroys a warehouse → natural. (b) Cashier runs away with cash → human. (c) Customers shift to smartphones, killing feature-phone demand → economic (technology/demand). (d) Sudden change in import duty → other (political/government).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing “profit is the only objective”.
- Calling technology change a natural cause.
- Saying risk can be fully eliminated — it can be reduced and partly insured, not removed.

activity.prompt: Match the example with the cause of business risk

quiz.why: Profit is the reward the owner gets for bearing the risk of business, because returns are uncertain.
Productivity is the ratio of output to input. It shows how well resources are used to produce goods.

quiz.q: A flood destroying stock is a…
quiz.why: A flood is a natural event, outside human control, so loss of stock due to it is a natural cause of risk.
Business risk can be reduced by insurance and good planning, but it cannot be removed completely, because it is part of every business.
Market standing means the position of the firm compared with its competitors, such as its share of the market.

lessons.title: Starting a business: basic factors

scenes.text: Priya bakes amazing cakes and wants to start a cake studio.
Her mentor gives her a list: product, form, location, finance, people, machines, licences, plan.
Every new business must think through these factors.

steps.title: Basic factors
steps.body:
1. **Selection of line of business** — demand, competition, skills, capital.
2. **Size of the firm** — small or large depending on finance, demand, technology.
3. **Choice of form of ownership** — sole proprietorship, partnership, company, etc.
4. **Location** — nearness to raw materials, market, labour, transport, power.
5. **Financing the proposition** — fixed and working capital needs and sources.
6. **Physical facilities** — machines, buildings, utilities.
7. **Plant layout** — arrangement of facilities for smooth flow.
8. **Competent and committed workforce**.
9. **Tax planning** — tax implications of choices.
10. **Launching the enterprise** — mobilise resources and start operations.

steps.title: Solved example 1: Location
steps.body: Priya compares a mall (high rent, many buyers) and a residential market (lower rent, regular customers). For a cake studio relying on birthdays and repeat orders, the residential market near schools may be better → *location* depends on the market.

steps.title: Solved example 2: Finance
steps.body: She needs ₹4 lakh for ovens and fit-out (fixed capital) and ₹60,000 for ingredients, rent and wages for 2 months (working capital). Sources: savings, a MUDRA-type small loan or family. → *financing the proposition*.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Ignoring working capital and running out of cash.
- Choosing a location only for low rent.
- Forgetting tax planning and licences (e.g., FSSAI registration for food businesses).

activity.prompt: Arrange the factors in a sensible order

quiz.why: Plant layout is how machines, equipment and other physical facilities are arranged in a plant. It is not about finance, tax or ownership.

quiz.q: Money for ingredients and wages is…
quiz.why: Money needed for day-to-day expenses such as ingredients and wages is working capital. Fixed capital is for long-term assets like machines.

quiz.q: Which factor depends most on nearness to market and raw materials?
quiz.why: Location, the place where a business is set up, depends mostly on nearness to the market and to raw materials.
Launching the enterprise is the last step in setting up a business, after the earlier decisions such as ownership form, location and finance.

quiz.q: Choosing between sole proprietorship and company is…
quiz.why: Choosing between a sole proprietorship, a partnership or a company is deciding the form of ownership.

questions.q: Business is an activity done mainly to…
questions.why: Business is an economic activity of producing or selling goods and services to satisfy needs, with the main aim of earning profit.

questions.q: A one-time sale of a used car by its owner is…
questions.why: A one-time sale of a used car lacks regularity of dealing, which is a key feature of business. So it is not a business activity.

questions.q: Mining is…
questions.why: Mining takes materials from the earth, so it is an extractive industry. Manufacturing and construction change or build things.

questions.q: Sugar from sugarcane is an example of…
questions.why: Making sugar from sugarcane changes the raw material into a finished product, so it is a processing activity of a manufacturing industry.

questions.q: Hindrance of place is removed by…
questions.why: Transport moves goods from the place of production to where they are needed, so it removes the hindrance of place.

questions.q: A professional must…
options: be a member of a professional body
questions.why: A professional, such as a lawyer, must be a member of a professional body (like the Bar Council), which sets rules and qualifications. They need the required qualifications.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Profit cannot be the only objective of business. Reason (R): Business must balance many objectives including social responsibility.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true and R explains A. Business has to balance several objectives, including social responsibility, so profit cannot be the only one.

questions.q: Hundi was mainly used for…
questions.why: A hundi was a credit instrument used for transferring money and credit from one place to another, much like a bill of exchange.

questions.q: Case: A company importing dates from Iraq and re-exporting them to Nepal is engaged in…
questions.why: Importing dates and re-exporting them to another country is entrepot trade, since the goods are not used in the home country.

questions.q: Which is a human cause of risk?
questions.why: Employee fraud is a human cause of business risk. Drought is natural, and inflation and a fall in demand are economic causes.

questions.q: Assembling industry example:
questions.why: Car manufacturing is an assembling industry, where many parts are put together to make one product. Cement is processing and a refinery is analytical.

questions.q: Case: A firm sets a target of 10 new products in 3 years. The objective is…
questions.why: A target of launching new products shows the objective of innovation, which is creating new or better products and methods.

questions.q: Which is NOT an auxiliary to trade?
questions.why: Auxiliaries to trade are services that help trade, such as banking, insurance, transport and warehousing. Retailing is itself trade.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Construction is a secondary industry. Reason (R): It creates structures like roads and dams.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true and R explains A. Construction makes structures such as roads and dams from materials, so it is a secondary industry.

questions.q: Case: Priya’s cake studio needs ovens worth ₹3 lakh and ₹50,000 for ingredients. Which statement is correct?
options: Ovens = fixed capital; ingredients = working capital
questions.why: Ovens are long-lasting assets, so they are fixed capital. The money for ingredients is used up in daily operations, so it is working capital.

questions.q: Which pair is correctly matched?
questions.why: Poultry raises birds by breeding, so it is a genetic industry. Cement is synthetical, an oil refinery is analytical and a car plant is assembling.

questions.q: A firm suffers losses because consumers switch to a rival’s cheaper product after a tax change. The risk is best classified as…
questions.why: Customers switching to a cheaper rival is a change in demand and competition, which are economic risks. The tax change is only the trigger.

courses.title: Ch 2 · Forms of Business Organisation
courses.summary: Sole proprietorship, Joint Hindu Family business, partnership (partners, deed, registration), cooperative societies, joint stock companies and how to choose the right form.
outcomes: Learners can explain features, merits and limitations of each form
Learners can identify types of partners and partnerships
Learners can distinguish private, public and one person companies
Learners can choose a suitable form for a given case

lessons.title: Sole proprietorship

scenes.text: Ramesh opens a kirana store with his savings and runs it alone.
He decides everything, keeps all the profit — and bears every loss himself.
That is a sole proprietorship.

steps.title: Meaning and features
steps.body:
A business owned, managed and controlled by **one person**, who bears all risk and receives all profit.

- Formation and closure are easy (few legal formalities; some licences may be needed).
- **Unlimited liability**: personal assets can be used to pay business debts.
- Sole risk-bearer and profit recipient.
- Full control and quick decisions.
- **No separate legal entity**; lack of business continuity (death, insanity or illness can end it).

steps.title: Merits and limitations
steps.body:
**Merits**: quick decision-making, confidentiality of information, direct incentive, sense of accomplishment, ease of formation and closure.

**Limitations**: limited resources (own savings, small loans), limited life, unlimited liability, limited managerial ability.

steps.title: Solved example 1: Liability
steps.body: Ramesh’s store owes suppliers ₹6 lakh; business assets fetch ₹4 lakh. Creditors can claim the remaining **₹2 lakh from his personal assets** (house, savings) — unlimited liability.

steps.title: Solved example 2: Suitability
steps.body: Suitable for: small retail, beauty parlours, tailoring, local services where personal attention matters and capital needs are small. Not suitable for: a steel plant needing huge capital.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying a sole proprietorship is a separate legal entity.
- Saying no licence is ever needed — some trades need permits.
- Confusing “limited life” with “limited liability”.

statements.s: A sole proprietor has unlimited liability.
A sole proprietorship has perpetual succession.
statements.why: It may end with the owner.

statements.s: Business secrets are easy to keep.
Large capital is easy to raise.

quiz.q: A sole proprietorship is owned by…
quiz.why: A sole proprietorship has only one owner, who runs the business and takes all profit and risk.
A sole proprietor has only his own savings and borrowings, so resources are limited. The others (quick decisions, secrecy, direct reward) are advantages.

quiz.q: Liability of a sole trader is…
quiz.why: A sole trader has unlimited liability. If the business cannot pay debts, his personal property can be used.

quiz.q: Which business suits sole proprietorship best?
quiz.why: A local bakery is small, needs little capital and personal attention, which suits a sole proprietorship. A steel plant, airline and refinery need huge capital.
In law a sole proprietor and the business are not separate, so the business and the owner are the same.

lessons.title: Joint Hindu Family business

story.title: The family firm run by the karta

scenes.text: The Agarwal family has run a cloth business for three generations.
The eldest member, the karta, manages it; children get a share by birth.
This is a Joint Hindu Family (JHF) business.

steps.title: Meaning and features
steps.body:
A business owned and carried on by members of a Hindu Undivided Family, governed by **Hindu law** (the Hindu Succession Act, 1956). Membership is by **birth**; members are **co-parceners**; management is with the **karta** (eldest member).

- Formation: at least two members and ancestral property; no agreement needed.
- **Liability**: karta — unlimited; co-parceners — limited to their share.
- Control: karta.
- Continuity: not affected by death of the karta (next eldest takes over).
- Two systems: *Dayabhaga* (West Bengal, Assam) — only male members as co-parceners traditionally; *Mitakshara* (rest of India). After the 2005 amendment, daughters are also co-parceners by birth.

steps.title: Merits and limitations
steps.body:
**Merits**: effective control by karta, continued existence, limited liability of members, increased loyalty and cooperation.

**Limitations**: limited resources (ancestral property), unlimited liability of karta, dominance of karta, limited managerial skills.

steps.title: Solved example 1: Liability
steps.body: Debts ₹50 lakh; business assets ₹35 lakh. The karta’s personal assets can be used for the ₹15 lakh balance; other co-parceners lose only their share in the business.

steps.title: Solved example 2: Continuity
steps.body: The karta dies. The business does not end; the next senior member becomes karta → **continuity**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying membership is by agreement — it is by birth.
- Saying all members have unlimited liability.
- Forgetting that the 2005 amendment made daughters co-parceners.

pairs: System in West Bengal and Assam

quiz.q: Membership in a JHF business is by…
quiz.why: Membership of a Hindu Undivided Family (JHF) business is by birth into the family, and not by agreement or registration.
The karta, who manages the JHF business, has unlimited liability. Other members' liability is limited to their share in the business.

quiz.q: JHF continues after the karta’s death because…
quiz.why: The JHF business continues even after the karta dies, because the next eldest member takes over as karta.
After the 2005 amendment, daughters became co-parceners with the same rights as sons in a Hindu undivided family.

quiz.q: A limitation of JHF business is…
quiz.why: The karta has dominance in running the business, and other members may feel the karta is not fair, which is a limitation. Continuity and loyalty are advantages.

lessons.title: Partnership: meaning, features, merits and limitations

scenes.text: Aman has money; Sara has café experience. They agree to run a café and share profits 3:2.
Their agreement makes them partners.
The Indian Partnership Act, 1932 governs them.

steps.title: Meaning and features
steps.body:
Section 4 of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932 (in our words): partnership is the relation between persons who have agreed to share profits of a business carried on by all or any of them acting for all.

- **Formation** by agreement (oral or written); at least 2 partners; maximum **50** (under the Companies Act, 2013 rules).
- **Unlimited and joint liability** of general partners.
- Risk bearing and profit sharing by agreement.
- Decision making and control shared.
- **Mutual agency**: each partner is an agent and principal of the others.
- Continuity can end on death, retirement, insolvency or insanity of a partner unless the others agree to continue.
- Not a separate legal entity.

steps.title: Merits and limitations
steps.body:
**Merits**: ease of formation and closure, balanced decisions, more funds, sharing of risks, secrecy.

**Limitations**: unlimited liability, limited resources (cap on members), possibility of conflicts, lack of continuity, lack of public confidence (accounts not published).

steps.title: Solved example 1: Mutual agency
steps.body: Sara orders ₹80,000 of coffee machines for the café without telling Aman. The seller can recover the money from the firm (and from Aman personally if needed) because Sara acted as an **agent** of the firm.

steps.title: Solved example 2: Joint liability
steps.body: Firm debts ₹10 lakh, firm assets ₹6 lakh. Aman is wealthy, Sara is not. Creditors may recover the full ₹4 lakh from Aman; Aman can later claim Sara’s share from her.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing maximum partners as 10/20 (older limits) — the current limit is 50 under the Companies Act, 2013 rules.
- Saying a written agreement is compulsory — oral is valid, though written is advisable.
- Saying a partnership is a separate legal person.

statements.s: A partnership can be formed by an oral agreement.
statements.why: Written deed is advisable but not compulsory.

statements.s: Each partner is an agent of the firm.
Partners always have limited liability.
The maximum number of partners is 50.

quiz.q: Partnership in India is governed by…
quiz.why: Partnership in India is governed by the Indian Partnership Act, 1932. The Companies Act is for companies.
A partnership needs at least two persons, so the minimum number of partners is 2.

options: each partner is agent and principal
quiz.why: Mutual agency means each partner is both an agent and a principal for the others. So one partner's acts bind the firm and the other partners.
A limitation of partnership is the possibility of conflicts among partners, since decisions are made jointly. Shared risk and more funds are advantages.
Partnership firms are not required to publish their accounts, so the public has less confidence than in a company.

lessons.title: Partnership: types of partners, partnership deed and registration

scenes.text: Aman’s uncle invests ₹5 lakh in the café but never comes to work.
A famous chef lets the café use his name, though he has no share.
Partners differ — and the deed sets the rules.

steps.title: Types of partners
steps.body:
- **Active**: contributes capital, takes part in management, unlimited liability.
- **Sleeping/dormant**: contributes capital and shares profit but does not take part; unlimited liability.
- **Secret**: participates, but association not known to the public; unlimited liability.
- **Nominal**: lends only name; no capital or profit share; liable to third parties.
- **Partner by estoppel**: by words or conduct gives an impression of being a partner → liable to those who relied on it.
- **Partner by holding out**: declared as a partner and does not deny it publicly → liable.
- **Minor**: can be admitted to the *benefits* only, with consent of all; liability limited to his share; on majority, must decide within 6 months whether to become a partner.

steps.title: Types of partnership
steps.body:
- By **duration**: *partnership at will* (no fixed term, ends by notice) and *particular partnership* (for a specific venture or period).
- By **liability**: *general* (all unlimited) and *limited partnership* (at least one unlimited; others limited — in India the separate **LLP Act, 2008** created Limited Liability Partnerships).

steps.title: Partnership deed
steps.body: A written agreement, preferably stamped: name of firm, nature and location of business, duration, capital contribution, profit-sharing ratio, interest on capital/drawings, salaries/commission, duties and rights, admission/retirement/expulsion rules, settlement of accounts on dissolution, dispute resolution.

steps.title: Registration
steps.body:
Registration with the **Registrar of Firms** is *optional* in India, but an unregistered firm suffers: a partner cannot sue the firm or other partners; the firm cannot sue third parties; the firm cannot claim set-off. Third parties can still sue the firm.

Steps: application in prescribed form (name, place, date of joining, duration, partners’ addresses), signed by all partners, fee paid; Registrar enters it in the Register of Firms and issues a certificate.

steps.title: Solved example 1: Identify the partner
steps.body: (a) Uncle invests, no work → *sleeping partner*. (b) Chef lends name only → *nominal partner*. (c) Aman tells a supplier that his friend Tina is a partner and Tina keeps quiet → Tina may be liable as a *partner by holding out*.

steps.title: Solved example 2: Effect of non-registration
steps.body: An unregistered firm’s customer refuses to pay ₹2 lakh. The firm **cannot sue** the customer. Lesson: register to protect legal rights.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying registration is compulsory in India.
- Saying a minor can be a full partner with unlimited liability.
- Confusing sleeping (has capital) with nominal (only name).

pairs: Implies he is a partner by conduct

quiz.q: Registration of a partnership in India is…
quiz.why: Registration of a partnership firm in India is optional, but an unregistered firm faces some disabilities, so it is advised.
An unregistered firm cannot sue third parties to enforce its claims. It can still do business and be sued by others.
A minor admitted to the benefits of a partnership has liability limited to his share in the firm. He is not personally liable.

quiz.q: A partnership for building one bridge is…
quiz.why: A particular partnership is formed for a specific project, such as building one bridge, and ends when the work is done.
A sleeping (silent) partner gives capital and shares in profit but does not take part in management. Still, he has unlimited liability like the others.

lessons.title: Cooperative societies

scenes.text: Hundreds of small dairy farmers in a village each sell a few litres of milk.
Alone, middlemen pay them little; together, they form a cooperative and sell directly.
India’s dairy cooperatives became a global success story.

steps.title: Meaning and features
steps.body:
A voluntary association of persons who join together for mutual welfare. Registration under the **Cooperative Societies Act, 1912** (or the relevant State Act) is **compulsory**; minimum **10 adult members**.

- Voluntary membership; open to all with common interest.
- **Legal status**: separate entity after registration.
- **Limited liability** to capital contributed.
- Control by elected managing committee — **one member, one vote**.
- Service motive (not profit maximisation).

steps.title: Merits and limitations
steps.body:
**Merits**: equality in voting, limited liability, stable existence, economy in operations, government support (tax, loans), ease of formation.

**Limitations**: limited resources, inefficient management (honorary members), lack of secrecy, government control (audit, returns), differences of opinion.

steps.title: Types
steps.body:
- **Consumers’ cooperative**: buy in bulk, sell to members at fair prices.
- **Producers’ cooperative**: supply inputs to small producers.
- **Marketing cooperative**: pool output of small producers and sell.
- **Farmers’ cooperative**: joint farming for large-scale benefits.
- **Credit cooperative**: loans to members at low interest.
- **Cooperative housing society**: houses for members at reasonable cost.

steps.title: Solved example 1: Identify the type
steps.body: (a) Farmers pool milk and sell to the city → *marketing* cooperative. (b) Employees of a bank form a society giving loans at 8% → *credit*. (c) Teachers form a society to build flats → *housing*.

steps.title: Solved example 2: Voting
steps.body: A member holding 100 shares and another holding 2 shares each get **one vote** — unlike a company, where votes depend on shares.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying registration is optional (it is compulsory).
- Saying votes depend on capital.
- Saying the main aim is profit — the aim is service to members.

items.text: Shop selling groceries to members at fair prices
Weavers pool cloth and sell abroad

quiz.q: Minimum members for a cooperative society:
quiz.why: A cooperative society needs at least 10 adult members to be formed.
In a cooperative, each member has one vote, whatever the number of shares held. This makes it democratic.

quiz.q: Main motive of a cooperative is…
quiz.why: The main motive of a cooperative is service to its members and mutual welfare, rather than profit.
A cooperative member's liability is limited to the capital he has contributed.
Cooperatives often have limited resources because their members are usually small contributors. Limited liability and equal voting are advantages.

lessons.title: Joint stock company and choosing a form

scenes.text: Aman and Sara now want 50 cafés across India.
They need crores of rupees and want limited liability.
They form a company under the Companies Act, 2013.

steps.title: Meaning and features
steps.body:
A **company** is an artificial person created by law, with a separate legal entity, perpetual succession and a common seal (optional now), whose capital is divided into transferable shares.

- **Artificial person**, **separate legal entity** (can own property, sue and be sued).
- **Formation** is time-consuming and costly (incorporation under the Companies Act, 2013).
- **Perpetual succession**: not affected by death/insolvency of members.
- **Control** by a Board of Directors elected by shareholders.
- **Limited liability** of members to the unpaid amount of their shares.
- **Risk bearing** by shareholders.

steps.title: Private vs public company
steps.body:
- **Private company**: minimum **2** members, maximum **200** (excluding employees); restricts transfer of shares; cannot invite the public to subscribe to securities; minimum 2 directors; name ends with “Private Limited”.
- **Public company**: minimum **7** members, no maximum; shares freely transferable; can invite the public; minimum 3 directors; name ends with “Limited”.
- **One Person Company (OPC)**: a private company with a single member.

steps.title: Merits and limitations
steps.body:
**Merits**: limited liability, transfer of interest, perpetual existence, scope for expansion, professional management.

**Limitations**: complexity in formation, lack of secrecy, impersonal work environment, numerous regulations, delay in decision-making, oligarchic management (a few directors control), conflict of interests among stakeholders.

steps.title: Choice of form of business
steps.body:
Consider: **cost and ease of set-up**, **liability**, **continuity**, **management ability**, **capital considerations**, **degree of control**, **nature of business**.

- Small capital, personal service → sole proprietorship/partnership.
- Large capital, limited liability, continuity → company.
- Mutual welfare of weaker sections → cooperative.

steps.title: Solved example 1: Limited liability
steps.body: Ravi holds 1,000 shares of ₹10 each, ₹6 paid. On winding up, he can be asked to pay at most the unpaid ₹4 × 1,000 = **₹4,000**, not more.

steps.title: Solved example 2: Choose the form
steps.body: (a) A large steel plant → public company. (b) A family-owned software start-up wanting to avoid public offering → private company. (c) Ten tea growers wanting joint marketing → cooperative. (d) A single tailor → sole proprietorship.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing that a private company can invite the public to buy shares.
- Using the old limit of 50 members for private companies (now 200).
- Saying shareholders manage the company directly — the Board does.

a.text: Aman and Sara want ₹20 crore to open 50 cafés and want to protect their personal assets. Which form should they choose?

choices.label: Stay a partnership
choices.feedback: Partners have unlimited liability and the firm can have at most 50 partners.

choices.label: Form a company
choices.feedback: Limited liability and capital from many shareholders.

p.text: A creditor sues after a loss — their homes are at risk. Try again?

choices.label: Convert to a company
choices.feedback: Good recovery.

c.text: They want to stay closely held for now, with transfer restrictions. Private or public?

choices.label: Private company
choices.feedback: 2–200 members, no public invitation.

choices.label: Public company
choices.feedback: Possible later, but needs 7+ members and more compliance.

end1.text: They incorporate a private limited company. Later, an IPO can convert it to a public company.

end2.text: A public company works but brings heavier compliance before they need it.

quiz.q: Maximum members in a private company:
quiz.why: A private company can have at most 200 members, not counting employees who are members. A public company has no upper limit.

quiz.q: Minimum members for a public company:
quiz.why: A public company needs a minimum of 7 members. A private company needs at least 2.
Perpetual succession means the company continues to exist even if members die, leave or change, since it is a separate legal entity.
A shareholder's liability is limited to the unpaid amount on the shares held. Personal assets cannot be used to pay the company's debts.
A private company restricts the transfer of its shares. It cannot invite the public to subscribe, and it has a limit on members.

questions.q: A sole proprietor’s liability is…
questions.why: A sole proprietor has unlimited liability, so his personal assets can be used to pay the business's debts.

questions.q: JHF business is managed by the…
questions.why: The JHF business is managed by the eldest member, who is called the karta.

questions.q: Partnership in India is governed by the Act of…
questions.why: Partnership in India is governed by the Indian Partnership Act of 1932.

questions.q: Registration of a cooperative society is…
questions.why: Registration of a cooperative society is compulsory, and it gives the society a separate legal identity.

questions.q: A nominal partner…
questions.why: A nominal partner lends only his name to the firm. He gives no capital and takes no part in management or profit, but is liable to outsiders.

questions.q: Maximum number of partners (current rules):
questions.why: The maximum number of partners is 50 under current rules (Companies Act 2013 and its rules).

questions.q: Assertion (A): A company has perpetual succession. Reason (R): It is a separate legal entity created by law.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true and R explains A. A company is a separate legal entity created by law, so it continues even if members change. That is perpetual succession.

questions.q: Case: Meena holds 500 shares of ₹10 each, ₹7 paid. Maximum further liability?
questions.why: Shares are ₹10 each with ₹7 paid, so ₹3 per share is unpaid. Further liability = ₹3 × 500 = ₹1,500.

questions.q: Which has “one member, one vote”?
questions.why: In a cooperative each member has one vote, whatever their share capital. In a company, votes depend on shares.

questions.q: An unregistered partnership firm cannot…
options: sue third parties for its claims
questions.why: An unregistered partnership cannot sue third parties to enforce its claims. It can still be sued, hire staff and buy goods.

questions.q: Case: Tina is introduced by partners as a partner and she does not deny it. A supplier gives credit relying on it. Tina is…
options: liable as partner by holding out
questions.why: Tina allowed herself to be shown as a partner and did not deny it, and the supplier relied on that. So she is liable as a partner by holding out (estoppel).

questions.q: Which statement about a private company is FALSE?
questions.why: A private company cannot invite the public to subscribe to its shares, so that statement is false. The other three statements are true.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Co-parceners in a JHF have limited liability. Reason (R): Only the karta has unlimited liability.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both statements are true and R explains A. In a JHF only the karta has unlimited liability, so the other co-parceners are liable only up to their share in the business.

questions.q: Case: Weavers in Varanasi pool their saris and sell them in Delhi to avoid middlemen. This is a…
questions.why: Weavers pooling their products to sell directly and avoid middlemen are forming a marketing cooperative. A consumers' cooperative serves buyers.

questions.q: A minor admitted to benefits of partnership must, on attaining majority, decide within…
questions.why: A minor admitted to partnership benefits must decide within 6 months of becoming an adult whether to become a partner or leave.

questions.q: Which form best suits a business needing huge capital, limited liability and continuity?
questions.why: A public company can raise huge capital from the public, offers limited liability and has perpetual succession. Sole proprietorship and partnership do not.

questions.q: Case: A firm has assets ₹8 lakh and debts ₹14 lakh. Partners A (rich) and B (insolvent). A pays ₹6 lakh. A can…
options: claim B’s share from B’s estate
questions.why: Partners are jointly and severally liable. If B cannot pay his share, A, having paid more than his share, can claim B's share from B's estate.

courses.title: Ch 3 · Private, Public and Global Enterprises
courses.summary: Private and public sectors, departmental undertakings, statutory corporations and government companies, the changing role of the public sector after 1991, global enterprises, joint ventures and public–private partnership.
outcomes: Learners can compare the three forms of public enterprise
Learners can explain the public sector’s changing role
Learners can describe features of MNCs
Learners can explain JVs and PPPs with examples

lessons.title: Private and public sectors; departmental undertakings

scenes.text: Indian Railways is run by a government ministry.
A mobile phone brand is owned by private shareholders.
India’s mixed economy has both sectors side by side.

steps.title: Private and public sector
steps.body: India follows a **mixed economy**. The **private sector** consists of businesses owned by individuals or groups (sole proprietorship, partnership, private and public companies). The **public sector** consists of organisations owned wholly or partly by the government (Central, State or local) — **public sector enterprises (PSEs)**. Industrial Policy Resolutions (1948, 1956) and the 1991 policy shaped their roles.

steps.title: Departmental undertakings
steps.body:
Run as a part of a ministry; e.g., Indian Railways, Posts and Telegraphs (India Post), broadcasting historically.

- **Features**: funded by the Government treasury from budget; subject to accounting and audit like other government departments; employees are government employees; accountable to the ministry; part of government.
- **Merits**: effective control by Parliament, high public accountability, revenue goes to the treasury, suitable for national security matters.
- **Limitations**: lack of flexibility, delays due to red tape, political interference, insensitivity to consumer needs.

steps.title: Solved example 1: Classify
steps.body: (a) India Post → departmental undertaking (public sector). (b) A family-owned tea company → private sector. (c) A listed private bank → private sector (public *company* but not public *sector*).

steps.title: Solved example 2: Why departmental form for defence?
steps.body: Defence production needs secrecy and strict government control → departmental form gives control and accountability, accepting less flexibility.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing a “public company” (private sector, listed) with a “public sector” enterprise.
- Thinking departmental undertakings have their own separate budget and legal entity — they do not.

statements.s: A public company is always in the public sector.
statements.why: Listed private companies are private sector.

statements.s: Departmental undertakings are financed from the government budget.
Departmental undertakings enjoy high flexibility.
India is a mixed economy.

quiz.why: Indian Railways is run by a government ministry as a departmental undertaking. It is not a company or a corporation.

quiz.q: Employees of a departmental undertaking are…
quiz.why: Employees of a departmental undertaking are government employees (civil servants) and follow government service rules.

quiz.q: A limitation of departmental undertakings is…
quiz.why: A limitation of departmental undertakings is red tape, or slow, rule-bound procedures. Accountability and parliamentary control are features, not limitations.
A mixed economy has both private and public sectors working together.
The departmental form suits activities needing secrecy and tight government control, like defence and security.

lessons.title: Statutory corporations and government companies

scenes.text: LIC was created by a special Act of Parliament in 1956.
Many central PSUs are registered under the Companies Act with the government holding a majority of shares.
Two different public-enterprise forms.

steps.title: Statutory corporations
steps.body:
Public enterprises created by a **special Act** of Parliament or State Legislature, which defines powers, functions and rules. Examples: Life Insurance Corporation (LIC Act 1956), Reserve Bank of India (RBI Act 1934), Food Corporation of India, Airports Authority of India.

- **Features**: separate legal entity; financially independent (can borrow, use revenue); employees not government servants; not subject to budget/audit procedures of departments (though audited); wholly owned by the government.
- **Merits**: high independence and flexibility, government does not interfere in finances, autonomy of operations.
- **Limitations**: autonomy limited in practice, rigidity (changes need amending the Act), political interference, corruption risk.

steps.title: Government companies
steps.body:
A company in which **not less than 51% of paid-up share capital** is held by the Central and/or State Governments (Companies Act, 2013). Examples include Hindustan Aeronautics Ltd, Coal India Ltd, SAIL.

- **Features**: registered under the Companies Act; separate legal entity; management under the Act and its articles; employees appointed under its own rules; funds from government and private shareholders; can raise money from capital markets.
- **Merits**: easy to form (Companies Act, no separate Act), own memorandum and articles, efficient management, healthy competition with private sector.
- **Limitations**: Companies Act provisions not fully applied in practice, government sole/main shareholder → constitutional responsibility evaded, government appoints directors (political influence).

steps.title: Solved example 1: Identify the form
steps.body: (a) Created by a special Act, fully government-owned → statutory corporation. (b) Registered company with government holding 60% → government company. (c) Run as a branch of the Ministry → departmental undertaking.

steps.title: Solved example 2: Shareholding test
steps.body: Government holds 45% of a listed company and private investors 55% → **not** a government company (below 51%).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying government companies are created by special Acts — that is statutory corporations.
- Using 50% instead of “not less than 51%”.
- Thinking statutory corporations’ employees are civil servants.

items.text: Powers defined in its own Act

quiz.why: LIC was set up by an Act of Parliament (LIC Act 1956), so it is a statutory corporation.

quiz.q: A government company needs government shareholding of at least…
quiz.why: A government company needs the government to hold at least 51% of its paid-up share capital.
A statutory corporation is created by a special Act of Parliament or a state legislature.

quiz.q: A government company is registered under the…
quiz.why: A government company is registered under the Companies Act, like any other company, but with government shareholding.

quiz.q: A limitation of statutory corporations is…
quiz.why: A statutory corporation works under its Act, so it is rigid and the Act has to be amended to change its powers. Flexibility and financial autonomy are advantages.

lessons.title: Changing role of the public sector

scenes.text: After independence, the government built steel plants, dams and power stations.
By 1991 many PSUs made losses; the economy needed reform.
The New Industrial Policy, 1991 changed the public sector’s role.

steps.title: Original role (1950s–1980s)
steps.body:
- **Development of infrastructure** — steel, power, transport.
- **Regional balance** — industries in backward areas (e.g., steel plants at Bhilai, Rourkela, Durgapur).
- **Economies of scale** in capital-intensive industries.
- **Check over concentration of economic power** in a few private hands.
- **Import substitution** — self-reliance in heavy industry.

steps.title: 1991 policy changes
steps.body:
- **Reduction in reserved industries**: from 17 to 8 in 1991, and later fewer (now mainly atomic energy and railways operations).
- **Disinvestment** — selling part of government shareholding to private investors/public.
- **Policy on sick units** — referred to bodies like BIFR (Board for Industrial and Financial Reconstruction) for revival or closure.
- **Memorandum of Understanding (MoU)** — targets agreed between management and government with more autonomy and accountability.

steps.title: Solved example 1: Identify the role
steps.body: Building a steel plant in a tribal district to create jobs → *regional balance*. Government producing heavy machinery in the 1960s instead of importing → *import substitution*.

steps.title: Solved example 2: Disinvestment
steps.body: The government sells 10% of its holding in a profitable PSU through an offer for sale; ownership is still majority-government → partial **disinvestment** raises funds and introduces market discipline.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying all PSUs were privatised in 1991 — the policy reduced reservation and began disinvestment gradually.
- Confusing disinvestment (selling shares) with liberalisation (removing controls).

events.text: Industrial Policy Resolution expands public sector role
BIFR set up for sick industrial companies
New Industrial Policy: dereservation, disinvestment, MoUs

quiz.q: Reserved industries in 1991 were cut from 17 to…
quiz.why: After the 1991 industrial policy, the number of industries reserved for the public sector was cut from 17 to 8 (later reduced further).

quiz.q: Selling part of government’s shares in a PSU is…
quiz.why: Selling part of the government's shareholding in a public sector undertaking is called disinvestment.
Under the MoU system, PSUs are given targets, and in return get more autonomy but are held accountable for results.

quiz.q: Locating steel plants in backward areas served…
quiz.why: Locating steel plants in backward areas helped balanced regional development, which was a public sector objective.
Sick public sector units were referred to the Board for Industrial and Financial Reconstruction (BIFR) for revival plans.

lessons.title: Global enterprises (MNCs)

scenes.text: A smartphone is designed in one country, its chips are made in another and it is assembled in India.
The company that controls all this operates in dozens of countries.
It is a multinational corporation (MNC).

steps.title: Features of global enterprises
steps.body:
- **Huge capital resources** — can raise funds from many markets.
- **Foreign collaboration** — tie-ups with local firms (technology, brands).
- **Advanced technology** — global quality standards.
- **Product innovation** — large R&D budgets.
- **Marketing strategies** — aggressive, global brands.
- **Expansion of market territory** — operations across countries.
- **Centralised control** — head office in the home country controls subsidiaries.

steps.title: Solved example 1: Identify the feature
steps.body: An MNC sets up an R&D centre in Bengaluru to design new medicines → *product innovation*. It decides prices for all countries from its global headquarters → *centralised control*.

steps.title: Solved example 2: Benefits and concerns for India
steps.body: Benefits: investment, jobs, technology, exports. Concerns: competition for small firms, profits sent abroad, dependence on foreign technology. Policy tries to balance both.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying MNCs have decentralised control in all matters — key decisions are centralised.
- Assuming only Western firms are MNCs; Indian firms also operate globally.

quiz.q: Key decisions in an MNC are…
quiz.why: In an MNC the key decisions are made at the headquarters, so control is centralised, even though it operates in many countries.
MNCs usually have huge capital resources, which they can raise from many countries. They also have advanced technology and R&D.
A concern about MNCs is that they compete with small local firms, which may be pushed out. Jobs, technology and investment are benefits.
Advertising a global brand worldwide reflects the marketing strategies of MNCs.
Yes, Indian companies can be MNCs when they operate in several countries, such as Tata or Infosys.

lessons.title: Joint ventures and public–private partnership

scenes.text: A foreign car maker partners an Indian firm to make cars in India.
A new expressway is built by a private company, with the government sharing risks.
Joint ventures and PPPs combine strengths.

steps.title: Joint ventures (JV)
steps.body:
Two or more firms join to achieve a common objective, sharing resources, risks and control. Types: **contractual JV** (no new firm; cooperation under contract, e.g., franchising) and **equity-based JV** (a new firm jointly owned).

**Benefits**: increased resources and capacity, access to new markets and distribution networks, access to technology, innovation, low cost of production, established brand name.

steps.title: Public–private partnership (PPP)
steps.body:
A model where the government and private sector share responsibilities to build and operate public infrastructure/services (roads, airports, metro, power, water).

**Features**: sharing of risks and rewards (allocated to the party best able to handle them); private sector brings investment, efficiency and technology; government provides regulation, land, approvals and may share revenue; a long-term contract (often 20–30 years).

steps.title: Solved example 1: Which JV type?
steps.body: (a) An Indian and a Japanese firm create a new company 51:49 to make motorcycles → *equity-based JV*. (b) A global coffee brand lets an Indian firm run outlets under its name for a fee → *contractual JV*.

steps.title: Solved example 2: PPP
steps.body: A private consortium builds and runs an airport for 30 years, collecting user charges and paying a revenue share to the government; at the end, the airport returns to the government. Risks of construction lie with the private partner; land acquisition with the government.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing a JV with a merger — in a JV both partners continue to exist separately.
- Saying in a PPP the government gives up ownership permanently.

a.text: An Indian firm with a strong dealer network wants advanced battery technology. A foreign firm has the technology but no Indian distribution. Best option?

choices.label: Compete separately
choices.feedback: Both miss what the other has.

choices.label: Form a joint venture
choices.feedback: Combine technology with distribution.

b.text: Both struggle — high cost and slow sales. Reconsider?

choices.label: Form a JV now
choices.feedback: Better.

c.text: Should they create a new jointly owned company or just sign a technology licence?

choices.label: New jointly owned company
choices.feedback: Equity-based JV — shared ownership and control.

choices.label: Technology licence only
choices.feedback: Contractual JV — simpler, less control sharing.

e1.text: Equity JV launched: shared risk, reward and control.

e2.text: Contractual JV: cooperation without a new firm.

quiz.why: An equity-based joint venture creates a new company that is jointly owned by the partners, who share ownership, risk and profits.
