A franchise is based on a contract between the franchisor and franchisee, so it is a contractual joint venture. No new firm is made.

quiz.q: In PPP, risks are allocated to…
options: the party best able to manage them
quiz.why: In a PPP, risks are shared in the way that each risk goes to the party best able to manage it, either the government or the private partner.
A joint venture gives access to new markets, along with shared costs, technology and risk. Unlimited liability and loss of identity are not benefits.
PPP (public–private partnership) is common in infrastructure such as roads, airports and metro rail.

questions.q: Mixed economy has…
questions.why: A mixed economy has both a public sector and a private sector.

questions.q: India Post is a…
questions.why: India Post is run by a government ministry (the Department of Posts), so it is a departmental undertaking.

questions.q: RBI was set up under a special Act. It is a…
questions.why: The RBI was set up under a special Act, so it is a statutory corporation.

questions.q: Government company: government shareholding of at least…
questions.why: For a company to be a government company, the government must hold at least 51% of its shares.

questions.q: Which is NOT a feature of MNCs?
questions.why: MNCs operate in many countries, so a small market territory is not their feature. They have huge capital, advanced technology and centralised control.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Statutory corporations are financially independent. Reason (R): They are funded only through the annual budget.
questions.why: The assertion is true: statutory corporations are financially independent and can use their revenues and borrow. The reason is false, as they are not funded only by the annual budget.

questions.q: Disinvestment means…
options: selling government shares to private parties/public
questions.why: Disinvestment is the sale of the government's shares in public sector undertakings to private parties or the public.

questions.q: Case: A foreign retailer allows an Indian firm to open stores in its brand name for a royalty. This is…
questions.why: Allowing another firm to use a brand name for royalty under a contract is a franchise, which is a contractual joint venture.

questions.q: Which was a role of the public sector before 1991?
questions.why: Before 1991 the public sector helped import substitution, making goods at home to cut imports, and aimed at self-reliance.

questions.q: Departmental undertakings are subject to…
options: budgeting, accounting and audit controls of government
questions.why: Departmental undertakings are under the budgeting, accounting and audit controls of the government, like any government department.

questions.q: Case: Government holds 74% in Company X registered under the Companies Act. X is…
questions.why: A company registered under the Companies Act with government holding of 74% (above 51%) is a government company.

questions.q: A key limitation of government companies is…
questions.why: A limitation of government companies is political influence, since the government appoints board members. This can reduce efficiency.

questions.q: Assertion (A): A public company can be in the private sector. Reason (R): “Public company” refers to share structure, “public sector” to ownership by government.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true and R explains A. 'Public company' refers to the way shares are held, which can be by private owners. 'Public sector' means ownership by government.

questions.q: Case: A metro line is built by a private firm, which operates it for 30 years and then hands it to the state. Model?
questions.why: A private firm builds, runs a metro for 30 years and then hands it to the state, which is a PPP, in the form of build-operate-transfer.

questions.q: MoU in PSUs relates to…
options: targets and autonomy agreed with government
questions.why: A Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) is a performance agreement between a PSU and the government, setting targets in return for autonomy.

questions.q: Which pair is wrongly matched?
questions.why: The RBI is a statutory body set up by a special Act, not a private company. The other pairs are correct.

questions.q: Case: An MNC sets prices in India from its head office and runs R&D in Pune. Which two features?
questions.why: Setting prices from the head office shows centralised control. Running R&D shows product innovation. These are features of MNCs.

courses.title: Ch 4 · Business Services
courses.summary: Nature and types of services; banking types, functions and e-banking; insurance principles and types; communication, transport and warehousing.
outcomes: Learners can explain the features of services
Learners can describe bank functions and digital payment systems
Learners can apply the principles of insurance to cases
Learners can classify warehouses and their functions

lessons.title: Nature and types of services

scenes.text: Neha gets a haircut; she cannot take it home in a box or return it.
Her friend buys a shampoo bottle — that she can store and return.
Services differ from goods in five key ways.

steps.title: Meaning and the 5 I’s
steps.body:
**Services** are intangible activities that satisfy needs and are offered for sale. Key features:

- **Intangibility**: cannot be touched; quality is judged by experience.
- **Inconsistency**: service quality varies from time to time and person to person (no standardisation).
- **Inseparability**: production and consumption happen together.
- **Inventory (less)**: cannot be stored for future use.
- **Involvement**: the customer participates in delivery (e.g., telling the tailor the fit).

steps.title: Goods vs services
steps.body: Goods are tangible, can be stored, standardised, production and consumption separable, ownership transfers. Services are intangible, cannot be stored, vary, produced and consumed simultaneously, no transfer of ownership (only experience/benefit).

steps.title: Types of services
steps.body:
- **Business services**: used by businesses — banking, insurance, transport, warehousing, communication.
- **Social services**: provided voluntarily for social goals — NGOs providing education/health in villages.
- **Personal services**: experienced differently by each customer — tourism, recreation, restaurants.

steps.title: Solved example 1: Identify the feature
steps.body: An empty seat on a flight that leaves cannot be sold later → *inventory (less)*. Two meals at the same restaurant taste slightly different → *inconsistency*.

steps.title: Solved example 2: Classify the service
steps.body: A courier company delivering parcels for an e-commerce firm → business service. A trust running free eye camps → social service. A holiday package → personal service.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling inconsistency “inseparability”.
- Saying services can be stored (empty hotel rooms cannot).
- Forgetting customer involvement as a feature.

activity.prompt: Match the feature with the example
pairs: You cannot touch a doctor’s advice
Concert is produced as you watch
Unsold cinema seat is lost forever
Customer explains the design to a tailor

quiz.q: Which is a feature of services?
quiz.why: Inseparability means a service is produced and used at the same time, so it cannot be separated from the provider. Services are intangible and cannot be stored.
Tourism is mainly a personal service, as it serves the individual traveller's experience. Business services serve other firms.
Banking for firms, such as loans and accounts, is a business service. It supports business activity.

quiz.q: Services cannot be standardised fully because of…
quiz.why: Services cannot be fully standardised because of inconsistency: the quality can differ each time, as it depends on people and conditions.

quiz.q: An empty train berth after departure shows…
quiz.why: A seat on a train that leaves empty is lost, because a service cannot be stored. This shows the feature of lack of inventory.

lessons.title: Banking: types, functions and e-banking

scenes.text: Priya’s cake studio needs a current account, a small loan and a way to accept payments.
Customers pay her by UPI; she pays suppliers by NEFT.
Banks and digital banking make this possible.

steps.title: Types of banks
steps.body:
- **Commercial banks**: accept deposits, give loans; public sector (e.g., SBI), private sector, foreign banks.
- **Cooperative banks**: under cooperative laws, serve members, often rural.
- **Specialised banks**: for specific purposes (e.g., export–import, industrial development).
- **Central bank**: the **Reserve Bank of India** — banker to government and banks, issues currency, controls credit and monetary policy.

steps.title: Functions of commercial banks
steps.body:
- **Acceptance of deposits**: savings, current, fixed (term), recurring.
- **Lending of funds**: loans, cash credit, overdraft, discounting of bills.
- **Cheque facility** and payment services.
- **Remittance of funds**: drafts, pay orders, NEFT/RTGS/IMPS.
- **Allied services**: lockers, collection of bills/dividends, underwriting, investment advice.

steps.title: E-banking
steps.body:
Banking through electronic channels: internet banking, mobile banking, ATMs, debit/credit cards, **NEFT** (National Electronic Funds Transfer — batch settlement), **RTGS** (Real Time Gross Settlement — individual, real-time, typically for ₹2 lakh and above), **IMPS** (instant, 24×7), **UPI** (instant mobile payments via virtual payment address/QR).

**Benefits**: 24×7 access, lower transaction cost, fewer cash risks, record of transactions, convenience. **Risks**: phishing, fraud — never share OTP/PIN.

steps.title: Solved example 1: Which account?
steps.body: Priya’s business makes many daily transactions → *current account* (no limit on transactions, usually no interest). Her personal savings → *savings account*. Surplus cash for one year → *fixed deposit*.

steps.title: Solved example 2: Overdraft vs cash credit
steps.body: Overdraft: allowed to withdraw beyond the current account balance up to a limit. Cash credit: a borrowing limit against security of stock/receivables, interest on amount used. Both charge interest only on the amount actually used.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying RBI gives loans to the public — it is a banker to banks and government.
- Mixing up RTGS (real-time, large value) and NEFT (batch).
- Sharing OTPs “to verify” — banks never ask for OTP/PIN.

pairs: Money locked for a term at higher interest
Withdraw beyond balance up to a limit

quiz.q: The central bank of India is…
quiz.why: The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) is the central bank of India. SBI is a commercial bank and NABARD deals with agriculture.

quiz.q: Which deposit suits a business with many daily transactions?
quiz.why: A current account has many transactions a day and no limit on withdrawals, so it suits businesses. Savings, fixed and recurring accounts are for saving.
NEFT settles payments in batches at set times, so it is not real time. RTGS settles in real time.

options: using public Wi-Fi for banking always
quiz.why: Never sharing your PIN or OTP with anyone is the safe practice. Callers who ask for them are usually fraudsters.

quiz.q: Discounting of bills is a form of…
quiz.why: Discounting a bill means the bank pays the money now, less a charge, and collects later. This is lending by the bank.

lessons.title: Insurance: meaning and principles

scenes.text: A fire destroys stock worth ₹5 lakh in Ravi’s shop; he had insured it for ₹4 lakh.
The insurer pays — but only what the policy and the principles allow.
Insurance works on seven fundamental principles.

steps.title: Meaning and function
steps.body: **Insurance** is a contract in which the **insurer** agrees, for a consideration called **premium**, to compensate the **insured** for a specified loss (or pay a sum on an event). It spreads the losses of a few over many (pooling of risk). Functions: provide certainty, protection, risk sharing, help capital formation.

steps.title: Principles
steps.body:
1. **Utmost good faith (uberrimae fidei)**: both parties must disclose all material facts.
2. **Insurable interest**: the insured must suffer financial loss if the subject is damaged.
3. **Indemnity**: compensation only up to the actual loss (no profit) — applies to non-life insurance.
4. **Proximate cause**: loss is covered only if the nearest (dominant) cause is an insured peril.
5. **Subrogation**: after paying, the insurer gets the insured’s rights against third parties/salvage.
6. **Contribution**: if insured with more than one insurer, they share the loss proportionately; total recovery cannot exceed loss.
7. **Mitigation**: the insured must take reasonable steps to minimise loss.

steps.title: Solved example 1: Indemnity
steps.body: Stock worth ₹5 lakh insured for ₹4 lakh; loss ₹3 lakh. Insurer pays **₹3 lakh** (actual loss, within sum insured) — not ₹4 lakh. (Under an *average clause*, if under-insured, payment may be proportionately reduced: 3 × 4/5 = ₹2.4 lakh.)

steps.title: Solved example 2: Contribution
steps.body: Property insured with A for ₹6 lakh and with B for ₹4 lakh; loss ₹5 lakh. A pays 5 × 6/10 = **₹3 lakh**; B pays **₹2 lakh**. Total = loss.

steps.title: Solved example 3: Proximate cause
steps.body: A ship is insured against fire, not against storms. A storm makes it sink. Not covered — the proximate cause (storm) is not an insured peril.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying indemnity applies to life insurance — life cannot be valued; a fixed sum is paid.
- Confusing subrogation (insurer steps into insured’s shoes) with contribution (sharing among insurers).
- Forgetting that hiding a medical condition breaks utmost good faith.

pairs: You must suffer loss if it is damaged
Insurer gets your rights after paying

quiz.why: The principle of indemnity applies to fire, marine and motor insurance, where loss can be valued in money. It does not apply to life insurance, as the value of a life cannot be measured.

quiz.q: Hiding a heart condition while buying a health policy breaks…
quiz.why: Insurance is based on utmost good faith, which means the insured must disclose all material facts. Hiding a heart condition breaks this principle.

quiz.q: Insured with X ₹3 lakh, Y ₹2 lakh; loss ₹2 lakh. X pays…
quiz.why: With two insurers, the loss is shared in proportion to the sums insured (3 : 2). X pays 3/5 of ₹2 lakh = ₹1.2 lakh.

quiz.q: After paying for a stolen car that is later found, the car belongs to the insurer by…
quiz.why: When the insurer pays for a stolen car in full, it takes over the rights to the car if it is found. This principle is subrogation, which stops the insured from gaining twice.

quiz.q: A tenant can insure the owner’s house against fire only if…
quiz.why: A person can insure a property only if he has insurable interest, meaning he would suffer a financial loss if it is damaged. Just paying the premium is not enough.

lessons.title: Types of insurance

scenes.text: Ravi buys a life policy to protect his family.
His exporter friend insures a shipment going by sea.
His sister buys health cover. Each policy suits a different risk.

steps.title: Life insurance
steps.body: A contract where the insurer pays a fixed sum on death of the insured or on maturity. Elements: contract, utmost good faith, insurable interest (own life, spouse, dependants), not a contract of indemnity. Types of policies: **whole life** (paid on death), **endowment** (paid on maturity or earlier death), **term** (pure protection for a term, low premium), **annuity**, **children’s endowment**.

steps.title: Fire insurance
steps.body: Covers loss or damage by fire during a specified period. Fire must be accidental and actual (ignition); loss must be proximately caused by fire. A contract of indemnity; insurable interest needed both at the time of contract and loss.

steps.title: Marine insurance
steps.body: Covers perils of the sea. Types: **ship (hull)** insurance, **cargo** insurance, **freight** insurance. Insurable interest is needed at the time of loss; indemnity applies.

steps.title: Health and other insurance
steps.body: **Health insurance**: covers hospitalisation and medical expenses (e.g., cashless at network hospitals). Others: **motor** (third-party cover is compulsory under the Motor Vehicles Act), **home**, **crop**, **travel**, **burglary**, **fidelity**, **liability** insurance.

steps.title: Solved example 1: Choose the policy
steps.body: A 30-year-old wants maximum cover at low cost → *term insurance*. A parent wants a lump sum when the child turns 18 → *children’s endowment*.

steps.title: Solved example 2: Marine
steps.body: An exporter ships tea worth ₹20 lakh to Dubai → *cargo insurance*. The shipping company insures its vessel → *hull insurance*. It also insures the freight it will earn → *freight insurance*.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling life insurance a contract of indemnity.
- Forgetting that third-party motor insurance is compulsory.
- Mixing up hull and cargo insurance.

items.text: Cargo of rice shipped to Africa

options: pure protection for a fixed term
quiz.why: Term insurance gives pure risk cover for a fixed number of years. It pays only if the insured dies in the term and has no savings or maturity element.

quiz.q: Insurable interest in marine insurance must exist at…
quiz.why: In marine insurance the insurable interest must exist at the time of the loss. It need not exist when the policy is taken.

quiz.q: Insurance on goods carried by sea is…
quiz.why: Insurance of goods carried by sea is cargo insurance. Hull insurance covers the ship, and freight insurance covers the shipping company's income.
Motor insurance that is compulsory by law covers third-party liability, which means injury or damage caused to others. Own-damage and theft cover are optional.
An endowment policy pays the sum assured on maturity, or earlier if the insured dies within the term. So it combines saving and protection.

lessons.title: Communication, transportation and warehousing

scenes.text: Priya sends a cake order confirmation by WhatsApp and ships ingredients by courier.
Bulk sugar comes by truck; flour is stored in a warehouse until needed.
These services remove hindrances of place, time and information.

steps.title: Communication services
steps.body:
- **Postal services**: letters, speed post, parcels, money orders, savings schemes, India Post Payments Bank.
- **Telecom services**: mobile and fixed-line phones, internet broadband, satellite and cable services, video conferencing.
- Digital channels help businesses reach customers instantly.

steps.title: Transportation
steps.body: Moves goods and people from one place to another: road, rail, water (inland, coastal, ocean), air, pipeline. Removes the **hindrance of place**; widens markets; helps specialisation. Choice depends on cost, speed, distance, nature of goods (perishables by air/refrigerated road).

steps.title: Warehousing
steps.body:
Storage of goods from production until sale; removes the **hindrance of time**.

- **Types**: private warehouses (own use), public warehouses (licensed, for anyone, fee-based), bonded warehouses (imported goods stored before payment of customs duty), government warehouses (e.g., Central Warehousing Corporation), cooperative warehouses.
- **Functions**: consolidation, break the bulk, stockpiling (seasonal goods), value-added services (packing, grading), price stabilisation, financing (warehouse receipts as security).

steps.title: Solved example 1: Type of warehouse
steps.body: An importer stores wine in a warehouse and pays duty only when releasing bottles for sale → *bonded warehouse*. A farmer stores potatoes in a cold storage run by a licensed operator → *public warehouse*.

steps.title: Solved example 2: Function
steps.body: A wholesaler receives one truckload of soap and divides it into small lots for retailers → *break the bulk*. Wheat harvested in April is stored and sold over the year → *stockpiling*, which also *stabilises prices*.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing bonded and public warehouses.
- Saying warehousing removes the hindrance of place (that is transport).
- Forgetting that warehouse receipts can help raise loans.

pairs: Licensed, open to any user for a fee
Large lot divided into small lots
Seasonal goods stored for year-round sale
Goods from many places combined into one load

quiz.why: Warehousing stores goods from the time of production until they are sold. This removes the hindrance of time.

quiz.q: Goods awaiting customs duty are kept in a…
quiz.why: Imported goods waiting for customs duty to be paid are kept in a bonded warehouse, which is under customs control, and duty is paid when they are taken out.

quiz.q: Fastest mode for perishable high-value goods over long distance is usually…
quiz.why: Air transport is the fastest, so it is used for perishable and high-value goods over long distances. Ships and bullock carts are too slow.

quiz.q: Price stabilisation is a function of…
quiz.why: Warehousing helps price stabilisation, because goods stored in plenty can be released when supply is short. This stops sudden price changes.
Speed post is a fast mail service offered by postal services, that is India Post. Banks, warehouses and insurers do not provide it.

questions.q: Services are…
questions.why: Services are intangible, meaning they cannot be touched or seen. Goods are tangible, and services cannot be stored.

questions.q: RBI is the…
questions.why: The RBI is the central bank of India. It controls money supply and regulates banks, and is not a commercial or cooperative bank.

questions.q: Which principle prevents profit from insurance?
questions.why: The principle of indemnity says the insured can get back only the actual loss and not more. So insurance cannot be used to make a profit.

questions.q: A bonded warehouse stores…
questions.why: A bonded warehouse is licensed by the government to store imported goods until the customs duty is paid.

questions.q: Which service feature means “produced and consumed together”?
questions.why: Inseparability means a service is produced and consumed at the same time, so the provider and the customer cannot be separated.

questions.q: RTGS is used for…
questions.why: RTGS (Real Time Gross Settlement) is used for large-value transfers, which are settled immediately, one by one. NEFT works in batches.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Life insurance is not a contract of indemnity. Reason (R): Loss of life cannot be measured in money.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true and R explains A. Loss of a human life cannot be measured in money, so life insurance is not a contract of indemnity.

questions.q: Insured with P ₹8 lakh and Q ₹2 lakh; loss ₹5 lakh. P pays…
questions.why: With two policies, the loss is shared in the ratio of sums insured: 8 : 2. P pays 5 × 8/10 = ₹4 lakh.

questions.q: Case: A cargo ship insured only against fire sinks in a storm. Claim?
questions.why: The ship was insured only against fire but it sank in a storm. The nearest cause of the loss (the storm) was not insured, so the claim is rejected under the principle of proximate cause.

questions.q: Which account is best for a trader with many daily transactions?
questions.why: A current account allows many deposits and withdrawals a day with no limit, so it suits a trader. FD, RD and PPF are for saving.

questions.q: Case: After a car theft claim is paid, the car is found. Insurer becomes owner under…
questions.why: After paying the full claim for the stolen car, the insurer gets the rights over the car if found. This is subrogation.

questions.q: Breaking bulk is a function of…
questions.why: Breaking bulk, splitting large lots into small lots for retailers, is a function of warehousing. Banks, telecom and insurers do not do this.

questions.q: Case: Stock worth ₹10 lakh insured for ₹6 lakh with an average clause; loss ₹5 lakh. Claim payable?
questions.why: With an average clause, the claim = loss × sum insured ÷ value of stock = 5 lakh × 6/10 = ₹3 lakh. The insured was under-insured, so only part is paid.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Services cannot be stored. Reason (R): Services are intangible and inseparable.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true and R explains A. Services are intangible and produced and consumed together, so they cannot be stored as inventory.

questions.q: Which is a social service?
questions.why: A social service is provided for the welfare of society, not for profit. An NGO running a free village school fits this. Bank loans, hotels and couriers are business services.

questions.q: Case: An exporter insures the freight the shipping company will earn. This is…
questions.why: Insurance of the freight that the shipping company will earn is called freight insurance. Hull covers the ship, and cargo covers the goods.

questions.q: Insured fails to call the fire brigade while the fire spreads. Principle violated?
questions.why: The insured must take reasonable steps to cut down a loss, such as calling the fire brigade. This is the principle of mitigation.

courses.title: Ch 5 · Emerging Modes of Business
courses.summary: E-business and its scope (B2B, B2C, C2C, intra-B, B2E), benefits and limitations, online transactions, payment and security, resources needed, and outsourcing (BPO and KPO).
outcomes: Learners can distinguish e-business from e-commerce
Learners can classify types of e-business
Learners can explain online payments and security risks
Learners can evaluate outsourcing benefits and concerns

lessons.title: E-business: meaning and scope

scenes.text: At midnight, Arjun orders a book on an app; at 7 a.m. it is dispatched.
The seller orders paper online from a mill; staff apply for leave on the company portal.
All of this is e-business.

steps.title: E-business vs e-commerce
steps.body: **E-business** means conducting industry, trade and commerce using computer networks (internet). **E-commerce** is a part of it — buying and selling online. E-business also covers production, inventory, HR, finance and other internal processes done electronically.

steps.title: Scope (types of e-business)
steps.body:
- **B2B** (business to business): a car maker orders parts from suppliers online; e-procurement.
- **B2C** (business to consumer): online retail, banking apps, ticket booking.
- **C2C** (consumer to consumer): selling used goods to other people on a marketplace.
- **Intra-B** (within a business): communication between departments via intranet, ERP.
- **B2E** (business to employees): online training, leave and payroll portals.
- **C2B**: consumers offer prices or services to firms (e.g., freelancers bidding).

steps.title: Solved example 1: Classify
steps.body: (a) A student sells his old bicycle on a classifieds site → C2C. (b) A cement firm buys coal through an online portal → B2B. (c) Employees download payslips from HR portal → B2E. (d) Production and marketing departments share a dashboard → intra-B.

steps.title: Solved example 2: Is it e-business or e-commerce?
steps.body: A company uses software to track inventory between its warehouses — this is **e-business** (internal process), not e-commerce (no buying/selling).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating e-business and e-commerce as the same.
- Calling an online marketplace sale between two individuals B2C.
- Forgetting intra-B and B2E as part of e-business.

items.text: You book a movie ticket on an app
Selling your old phone to a stranger online
Employees apply for leave on HR portal

quiz.why: E-commerce, which is buying and selling online, is a part of e-business. E-business is wider and also includes internal processes.

quiz.q: Online sale of used goods between individuals is…
quiz.why: Selling used goods online from one individual to another is consumer to consumer (C2C).

quiz.q: A supplier portal for a car maker is…
quiz.why: A portal through which a car maker deals with its suppliers is business to business (B2B).
Online payslips that the firm gives to its staff are business to employee (B2E).
E-business includes all the internal and external processes of a firm done online, not just selling or payments.

lessons.title: Benefits and limitations of e-business

scenes.text: A handicraft seller in Jaipur gets orders from Japan without opening a shop there.
But one customer complains: she could not touch the fabric before buying.
E-business brings big gains and some limits.

steps.title: Benefits
steps.body:
- **Ease of formation and lower investment** (no big showroom).
- **Convenience**: 24×7, anytime, anywhere.
- **Speed**: information and transactions move instantly.
- **Global reach/access**: sell worldwide.
- **Movement towards a paperless society**.
- Lower costs and better customer data.

steps.title: Limitations
steps.body:
- **Low personal touch**: no face-to-face interaction.
- **Incongruence between order taking/giving speed and order fulfilment speed** (delivery still takes time).
- **Lack of human touch for product checks**: cannot feel, smell or try.
- **Anonymity**: hard to verify identities.
- **Security risks**: hacking, fraud, viruses.
- **People’s resistance** to new technology.
- **Ethical fallouts**: data misuse, surveillance concerns.

steps.title: Solved example 1: Identify benefit
steps.body: A start-up begins selling T-shirts with just a website and a small warehouse → *ease of formation and lower investment*. A Jaipur seller ships to Japan → *global reach*.

steps.title: Solved example 2: Identify limitation
steps.body: You order in 10 seconds but get the product after 5 days → *incongruence between order and fulfilment speed*. You cannot try on shoes before buying → *lack of personal touch*.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying e-business has no costs — it needs servers, logistics, security.
- Listing “global reach” as a limitation.
- Ignoring ethics and data privacy.

quiz.why: A benefit of e-business is global reach, since a firm can sell to customers in any place. Security risk and low personal touch are limitations.

quiz.q: “You cannot try clothes before buying online” is…
quiz.why: Not being able to try clothes before buying online is a lack of personal touch, which is a limitation of online business.
A paperless society saves paper and reduces cost, so it is a benefit of e-business.

quiz.q: Order in seconds, delivery in days shows…
quiz.why: Order placement takes seconds but delivery takes days, so there is a mismatch between the speed of ordering and the speed of delivery. This is incongruence of speeds.

quiz.q: Data misuse is an example of…
quiz.why: Misuse of customer data is an ethical problem of online business, which is called ethical fallout.

lessons.title: Online transactions, payments and security

scenes.text: Arjun registers on a shopping site, adds headphones to his cart and checks out.
He chooses UPI; the site shows a padlock symbol in the address bar.
Each step has risks — and protections.

steps.title: Stages of an online transaction
steps.body:
1. **Pre-purchase/sale**: information about products via websites, ads, reviews.
2. **Purchase/sale**: registration, placing order (shopping cart), payment.
3. **Delivery/post-sale**: delivery (physical or digital download), tracking, after-sales service.

steps.title: Payment mechanisms
steps.body: **Cash on delivery (COD)**, cheque/DD, **net banking transfer**, **credit and debit cards**, **UPI and mobile wallets (digital cash)**. Card details are encrypted; payment gateways connect buyer, seller and bank.

steps.title: Security and safety
steps.body:
Risks: **transaction risks** (default on order taking/giving, delivery, payment), **data storage and transmission risks** (hacking, viruses, phishing), **threat to intellectual property and privacy**.

Protections: **encryption** (e.g., HTTPS/SSL/TLS), two-factor authentication/OTP, strong passwords, verified sellers, ratings, secure payment gateways, data backups, firewalls, antivirus.

steps.title: Solved example 1: Spot the risk
steps.body: A customer places an order with a fake address and refuses delivery → *transaction risk (order giving)*. Hackers steal card numbers from a site → *data storage/transmission risk*.

steps.title: Solved example 2: Safe payment habits
steps.body: Check for HTTPS and the correct domain; use UPI PIN only to *send* money (never to receive); never share OTP; prefer COD or trusted gateways on new sites.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Believing you must enter your UPI PIN to receive money — that is a common scam.
- Ignoring the padlock/HTTPS sign.
- Thinking COD has no risks for sellers (returns, refusals).

a.text: A caller says: “Sir, you won a cashback. Enter your UPI PIN on the request I sent to receive ₹2,000.” What do you do?

choices.label: Enter the PIN
choices.feedback: Entering a PIN always SENDS money. This is a scam.

choices.label: Decline and report
choices.feedback: Correct — PIN is only for paying.

bad.text: ₹2,000 leaves your account. Report immediately on the national cybercrime helpline 1930 and your bank.

good.text: You decline, block the number and report it. Your money is safe.

quiz.q: Encryption on a website is indicated by…
quiz.why: HTTPS and the padlock sign show that the connection to the site is encrypted and safe. Pop-ups and discounts do not show security.
COD stands for Cash on Delivery, where the customer pays in cash when the goods arrive.
Phishing is a fraud in which fake messages or sites trick people into giving passwords or card details. It is a security risk.
The post-purchase stage includes delivery of goods and after-sales service. Ordering and payment come earlier.
A UPI PIN is entered only when sending money. You never need it to receive money, so anyone asking for it to 'send' you money is cheating.

lessons.title: Resources for e-business and outsourcing

scenes.text: A customer in London calls about her internet bill; the call is answered in Gurugram.
A US firm’s data analysis is done by a team in Pune.
This is business process outsourcing.

steps.title: Resources for successful e-business
steps.body: A well-conceived **website** with good design; adequate **computer systems and network capacity**; skilled **technical and business staff**; secure **payment systems**; efficient **logistics**; and **customer support**.

steps.title: Outsourcing
steps.body:
Contracting out non-core (and some core) activities to specialised outside agencies. Features: contracting out, usually of non-core activities, to specialists; can be **in-house** or **offshore**.

- **BPO** (business process outsourcing): call centres, payroll, data entry.
- **KPO** (knowledge process outsourcing): research, analytics, legal, medical transcription and other expert work.
- **Need/benefits**: focus on core competency, quest for excellence, cost reduction (economies of scale), growth through relationships, stimulates entrepreneurship and employment in host countries.
- **Concerns**: confidentiality, sweat-shopping (long hours, low pay), ethical concerns, opposition in home countries due to job losses.

steps.title: Solved example 1: BPO or KPO?
steps.body: (a) Handling customer complaints by phone → BPO. (b) Analysing clinical trial data for a drug company → KPO. (c) Processing payroll → BPO.

steps.title: Solved example 2: Why outsource?
steps.body: A car company outsources canteen, security and IT support so managers can focus on design and manufacturing → *focus on core competency*.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying outsourcing always means offshore — it can be within the same country.
- Ignoring confidentiality risks.
- Calling expert research work BPO instead of KPO.

quiz.why: Outsourcing usually means giving non-core activities, such as payroll or call centres, to outside firms. The firm keeps its core business.
Knowledge process outsourcing (KPO) is for knowledge-intensive work, such as research and analysis, that needs expert skills.
A concern about outsourcing is confidentiality, as sharing business data with outside firms can lead to leaks. Cost reduction and focus on the core are benefits.

quiz.q: Which resource is essential for e-business?
quiz.why: An e-business depends on a well-designed website, because it is the place where customers see and buy. Showrooms and branches are not needed.
Outsourcing lets a firm give non-core work to specialists, so it can focus on its core competency.

questions.q: E-business is…
questions.why: E-business is wider than e-commerce. It includes all online business processes, including internal ones, while e-commerce is only buying and selling.

questions.q: Selling to other consumers online is…
questions.why: Selling to other consumers online is consumer to consumer (C2C).

questions.q: Which is a limitation of e-business?
questions.why: Low personal touch is a limitation of e-business, because customers cannot meet staff or touch goods. The other three are benefits.

questions.q: COD is a…
questions.why: Cash on delivery (COD) is a way of paying, so it is a payment mechanism.

questions.q: Outsourcing of call centre work is…
questions.why: Outsourcing call centre work is business process outsourcing (BPO). KPO needs knowledge work.

questions.q: An intranet linking departments is an example of…
questions.why: An intranet linking the departments of one firm is intra-business (intra-B), as the dealings are inside the business.

questions.q: Assertion (A): E-business needs lower initial investment. Reason (R): It does not require large physical infrastructure like showrooms.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true and R explains A. An online business does not need showrooms and big premises, so it needs less money to start.

questions.q: Case: A website’s customer card data is stolen by hackers. Risk type?
questions.why: Theft of card details from a site is a risk related to data storage and transmission. It is not a delivery or order risk.

questions.q: Case: Customers give fake addresses and refuse COD parcels. Risk?
questions.why: Fake addresses and refusing COD parcels mean the buyer fails to complete the order or pay. This is a transaction risk (order and payment default).

questions.q: Sweat-shopping is a concern related to…
questions.why: Sweat-shopping, paying workers very low wages in poor conditions, is a concern about outsourcing.

questions.q: Which statement is TRUE?
options: OTPs can be shared with bank staff
You must enter UPI PIN to receive money
questions.why: HTTPS shows that the connection is encrypted, so that statement is true. OTPs must never be shared, UPI PIN is not needed to receive money and COD has risks.

questions.q: Case: A pharmaceutical company in the US hires an Indian firm to analyse clinical trial data. This is…
questions.why: Analysing clinical trial data needs expert knowledge, so the work is knowledge process outsourcing (KPO), not simple BPO.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Outsourcing helps firms focus on core competencies. Reason (R): Non-core work is done by specialists.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true and R explains A. When specialists do the non-core work, the firm can use its time and resources on its core competencies.

questions.q: Which stage of an online transaction includes registration and payment?
questions.why: The purchase stage covers registration, placing the order and payment. Pre-purchase is search and information, and post-purchase is delivery and service.

questions.q: Case: A firm’s orders arrive instantly online but take a week to ship. Limitation illustrated?
options: Incongruence between order speed and fulfilment speed
questions.why: Orders arrive instantly but shipping takes a week. This mismatch is the incongruence between the speed of ordering and the speed of fulfilment.

questions.q: A freelancer offers design services to companies on a platform where firms choose bids. Model?
questions.why: A freelancer who offers a service to companies that bid for it is an individual selling to businesses. This is consumer to business (C2B).

courses.title: Ch 6 · Social Responsibilities of Business and Business Ethics
courses.summary: Concept and need for social responsibility, arguments for and against, kinds of responsibility, duties to interest groups, CSR in Indian law, environmental protection and the elements of business ethics.
outcomes: Learners can explain the case for and against social responsibility
Learners can classify economic, legal, ethical and discretionary responsibilities
Learners can describe business’s role in environmental protection
Learners can identify elements of business ethics in cases

lessons.title: Concept of social responsibility and why it is needed

scenes.text: A paint factory makes good profits, but its waste flows into a village river.
Fish die; villagers fall sick; the media notices.
Is the business only answerable to its owners?

steps.title: Meaning
steps.body: **Social responsibility** of business is its obligation to make decisions and take actions that are desirable in terms of the objectives and values of society — beyond just making profit and obeying the law. **Social obligation** (legal duty) is narrower; social responsibility includes voluntary actions too.

steps.title: Arguments for
steps.body:
- **Justification for existence and growth**: business exists because society allows it.
- **Long-term interest of the firm**: good image builds trust.
- **Avoidance of government regulation**: voluntary action reduces need for strict laws.
- **Maintenance of society**: unhappy groups may harm business.
- **Availability of resources with business**: money and talent to solve problems.
- **Converting problems into opportunities**.
- **Better environment for doing business**.
- **Holding business responsible for social problems** it may have caused.

steps.title: Arguments against
steps.body:
- **Violation of profit-maximisation objective**.
- **Burden on consumers** (costs passed on via prices).
- **Lack of social skills** among business people.
- **Lack of broad public support**.

steps.title: Solved example 1: Identify the argument
steps.body: A company sets up a water-treatment plant voluntarily, fearing that otherwise strict pollution laws will follow → *avoidance of government regulation*. A firm with large funds builds rural schools → *availability of resources*.

steps.title: Solved example 2: Reality today
steps.body: Under the Companies Act, 2013 (Section 135), companies above certain size thresholds (net worth ≥ ₹500 crore, or turnover ≥ ₹1,000 crore, or net profit ≥ ₹5 crore) must spend at least **2% of average net profits of the last three years** on CSR activities. So CSR is partly a legal duty in India.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating social responsibility as identical to legal obligation.
- Listing “burden on consumers” as an argument *for* CSR.
- Writing that CSR spending is mandatory for every company — only for those above thresholds.

activity.prompt: Argument FOR or AGAINST social responsibility?

quiz.why: Social responsibility goes beyond what the law requires. It includes voluntary actions for society, not only charity or legal duty.

quiz.q: Under Section 135, eligible companies spend at least…
quiz.why: Under Section 135 of the Companies Act, eligible companies must spend at least 2% of their average net profits of the last three years on CSR.

quiz.q: “Business has funds and talent to solve problems” argues…
quiz.why: The argument that business has the funds and talent to solve social problems is an argument in favour of social responsibility.
The argument that businesspeople lack the skills for social work is an argument against CSR. The others are arguments in favour.

quiz.q: CSR thresholds include net profit of at least…
quiz.why: One CSR threshold is a net profit of at least ₹5 crore in a year, along with the net worth and turnover thresholds.

lessons.title: Kinds of responsibility and responsibility towards groups

scenes.text: Shareholders want returns; workers want fair wages; customers want safe products.
The government wants taxes; the community wants clean air.
A responsible business balances all of them.

steps.title: Kinds of social responsibility
steps.body:
- **Economic**: produce goods and services society wants and sell at a profit.
- **Legal**: obey the law.
- **Ethical**: behave as society expects beyond the law (e.g., honest advertising).
- **Discretionary**: purely voluntary — donations, community programmes.

steps.title: Responsibility towards different interest groups
steps.body:
- **Shareholders/owners**: fair and regular return, safety of investment, accurate information.
- **Workers**: fair wages, safe working conditions, opportunities to grow, respect, right to form unions.
- **Consumers**: right quality and quantity at fair prices, no unfair trade practices (adulteration, hoarding, misleading ads), after-sales service, hearing complaints.
- **Government and community**: obey laws, pay taxes honestly, protect the environment, behave as a good citizen.

steps.title: Solved example 1: Identify the kind
steps.body: A firm recalls a car model with a faulty brake before any law requires it → *ethical*. A firm donates to a flood-relief fund → *discretionary*. It files GST returns on time → *legal*.

steps.title: Solved example 2: Identify the group
steps.body: A company sets up a crèche for employees’ children → *workers*. It publishes audited results on time → *shareholders*. It stops misleading “100% sugar-free” claims → *consumers*.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing ethical (expected, not legally required) with legal responsibility.
- Forgetting that responsibility to consumers includes complaint redress.

activity.prompt: Match the action with the group served

quiz.q: Donating to a school voluntarily is…
quiz.why: A voluntary donation to a school is not required by law, so it is a discretionary responsibility.

quiz.q: Paying minimum wages as per law is…
quiz.why: Paying minimum wages is required by law, so it is a legal responsibility.

quiz.q: Hoarding goods to raise prices violates responsibility to…
quiz.why: Hoarding goods to push up prices is an unfair trade practice, and it harms consumers. So it violates the responsibility to consumers.

quiz.q: Safety at workplace is a responsibility towards…
quiz.why: Providing safe working conditions is a responsibility towards workers (employees).

options: behaving as society expects beyond law
quiz.why: Ethical responsibility means behaving as society expects, even where the law does not say so. It goes beyond the law.

lessons.title: Business and environmental protection

scenes.text: Delhi’s winter smog chokes residents.
A factory’s generators keep a neighbourhood awake.
Businesses cause pollution — and can help reduce it.

steps.title: Causes and types of pollution
steps.body:
Industrial production and transport cause:
- **Air pollution**: emissions from vehicles, chimneys (carbon monoxide, sulphur dioxide, particulates).
- **Water pollution**: chemical and waste dumping into rivers.
- **Land pollution**: toxic waste, plastic, e-waste dumping.
- **Noise pollution**: machines, vehicles, generators.

steps.title: Need for pollution control
steps.body:
- Reduce health hazards (cancers, lung and heart disease).
- Reduce risk of liability (fines, lawsuits).
- Cost savings (efficient processes, less waste).
- Improve public image.
- Other social benefits (clean environment, natural beauty, better quality of life).

steps.title: Role of business in environmental protection
steps.body:
- Commitment by top management.
- Ensure the whole organisation is committed to environment-friendly practices.
- Clear policies for purchasing good-quality raw materials, better technology, scientific waste disposal.
- Comply with laws on pollution prevention.
- Participate in government programmes (hazardous waste management, river clean-up, tree planting).
- Periodic assessment of pollution control programmes.
- Educate suppliers, dealers and customers about pollution control.

steps.title: Solved example 1: Identify the pollution
steps.body: Bus depot diesel smoke → air. Dyeing unit discharging coloured water → water. Discarded batteries and phones in landfill → land (e-waste). Loudspeakers at night → noise.

steps.title: Solved example 2: Role of business
steps.body: A cement company installs dust filters, recycles water and trains truck drivers to avoid idling → *better technology, compliance and education of partners*.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying pollution control only adds cost; it often saves cost and avoids liability.
- Forgetting noise pollution in lists.

activity.prompt: Green business checklist for a small factory
items: Top management signs an environment policy
Switch to cleaner fuel or efficient machines

quiz.why: Dumped e-waste has toxic metals that seep into the soil, so it mainly causes land pollution.

quiz.q: A reason for pollution control is…
quiz.why: Pollution control reduces health hazards for people. Higher liability, poor image and more smoke are not reasons for it.

quiz.q: Educating dealers about pollution is a role of…
quiz.why: Business can help control pollution by educating dealers and others about it. It is a role of business, not only of the government.
Generators running at night make loud sound, so they cause noise pollution.

quiz.q: Efficient processes reduce waste and give…
quiz.why: Efficient processes reduce waste, and less waste means lower costs. So they give cost savings.

lessons.title: Business ethics: concept and elements

scenes.text: A salesperson can win a big order by offering a bribe.
Her manager says, “We don’t do business that way.”
That is business ethics in action.

steps.title: Meaning
steps.body: **Business ethics** refers to socially determined moral principles that should govern business activities — what is right and wrong in business conduct. Ethics guide behaviour even where the law is silent.

steps.title: Elements of business ethics
steps.body:
- **Top management commitment**: leaders must model ethical conduct.
- **Publication of a code of conduct**: written policies on fair dealing, conflicts of interest, gifts, bribery, harassment.
- **Establishment of compliance mechanisms**: reporting channels, audits, whistle-blower protection.
- **Involving employees at all levels**.
- **Measuring results**: monitor and review compliance.

steps.title: Solved example 1: Ethical or not?
steps.body: (a) Hiding a product defect to meet sales targets → unethical. (b) Refusing a bribe even if it loses a contract → ethical. (c) Using customers’ personal data without consent for ads → unethical (also may be illegal under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023).

steps.title: Solved example 2: Identify the element
steps.body: A company launches an anonymous hotline for reporting fraud and protects those who report → *compliance mechanism*. The CEO publicly refuses expensive gifts from suppliers → *top management commitment*.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking ethics = law. Some legal acts can still be unethical.
- Thinking a code on paper is enough without leaders following it.

a.text: A buyer hints that a “gift” to him will secure your ₹50 lakh order. Your company code bans bribes. What do you do?

choices.label: Give the gift quietly
choices.feedback: This is bribery — illegal and unethical.

choices.label: Refuse and report through the compliance channel
choices.feedback: Correct use of ethics and compliance mechanisms.

b.text: An audit uncovers the payment; the firm faces legal action and loses reputation.

c.text: You lose this order but your firm’s reputation stays strong; the buyer’s company also takes action.

quiz.why: Business ethics are the moral principles that guide how a business behaves, deciding what is right and wrong in business conduct.

quiz.q: A whistle-blower system is an example of…
quiz.why: A whistle-blower system lets employees report wrong acts, so it helps check that rules are followed. It is a compliance mechanism.

quiz.q: The most important element for ethics to work is…
quiz.why: Ethics work only if top management is committed to them and sets an example. Location, advertising and pricing do not decide this.
Hiding a defect in a product deceives customers, so it is unethical.
Ethics apply even where the law is silent. They guide behaviour in situations that the law does not cover, and apply to all businesses.

questions.q: Social responsibility is wider than…
questions.why: Social responsibility is wider than legal obligation, as it covers voluntary acts beyond what the law demands.

questions.q: Discretionary responsibility means…
questions.why: Discretionary responsibility means voluntary acts, such as donations or sponsoring a school, that the law does not require.

questions.q: Air pollution is mainly caused by…
questions.why: Air pollution is mainly caused by emissions from vehicles and factories. Noise, land and water pollution are other kinds.

questions.q: A code of conduct is an element of…
questions.why: A code of conduct is a written set of rules for behaviour, so it is an element of business ethics.

questions.q: An argument against social responsibility is…
questions.why: The argument that social spending is a burden on consumers, since it is added to prices, is against social responsibility. The others are in favour.

questions.q: Fair wages and safe workplace are responsibilities towards…
questions.why: Fair wages and a safe workplace are responsibilities of the business towards its workers.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Voluntary social action can reduce government regulation. Reason (R): If business behaves responsibly, there is less need for strict laws.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true and R explains A. If business acts responsibly on its own, there is less need for strict laws, so government regulation can be reduced.

questions.q: Case: A firm stops a misleading “doctor recommended” ad claim though no law forced it. Kind of responsibility?
questions.why: Withdrawing a misleading ad without any legal requirement is acting as society expects, beyond the law. That is ethical responsibility.

questions.q: CSR spending of 2% applies to companies with…
options: net worth ≥ ₹500 cr or turnover ≥ ₹1,000 cr or net profit ≥ ₹5 cr
questions.why: The 2% CSR rule applies to companies with net worth of ₹500 crore or more, or turnover of ₹1,000 crore or more, or net profit of ₹5 crore or more.

questions.q: Case: A cement firm installs dust filters to meet norms and also trains truck drivers. Which roles?
options: Compliance with laws and educating partners
questions.why: Installing dust filters to meet norms is compliance with laws, and training truck drivers is educating partners. Both are roles of business in controlling pollution.

questions.q: Which is NOT a reason for pollution control?
questions.why: Increasing noise is not a reason for pollution control. Pollution control reduces health hazards and liability and improves the image.

questions.q: Responsibility to shareholders includes…
questions.why: Business owes shareholders a fair return on their investment and accurate information about the company. It does not fix their wages or pay their taxes.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Everything legal is ethical. Reason (R): Laws cover all moral situations.
questions.why: Both statements are false. Not everything legal is ethical, because a legal act can still be unfair. Laws also do not cover all moral situations.

questions.q: Case: A firm’s hotline lets employees anonymously report fraud. Element of ethics?
questions.why: A hotline where employees can report fraud without giving their names is a compliance mechanism, which helps detect and stop wrong acts.

questions.q: Case: A company says “we will not spend on social causes because it lowers profits for shareholders.” This view reflects…
questions.why: A firm that refuses to spend on social causes, as it would lower profits, is using the profit-maximisation argument against CSR. The marked option states this view as being against CSR.

questions.q: Case: A factory’s waste reduction cut raw-material costs by 8% and fines to zero. Which two needs for pollution control does it show?
questions.why: Cutting waste lowered raw material cost (cost savings), and zero fines show reduced legal liability. These are two reasons for pollution control.

school-c11-business-b.title: Class 11 Business Studies (Part B)
school-c11-business-b.description: All chapters of Class 11 Business Studies: business and commerce, forms of organisation, services, ethics, finance, small business and trade, explained with Indian cases.

courses.title: Ch 7 · Sources of Business Finance
courses.summary: Fixed and working capital needs, classification of sources, equity and preference shares, retained earnings, debentures, bank and institutional loans, public deposits, trade credit, factoring, commercial paper, lease and international sources (ADR, GDR, IDR, FCCB).
outcomes: Learners can classify sources by period, ownership and generation
Learners can compare equity, preference and debt
Learners can explain short-term sources including factoring and CP
Learners can choose suitable sources for given cases

lessons.title: Business finance: meaning, needs and classification

story.title: How much money does a business need?

scenes.text: Kavya plans a small garment factory.
She needs money for machines and building — and for cloth, thread and wages every month.
These are fixed capital and working capital needs.

steps.title: Meaning and significance
steps.body: **Business finance** is the money required to carry out business activities. It is needed to start, run, modernise and expand a business, and to meet emergencies.

steps.title: Fixed and working capital
steps.body:
- **Fixed capital requirements**: to buy fixed assets — land, building, plant and machinery, furniture. Depends on nature of business (manufacturing needs more than trading).
- **Working capital requirements**: to run day-to-day operations — raw materials, wages, rent, holding stock, giving credit to customers. Depends on length of operating cycle, credit policy, scale, seasonality.

steps.title: Classification of sources
steps.body:
- **By period**: *long-term* (more than 5 years: shares, debentures, term loans, retained earnings), *medium-term* (1–5 years: public deposits, lease, bank loans), *short-term* (less than 1 year: trade credit, factoring, commercial paper, bank overdraft).
- **By ownership**: *owner’s funds* (equity, retained earnings) and *borrowed funds* (debentures, loans, public deposits, trade credit).
- **By source of generation**: *internal* (retained earnings, collecting receivables, disposing surplus stock) and *external* (shares, debentures, loans, trade credit, factoring, CP).

steps.title: Solved example 1: Classify
steps.body: (a) Equity shares → long-term, owner’s, external. (b) Retained earnings → long-term, owner’s, internal. (c) Trade credit → short-term, borrowed, external. (d) Bank loan for 3 years → medium-term, borrowed, external.

steps.title: Solved example 2: Fixed or working capital?
steps.body: Kavya buys sewing machines (₹12 lakh) → fixed capital. She keeps 2 months of cloth and wages (₹4 lakh) → working capital. Cloth sold on 30-day credit increases working capital needs.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating retained earnings as external.
- Using fixed capital funds (long-term) for daily needs and vice versa without planning.
- Calling public deposits owner’s funds.

quiz.q: Money for raw materials and wages is…
quiz.why: Money needed for raw materials and wages is working capital, as it is for day-to-day operations. Fixed capital is for long-term assets.
Retained earnings are profits kept in the business, so they are generated inside the firm. They are an internal source of finance.

quiz.q: Long-term finance usually means more than…
quiz.why: Long-term finance is usually needed for a period of more than 5 years. Medium-term is 1 to 5 years and short-term is up to 1 year.

quiz.q: A manufacturing firm needs more fixed capital than a…
quiz.why: A manufacturing firm needs more fixed capital than a trading firm, since it needs plant and machinery. A trading firm mostly needs stock.
Trade credit is credit given by suppliers, allowing the buyer to pay later. It is a short-term borrowed source.

lessons.title: Owner’s funds: equity, preference shares and retained earnings

story.title: Selling a slice of the company

scenes.text: To raise ₹50 crore, a company sells shares to thousands of investors.
Equity holders get votes and residual profits; preference holders get a fixed dividend first.
Retained profits are a third source.

steps.title: Equity shares
steps.body:
Represent ownership; holders are owners with **voting rights** and a claim on **residual** income and assets.

- **Merits**: permanent capital (no repayment), no fixed burden of dividend, voting rights for investors, creates a base for borrowing, suits investors wanting capital growth.
- **Limitations**: costlier than other sources (higher expected return), issue costs, dilution of control, delay in raising (formalities), investors bear high risk.

steps.title: Preference shares
steps.body:
Get **preference** over equity in dividend (at a fixed rate) and in repayment of capital on winding up. Usually no voting rights (except on matters affecting them). Types: cumulative/non-cumulative, participating/non-participating, convertible/non-convertible, redeemable.

- Merits: fixed dividend for cautious investors, no dilution of control, no charge on assets. Limitations: not suitable for investors wanting control, dividend not tax-deductible, higher cost than debt.

steps.title: Retained earnings (ploughing back of profits)
steps.body: Profits kept in the business instead of being distributed. Merits: permanent, no explicit cost, no dilution of control, increases share value. Limitations: may cause dissatisfaction among shareholders (less dividend), uncertain, opportunity cost.

steps.title: Solved example 1: Dividend priority
steps.body:
Profit available for dividend ₹10 lakh; 10% preference shares ₹40 lakh; equity shares ₹1 crore.

- Step 1: Preference dividend = 10% × 40 lakh = ₹4 lakh (paid first).
- Step 2: Balance for equity = ₹6 lakh → 6% on equity.

steps.title: Solved example 2: Cumulative preference
steps.body: If no dividend is paid in a loss year on cumulative preference shares, the arrears (₹4 lakh) are carried forward and must be paid before any equity dividend in future years.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying equity dividend is fixed.
- Saying preference shareholders always vote.
- Saying retained earnings are “free” — they have an opportunity cost.

activity.prompt: Profit available ₹15 lakh. 12% preference shares of ₹50 lakh. How much (₹ lakh) is left for equity shareholders?

quiz.why: Equity shareholders are the owners of the company. Debenture holders and lenders are creditors.
Preference shareholders get a fixed dividend before equity shareholders, and get their capital back first at winding up.
Ploughing back of profits means keeping a part of profits in the business instead of paying it all out as dividend. It forms retained earnings.

quiz.q: Issue of more equity can cause…
quiz.why: Issuing more equity shares brings in new owners with voting rights, so the control of existing owners is diluted.
If a cumulative preference dividend is not paid in a year, the arrears are carried forward and must be paid later, before equity holders get anything.

lessons.title: Borrowed funds: debentures, banks, financial institutions and public deposits

scenes.text: A company wants ₹20 crore but does not want new owners.
It issues debentures at 9% interest and takes a term loan.
Lenders get interest, not ownership.

steps.title: Debentures
steps.body:
Instruments acknowledging a debt; holders are **creditors** and receive **fixed interest**. Types: secured/unsecured, registered/bearer, convertible/non-convertible, redeemable.

- Merits: preferred by investors seeking fixed income, no dilution of control, interest is **tax-deductible**, suitable when sales are stable.
- Limitations: fixed charge even in losses, assets may be mortgaged (charge), reduces further borrowing capacity.

steps.title: Commercial banks and financial institutions
steps.body:
- **Commercial banks**: loans and advances for short, medium and long periods — cash credit, overdraft, term loans, discounting of bills. Merits: timely funds, confidentiality, easy to arrange. Limitations: usually short/medium term, need security, strict conditions.
- **Financial institutions** (e.g., development banks, SIDBI for small industries): long-term finance for expansion and modernisation; also give managerial and technical advice. Limitations: rigid procedures, may restrict dividend/management freedom.

steps.title: Public deposits
steps.body: Deposits raised by companies directly from the public, usually for **6 months to 3 years**, at interest higher than bank deposits; regulated by the Companies Act and RBI (for NBFCs). Merits: simple procedure, no charge on assets, no dilution of control, cheaper than bank loan. Limitations: new firms find it hard, unreliable for large amounts, collection costly.

steps.title: Solved example 1: Tax shield
steps.body: Debentures ₹1 crore at 10% → interest ₹10 lakh. With 25% tax, after-tax cost = 10 × (1 − 0.25) = **₹7.5 lakh** (7.5%). Dividends on equity give no such deduction.

steps.title: Solved example 2: Choose a source
steps.body: A firm with stable profits that does not want to dilute control → debentures or term loan. A firm expecting erratic profits → avoid heavy fixed interest; prefer equity.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling debenture holders owners.
- Saying interest on debentures is paid only when there is profit.
- Forgetting that public deposits are unsecured.

activity.prompt: Debentures ₹50 lakh at 12% interest; tax rate 30%. After-tax interest cost (₹ lakh)?

quiz.why: Debenture holders have lent money to the company, so they are its creditors, not owners.
Interest on debentures is a fixed charge that must be paid whether or not there is a profit. It is deductible as an expense for tax.
SIDBI (Small Industries Development Bank of India) mainly supports small industries by giving them finance.
Public deposits are usually accepted for a period of 6 months to 3 years, so they are short-to-medium term.

quiz.q: A limitation of bank loans is…
quiz.why: A limitation of bank loans is that the bank asks for security and sets strict conditions. This makes them harder for some firms to get.

lessons.title: Short-term sources: trade credit, factoring, commercial paper and lease

story.title: Cash flow tricks of a growing business

scenes.text: Kavya’s cloth supplier lets her pay after 60 days.
A factoring company buys her unpaid customer bills for cash today.
She leases a delivery van instead of buying it.

steps.title: Trade credit
steps.body: Credit extended by one trader to another when buying goods, shown as *sundry creditors/accounts payable*. Merits: convenient, continuous, no charge on assets, helps increase stock when demand rises. Limitations: may encourage over-trading, limited amount, costlier if discounts are lost.

steps.title: Factoring
steps.body: A financial service where a **factor** buys the firm’s receivables (book debts) at a discount and/or collects them, provides credit information, and may bear bad-debt risk (*non-recourse* factoring). Merits: cheaper than some loans, steady cash flow, no charge on assets, saves collection effort. Limitations: costly if invoices are numerous and small; customers may feel pressure from a third party.

steps.title: Commercial paper and lease financing
steps.body:
- **Commercial paper (CP)**: an unsecured promissory note issued by large, creditworthy companies for short-term funds; maturity **7 days to 1 year**; issued at discount. Merits: no security, freely transferable, cheaper than bank loans. Limitations: only for big firms, cannot be extended easily, amount limited by liquidity in market.
- **Lease financing**: the **lessor** (owner) lets the **lessee** use an asset for a periodic **lease rent**. Merits: no large initial outlay, lease rent is tax-deductible, risk of obsolescence with lessor (in operating leases). Limitations: restrictions on use, firm does not own the asset.

steps.title: Solved example 1: Factoring cash
steps.body:
Receivables ₹10 lakh; factor advances 80% now and charges 2% fee on invoice value.

- Advance = ₹8 lakh. Fee = ₹20,000.
- On collection, the balance ₹2 lakh − 20,000 = **₹1,80,000** is paid to Kavya (ignoring interest).

steps.title: Solved example 2: Commercial paper discount
steps.body: CP face value ₹1 crore for 1 year issued at ₹93 lakh → implied cost ≈ 7/93 = **7.5%** p.a.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling CP a secured instrument.
- Saying the lessee owns the leased asset.
- Assuming small firms can easily issue CP.

pairs: Unsecured short-term note by big firms
Use an asset for periodic rent
Withdraw beyond balance up to limit

quiz.why: Commercial paper is an unsecured short-term promissory note issued by large, creditworthy companies to raise funds.

quiz.q: In a lease, the owner is the…
quiz.why: In a lease, the lessor is the owner of the asset and the lessee is the user, who pays the rent.
Factoring is the sale of a firm's receivables (book debts) to a factor, who pays most of the amount in advance.
Commercial paper has a short maturity, from 7 days to 1 year.
Lease rent is treated as a business expense, so it is tax-deductible.

lessons.title: International finance and choosing a source

scenes.text: An Indian IT company wants dollars for a US acquisition.
It lists depository receipts in New York and issues convertible bonds.
It must also decide which source is best overall.

steps.title: International sources
steps.body:
- **Commercial banks abroad**: foreign currency loans.
- **International agencies and development banks**: e.g., International Finance Corporation (IFC), Asian Development Bank.
- **International capital markets**:
  - **GDR** (Global Depository Receipt): shares of an Indian company converted into depository receipts traded on exchanges outside the US (e.g., Luxembourg, London); denominated in USD.
  - **ADR** (American Depository Receipt): depository receipts issued and traded only in the USA.
  - **IDR** (Indian Depository Receipt): issued in India by a *foreign* company to raise rupees from Indian investors.
  - **FCCB** (Foreign Currency Convertible Bonds): bonds in foreign currency convertible into equity; fixed interest until conversion.

steps.title: Factors affecting choice of source
steps.body: **Cost** (issue cost and return expected), **financial strength and stability** of the firm, **form of organisation and legal status**, **purpose and time period**, **risk profile**, **control** considerations, **effect on credit-worthiness**, **flexibility and ease**, **tax benefits**.

steps.title: Solved example 1: Identify the instrument
steps.body: (a) A UK company raises rupees in India → IDR. (b) An Indian company’s receipts listed in New York → ADR. (c) An Indian company issues dollar bonds convertible into shares → FCCB. (d) Receipts listed in Luxembourg → GDR.

steps.title: Solved example 2: Choosing
steps.body: A start-up with uncertain profits needing long-term funds and willing to share control → equity (venture capital/private equity). A profitable firm with stable cash flows wanting to keep control → debentures/term loans. Short seasonal need → trade credit, overdraft, CP (if large).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing ADR (USA) with GDR (outside USA).
- Saying IDRs are issued abroad by Indian firms — they are issued in India by foreign firms.
- Ignoring control when choosing equity.

pairs: Traded on exchanges outside the USA
Foreign company raises money in India
International agency lending to private sector

quiz.why: An Indian Depository Receipt (IDR) is issued by a foreign company to raise funds in India from Indian investors.
American Depository Receipts (ADRs) are issued and traded in the USA, by non-US companies.
Foreign Currency Convertible Bonds (FCCBs) are debt that holders can convert into equity shares after a set time.

quiz.q: A key factor in choosing a source is…
quiz.why: Cost is a key factor in choosing a source of finance. Logo colour, office size and festival dates do not matter.

quiz.q: A firm wanting to retain control prefers…
quiz.why: A firm that wants to keep control prefers debt, since lenders get interest but have no voting rights. Equity gives votes to new shareholders.

questions.q: Fixed capital is required for…
questions.why: Fixed capital is needed to buy long-term assets like machinery and buildings. Rent, wages and raw materials are paid from working capital.

questions.q: Retained earnings are an…
questions.why: Retained earnings are profits kept inside the business, so they are an internal source of finance.

questions.q: Debenture holders receive…
questions.why: Debenture holders are lenders, so they receive interest at a fixed rate. Dividend and voting rights belong to shareholders.

questions.q: CP is issued by…
questions.why: Commercial paper is issued by large, creditworthy companies, as it is unsecured and depends on the issuer's credit rating.

questions.q: Lessee is the…
questions.why: The lessee is the user of the asset who pays rent. The owner is the lessor.

questions.q: Which source involves no dilution of control and has tax-deductible cost?
questions.why: Debentures do not give voting rights, so control is not diluted, and the interest is deductible for tax. Equity dilutes control, and dividends on preference shares are not deductible.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Equity capital is permanent capital. Reason (R): It is repaid only on winding up.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true and R explains A. Equity capital is repaid only when the company is wound up, so it stays in the business as permanent capital.

questions.q: Profit ₹20 lakh; 8% preference shares ₹1 crore. Balance for equity?
questions.why: Preference dividend = 8% of ₹1 crore = ₹8 lakh. Balance for equity = ₹20 lakh − ₹8 lakh = ₹12 lakh.

questions.q: Case: Receivables ₹5 lakh; factor pays 85% now; fee 1%. Advance received?
questions.why: The factor advances 85% of the receivables: 85% × ₹5 lakh = ₹4.25 lakh now. The rest is paid later, less the factor's fee.

questions.q: A foreign company raising funds from Indian investors uses…
questions.why: A foreign company that raises funds from Indian investors issues Indian Depository Receipts (IDRs). ADR is for the USA and GDR is for global markets.

questions.q: Case: ₹80 lakh debentures at 10%; tax 30%. After-tax cost (₹ lakh)?
questions.why: Interest = 10% of ₹80 lakh = ₹8 lakh. Interest is tax-deductible, so after-tax cost = 8 × (1 − 0.30) = ₹5.6 lakh.

questions.q: Which is a short-term source?
questions.why: Trade credit is a short-term source, since it is repaid within a short period. Equity, debentures and retained earnings are long-term.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Public deposits create a charge on assets. Reason (R): Public deposits are unsecured.
questions.why: The assertion is false: public deposits are unsecured, so they do not create a charge on assets. The reason is true.

questions.q: Case: A seasonal firm needs funds for 3 months each Diwali. Best choice?
questions.why: A seasonal need for 3 months suits a short-term source such as bank overdraft or cash credit. Equity and debentures are long-term.

questions.q: Case: CP of face value ₹50 crore for 1 year issued at ₹46 crore. Approximate cost?
questions.why: CP was issued at ₹46 crore and repaid at ₹50 crore after a year, so the cost is ₹4 crore on ₹46 crore = 4/46 ≈ 8.7%.

questions.q: Which is NOT a factor affecting choice of source?
questions.why: The colour of the brand has nothing to do with choosing a source of finance. Cost, tax benefits and control do.

questions.q: Case: A loss-making year — which source still requires payment?
questions.why: Debenture interest is a fixed charge and must be paid even in a loss. Equity dividend, retained earnings and non-cumulative preference dividend need profits.

courses.note: Part B chapters (7–10) follow the rationalised NCERT sequence; topic order may differ by edition

courses.title: Ch 8 · Small Business and Entrepreneurship
courses.summary: Entrepreneurship and its process, Startup India, intellectual property rights, MSME definitions (current composite limits), role of small business in India and rural areas, problems and government support.
outcomes: Learners can explain characteristics and process of entrepreneurship
Learners can identify the right IPR for a creation
Learners can classify MSMEs using investment and turnover
Learners can match small-business problems with government support

lessons.title: Entrepreneurship: concept, characteristics and need

story.title: From a college project to a company

scenes.text: Ananya notices farmers in her village lose tomatoes because they cannot store them.
She builds a low-cost solar cold box with two friends.
Spotting a problem, taking a risk and creating value — that is entrepreneurship.

steps.title: Meaning
steps.body: **Entrepreneurship** is the process of setting up one’s own business as distinct from pursuing any other economic activity (employment or profession). The person is the **entrepreneur**; the output is the **enterprise**.

steps.title: Characteristics
steps.body:
- **Systematic activity** — needs knowledge, skills and competencies that can be learnt.
- **Lawful and purposeful** — aims at legal profit and value creation.
- **Innovation** — new products, processes, markets or business models.
- **Organisation of production** — brings together land, labour, capital and technology.
- **Risk-taking** — moderate, calculated risks.

steps.title: Need / importance
steps.body: Creates jobs, develops new products and industries, uses local resources, supports balanced regional development, increases GDP and exports, improves standard of living and spreads innovation.

steps.title: Process of entrepreneurship
steps.body:
1. Opportunity identification (spotting a problem worth solving)
2. Idea evaluation and feasibility (market, technical, financial)
3. Business plan (resources, marketing, finance)
4. Mobilising resources (funding, team, licences)
5. Launch and manage the enterprise
6. Grow/scale and innovate continuously

steps.title: Solved example 1: Identify the characteristic
steps.body: Ananya studies costs, tests prototypes and plans carefully → *systematic activity*. Her solar cold box is a new solution → *innovation*. She invests savings knowing she may lose them → *risk-taking*.

steps.title: Solved example 2: Employment vs entrepreneurship
steps.body: A salaried engineer earns a fixed salary with low risk; Ananya earns uncertain profits with higher risk but creates jobs for others.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking entrepreneurs are “born, not made” — skills can be learnt.
- Equating risk-taking with gambling; entrepreneurs take calculated risks.

quiz.why: An entrepreneur takes calculated risks, based on analysis. Reckless risk is gambling, and no risk means no enterprise.
