Entrepreneurship is a systematic, planned activity of finding opportunities and building a business. It is not random.
Bringing a new product to the market is innovation, creating something new. Imitation copies others.

quiz.q: A benefit of entrepreneurship to society is…
quiz.why: Entrepreneurship creates jobs, which benefits society. Monopoly and unemployment are not benefits.

quiz.q: The first step in the process is…
quiz.why: The first step in the entrepreneurial process is identifying an opportunity, such as spotting a problem to solve. Launch and hiring come later.

lessons.title: Startup India and intellectual property rights

scenes.text: Ananya’s team names their product “ThandaBox” and designs a unique logo.
An investor asks: “Have you registered the trademark? Is the design patentable?”
Startup India and IPR laws can help.

steps.title: Startup India
steps.body:
Launched by the Government of India on **16 January 2016** to build an ecosystem for start-ups: simplified compliance and self-certification, a **Fund of Funds** for start-ups (through SIDBI), tax benefits for eligible start-ups (on approval), faster exit, support for patents/trademarks (fee rebates, facilitators), incubation and industry–academia links.

Ways to fund a start-up: bootstrapping, crowdfunding, angel investors, venture capital, business incubators/accelerators, microfinance, government programmes.

steps.title: Intellectual property rights (IPR)
steps.body:
Legal rights over creations of the mind. In India:

- **Copyright**: original literary, artistic, musical works, films, software — generally author’s life + 60 years.
- **Trademark**: word, logo, symbol identifying goods/services — 10 years, renewable.
- **Patent**: new invention with industrial application — 20 years.
- **Geographical Indication (GI)**: product from a specific region with qualities due to it (Darjeeling tea, Banarasi saree).
- **Industrial design**: shape/pattern/ornamentation of an article.
- **Plant variety** and **semiconductor integrated circuit layout design** protections.

steps.title: Solved example 1: Which IPR?
steps.body: (a) Name and logo “ThandaBox” → trademark. (b) The new cooling mechanism → patent. (c) The user manual and app code → copyright. (d) Shape of the box → industrial design.

steps.title: Solved example 2: Funding path
steps.body: Ananya’s team uses savings (bootstrapping), wins an incubator grant, then raises money from an angel investor in exchange for 10% equity.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying a patent lasts forever — 20 years.
- Confusing trademark (brand) with patent (invention).
- Thinking GI belongs to one company — it belongs to producers of a region.

activity.prompt: Match the IPR with the example

quiz.why: The Startup India initiative was launched on 16 January 2016.
A patent in India is granted for 20 years from the filing date. After that, others can use the invention.
Banarasi saree is protected by a Geographical Indication (GI), which links a product's quality to its place of origin.
A trademark in India is registered for 10 years, and it can be renewed again and again.

quiz.q: Funding a start-up from own savings is…
quiz.why: Funding a start-up from the founder's own savings is bootstrapping. Venture capital and crowdfunding use outside money.

lessons.title: MSMEs: definition and role

story.title: The small units that employ millions

scenes.text: A town has hundreds of small units making garments, utensils and auto parts.
Together they employ more people than the big factory nearby.
Small businesses are the backbone of India’s economy.

steps.title: Definition (MSMED Act, 2006 as revised)
steps.body:
Since 2020 MSMEs are classified on a **composite criterion of investment in plant & machinery/equipment AND annual turnover**, the same for manufacturing and services. Revised limits effective **1 April 2025**:

- **Micro**: investment ≤ ₹2.5 crore and turnover ≤ ₹10 crore.
- **Small**: investment ≤ ₹25 crore and turnover ≤ ₹100 crore.
- **Medium**: investment ≤ ₹125 crore and turnover ≤ ₹500 crore.

(The 2020 limits were ₹1/5, ₹10/50 and ₹50/250 crore; some textbooks still show those. Registration is on the **Udyam** portal — check it for the current limits.) Village and khadi industries and cottage industries are also part of small business.

steps.title: Role of small business in India
steps.body:
- Large share of industrial units, manufacturing output and exports.
- **Employment**: second largest employer after agriculture.
- Wide variety of products; use of local resources and skills.
- **Balanced regional development** — set up in rural and backward areas.
- Low capital per job; flexible, personal service; quick decisions.
- **Role in rural India**: non-farm jobs, reduced migration to cities, use of local raw material, development of traditional crafts.

steps.title: Solved example 1: Classify the unit
steps.body: Investment ₹8 crore, turnover ₹60 crore → **small** (investment ≤ 25 and turnover ≤ 100; but not micro since turnover > 10). Investment ₹2 crore, turnover ₹9 crore → **micro**.

steps.title: Solved example 2: Rural role
steps.body: A bamboo craft cluster in Assam employs 300 women at home → non-farm rural jobs, uses local material, preserves a traditional craft.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using only investment (old criterion) instead of investment *and* turnover.
- Treating manufacturing and services with different limits (they are now the same).
- Quoting limits without saying which year they apply to.

quiz.why: MSMEs are classified by both investment in plant and machinery and turnover, not by employees or profit alone.
Small businesses are the second largest employer in India after agriculture.

quiz.q: A role of rural small industries is…
quiz.why: Rural small industries give non-farm jobs in villages, which reduces dependence on agriculture and migration to cities.
MSMEs register on the Udyam portal, which gives them a recognised status.

quiz.q: Small businesses help regional balance because they…
options: can be set up in backward areas
quiz.why: Small businesses need little capital and can be set up in backward and rural areas, which helps balanced regional development.

lessons.title: Problems of small business and government support

scenes.text: Ravi’s small auto-parts unit cannot get a bank loan without collateral.
A big buyer pays him after 120 days; power cuts halt production.
Government schemes try to address such problems.

steps.title: Problems of small business
steps.body:
- **Finance**: lack of collateral, high interest, delays in payment by buyers.
- **Raw materials**: poor quality, high prices, small bulk purchase.
- **Managerial skills**: owner manages everything.
- **Marketing**: weak bargaining power, poor branding.
- **Quality**: cannot invest in quality testing.
- **Capacity utilisation**: under-use due to lack of demand/power.
- **Technology**: outdated, low productivity.
- **Sickness**: many units become sick.
- **Global competition** after liberalisation.

steps.title: Government assistance (institutions and schemes)
steps.body:
- **NSIC** (National Small Industries Corporation): machinery on hire-purchase, raw material, marketing support, technology support.
- **District Industries Centres (DICs)**: single-window support at the district level.
- **SIDBI** (Small Industries Development Bank of India): finance and refinance to MSMEs.
- **NABARD**: rural credit and support to rural industries.
- **KVIC**: khadi and village industries.
- **Credit Guarantee Fund Trust (CGTMSE)**: collateral-free loans guarantee.
- **SFURTI**: clusters of traditional industries.
- **MSME Samadhaan** portal for delayed-payment complaints (buyers must pay MSMEs within 45 days under MSMED Act).
- **Udyam registration**, public procurement preference, PM Mudra loans (Shishu, Kishore, Tarun).

steps.title: Solved example 1: Match problem to support
steps.body: No collateral → CGTMSE guarantee / Mudra loan. Delayed payment of 120 days → MSME Samadhaan (45-day rule). Needs new machinery on easy terms → NSIC hire-purchase.

steps.title: Solved example 2: Rural craft cluster
steps.body: Weavers needing common facilities and design support → SFURTI cluster scheme; rural credit through NABARD-supported banks.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing up SIDBI (MSME finance) with SEBI (market regulator).
- Saying all small units must have collateral for loans — guarantee schemes exist.
- Forgetting the 45-day payment rule.

activity.prompt: Match the problem with the support

quiz.why: SIDBI provides finance to MSMEs. It does not regulate markets or deal in foreign exchange or insurance.
Under the MSMED Act, buyers must pay MSMEs within 45 days of acceptance of goods or services.
District Industries Centres (DICs) work at the district level, helping small entrepreneurs with licences, finance and training.

quiz.q: A common problem of small business is…
quiz.why: Lack of finance is a common problem of small businesses. They often have little capital and find it hard to borrow.
The Khadi and Village Industries Commission (KVIC) supports khadi and village industries, mostly in rural areas.

questions.q: Entrepreneurship is a…
questions.why: Entrepreneurship is a systematic activity, with planned steps from spotting an opportunity to running the business.

questions.q: An entrepreneur takes…
questions.why: An entrepreneur takes calculated risks, which are moderate and thought through, not reckless ones.

questions.q: Startup India was launched on…
questions.why: Startup India was launched on 16 January 2016.

questions.q: A patent protects…
questions.why: A patent protects inventions. Copyright protects books and artworks, trademarks protect brand names, and GI protects regional products.

questions.q: MSMEs are classified on…
questions.why: MSMEs are classified on the basis of investment and turnover, using composite criteria.

questions.q: Darjeeling tea is protected as a…
questions.why: Darjeeling tea is protected as a Geographical Indication (GI) because its quality comes from the region.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Small industries help balanced regional development. Reason (R): They can be set up in rural and backward areas with low capital.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true and R explains A. Small industries can be set up in rural and backward areas with little capital, which spreads development.

questions.q: Case (2025 limits): investment ₹20 crore, turnover ₹120 crore. The unit is…
questions.why: Investment of ₹20 crore is within the small limit, but turnover of ₹120 crore is above ₹100 crore and within ₹500 crore, so the unit is medium.

questions.q: CGTMSE helps by…
questions.why: CGTMSE guarantees loans given to MSMEs without collateral, so banks lend to small units that have no security.

questions.q: Copyright on literary works in India generally lasts…
questions.why: Copyright on literary works in India generally lasts for the author's life plus 60 years.

questions.q: Case: A buyer delays payment to a micro unit by 100 days. The unit can complain on…
questions.why: MSME Samadhaan is the portal where MSMEs can file complaints about delayed payments from buyers. The legal limit is 45 days.

questions.q: Which is NOT a problem of small business?
questions.why: Excess bargaining power is not a problem of small businesses. They actually have weak bargaining power. Finance, marketing and technology are common problems.

questions.q: Case: Three students raise ₹5 lakh from 400 people online who each give small amounts. Funding type?
questions.why: Raising money from many people who each give small amounts online is crowdfunding.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Trademarks protect inventions. Reason (R): Trademarks identify goods of one trader.
questions.why: The assertion is false: a trademark protects a brand name or mark, not an invention (a patent does that). The reason is true.

questions.q: Case: Investment ₹2 crore, turnover ₹12 crore (2025 limits). Classification?
questions.why: Investment of ₹2 crore is within the micro limit, but turnover of ₹12 crore is above ₹10 crore, so the unit is small.

questions.q: NSIC provides…
options: machinery on hire-purchase and marketing support
questions.why: The National Small Industries Corporation (NSIC) helps small units with machinery on hire-purchase and with marketing support.

courses.note: Part B chapters (7–10) follow the rationalised NCERT sequence; topic order may differ by edition; MSME limits shown are those effective from 1 April 2025

courses.title: Ch 9 · Internal Trade
courses.summary: Internal trade, services of wholesalers and retailers, itinerant and fixed-shop retailers, large-scale retail formats, and the role of GST and chambers of commerce.
outcomes: Learners can explain services of wholesalers and retailers
Learners can classify itinerant and fixed-shop retailers
Learners can compare departmental stores, chain stores, supermarkets and others
Learners can explain how GST and chambers of commerce support internal trade

lessons.title: Internal trade and wholesale trade

scenes.text: A biscuit factory in Indore makes 10 lakh packets a day.
Wholesalers buy truckloads and sell cartons to thousands of shops.
Your local shop sells you one packet.

steps.title: Internal trade
steps.body: Buying and selling of goods and services **within the boundaries of a nation**. No customs duty or import duty; payment in domestic currency. Two types: **wholesale trade** (buying in large quantities from producers and selling to retailers/industrial users) and **retail trade** (selling to final consumers in small quantities).

steps.title: Services of wholesalers to manufacturers
steps.body:
- Facilitating large-scale production (bulk orders).
- Bearing risk (price fall, theft, spoilage).
- Financial assistance (cash payment, advance).
- Expert advice on consumer preferences and prices.
- Help in marketing (reach many retailers).
- Facilitate production continuity (buying even off-season).
- Storage — holding stock from production until sale.

steps.title: Services of wholesalers to retailers
steps.body:
- Availability of goods (variety from many producers).
- Marketing support (ads, promotions).
- Grant of credit to retailers.
- Specialised knowledge of products.
- Risk sharing — retailers buy small lots, avoid holding large stocks.

steps.title: Solved example 1: Identify the service
steps.body: A wholesaler buys raincoats from a manufacturer in January (off-season) → *continuity of production* and *storage*. He tells the manufacturer that customers want lighter fabric → *expert advice*.

steps.title: Solved example 2: To whom?
steps.body: The wholesaler gives a shop 30 days to pay → service to *retailer* (credit). He pays the factory in cash on delivery → service to *manufacturer* (financial assistance).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying wholesalers sell mainly to final consumers.
- Mixing services to manufacturers and services to retailers in answers.

items.text: Buying in bulk so factory can produce at scale
Supplying a variety from many producers
Small lots so shops avoid big stocks

quiz.why: Internal trade takes place within the borders of a country. Trade between countries is external trade.
Wholesalers buy in bulk and sell mainly to retailers and industrial users. Retailers sell to final consumers.

options: bridge time gap between production and sale
quiz.why: Wholesalers store goods and release them over time, which bridges the time gap between production and sale.

quiz.q: Credit to retailers is a service of…
quiz.why: Wholesalers often give goods on credit to retailers. This helps small retailers.

quiz.q: Import duty applies to internal trade?
quiz.why: No, import duty does not apply to internal trade, since goods do not cross a national border. Customs duty applies to foreign trade.

lessons.title: Retail trade, services of retailers and itinerant retailers

story.title: The vegetable cart and the weekly haat

scenes.text: A vegetable seller pushes a cart through Meena’s lane every morning.
On Sundays, traders gather at the weekly haat.
Retailers come in many forms — some do not even have a shop.

steps.title: Services of retailers
steps.body:
**To manufacturers/wholesalers**: help in distribution, personal selling, enabling large-scale operations, collecting market information, help in promotion.
**To consumers**: regular availability of products, new product information, convenience in buying (small quantities, near home, long hours), wide selection, after-sales services, credit facilities.

steps.title: Itinerant retailers (no fixed shop)
steps.body:
- **Peddlers and hawkers**: carry goods on carts/bicycles/heads, door to door — toys, vegetables, fruits.
- **Market traders**: open shops at different places on fixed days (weekly haats).
- **Street traders (pavement vendors)**: at busy places — railway stations, bus stops.
- **Cheap jacks**: have independent shops of a temporary nature in a locality; move when business slows; deal in household goods, repairs.

steps.title: Solved example 1: Identify the retailer
steps.body: A man selling balloons and toys door to door → *hawker/peddler*. A woman selling bangles at the Tuesday market in different villages each day → *market trader*. A vendor at a bus stand selling magazines → *street trader*.

steps.title: Solved example 2: Service to consumer
steps.body: A shopkeeper lets regular customers pay at month-end → *credit facility*. He delivers a new washing machine and installs it → *after-sales service*.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing market traders (fixed days, different places) with street traders (busy fixed spots).
- Thinking cheap jacks are door-to-door sellers — they have temporary shops.

pairs: Sells door to door from a cart
Sells at weekly markets on fixed days
Sits at busy spots like bus stops
Temporary shop, moves when business drops

quiz.q: A vendor at a railway station sitting on the pavement is a…
quiz.why: A vendor sitting on the pavement at a railway station or busy place is a street trader, a type of small itinerant retailer.

quiz.q: Collecting market information is a service of retailers to…
quiz.why: Retailers collect information about customer tastes and send it to manufacturers and wholesalers. This helps them plan their products.

options: have no fixed place of business
quiz.why: Itinerant retailers have no fixed place of business and move from place to place to sell their goods.
Weekly haats are markets on fixed days, where market traders sell their goods in different places.

quiz.q: After-sales service is a service to…
quiz.why: After-sales service, such as repairs and installation, is a service to consumers.

lessons.title: Fixed shop retailers: small shops

scenes.text: Meena’s market has a general store, a shoe shop, a second-hand bookshop and a corner stall.
Each type serves customers differently.
These are small-scale fixed shop retailers.

steps.title: Types of small fixed shops
steps.body:
- **General stores**: daily needs (grocery, toiletries, stationery) in residential areas; credit and home delivery; personal touch.
- **Speciality shops**: one type of product (children’s garments, sweets, medicines).
- **Street stall holders**: small stalls at street crossings or busy places — cheap items like hosiery, toys, newspapers.
- **Second-hand goods shops**: used books, clothes, furniture, vehicles — at lower prices.
- **Single-line stores**: a single line of products with variety (e.g., only readymade garments, only watches, only shoes).

steps.title: Solved example 1: Classify
steps.body: (a) A shop with grocery, soap and notebooks near homes → general store. (b) A shop selling only watches of many brands → single-line store. (c) A shop selling used laptops → second-hand goods shop.

steps.title: Solved example 2: Why do general stores survive large retailers?
steps.body: Convenience (close to home), long hours, credit to known customers, small quantities, home delivery and a personal relationship.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing single-line stores (one line, many varieties) with speciality shops (a specific product).
- Assuming small shops never give credit.

quiz.q: Used books are sold at a…
quiz.why: Used books are sold in second-hand goods shops, which deal in goods that have been used before.

quiz.q: A shop selling only watches is a…
quiz.why: A shop that sells only one line of goods, such as watches, is a single-line store.

quiz.q: General stores are usually located in…
quiz.why: General stores are usually in residential areas, near homes, and they sell daily-use goods.

quiz.q: A strength of small shops is…
quiz.why: Small shops give personal attention and often give credit to regular customers. Large variety and central buying belong to big stores.
Street stall holders sell cheap, daily-use items at busy places such as bus stops.

lessons.title: Large-scale retailers

scenes.text: Meena visits a big store that sells clothes, kitchenware and toys under one roof.
The same burger brand has 200 identical outlets.
A vending machine at the metro gives her a cold drink.

steps.title: Departmental stores
steps.body: Large establishments offering a wide variety of products, classified into departments, under one roof; usually in central locations. Features: shopping convenience, centralised purchasing, decentralised selling, attractive services (restaurants, rest rooms). **Merits**: attract many customers, convenience, economies of large-scale buying, promotion. **Limitations**: lack of personal attention, high operating costs, high possibility of loss, inconvenient location for some.

steps.title: Chain stores (multiple shops)
steps.body: A network of retail shops owned and operated by one organisation, selling standardised products at uniform prices; centrally managed, located in busy localities. **Merits**: economies of scale, elimination of middlemen, no bad debts (cash sales), transfer of goods between branches, diffusion of risk, low cost. **Limitations**: limited products, lack of initiative by branch managers, lack of personal touch, difficult to change demand quickly.

steps.title: Other large-scale formats
steps.body:
- **Mail order houses**: sell through post/courier after receiving orders (catalogues, ads); goods sent by VPP/cash on delivery. Suit standardised, graded, easy-to-transport goods. Today largely replaced by e-commerce.
- **Consumer cooperative stores**: owned by consumers; low prices, cash sales, profit shared as bonus.
- **Supermarkets**: large self-service stores selling mainly food and household items at low prices; cash and carry.
- **Vending machines**: coin/card/UPI-operated machines for snacks, drinks, tickets; useful for pre-packed, low-price, standardised goods; high installation and maintenance cost.

steps.title: Solved example 1: Departmental vs chain store
steps.body: Location: central (departmental) vs many localities (chain). Range: wide variety (departmental) vs limited line (chain). Credit: may offer credit (departmental) vs cash only (chain). Prices: may vary by department vs uniform prices (chain).

steps.title: Solved example 2: Identify the format
steps.body: (a) Customers pick items in trolleys and pay at checkout → supermarket. (b) A residents’ society runs a store owned by members → consumer cooperative store. (c) Orders from a catalogue delivered by post → mail order house.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying chain stores give wide variety — they specialise.
- Saying departmental stores have uniform prices across branches — that is chain stores.
- Forgetting vending machine limitations (maintenance, breakdowns).

items.text: Same brand, uniform prices, many outlets
Centralised purchasing, decentralised selling, central location

quiz.q: Uniform prices across outlets are typical of…
quiz.why: Chain stores are owned by one company and sell standard goods at the same prices in all outlets.

quiz.q: Self-service is a key feature of…
quiz.why: Self-service, where customers take goods from the shelves themselves, is a key feature of supermarkets.

quiz.q: A limitation of departmental stores is…
quiz.why: A limitation of departmental stores is their high operating costs, which mean higher prices. Attractive services and convenience are advantages.

quiz.q: Mail order suits goods that are…
quiz.why: Mail order suits goods that are standardised, light and easy to transport. Perishable or custom-made goods do not suit it.
Chain stores sell mostly for cash. So they have no bad debts.

lessons.title: GST and chambers of commerce in internal trade

scenes.text: Before GST, trucks waited for hours at state check-posts.
Since July 2017, one GST system covers the whole country.
Chambers of commerce also help traders across states.

steps.title: GST and internal trade
steps.body: GST (from 1 July 2017) unified many indirect taxes and created a **common national market**: removal of cascading, input tax credit across states, abolition of state check-posts and **e-way bills** for movement of goods, easier compliance online through GSTN. This reduces cost and time of moving goods across states.

steps.title: Role of chambers of commerce and industry
steps.body:
Associations of businesses (e.g., FICCI, CII, ASSOCHAM and state/city chambers) that:
- Help in **transportation and interstate movement** of goods (dialogue with government on transport and taxes).
- Promote **harmonisation of taxes** and levies.
- Improve **marketing of agro-products** and support **infrastructure** (roads, power, ports).
- Simplify **labour legislation** issues, and promote **standardisation** of weights and measures and product quality.
- Act as a link between business and government; arrange training, trade fairs and dispute resolution.

steps.title: Solved example 1: Effect of GST
steps.body: A trader sending goods from Gujarat to Punjab previously paid entry tax and waited at check-posts; under GST, IGST is charged with credit available to the buyer, and goods move with an e-way bill → faster, cheaper trade.

steps.title: Solved example 2: Chamber role
steps.body: A state chamber lobbies for a cold-chain corridor for fruits from the hills to the plains → *marketing of agro-products and infrastructure*.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying GST is a direct tax — it is indirect.
- Thinking chambers of commerce are government departments — they are business associations.

statements.s: GST helped remove state check-posts.
Chambers of commerce are government ministries.
GST created a common national market.
Input tax credit is available only within one state.

quiz.why: GST came into force on 1 July 2017.
An e-way bill is an electronic document for the movement of goods, which is needed above a set value.

quiz.q: A role of chambers of commerce is…
quiz.why: Chambers of commerce help in harmonising taxes and levies, by representing business views to government. They do not print currency or run railways.
GST is an indirect tax, because the tax is collected by the seller from the buyer and paid to the government.
Removing cascading means eliminating tax on tax, through input tax credit under GST.

questions.q: Internal trade is trade…
questions.why: Internal trade is trade within a nation. Trade between nations is international trade.

questions.q: Wholesalers buy from…
questions.why: Wholesalers buy goods in bulk from manufacturers, and then sell to retailers.

questions.q: Peddlers sell…
questions.why: Peddlers sell goods door to door, carrying them with them, so they have no fixed shop.

questions.q: Self-service stores selling groceries are…
questions.why: Self-service stores selling groceries and daily items under one roof are supermarkets.

questions.q: Centralised purchasing and decentralised selling is a feature of…
questions.why: Departmental stores buy goods centrally in bulk and sell them through different departments, so purchasing is centralised and selling is decentralised.

questions.q: A chain store sells on…
questions.why: Chain stores sell on a cash basis, so they have no bad debts.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Wholesalers help manufacturers in large-scale production. Reason (R): They place bulk orders.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true and R explains A. Wholesalers place bulk orders with manufacturers, which allows the manufacturer to produce on a large scale.

questions.q: Case: A trader sets up stalls in different villages on fixed weekdays. Type?
questions.why: A trader who sets up stalls on fixed days in different villages is a market trader, as in weekly haats.

questions.q: Case: A shop sells only watches but of 20 brands. Type?
questions.why: A shop that sells only watches is a single-line store, even though it carries many brands. It deals in one line of goods.

questions.q: Which is NOT a service of retailers to consumers?
questions.why: Bulk production is done by manufacturers, not retailers. Credit, regular supply and after-sales service are retailer services.

questions.q: Vending machines are suitable for…
questions.why: Vending machines suit pre-packed, standardised, low-priced items such as drinks. They cannot sell cars, heavy furniture or custom-made goods.

questions.q: Case: A burger brand has 300 outlets with identical menus and prices managed from a head office. Type?
questions.why: A chain of outlets with the same menu and prices, run from a head office, is a chain store (multiple shop).

questions.q: Assertion (A): Chain stores do not suffer bad debts. Reason (R): They sell on cash basis.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true and R explains A. Chain stores sell for cash, so they have no credit sales and therefore no bad debts.

questions.q: Case: Goods move from Maharashtra to Karnataka without check-post delays, with an e-way bill and IGST. Which development enabled this?
questions.why: GST made one tax for the country and removed check-posts, with e-way bills and IGST for inter-state movement. So goods move smoothly between states.

questions.q: Which pair is wrongly matched?
options: Supermarket – credit sales and personal attention
Cheap jack – temporary shop in a locality
questions.why: A supermarket is self-service and sells for cash, so it does not give credit or personal attention. That pair is wrong. The others are right.

questions.q: A role of chambers of commerce is…
questions.why: Chambers of commerce can support the marketing of agro-products by representing and assisting traders. They do not run courts, collect GST or issue currency.

courses.title: Ch 10 · International Business
courses.summary: Meaning, scope and benefits of international business, modes of entry, export and import procedures and documents, export promotion schemes and international institutions (WTO, IMF, World Bank).
outcomes: Learners can distinguish international from domestic business
Learners can compare modes of entry by investment, control and risk
Learners can sequence export and import procedures and identify documents
Learners can describe export promotion measures and global institutions

lessons.title: International business: meaning, scope and benefits

story.title: Basmati to Dubai, iPhones to India

scenes.text: A Haryana rice mill ships basmati to Dubai.
An Indian IT firm writes software for a bank in London.
Both are doing international business.

steps.title: Meaning and differences from domestic business
steps.body:
**International business** is manufacturing and trade beyond national boundaries — trade in goods and services, transfer of capital, technology, people and intellectual property.

Differences: nationality of buyers/sellers, mobility of factors (restricted internationally), different currencies (exchange rate risk), different customs and laws, government regulation (tariffs, quotas), different business systems, higher risk.

steps.title: Scope
steps.body:
- **Merchandise exports and imports** (tangible goods).
- **Service exports and imports** (tourism, transport, IT, consultancy).
- **Licensing and franchising** (allowing foreign firms to use patents, trademarks or business formats for a fee).
- **Foreign investment**: *FDI* (direct investment in plant, with control) and *FPI* (portfolio investment in shares/bonds without control).

steps.title: Benefits
steps.body:
**To nations**: earn foreign exchange, efficient use of resources (comparative advantage), improve growth prospects and employment, increase standard of living.
**To firms**: higher profits, use surplus capacity, improve growth prospects, way out of intense domestic competition, improve business vision.

steps.title: Solved example 1: Classify the activity
steps.body: (a) Exporting tea → merchandise export. (b) Foreign tourists staying in Goa → service export (tourism). (c) An Indian firm builds a factory in Kenya with 100% ownership → FDI. (d) A US fund buys shares of an Indian bank → FPI.

steps.title: Solved example 2: Why go global?
steps.body: A pharma firm with spare capacity in India exports generic medicines to Africa → *use of surplus capacity* + *higher profits* + *foreign exchange for India*.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating international trade and international business as identical — business is wider (includes investment, licensing).
- Confusing FDI (control) with FPI (no control).

items.text: Software services for a UK bank
Pizza brand lets an Indian firm use its name

quiz.why: International business is wider than international trade, as it includes investment, licensing and other dealings, as well as trade in goods and services.
Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) involves owning and controlling business operations in another country. Foreign portfolio investment gives no control.

quiz.q: Tourism by foreigners in India is a…
quiz.why: Foreign tourists in India bring in foreign exchange for a service, so tourism is a service export.
International business earns foreign exchange for a nation. Higher tariffs, less employment and isolation are not benefits.
Exchange-rate risk exists because countries use different currencies, whose values change against each other.

lessons.title: Modes of entry into international business

story.title: How to enter a foreign market

scenes.text: An Indian ice-cream brand wants to sell in Singapore.
Should it export, license its brand, form a JV or build its own factory?
Each mode has different cost, control and risk.

steps.title: Exporting and importing
steps.body: Simplest mode: *direct* (firm handles everything) or *indirect* (through intermediaries such as export houses). Merits: easy, less investment, less risk. Limitations: extra packaging/transport costs, trade barriers, limited contact with foreign market.

steps.title: Contract manufacturing (outsourcing)
steps.body: A firm contracts local manufacturers abroad to produce components or goods to its specifications. Merits: no investment in plant, low cost, local suppliers benefit. Limitations: quality issues, less control, local firm cannot sell freely.

steps.title: Licensing and franchising
steps.body: The licensor allows a foreign licensee to use patents, trademarks, technology, for a **royalty**. **Franchising** is a similar arrangement for services/business formats (fast food, hotels). Merits: little investment, low risk, licensee handles local operations. Limitations: licensee may become a competitor, trade secrets may leak, conflicts over royalty.

steps.title: Joint ventures and wholly owned subsidiaries
steps.body:
- **JV**: share ownership with a local partner. Merits: shared cost and risk, local knowledge, distribution. Limitations: shared profits, conflicts.
- **Wholly owned subsidiary (WOS)**: 100% ownership (new or acquired). Merits: full control, all profits, protection of technology. Limitations: huge investment, entire risk, political risk.

steps.title: Solved example 1: Choose the mode
steps.body: A small firm with little capital and no foreign experience → *indirect exporting*. A firm with a strong brand wanting fast expansion with low investment → *franchising*. A tech firm needing full control of secret technology → *wholly owned subsidiary*.

steps.title: Solved example 2: Rank by control and risk
steps.body: Lowest to highest control (and investment/risk): Exporting → Contract manufacturing → Licensing/franchising → Joint venture → Wholly owned subsidiary.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying licensing gives full control.
- Saying WOS is low risk.
- Confusing contract manufacturing with licensing (licensing sells rights; contract manufacturing buys production).

activity.prompt: Arrange modes from LOWEST to HIGHEST investment and control

quiz.why: Royalty is a payment for the right to use a brand, technology or patent. It is paid in licensing and franchising.
A wholly owned subsidiary is 100% owned by the parent, so it gives full control. In a joint venture control is shared.
A risk of licensing is that the licensee may learn the technology and become a competitor.
Exporting is the simplest way to enter a foreign market, since it needs little investment and no operations abroad.

quiz.q: A fast-food brand entering via local operators uses…
quiz.why: A fast-food brand that lets local operators run outlets under its name is using franchising.

lessons.title: Export procedure and documents

scenes.text: A Dubai importer emails an enquiry for 20 tonnes of basmati.
The exporter must arrange licences, inspection, customs and shipping.
Here is the step-by-step export procedure.

steps.title: Steps in exporting
steps.body:
1. **Receipt of enquiry and sending quotation** (*proforma invoice*: price, quality, terms).
2. **Receipt of order/indent**.
3. **Assessing importer’s creditworthiness / securing payment** — usually by **letter of credit (L/C)** from importer’s bank.
4. **Obtaining export licence**: IEC (Importer Exporter Code) from DGFT; registration with the relevant **Export Promotion Council**; RCMC.
5. **Pre-shipment finance** from bank (packing credit).
6. **Production/procurement of goods**.
7. **Pre-shipment inspection** (for certain goods) and certificate.
8. **Excise/GST clearance** formalities (refund/LUT as applicable).
9. **Certificate of origin** (needed for tariff concessions).
10. **Reservation of shipping space** (shipping order).
11. **Packing and forwarding** (clearing & forwarding agent).
12. **Insurance** of goods.
13. **Customs clearance**: *shipping bill* filed; goods examined; *let export* order.
14. **Mate’s receipt** from ship’s captain → exchanged for **bill of lading** after paying freight.
15. **Preparation of invoice** and **securing payment** — documents sent through bank (bill of exchange: *sight draft* — D/P, or *usance draft* — D/A).

steps.title: Key export documents
steps.body:
- **Proforma invoice**: quotation with details of goods and terms.
- **Letter of credit**: importer’s bank guarantees payment to exporter on presenting documents.
- **Shipping bill**: main document for customs permission to export.
- **Mate’s receipt**: issued by the ship’s captain on loading goods.
- **Bill of lading** (sea) / **Airway bill** (air): receipt by carrier and document of title.
- **Certificate of origin**, **certificate of inspection**, **marine insurance policy**, **commercial invoice**, **packing list**.

steps.title: Solved example 1: Order the steps
steps.body: Enquiry → proforma invoice → order → L/C → IEC/licence → packing credit → production → inspection → certificate of origin → shipping space → packing → insurance → customs (shipping bill) → mate’s receipt → bill of lading → documents through bank → payment.

steps.title: Solved example 2: Identify the document
steps.body: The captain gives a receipt when rice is loaded → *mate’s receipt*. The shipping company issues a document that the importer uses to claim the goods → *bill of lading*. Customs needs permission application → *shipping bill*.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing shipping bill (customs) with bill of lading (carrier).
- Thinking mate’s receipt is issued by customs — it is issued by the ship’s captain.
- Shipping before arranging payment security (L/C).

items: Receive enquiry and send proforma invoice
Get mate’s receipt then bill of lading
Send documents through bank and receive payment

quiz.q: The document used for customs clearance of exports is…
quiz.why: A shipping bill is the document filed with customs for clearance of exports. A bill of entry is used for imports.
The mate's receipt is issued by the captain of the ship, as proof that the goods were loaded on the vessel.
The Import Export Code (IEC) is issued by the Directorate General of Foreign Trade (DGFT).

quiz.q: Letter of credit is issued by…
quiz.why: A letter of credit is issued by the importer's bank, which promises to pay the exporter once the conditions are met.
A bill of lading is issued by the shipping company, and it is a document of title to the goods. It can be used to claim the goods.

lessons.title: Import procedure and documents

scenes.text: An Indian textile mill wants a high-speed loom from Germany.
It needs foreign exchange, an import licence check and customs clearance.
Here is the import procedure.

steps.title: Steps in importing
steps.body:
1. **Trade enquiry** → receive quotation/proforma invoice.
2. **Procurement of import licence** (check EXIM/Foreign Trade Policy; obtain IEC).
3. **Obtaining foreign exchange** (apply to an authorised dealer bank, under FEMA rules).
4. **Placing order or indent**.
5. **Obtaining letter of credit** (arrange L/C through own bank).
6. **Arranging finance** for payment.
7. **Receipt of shipment advice** from exporter.
8. **Retirement of import documents** (pay or accept bill to obtain documents incl. bill of lading).
9. **Arrival of goods** — ship’s captain files **import general manifest**.
10. **Customs clearance and release of goods**: obtain *delivery order* (by endorsing bill of lading), pay port dues (*port trust dues receipt*), file **bill of entry**, pay customs duty, goods examined and released.

steps.title: Key import documents
steps.body:
- **Bill of entry**: form filled for customs assessment of import duty.
- **Import general manifest**: list of goods on the ship, filed by the carrier.
- **Delivery order**: issued by shipping company to take delivery.
- **Dock challan / port trust dues receipt**.
- **Shipment advice**, **bill of lading**, **commercial invoice**, **certificate of origin**.

steps.title: Solved example 1: Identify the document
steps.body: The mill’s agent fills a form showing value of the loom for customs duty → *bill of entry*. The ship’s captain submits a list of all cargo → *import general manifest*.

steps.title: Solved example 2: Retiring documents
steps.body: Under D/P (documents against payment), the mill pays its bank to receive the bill of lading; it then endorses it to the shipping company for a delivery order.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing bill of entry (import) with shipping bill (export).
- Forgetting foreign exchange approval under FEMA through an authorised dealer.

pairs: Permission to take goods from ship
Exporter informs goods have been shipped
Bank guarantee of payment to exporter

quiz.q: Bill of entry is used in…
quiz.why: A bill of entry is filed with customs by an importer to clear imported goods. Exports use a shipping bill.

quiz.q: Foreign exchange for imports is obtained from…
quiz.why: Importers get foreign exchange through an authorised dealer, which is a bank allowed by the RBI to deal in foreign exchange.

quiz.q: Import general manifest is filed by…
options: person in charge of the carrier
quiz.why: The import general manifest is filed with customs by the person in charge of the carrier (ship or aircraft), listing the cargo.
The shipping company issues the delivery order, which allows the importer to take delivery of goods from the port.

quiz.q: Under D/P, documents are released on…
quiz.why: Under D/P (documents against payment), the bank gives the shipping documents to the importer only on payment.

lessons.title: Export promotion and international institutions

scenes.text: India is a founder member of the WTO.
An exporter sets up in an SEZ to get duty-free inputs.
Global institutions and national schemes shape trade.

steps.title: Export promotion measures in India
steps.body:
- **Duty drawback**: refund of customs/excise duties paid on inputs of exported goods.
- **Export manufacturing under bond**: produce for export without paying duties.
- **Exemption from GST/zero-rating** of exports.
- **Advance authorisation**: duty-free import of inputs for export production.
- **Export Promotion Capital Goods (EPCG)** scheme.
- **Status holders / export houses** recognition.
- **Export processing zones (EPZs) → Special Economic Zones (SEZs)** (SEZ Act 2005): duty-free enclaves with simplified procedures.
- **100% Export Oriented Units (EOUs)**.
- Export credit insurance (ECGC) and pre-shipment/post-shipment finance.

steps.title: International institutions
steps.body:
- **WTO** (World Trade Organization): set up **1 January 1995**, successor of **GATT** (1948); headquarters Geneva. Objectives: reduce tariffs and trade barriers, non-discrimination (MFN), dispute settlement, trade in goods, services (GATS) and IP (TRIPS).
- **IMF** (International Monetary Fund): Bretton Woods institution (1944 conference, operations from 1947); promotes exchange stability, short-term balance-of-payments support.
- **World Bank (IBRD)**: Bretton Woods; long-term development loans; with IDA (soft loans), IFC (private sector), MIGA (investment guarantees), ICSID (investment disputes).

steps.title: Solved example 1: Which scheme?
steps.body: An exporter gets refund of duty paid on imported fabric used in shirts sent abroad → *duty drawback*. A firm imports machinery at concessional duty with an export obligation → *EPCG*.

steps.title: Solved example 2: Which institution?
steps.body: A country facing a temporary balance-of-payments crisis → *IMF*. A long-term loan for a dam → *World Bank*. A tariff dispute between two countries → *WTO dispute settlement*.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying WTO was founded in 1948 — that was GATT; WTO came in 1995.
- Mixing IMF (short-term BoP) with World Bank (long-term development).

events.text: Bretton Woods conference (IMF and World Bank planned)

quiz.why: The World Trade Organization (WTO) was established on 1 January 1995.

quiz.q: Refund of duties on inputs used in exports is…
quiz.why: Duty drawback is the refund of customs and excise duties paid on inputs that were used for exports.

quiz.q: Short-term BoP support is given by…
quiz.why: The IMF (International Monetary Fund) gives short-term help to countries with balance of payments problems.

quiz.q: SEZs in India are governed by the…
quiz.why: Special Economic Zones in India are set up under the SEZ Act, 2005.

quiz.q: IDA of the World Bank group provides…
quiz.why: The International Development Association (IDA) of the World Bank group gives soft, concessional loans to the poorest countries.

questions.q: International business includes…
questions.why: International business includes trade, investment, licensing and other dealings across countries, so it is wide in scope.

questions.q: FPI involves…
questions.why: Foreign portfolio investment (FPI) is investment in securities such as shares and bonds of another country, without controlling the company.

questions.q: The simplest entry mode is…
questions.why: Exporting is the simplest mode of entering a foreign market. It needs the lowest investment and risk.

questions.q: Shipping bill is required for…
questions.why: A shipping bill is required for exports, to get customs clearance. Imports need a bill of entry.

questions.q: WTO replaced…
questions.why: The WTO replaced GATT (General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade) in 1995.

questions.q: Bill of entry is filed by…
questions.why: A bill of entry is filed with customs by the importer, to get imported goods cleared. The exporter files a shipping bill.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Licensing requires little investment. Reason (R): The licensee bears the cost of local operations.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true and R explains A. In licensing, the licensee sets up and runs the local operations, so the licensor needs little investment.

questions.q: Case: A firm wants full control over secret technology abroad. Best mode?
questions.why: To keep full control over secret technology abroad, a wholly owned subsidiary is best, as the parent owns 100%. Licensing, franchising and contract manufacturing share the know-how with others.

questions.q: Case: Captain issues a receipt when goods are loaded. It is exchanged for…
questions.why: The captain's receipt for loaded goods (mate's receipt) is handed to the shipping company, which gives the bill of lading in exchange, usually after freight is paid.

questions.q: Duty drawback is…
options: refund of duties on inputs used in exports
questions.why: Duty drawback is a refund of customs and excise duties paid on inputs used in making exported goods.

questions.q: Which is a Bretton Woods institution?
questions.why: The IMF is a Bretton Woods institution, set up in 1944 along with the World Bank. SAARC and ASEAN are regional groups, and the WTO started in 1995.

questions.q: Case: An Indian garment firm gets a Bangladeshi factory to stitch shirts to its design and sells them under its own brand. Mode?
questions.why: The Indian firm has the shirts made by another firm abroad to its design and sells them under its own brand. This is contract manufacturing.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Exporters prefer a letter of credit. Reason (R): It assures payment by the importer’s bank against documents.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true and R explains A. In a letter of credit, the importer's bank promises to pay the exporter on receiving the documents, so payment is assured.

questions.q: Which document is the evidence of title for goods shipped by sea?
questions.why: The bill of lading is the document of title for goods sent by sea, as the holder can claim the goods. A mate's receipt is only proof of loading.

questions.q: Case: Importer’s documents are released only when he accepts a bill payable in 90 days. Type?
questions.why: When documents are given against acceptance of a bill payable after a period (here 90 days), it is called documents against acceptance (D/A).

questions.q: Which sequence is correct for exports?
options: Bill of lading → shipping bill → mate’s receipt
Shipping bill → mate’s receipt → bill of lading
questions.why: For exports, the shipping bill comes first (customs clearance), then goods are loaded and a mate's receipt is given, and finally the bill of lading is issued.

questions.q: Case: A country needs a 20-year loan for a highway. Approach?
questions.why: The World Bank gives long-term loans for development projects, such as a highway. The IMF handles short-term balance-of-payments needs, and ECGC insures exports.
