courses.title: Revision & Practice · Class 11 Business Studies
courses.summary: Chapter-by-chapter revision sheets for all ten chapters, a method for case-based questions, and two mixed mock papers.
outcomes: Learners can recall key terms and distinctions across all chapters
Learners can answer case-based questions with evidence
Learners can attempt full-length mixed practice

lessons.title: Quick-revision sheet: Part A (Chapters 1–6)

scenes.text: Ten days to the exam, and Sara wants short notes.
Business Studies is about definitions, features, merits, limitations and cases.
Here is the condensed sheet.

steps.title: Ch 1 Business, trade and commerce
steps.body: Hundi, shrenis, ports (Bharuch, Tamralipti). Business features: economic, regular, profit, risk. Industry: primary (extractive, genetic), secondary (manufacturing: analytical, synthetical, processing, assembling; construction), tertiary. Commerce = trade + auxiliaries (transport–place, warehousing–time, insurance–risk, banking–finance, advertising–information). Multiple objectives; risk causes: natural, human, economic, other.

steps.title: Ch 2 Forms of organisation
steps.body: Sole proprietor (unlimited liability, no separate entity). JHF (karta unlimited; co-parceners limited; by birth; Hindu Succession Act 1956). Partnership (1932 Act; 2–50; mutual agency; registration optional; partner types). Cooperative (1912 Act; min 10; one member one vote). Company (2013 Act; private 2–200; public 7+; OPC; perpetual succession; limited liability).

steps.title: Ch 3 Enterprises
steps.body: Departmental (ministry, budget), statutory corporation (special Act: LIC, RBI), government company (≥51%). 1991: dereservation, disinvestment, BIFR, MoU. MNC features. JV (contractual/equity). PPP (risk sharing).

steps.title: Ch 4 Services
steps.body: 5 I’s. Banks (RBI, commercial, cooperative), deposits, NEFT/RTGS/IMPS/UPI. Insurance principles: utmost good faith, insurable interest, indemnity, proximate cause, subrogation, contribution, mitigation. Life/fire/marine/health. Warehouses: private, public, bonded, government, cooperative.

steps.title: Ch 5–6
steps.body: E-business types (B2B, B2C, C2C, intra-B, B2E), benefits/limitations, payments and security, BPO/KPO. Social responsibility: for/against, kinds (economic, legal, ethical, discretionary), CSR Section 135 (2%), pollution, ethics elements.

steps.title: Answer-writing tips
steps.body: Define → list points with headings → one-line explanation each → example. For “case” questions, quote the line from the case that shows the concept.

quiz.q: Hindrance of risk is removed by…
quiz.why: Insurance covers losses from fire, accident, theft and so on, so it removes the hindrance of risk.
A partnership can have at most 50 partners under current rules.
The RBI was created by the RBI Act, so it is a statutory corporation.

quiz.q: Selling used goods person-to-person online is…
quiz.why: Selling used goods online from one person to another is consumer to consumer (C2C).
Ethical responsibility goes beyond the law. It means doing what society expects even when no law requires it.

lessons.title: Quick-revision sheet: Part B (Chapters 7–10)

scenes.text: Part B has the most case-based questions.
Learn the key terms and their differences.
Here is the sheet.

steps.title: Ch 7 Finance
steps.body: Fixed vs working capital. Classification: period, ownership, generation. Equity (owners, residual, votes), preference (fixed dividend, priority), retained earnings (internal), debentures (creditors, fixed interest, tax-deductible), banks, FIs, public deposits (6 months–3 years, unsecured), trade credit, factoring, CP (7 days–1 year, unsecured), lease (lessor/lessee), ADR/GDR/IDR/FCCB.

steps.title: Ch 8 Small business
steps.body: Entrepreneurship features (systematic, lawful, innovation, organisation, risk). Startup India 2016. IPR: patent 20 years, trademark 10 years renewable, copyright (life+60), GI, design. MSME composite limits (2025): micro 2.5/10, small 25/100, medium 125/500 (₹ crore investment/turnover). Support: NSIC, DIC, SIDBI, NABARD, KVIC, CGTMSE, MSME Samadhaan (45 days).

steps.title: Ch 9 Internal trade
steps.body: Wholesaler services to manufacturers and retailers; retailer services. Itinerant: hawkers, market traders, street traders, cheap jacks. Small fixed: general, speciality, street stall, second-hand, single-line. Large: departmental, chain, mail order, cooperative, supermarket, vending machines. GST (1 July 2017), chambers of commerce.

steps.title: Ch 10 International business
steps.body: Scope: goods, services, licensing/franchising, FDI/FPI. Entry modes by control: export → contract manufacturing → licensing/franchising → JV → WOS. Export: proforma, L/C, IEC, packing credit, inspection, certificate of origin, shipping bill, mate’s receipt, bill of lading. Import: licence, forex, L/C, IGM, bill of entry, delivery order. WTO 1995, IMF, World Bank. Duty drawback, EPCG, SEZ.

steps.title: Frequent confusions
steps.body: Shipping bill (export customs) vs bill of entry (import customs) vs bill of lading (carrier title). ADR (USA) vs GDR (outside USA) vs IDR (foreign firm in India). Departmental vs chain store.

pairs: Foreign company raising money in India

quiz.why: Commercial paper is an unsecured short-term promissory note, as no asset is pledged against it.
MSMEs are classified by investment and turnover, not by location or profit.
Supermarkets are self-service stores where customers pick goods from the shelves and pay at the counter.

quiz.q: Bill of lading is issued by…
quiz.why: A bill of lading is issued by the shipping company (the carrier), as a receipt and document of title for the goods.
Duty drawback is a refund of duties paid on inputs that are used in exported goods.

lessons.title: How to answer case-based questions

scenes.text: Case questions hide the concept in one sentence.
Students lose marks by writing theory without quoting the case.
Here is a method.

steps.title: Four-step method
steps.body:
1. Read the question first, then the case.
2. Underline the key line(s).
3. Name the concept exactly (e.g., “Principle of subrogation”).
4. Quote the line and explain in one or two sentences; add extra points if marks allow.

steps.title: Worked case 1
steps.body: “After paying for the stolen car, the insurance company recovered the car and sold it.” → Concept: **subrogation**. Quote: “recovered the car and sold it”. Explanation: after compensating, the insurer steps into the insured’s rights.

steps.title: Worked case 2
steps.body: “Rita runs a shop that sells only shoes but of many brands and sizes.” → **single-line store**. Quote: “only shoes but of many brands”.

steps.title: Worked case 3
steps.body: “A company issued bonds in dollars that investors can convert into its shares after 3 years.” → **FCCB**. Quote: “bonds in dollars… convert into shares”.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing the right concept but no quote from the case.
- Writing an unrelated concept with similar words (e.g., contribution vs subrogation).

a.text: Case: “Two insurers covered the same warehouse and shared the ₹10 lakh loss in proportion to their policies.” Which principle?

choices.label: Subrogation
choices.feedback: No — subrogation is about the insurer taking the insured’s rights.

choices.label: Contribution
choices.feedback: Correct — insurers share proportionately.

w.text: Look again at the phrase “shared the loss”. Try again.

choices.label: Contribution
choices.feedback: Right.

r.text: Answer: Principle of contribution — quote “shared the ₹10 lakh loss in proportion to their policies”.

quiz.q: First step in a case question:
quiz.why: In a case question, first read the question so you know what is asked, then use the case facts to answer.

quiz.q: “Buys in bulk from manufacturers and sells to shops” describes…
quiz.why: A wholesaler buys in bulk from manufacturers and sells to shops (retailers).

quiz.q: “Lets a café use its brand for a royalty” describes…
quiz.why: Letting a café use a brand name for a royalty is franchising.

quiz.q: “Profit kept in business for expansion” describes…
quiz.why: Profit kept in the business for expansion is called retained earnings (ploughing back of profit).
Quoting the line from the case shows evidence for your answer and earns marks in case-based questions.

questions.q: [Mock A] Genetic industry example:
questions.why: Poultry farming raises birds by breeding, so it is a genetic industry. Mining is extractive, a refinery is analytical and car assembly is assembling.

questions.q: [Mock A] Registration of a partnership in India is…
questions.why: Registration of a partnership firm in India is optional, though an unregistered firm cannot sue third parties.

questions.q: [Mock A] Insurable interest must exist in marine insurance at the time of…
questions.why: In marine insurance the insurable interest must exist at the time of the loss.

questions.q: [Mock A] Which is a statutory corporation?
questions.why: LIC was set up by the LIC Act, so it is a statutory corporation. SAIL and Coal India are government companies, and India Post is a departmental undertaking.

questions.q: [Mock A] Case: A firm buys tea in bulk and sells it to 500 shops on credit. It is a…
questions.why: A firm that buys tea in bulk and sells to 500 shops on credit is a wholesaler.

questions.q: [Mock A] Assertion (A): A sole proprietor enjoys quick decision-making. Reason (R): He need not consult anyone.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true and R explains A. A sole proprietor does not need to consult anyone, so he can decide quickly.

questions.q: [Mock A] Case: An insurer pays ₹3 lakh for a stolen bike and later recovers it. The bike belongs to the insurer under…
questions.why: After paying the full claim for the stolen bike, the insurer gets the right to the bike when it is recovered. This is subrogation.

questions.q: [Mock A] Case: A software firm in Pune writes code for a German bank. Scope of international business?
questions.why: Writing software for a foreign bank earns foreign exchange for a service, so it is a service export.

questions.q: [Mock A] Case: Shareholding of government in X Ltd falls from 55% to 49%. X Ltd is now…
questions.why: A government company needs at least 51% government holding. At 49% the company is no longer a government company.

questions.q: [Mock A] Case: Insured with A ₹4 lakh and B ₹6 lakh; loss ₹5 lakh. B pays…
questions.why: The loss is shared in the ratio of the sums insured, 4 : 6. B pays 5 × 6/10 = ₹3 lakh.

questions.q: [Mock A] Which is NOT an element of business ethics?
questions.why: Price fixing with rivals is unfair and unethical, so it is not an element of ethics. Code of conduct, top management commitment and compliance mechanism are elements.

questions.q: [Mock A] Case: An NGO runs free schools in villages. Type of service?
questions.why: An NGO running free schools serves society without profit, so it provides a social service.

questions.q: [Mock B] Debenture holders are…
questions.why: Debenture holders lend money to the company, so they are its creditors. They are not owners.

questions.q: [Mock B] Patent term in India:
questions.why: A patent in India lasts for 20 years from the date of filing.

questions.q: [Mock B] Customs document for imports:
questions.why: The importer files a bill of entry with customs for clearing imports. A shipping bill is for exports.

questions.q: [Mock B] Case: A mall store has departments for clothing, toys and electronics under one roof. Type?
questions.why: A store with different departments, such as clothing, toys and electronics, under one roof is a departmental store.

questions.q: [Mock B] Case: A firm sells its receivables to a specialist for immediate cash. Source?
questions.why: Selling receivables to a specialist for immediate cash is factoring.

questions.q: [Mock B] Case (2025 limits): investment ₹30 crore; turnover ₹80 crore. The enterprise is…
questions.why: Investment of ₹30 crore is above the small limit (₹25 crore) but within the medium limit (₹125 crore), and turnover of ₹80 crore is also within limits. So it is medium.

questions.q: [Mock B] Assertion (A): Preference shareholders usually have no voting rights. Reason (R): They get priority in dividend.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true, but R does not explain A. Preference shareholders have no voting rights, and they get priority in dividend, but priority does not cause the lack of votes.

questions.q: [Mock B] Case: Ten firms in a state lobby together for better roads and simpler state taxes. They act through a…
questions.why: A chamber of commerce is a business association that puts forward the common needs of firms, such as better roads and simpler taxes, to the government.

questions.q: [Mock B] Case: An Indian firm lists its depository receipts in Luxembourg. Instrument?
questions.why: Depository receipts of an Indian firm listed outside the USA, such as in Luxembourg, are Global Depository Receipts (GDRs). ADRs are issued in the USA.

questions.q: [Mock B] Which sequence of entry modes shows rising control?
questions.why: Control rises from exporting (least), to licensing, to a joint venture, to a wholly owned subsidiary (full control).

questions.q: [Mock B] Case: ₹50 crore CP issued at ₹47 crore for one year. Approximate cost?
questions.why: CP is issued at ₹47 crore and repaid at ₹50 crore after one year. Cost = 3/47 ≈ 6.4%.

school-c11-chemistry-a.title: Class 11 Chemistry · Part A (Ch 1–3)
school-c11-chemistry-a.description: Class 11 Chemistry chapter by chapter: Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry, Structure of Atom, and Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties — with solved numericals and JEE/NEET bridge practice.

courses.title: Ch 1 · Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry
courses.summary: Matter and measurement, laws of chemical combination, Dalton's theory, atomic and molecular masses, the mole concept, empirical and molecular formulas, stoichiometry, limiting reagent and concentration terms.
outcomes: Learners can state and apply the laws of chemical combination
Learners can convert between mass, moles, particles and gas volume
Learners can derive empirical and molecular formulas from percentage composition
Learners can solve stoichiometry and limiting-reagent problems
Learners can express concentration as mass %, mole fraction, molarity and molality

lessons.title: Matter, measurement and laws of chemical combination

scenes.text: A baker always uses flour and yeast in the same ratio, whatever the batch size.
Chemists in the 1700s–1800s found that compounds behave the same way — elements combine in fixed mass ratios.

steps.title: Matter and measurement
steps.body:
- Matter: solid, liquid, gas; pure substances (elements, compounds) and mixtures (homogeneous, heterogeneous).
- Physical properties can be measured without changing identity (colour, m.p.); chemical properties need a chemical change (reactivity, combustibility).
- SI units; mass in kg, amount in mol, temperature in K. Use scientific notation and significant figures (same rules as physics).

steps.title: Laws of chemical combination
steps.body:
1. **Conservation of mass** (Lavoisier): mass is neither created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction.
2. **Definite proportions** (Proust): a compound always contains the same elements in the same mass ratio, whatever its source.
3. **Multiple proportions** (Dalton): when two elements form more than one compound, masses of one that combine with a fixed mass of the other are in small whole-number ratios.
4. **Gay Lussac's law of gaseous volumes:** gases react in simple whole-number volume ratios (same T, P).
5. **Avogadro's law:** equal volumes of gases at the same T and P contain equal numbers of molecules.

**Dalton's atomic theory:** matter is made of indivisible atoms; atoms of an element are identical; compounds form when atoms combine in fixed ratios; reactions rearrange atoms.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1 (multiple proportions):** H₂O has 2 g H : 16 g O; H₂O₂ has 2 g H : 32 g O. Masses of O per 2 g H are 16 : 32 = **1 : 2** — a simple ratio.

**Example 2 (gaseous volumes):** 2 volumes H₂ + 1 volume O₂ → 2 volumes water vapour: ratio **2 : 1 : 2**.

**Example 3 (conservation):** 12 g carbon burns completely in 32 g oxygen; mass of CO₂ formed = **44 g**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking Dalton's 'indivisible atom' is still fully correct — atoms have subatomic particles and isotopes exist.
- Applying Gay Lussac's law to masses (it is about gas volumes).
- Mixing up definite proportions (one compound) with multiple proportions (two or more compounds).

activity.prompt: Match the law to its scientist

quiz.q: CO and CO₂ illustrate the law of
quiz.why: Carbon and oxygen make CO and CO₂. For a fixed 12 g of carbon, the oxygen is 16 g and 32 g, which is a simple ratio of 1 : 2. This is the law of multiple proportions.

quiz.q: Pure water from a river or from a lab always has H:O mass ratio 1:8. This is the law of
quiz.why: Pure water always has hydrogen and oxygen in the same mass ratio of 1 : 8, whatever the source. This is the law of definite proportions.
A salt solution is a homogeneous mixture, as its composition is the same throughout. Sand in water, oil and water, and granite are not uniform.

quiz.q: 1 volume N₂ + 3 volumes H₂ give how many volumes of NH₃?
quiz.why: N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃. By Gay-Lussac's law, 1 volume of N₂ with 3 volumes of H₂ gives 2 volumes of NH₃.

quiz.q: Which postulate of Dalton's theory is not valid today?
quiz.why: Atoms are no longer thought to be indivisible, since they contain electrons, protons and neutrons. The other postulates are still accepted.

sources: NCERT Chemistry Class 11 (topic: laws of chemical combination)

lessons.title: Atomic and molecular masses and the mole

scenes.text: A shopkeeper doesn't count grains of rice — he weighs them.
Chemists count atoms the same way: one mole is a fixed number of particles with a known mass.

steps.title: Atomic and molecular mass
steps.body:
- **Atomic mass unit:** 1 u = 1/12 of the mass of one ¹²C atom ≈ 1.66 × 10⁻²⁴ g.
- **Average atomic mass** uses isotope abundances: e.g. chlorine ≈ 0.7577 × 34.97 + 0.2423 × 36.97 ≈ 35.45 u.
- **Molecular mass** = sum of atomic masses (H₂O = 18 u; CO₂ = 44 u; C₆H₁₂O₆ = 180 u).
- **Formula mass** for ionic compounds (NaCl = 58.5 u).

steps.title: Mole concept
steps.body:
- 1 mole = **6.022 × 10²³** particles (Avogadro constant N_A) = number of atoms in exactly 12 g of ¹²C.
- **Molar mass** (g/mol) numerically equals the atomic/molecular mass in u.
- n = mass/molar mass = N/N_A.
- 1 mol of an ideal gas at STP (273 K, 1 bar) occupies 22.7 L (22.4 L at 1 atm).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** Moles and molecules in 36 g of water.
- n = 36/18 = **2 mol**; N = 2 × 6.022 × 10²³ = **1.204 × 10²⁴** molecules
- Atoms: 3 per molecule → 3.61 × 10²⁴ atoms

**Example 2:** Mass of one molecule of CO₂ = 44/(6.022 × 10²³) ≈ **7.31 × 10⁻²³ g**.

**Example 3:** Moles in 4.4 g CO₂ = 0.1 mol → volume at STP (1 atm) = **2.24 L**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing molecules with atoms (1 mol O₂ has 2 mol O atoms).
- Using 22.4 L for gases not at STP.
- Writing molar mass in u instead of g/mol.

activity.prompt: How many moles are present in 9.8 g of H₂SO₄ (molar mass 98 g/mol)?

quiz.q: Number of atoms in 1 mol of O₂
quiz.why: One mole of O₂ has 6.022 × 10²³ molecules, and each molecule has 2 atoms. So atoms = 2 × 6.022 × 10²³ = 1.204 × 10²⁴.
Molar mass of C₆H₁₂O₆ = 6 × 12 + 12 × 1 + 6 × 16 = 72 + 12 + 96 = 180 g/mol.
One atomic mass unit (u) is defined as one twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom. The old oxygen-based definition is no longer used.
Mass = moles × molar mass = 0.5 × 58.5 = 29.25 g.
1 g of H₂ is 0.5 mol of molecules, which is 1 mol of atoms. 1 g of He is 0.25 mol, and 1 g of N₂ or O₂ is much less in atoms, so H₂ has the most atoms.

sources: NCERT Chemistry Class 11 (topic: mole concept)

lessons.title: Percentage composition, empirical and molecular formula

scenes.text: A forensic lab analyses a sweet white powder: 40% C, 6.7% H, 53.3% O.
From the percentages and molar mass 180 g/mol, they identify the formula C₆H₁₂O₆ — glucose.

steps.title: Percentage composition
steps.body:
Mass % of an element = (mass of that element in 1 mol of compound / molar mass) × 100.
- Water: H = 2.016/18.02 × 100 ≈ 11.19%; O ≈ 88.81%.
- Ethanol C₂H₅OH (46.07 g/mol): C ≈ 52.14%, H ≈ 13.13%, O ≈ 34.73%.

steps.title: Empirical → molecular formula
steps.body:
1. Take 100 g → percentages become grams.
2. Convert each to moles (÷ atomic mass).
3. Divide all by the smallest mole value.
4. If not whole numbers, multiply by a small integer (e.g. 1.5 × 2 = 3).
5. n = molar mass / empirical formula mass; molecular formula = (empirical)ₙ.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Rounding 1.5 to 2 instead of multiplying through.
- Dividing by molecular mass of diatomic elements (use atomic mass of O = 16, not 32).
- Forgetting that the empirical formula may equal the molecular formula (n = 1).

activity.prompt: Order the steps to find a molecular formula from % composition
items: Convert mass of each element to moles
Divide by the smallest number of moles
Make the ratio whole numbers to get the empirical formula
Divide molar mass by empirical formula mass to get n

quiz.why: Benzene is C₆H₆. The simplest whole-number ratio of C to H is 1 : 1, so the empirical formula is CH.
% O in CO₂ = (32 ÷ 44) × 100 = 72.7%. The molar mass of CO₂ is 12 + 32 = 44.

quiz.q: Empirical formula CH₂, molar mass 42 g/mol. Molecular formula
quiz.why: The empirical formula mass of CH₂ is 14. n = 42/14 = 3, so the molecular formula is C₃H₆.

quiz.q: A mole ratio of 1 : 1.33 should be converted by multiplying by
quiz.why: To get whole numbers from 1 : 1.33, multiply by 3. This gives 3 : 3.99, which is about 3 : 4.
% N in NH₃ = (14 ÷ 17) × 100 = 82.4%. NH₃ has a molar mass of 14 + 3 = 17.

sources: NCERT Chemistry Class 11 (topic: empirical formula)

lessons.title: Stoichiometry and limiting reagent

scenes.text: With 10 slices of bread and 3 cheese slices, Kavya can make only 3 cheese sandwiches.
Cheese is the limiting ingredient. In reactions, the limiting reagent decides how much product forms.

steps.title: Using balanced equations
steps.body:
A balanced equation gives **mole ratios**. E.g. CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O: 1 mol CH₄ needs 2 mol O₂ and gives 1 mol CO₂ and 2 mol H₂O.

Steps: balance → convert given masses to moles → use mole ratio → convert back to mass/volume.

steps.title: Limiting reagent
steps.body:
The reactant that is completely used up first; it limits the amount of product. The other is in **excess**.

Method: for each reactant, divide its moles by its coefficient. The smallest value marks the limiting reagent.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** Mass of CO₂ from burning 16 g CH₄.
- 16 g = 1 mol CH₄ → 1 mol CO₂ = **44 g**
- O₂ needed = 2 mol = 64 g

**Example 2:** 28 g N₂ and 3 g H₂ react: N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃.
- N₂ = 1 mol (1/1 = 1); H₂ = 1.5 mol (1.5/3 = 0.5) → **H₂ is limiting**
- NH₃ = 1.5 × 2/3 = 1 mol = **17 g**; N₂ left = 0.5 mol = 14 g

**Example 3:** Volume of O₂ at STP (22.4 L/mol) needed to burn 2 mol of H₂: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O → 1 mol O₂ = **22.4 L**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using an unbalanced equation.
- Choosing the reactant with the smaller MASS as limiting — compare moles divided by coefficients.
- Forgetting to report the excess reagent remaining when asked.

activity.prompt: How many grams of water form when 4 g of H₂ reacts with excess O₂ (2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O)?

quiz.q: In 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, the mole ratio H₂ : H₂O is
quiz.why: In 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, 2 moles of H₂ give 2 moles of water. So the ratio H₂ : H₂O is 2 : 2 = 1 : 1.

quiz.q: 5 mol H₂ and 2 mol O₂ react to form water. Limiting reagent
quiz.why: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. O₂ available 2 mol needs 4 mol H₂, but 5 mol H₂ is present. O₂ runs out first, so it is the limiting reagent.

quiz.q: Mass of O₂ needed to burn 12 g of carbon to CO₂
quiz.why: C + O₂ → CO₂. 12 g of carbon is 1 mol, and it needs 1 mol of O₂, which weighs 32 g.
The limiting reagent is used up first, so it decides how much product can form.

quiz.q: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂. CO₂ from 50 g CaCO₃ (M = 100)
quiz.why: 50 g of CaCO₃ (M = 100) is 0.5 mol. It gives 0.5 mol of CO₂ = 0.5 × 44 = 22 g.

sources: NCERT Chemistry Class 11 (topic: stoichiometry)

lessons.title: Concentration of solutions

scenes.text: An ORS packet says: dissolve in exactly one litre of clean water.
Too concentrated or too dilute and it won't work well — concentration matters in medicine as in the lab.

steps.title: Concentration terms
steps.body:
- **Mass percent** = (mass of solute / mass of solution) × 100
- **Mole fraction** x_A = n_A/(n_A + n_B); Σx = 1
- **Molarity** M = moles of solute / volume of solution in L (changes with temperature)
- **Molality** m = moles of solute / mass of solvent in kg (independent of temperature)
- Dilution: M₁V₁ = M₂V₂

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** 4 g NaOH (40 g/mol) in 250 mL solution.
- n = 0.1 mol; M = 0.1/0.25 = **0.4 M**

**Example 2:** 4 g NaOH dissolved in 500 g water: m = 0.1/0.5 = **0.2 mol/kg**.

**Example 3:** 2 g of a solute in 18 g of solution → mass % = **11.1%**.

**Example 4:** How much 2 M HCl is needed to make 500 mL of 0.5 M? V₁ = 0.5 × 500/2 = **125 mL**.

**Example 5:** Mole fraction of ethanol in a mix of 46 g ethanol and 36 g water: 1/(1 + 2) = **0.33**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using volume of SOLVENT for molarity (it is volume of solution).
- Using mass of solution for molality (it is mass of solvent, in kg).
- Forgetting to convert mL to L.

activity.prompt: Match each concentration term to its definition

quiz.q: Which does not change with temperature?
quiz.why: Molality depends on masses only (mol per kg of solvent), so it does not change with temperature. Molarity and normality depend on volume, which changes.

quiz.q: 5.85 g NaCl in 500 mL solution. Molarity
Sum of mole fractions in a solution
quiz.why: The mole fractions of all components of a solution add up to 1, by definition.

quiz.q: 100 mL of 1 M solution is diluted to 1 L. New molarity
quiz.why: Use M₁V₁ = M₂V₂. 1 × 100 = M₂ × 1000, so M₂ = 0.1 M.

quiz.q: 18 g glucose in 1 kg water. Molality
quiz.why: 18 g glucose (M = 180) is 0.1 mol. In 1 kg of water, molality = 0.1 mol/kg = 0.1 m.

sources: NCERT Chemistry Class 11 (topic: concentration)

questions.q: Avogadro constant
questions.why: The Avogadro constant is 6.022 × 10²³ per mole, the number of particles in one mole.

questions.q: Molar mass of CO₂
questions.why: Molar mass of CO₂ = 12 + 2 × 16 = 44 g/mol.

questions.q: Law of conservation of mass was given by
questions.why: Antoine Lavoisier gave the law of conservation of mass. Proust gave definite proportions and Dalton the atomic theory.

questions.q: Number of moles in 11.2 L of O₂ at STP (22.4 L/mol)
questions.why: At STP, one mole of gas has a volume of 22.4 L. So 11.2 L of O₂ = 11.2/22.4 = 0.5 mol.

questions.q: Assertion: Molality is preferred over molarity in experiments at varying temperature. Reason: Volume changes with temperature but mass does not.
options: Both true, Reason does not explain
questions.why: Both are true and R explains A. Molality uses masses, which do not change with temperature, while molarity uses volume, which does.

questions.q: Number of atoms in 0.1 mol of H₂O
questions.why: 0.1 mol of H₂O has 3 atoms per molecule. Atoms = 0.1 × 3 × 6.022 × 10²³ = 1.806 × 10²³.

questions.q: A compound has 85.7% C and 14.3% H; molar mass 56. Molecular formula
questions.why: For 85.7% C and 14.3% H, the ratio of moles is C : H = 7.14 : 14.3 = 1 : 2, so the empirical formula is CH₂ (mass 14). 56 ÷ 14 = 4, so the molecular formula is C₄H₈.

questions.q: Case: In a lab, 10 g of CaCO₃ (M = 100) reacts with excess HCl. Volume of CO₂ at STP (22.4 L/mol)
questions.why: 10 g CaCO₃ (M = 100) is 0.1 mol and gives 0.1 mol CO₂. Volume at STP = 0.1 × 22.4 = 2.24 L.

questions.q: Molarity of a solution with 49 g H₂SO₄ in 2 L
questions.why: 49 g H₂SO₄ (M = 98) is 0.5 mol. Molarity = 0.5 mol ÷ 2 L = 0.25 M.

questions.q: 10 g H₂ and 64 g O₂ react to form water. Mass of water formed
questions.why: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. 64 g O₂ is 2 mol and needs 4 mol (8 g) of H₂, out of 10 g, so O₂ is limiting. It gives 4 mol water = 4 × 18 = 72 g.

questions.q: Chlorine has isotopes ³⁵Cl (75%) and ³⁷Cl (25%). Average atomic mass
Mole fraction of solute in a 1 molal aqueous solution
questions.why: A 1 molal solution has 1 mol of solute in 1 kg (55.5 mol) of water. Mole fraction of solute = 1/(1 + 55.5) ≈ 0.018.

questions.q: Density of a 3 M NaCl solution is 1.25 g/mL. Its molality is about (M_NaCl = 58.5)
questions.why: 1 L of solution weighs 1250 g. Solute = 3 × 58.5 = 175.5 g, so solvent = 1250 − 175.5 = 1074.5 g. Molality = 3/1.0745 ≈ 2.79 m.

questions.q: An oxide of a metal M contains 40% oxygen by mass; the metal is divalent. Atomic mass of M
questions.why: For divalent M the oxide is MO. 40% oxygen means 16/(M + 16) = 0.4, so M + 16 = 40 and M = 24.

questions.q: Volume of 0.1 M NaOH needed to neutralise 25 mL of 0.2 M H₂SO₄
questions.why: 25 mL of 0.2 M H₂SO₄ is 5 mmol. It has 2 H⁺, so it needs 10 mmol NaOH. At 0.1 M, the volume = 10/0.1 = 100 mL.

questions.q: How many significant figures in 0.00250?
questions.why: In 0.00250, the leading zeros are not significant. The digits 2, 5 and the trailing 0 are significant, so there are 3 significant figures.

courses.title: Ch 2 · Structure of Atom
courses.summary: Subatomic particles and early atomic models, electromagnetic radiation and Planck's quantum theory, the photoelectric effect, hydrogen spectrum and Bohr's model, dual nature, uncertainty principle, quantum numbers, orbitals and electronic configuration.
outcomes: Learners can describe the discovery of electron, proton and neutron and the Thomson and Rutherford models
Learners can calculate photon energies and photoelectric kinetic energies
Learners can apply Bohr's model and the Rydberg formula to hydrogen-like species
Learners can use de Broglie and Heisenberg relations
Learners can assign quantum numbers and write electronic configurations

lessons.title: Subatomic particles and atomic models

scenes.text: Rutherford's team fired alpha particles at thin gold foil, expecting them all to pass straight through.
A tiny fraction bounced back — 'like a shell bouncing off tissue paper'. The atom must have a tiny, dense nucleus.

steps.title: Discovery of particles
steps.body:
- **Electron:** cathode-ray tube experiments (J.J. Thomson measured e/m ≈ 1.76 × 10¹¹ C/kg). Millikan's oil-drop experiment gave charge e = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C → mass ≈ 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg.
- **Proton:** from canal (anode) rays; charge +e, mass ≈ 1.673 × 10⁻²⁷ kg.
- **Neutron:** Chadwick (1932), by bombarding beryllium with α-particles; neutral, mass ≈ 1.675 × 10⁻²⁷ kg.

steps.title: Atomic models
steps.body:
- **Thomson (plum pudding):** positive sphere with embedded electrons — could not explain α-scattering.
- **Rutherford (nuclear model):** most α-particles pass straight → atom mostly empty; few deflected at large angles → tiny positive nucleus (≈ 10⁻¹⁵ m vs atom ≈ 10⁻¹⁰ m) containing almost all mass; electrons revolve around it.
- **Drawbacks of Rutherford:** an accelerating electron should radiate and spiral in (atom unstable); cannot explain line spectra.

**Atomic number Z** = protons; **mass number A** = protons + neutrons. Isotopes: same Z, different A (¹H, ²H, ³H). Isobars: same A, different Z (¹⁴C, ¹⁴N).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** ³⁵₁₇Cl: protons **17**, electrons 17, neutrons 35 − 17 = **18**.

**Example 2:** An ion has 18 electrons, 16 protons, 16 neutrons. Charge = 16 − 18 = −2, A = 32 → **³²S²⁻**.

**Example 3:** ⁴⁰₁₈Ar and ⁴⁰₂₀Ca are **isobars**; ¹²C and ¹⁴C are **isotopes**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Subtracting electrons instead of protons from A to get neutrons.
- Mixing isotopes and isobars.
- Saying the nucleus is large — it is about 10⁵ times smaller than the atom.

events.text: Millikan's oil-drop experiment begins measuring e

quiz.why: Neutrons = mass number − atomic number = 23 − 11 = 12.
James Chadwick discovered the neutron in 1932. Thomson found the electron, Rutherford the nucleus, and Millikan the electron's charge.

options: the atom is mostly empty space
quiz.why: Most α-particles passed straight through the gold foil because most of the atom is empty space. The nucleus is tiny, so only a few were deflected.
¹⁴C and ¹⁴N have the same mass number (14) but different atomic numbers. Species like this are isobars.
The charge of an electron is 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, measured by Millikan. 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ is its mass in kg.

sources: NCERT Chemistry Class 11 (topic: subatomic particles)

lessons.title: Electromagnetic radiation, Planck's theory and photoelectric effect

scenes.text: A mall door opens when you break a light beam. Its sensor relies on light knocking electrons out of a metal.
Strangely, dim blue light can do it but bright red light cannot — energy comes in packets called photons.

steps.title: Wave properties
steps.body:
- c = νλ (c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s); wavenumber ν̄ = 1/λ (m⁻¹ or cm⁻¹).
- EM spectrum (increasing frequency): radio, microwave, infrared, visible (≈ 400–750 nm), ultraviolet, X-rays, γ-rays.

steps.title: Planck's quantum theory and photoelectric effect
steps.body:
- Energy is emitted/absorbed in discrete packets (quanta): **E = hν**, h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J s. Explained black-body radiation.
- **Photoelectric effect:** electrons are ejected from a metal only if ν ≥ threshold ν₀, instantly; their KE depends on frequency, number depends on intensity.
- **Einstein:** hν = hν₀ + ½mₑv² (W₀ = hν₀ = work function).
- 1 eV = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** Yellow light λ = 580 nm.
- ν = 3 × 10⁸/5.8 × 10⁻⁷ = **5.17 × 10¹⁴ Hz**
- E = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ × 5.17 × 10¹⁴ ≈ **3.43 × 10⁻¹⁹ J** per photon

**Example 2:** A metal has W₀ = 2.0 eV. Light of photon energy 4.0 eV falls on it. Maximum KE of electrons = **2.0 eV = 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁹ J**.

**Example 3:** Photons in 1 J of 580 nm light = 1/3.43 × 10⁻¹⁹ ≈ **2.9 × 10¹⁸**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking more intense light gives faster electrons — intensity changes the NUMBER, frequency changes the KE.
- Forgetting nm → m conversion (10⁻⁹).
- Mixing J and eV.

statements.s: Below the threshold frequency no electrons are emitted however bright the light.
statements.why: Each photon must have enough energy.

statements.s: Increasing intensity increases the KE of photoelectrons.
E = hν links photon energy to frequency.
X-rays have longer wavelength than visible light.

quiz.why: Planck's constant h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J s.

quiz.q: Energy of a photon is proportional to
quiz.why: E = hν, so photon energy is directly proportional to its frequency. Intensity only changes the number of photons.

quiz.q: Work function 3 eV, photon 5 eV. Max KE of electron
quiz.why: Maximum KE = photon energy − work function = 5 − 3 = 2 eV.
γ-rays have the shortest wavelength, so the highest frequency in the electromagnetic spectrum. Radio waves have the lowest.

sources: NCERT Chemistry Class 11 (topic: quantum theory)

lessons.title: Hydrogen spectrum and Bohr's model

scenes.text: Every gas in a discharge tube glows with its own set of coloured lines.
Like fingerprints, these line spectra identify elements — even in stars. Bohr explained hydrogen's lines.

steps.title: Line spectrum of hydrogen
steps.body:
**Rydberg formula:** ν̄ = 109,677 (1/n₁² − 1/n₂²) cm⁻¹ with n₂ > n₁.
- Lyman (n₁ = 1, UV), Balmer (n₁ = 2, visible), Paschen (3, IR), Brackett (4, IR), Pfund (5, IR).
- Max number of lines when an electron falls from level n to the ground state: n(n − 1)/2.

steps.title: Bohr's model
steps.body:
Postulates: electrons move in fixed circular orbits (stationary states) without radiating; angular momentum is quantised (mvr = nh/2π); energy is absorbed/emitted only when jumping between orbits: ΔE = hν.

Results for hydrogen-like species (nuclear charge Z):
- **Eₙ = −2.18 × 10⁻¹⁸ (Z²/n²) J** = −13.6 Z²/n² eV
- **rₙ = 52.9 (n²/Z) pm**
- Ionisation energy of H = 13.6 eV; He⁺ = 54.4 eV.

**Limitations:** fails for multi-electron atoms, cannot explain fine structure, Zeeman/Stark effects, or chemical bonding; contradicts the uncertainty principle.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** H electron from n = 3 to n = 2 (Balmer Hα).
- ΔE = 2.18 × 10⁻¹⁸ (1/4 − 1/9) = 3.03 × 10⁻¹⁹ J
- λ = hc/ΔE = (6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ × 3 × 10⁸)/3.03 × 10⁻¹⁹ ≈ **656 nm** (red)

**Example 2:** Radius of the 2nd orbit of He⁺: r = 52.9 × 4/2 = **105.8 pm**.

**Example 3:** Energy of the n = 2 level of Li²⁺: −13.6 × 9/4 = **−30.6 eV**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting Z² for hydrogen-like ions.
- Putting n₂ < n₁ in Rydberg's formula (gives negative values).
- Applying Bohr's formulas to neutral He or other multi-electron atoms.

activity.prompt: Match the spectral series to its lower level and region

quiz.q: Energy of electron in the 1st Bohr orbit of H
quiz.why: The energy of the electron in the first Bohr orbit of hydrogen is −13.6 eV. The negative sign means it is bound to the nucleus.

quiz.q: Radius of the 3rd orbit of H
quiz.why: Bohr radius rₙ = 52.9 pm × n². For n = 3, r = 52.9 × 9 ≈ 476 pm.
The Balmer series arises from transitions to n = 2 and lies in the visible region. Lyman is in UV and Paschen is in IR.
For a one-electron ion, IE = 13.6 × Z² eV. For He⁺, Z = 2, so IE = 13.6 × 4 = 54.4 eV.

quiz.q: Max spectral lines when electrons fall from n = 4 to ground
quiz.why: Number of possible lines for transitions among n levels = n(n−1)/2 = 4 × 3/2 = 6.

sources: NCERT Chemistry Class 11 (topic: Bohr model)

lessons.title: Dual nature, uncertainty principle, quantum numbers and orbitals

scenes.text: A light microscope cannot show a virus clearly; an electron microscope can.
Fast electrons have tiny wavelengths — matter behaves like waves too.

steps.title: de Broglie and Heisenberg
steps.body:
- **de Broglie:** λ = h/mv = h/p — significant only for tiny masses.
- **Heisenberg uncertainty principle:** Δx · Δp ≥ h/4π. Position and momentum of an electron cannot both be known exactly, so definite Bohr orbits are meaningless; we use **orbitals** — regions of high probability (|ψ|²) from the Schrödinger equation.

steps.title: Quantum numbers
steps.body:
- **Principal n** = 1, 2, 3…: shell, size and energy.
- **Azimuthal l** = 0 … (n − 1): subshell s(0), p(1), d(2), f(3); shape.
- **Magnetic mₗ** = −l … +l: orientation; (2l + 1) orbitals per subshell.
- **Spin mₛ** = +½ or −½.
- Orbitals in shell n = n²; electrons = 2n².
- Nodes: radial = n − l − 1; angular = l; total = n − 1.
- Shapes: s spherical; p dumbbell (pₓ, p_y, p_z); d mostly cloverleaf (d_z² has a ring).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** de Broglie λ of an electron (9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg) at 10⁶ m/s.
- λ = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴/(9.1 × 10⁻²⁵) ≈ **7.3 × 10⁻¹⁰ m** (comparable to atomic sizes)
- A 0.1 kg ball at 10 m/s: λ ≈ 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ m — undetectable

**Example 2:** Quantum numbers for 3d: n = 3, l = 2, mₗ = −2 … +2 (5 orbitals, 10 electrons).

**Example 3:** Nodes in a 3p orbital: radial = 3 − 1 − 1 = **1**; angular = **1**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Allowing l = n (max l is n − 1), e.g. '2d' does not exist.
- Thinking an orbital is a fixed path like an orbit.
- Forgetting that uncertainty matters only for microscopic particles.

quiz.why: For a given n, l can be 0 to n − 1. For n = 3, l = 0, 1, 2.
The number of orbitals in a shell is n². For n = 4, that is 16 orbitals.

quiz.q: Angular nodes in a d orbital
quiz.why: The number of angular nodes equals l. For a d orbital l = 2, so there are 2 angular nodes.

quiz.q: de Broglie wavelength is inversely proportional to
quiz.why: The de Broglie wavelength is λ = h/p, so it is inversely proportional to momentum.
Heisenberg's uncertainty principle: Δx · Δp ≥ h/4π, so position and momentum cannot both be known exactly.

sources: NCERT Chemistry Class 11 (topic: quantum mechanical model)

lessons.title: Filling orbitals: aufbau, Pauli, Hund and configurations

scenes.text: Passengers fill the nearest empty seats first and avoid sharing a double seat until all singles are taken.
Electrons do the same: lowest energy first (aufbau), single occupancy first (Hund), and only two per orbital with opposite spins (Pauli).

steps.title: Rules
steps.body:
- **Aufbau:** fill orbitals in increasing energy, using the **(n + l) rule**; if equal, lower n first. Order: 1s 2s 2p 3s 3p 4s 3d 4p 5s 4d 5p 6s 4f 5d 6p 7s …
- **Pauli exclusion:** no two electrons in an atom have all four quantum numbers the same → max 2 electrons per orbital with opposite spins.
- **Hund's rule:** in degenerate orbitals, electrons occupy singly with parallel spins before pairing.

steps.title: Configurations and stability
steps.body:
- N (7): 1s² 2s² 2p³ (3 unpaired)
- O (8): 1s² 2s² 2p⁴ (2 unpaired)
- Fe (26): [Ar] 3d⁶ 4s²
- **Exceptions:** Cr (24): [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹; Cu (29): [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹ — half-filled and fully filled subshells are extra stable due to symmetry and larger **exchange energy**.
- For cations of transition elements, 4s electrons leave first: Fe²⁺ = [Ar] 3d⁶.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** Unpaired electrons in Mn (25): [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s² → **5**.

**Example 2:** Which fills first, 4s or 3d? 4s: n + l = 4; 3d: n + l = 5 → **4s first**.

**Example 3:** Configuration of Cu⁺: Cu [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹ → remove 4s → **[Ar] 3d¹⁰** (no unpaired electrons, colourless salts).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing Cr as 3d⁴ 4s² and Cu as 3d⁹ 4s².
- Removing 3d electrons before 4s when forming transition-metal ions.
- Pairing electrons in p orbitals before each has one (violates Hund).

quiz.why: Chromium has the configuration [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹, not 3d⁴ 4s², because a half-filled d subshell is extra stable.
Nitrogen is 1s² 2s² 2p³. By Hund's rule the three 2p electrons occupy separate orbitals, so there are 3 unpaired electrons.

quiz.q: Pauli principle limits each orbital to
quiz.why: The Pauli exclusion principle allows at most 2 electrons in an orbital, and they must have opposite spins.

quiz.q: Which orbital has the higher energy (multi-electron atom)?
quiz.why: In a multi-electron atom, energy depends on n + l. For 3d, n + l = 5, and for 4s, n + l = 4. So 3d has higher energy and fills after 4s.

quiz.q: Fe³⁺ has how many unpaired electrons?
quiz.why: Fe is [Ar] 3d⁶ 4s². Losing 3 electrons gives Fe³⁺ = [Ar] 3d⁵, with 5 unpaired electrons.

sources: NCERT Chemistry Class 11 (topic: electronic configuration)

questions.q: Charge-to-mass ratio of the electron was measured by
questions.why: J.J. Thomson measured the charge-to-mass ratio (e/m) of the electron from cathode ray experiments. Millikan measured its charge.

questions.q: Shape of an s orbital
questions.why: An s orbital has l = 0 and is spherical. A p orbital is dumbbell-shaped.

questions.q: Maximum electrons in n = 3
questions.why: The maximum number of electrons in a shell is 2n². For n = 3, that is 2 × 9 = 18.

questions.q: Number of protons, neutrons in ⁵⁶₂₆Fe
questions.why: In ⁵⁶₂₆Fe, protons = atomic number = 26, and neutrons = 56 − 26 = 30.

questions.q: Assertion: Cu has configuration [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹. Reason: Completely filled d subshell has extra stability.
options: Both true, Reason does not explain
questions.why: Both are true and R explains A. A completely filled d subshell is extra stable because of symmetry and exchange energy, so one 4s electron moves to 3d, giving 3d¹⁰ 4s¹.

questions.q: Quantum numbers n = 2, l = 1 describe
questions.why: n = 2 and l = 1 means a p subshell in the second shell, so it is 2p.

questions.q: Energy of a photon of wavelength 400 nm (hc = 1.986 × 10⁻²⁵ J m)
Case: A sodium lamp emits light with photons of 2.1 eV onto a metal of work function 2.3 eV. What happens?
questions.why: The photon energy (2.1 eV) is less than the work function (2.3 eV), so it cannot free an electron. No photoelectrons are emitted, however intense the light.

questions.q: Wavelength of the first Lyman line (n = 2 → 1) of H (R = 109,677 cm⁻¹)
Ratio of radii of the 2nd orbit of H and the 3rd orbit of Li²⁺
questions.why: Radius is proportional to n²/Z. H, n = 2: 4/1 = 4. Li²⁺, n = 3: 9/3 = 3. The ratio is 4 : 3.

questions.q: Number of radial nodes in a 4s orbital
questions.why: Number of radial nodes = n − l − 1. For 4s, n = 4, l = 0, so 4 − 0 − 1 = 3.

questions.q: de Broglie wavelength of an electron accelerated so its momentum is 6.626 × 10⁻²⁴ kg m/s
Minimum uncertainty in the velocity of an electron (9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg) located within 1 × 10⁻¹⁰ m (h/4π = 5.27 × 10⁻³⁵ J s)
Which set of quantum numbers is NOT possible?
questions.why: For a given n, l can only go from 0 to n − 1. So l = 2 is impossible for n = 2.

questions.q: Energy required to remove an electron from the n = 2 level of hydrogen
questions.why: The energy needed to remove the electron from level n of hydrogen is 13.6/n² eV. For n = 2, it is 13.6/4 = 3.4 eV.

questions.q: Number of electrons with l = 1 in a ground-state chlorine atom (Z = 17)
questions.why: Chlorine is 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁵. Electrons with l = 1 are in p orbitals: 6 + 5 = 11.

courses.title: Ch 3 · Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
courses.summary: History of classification, the modern periodic law, IUPAC names for Z > 100, s/p/d/f blocks, and periodic trends in atomic and ionic radii, ionisation enthalpy, electron gain enthalpy, electronegativity, valence and reactivity.
outcomes: Learners can trace the development from Döbereiner to the modern periodic law
Learners can name elements with Z > 100 by IUPAC rules
Learners can relate block, period and group to electronic configuration
Learners can explain trends and exceptions in radius, ionisation enthalpy and electron gain enthalpy
Learners can predict chemical behaviour from periodic position

lessons.title: History and the modern periodic law

scenes.text: Imagine a library with books scattered everywhere. Arranging them by subject makes any book easy to find.
Chemists arranged elements by properties — and Mendeleev even left gaps for books not yet written.

steps.title: Early attempts
steps.body:
- **Döbereiner's triads** (1829): groups of three with the middle element's atomic mass ≈ average of the others (Li, Na, K; Cl, Br, I).
- **Newlands' law of octaves** (1865): every eighth element resembled the first — worked only up to calcium.
- **Mendeleev's periodic law** (1869): properties are periodic functions of atomic mass. He left gaps and predicted **eka-aluminium (gallium)** and **eka-silicon (germanium)** with remarkable accuracy, and corrected some atomic masses.

steps.title: Modern periodic law and table
steps.body:
Moseley showed X-ray frequencies depend on atomic number. **Modern periodic law:** physical and chemical properties are periodic functions of **atomic number**.
- Long form: 7 periods, 18 groups.
- Period number = highest principal quantum number of the element.
- Lanthanoids and actinoids placed separately at the bottom.

steps.title: IUPAC names for Z > 100
steps.body:
Digit roots: 0 nil, 1 un, 2 bi, 3 tri, 4 quad, 5 pent, 6 hex, 7 sept, 8 oct, 9 enn; join them and add '-ium'; the symbol uses the first letters of the roots.
- Z = 119 → un-un-enn-ium = **ununennium (Uue)**
- Z = 120 → un-bi-nil-ium = **unbinilium (Ubn)**
These are temporary names until a permanent name is approved.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying Mendeleev's law used atomic number (it used atomic mass).
- Forgetting elision: the final 'i' of bi and tri is dropped before 'ium' (Z = 112 → un-un-bi-ium = ununbium), and the final 'n' of enn is dropped before 'nil' (Z = 190 → unennilium).
- Forgetting that period number equals the outermost shell number.

events.text: Moseley links properties to atomic number

quiz.q: Modern periodic law is based on
quiz.why: The modern periodic law says properties of elements are periodic functions of their atomic number, as found by Moseley. Mendeleev used atomic mass.
Mendeleev predicted eka-aluminium, which was later discovered and named gallium. Eka-silicon is germanium.
IUPAC temporary names come from the digits of the atomic number: 1 = un, 2 = bi, 0 = nil. So element 120 is un-bi-nil-ium = unbinilium.

quiz.q: Number of groups in the long form table
quiz.why: The long form periodic table has 18 groups, numbered 1 to 18 under the IUPAC system.
Newlands' law of octaves worked only up to calcium. After that, it did not hold for heavier elements.

sources: NCERT Chemistry Class 11 (topic: history of the periodic table)

lessons.title: Electronic configuration and blocks

scenes.text: A PIN code tells you the region, district and post office.
An element's configuration tells its period, block and group — its address in the periodic table.

steps.title: The four blocks
steps.body:
- **s-block** (groups 1, 2): ns¹⁻²; reactive metals (alkali, alkaline earth), low ionisation enthalpy.
- **p-block** (groups 13–18): ns² np¹⁻⁶; metals, non-metals, metalloids; noble gases ns² np⁶ (He 1s²).
- **d-block** (groups 3–12): (n−1)d¹⁻¹⁰ ns⁰⁻²; transition metals, coloured ions, variable oxidation states, catalysts.
- **f-block:** (n−2)f¹⁻¹⁴ (n−1)d⁰⁻¹ ns²; lanthanoids (4f) and actinoids (5f, mostly radioactive).

steps.title: Metals, non-metals, metalloids
steps.body: Metals (> 78% of elements) are on the left and centre; non-metals at the top right; **metalloids** (B, Si, Ge, As, Sb, Te) lie along the zig-zag boundary and show intermediate properties. Metallic character decreases across a period and increases down a group.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** Element with configuration [Ne] 3s² 3p⁴: period **3**, p-block, group 10 + 6 = **16** → sulphur.

**Example 2:** [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s²: period 4, d-block, group = 5 + 2 = **7** → manganese.

**Example 3:** Z = 37: [Kr] 5s¹ → period 5, group 1 (rubidium, an alkali metal).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Placing helium in the s-block by chemistry — it is in group 18 because it is a noble gas, though its configuration is 1s².
- Using group = number of valence electrons for d-block without adding (n−1)d and ns electrons.
- For p-block group number = 10 + (ns + np electrons).

activity.prompt: Place each configuration in its block

quiz.q: Group of an element with outer configuration 3s² 3p³
quiz.why: The outer configuration 3s² 3p³ has 5 valence electrons in a p-block element. The group number is 10 + 5 = 15.
Silicon is a metalloid, with properties between metals and non-metals. Cl is a non-metal, and Fe and Na are metals.
The d-block (transition) elements have the general configuration (n−1)d¹⁻¹⁰ ns⁰⁻². The d orbitals are being filled.

quiz.q: Period of an element with Z = 20
quiz.why: The element with Z = 20 is calcium, [Ar] 4s². The highest shell is n = 4, so it is in period 4.
The lanthanoids are the elements in which the 4f orbitals are being filled.

sources: NCERT Chemistry Class 11 (topic: blocks)

lessons.title: Atomic and ionic radii and ionisation enthalpy

story.title: Why sodium is stored in kerosene

scenes.text: In the school lab, sodium is kept under kerosene, but magnesium ribbon lies in an open box.
Sodium's single outer electron is lost very easily (low ionisation enthalpy) — it reacts with air and moisture.

steps.title: Radii
steps.body:
- **Atomic radius:** covalent radius for non-metals, metallic radius for metals.
- Across a period: **decreases** (effective nuclear charge rises, same shell).
- Down a group: **increases** (new shells).
- Cation < parent atom; anion > parent atom.
- **Isoelectronic species** (same number of electrons): radius decreases as nuclear charge increases: O²⁻ > F⁻ > Na⁺ > Mg²⁺ > Al³⁺ (all 10 e⁻).

steps.title: Ionisation enthalpy (ΔᵢH)
steps.body:
Energy to remove the most loosely bound electron from an isolated gaseous atom: X(g) → X⁺(g) + e⁻. Always positive; ΔᵢH₂ > ΔᵢH₁.
- Generally increases across a period, decreases down a group (shielding, size).
- **Exceptions:** Be > B (2s electrons penetrate more than 2p); N > O (half-filled 2p³ is stable, and O's paired 2p electron is repelled). Similarly Mg > Al and P > S.
- Noble gases have the highest values in each period; alkali metals the lowest.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** Arrange Na, Mg, Al in increasing first ionisation enthalpy: **Na < Al < Mg** (Al's 3p electron is easier to remove than Mg's 3s).

**Example 2:** Arrange N³⁻, O²⁻, F⁻, Na⁺ by size: **N³⁻ > O²⁻ > F⁻ > Na⁺** (Z = 7, 8, 9, 11).

**Example 3:** Why is ΔᵢH₂ of Na very large? Removing a second electron breaks into the stable neon core.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Assuming IE strictly increases across a period — remember the B and O dips.
- Saying anions are smaller than their atoms.
- Comparing isoelectronic ions by mass instead of nuclear charge.

activity.prompt: Arrange the isoelectronic species from LARGEST to SMALLEST

quiz.q: Which has a higher first ionisation enthalpy?
quiz.why: Nitrogen has a higher first ionisation enthalpy than oxygen, because its 2p³ half-filled configuration is extra stable.
Across a period, atomic radius decreases, because the effective nuclear charge increases while electrons are added to the same shell.

quiz.q: Largest among Na⁺, Mg²⁺, F⁻, O²⁻
quiz.why: Na⁺, Mg²⁺, F⁻ and O²⁻ all have 10 electrons. Among such ions, the one with the fewest protons (O²⁻, Z = 8) is largest.
Sodium, an alkali metal at the start of the period, has the lowest ionisation enthalpy in period 3.

quiz.q: First IE of Be > B because
quiz.why: In boron the 2p electron is shielded by the 2s electrons and is easier to remove than a 2s electron of Be. So Be has a higher first ionisation enthalpy than B.

sources: NCERT Chemistry Class 11 (topic: radius, ionisation enthalpy)

lessons.title: Electron gain enthalpy, electronegativity, valence and reactivity

scenes.text: In a bond, two atoms pull on the shared electrons like a tug-of-war.
Fluorine is the strongest puller of all — the most electronegative element.

steps.title: Electron gain enthalpy (Δ_egH)
steps.body:
Enthalpy change when a gaseous atom gains an electron: X(g) + e⁻ → X⁻(g).
- Halogens have large negative values (one electron short of a noble-gas configuration).
- **Cl is more negative than F**: fluorine's small 2p shell causes strong electron–electron repulsion.
- Noble gases have large positive values (electron must enter a new shell).
- Second gain enthalpy (e.g. O⁻ → O²⁻) is positive (repulsion by the negative ion).

steps.title: Electronegativity and other trends
steps.body:
- **Electronegativity:** ability of an atom in a molecule to attract shared electrons; not measurable directly. Pauling scale: F 4.0 (highest), O 3.5, N 3.0, Cl 3.0, C 2.5, H 2.1, Na 0.9, Cs 0.7.
- Increases across a period, decreases down a group.
- **Valence:** for s/p elements, usually the number of valence electrons or 8 minus that number. Oxidation state in compounds depends on electronegativity: in OF₂, O is +2.
- **Reactivity:** metals most reactive at the bottom left (Cs), non-metals at the top right (F).
- **Anomalous behaviour of second-period elements** (Li, Be, B…): small size, high charge density, no d orbitals → max covalency 4; resemble the diagonal element of the next group (**diagonal relationship**: Li–Mg, Be–Al).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** Most negative electron gain enthalpy among F, Cl, Br, I → **Cl**.

**Example 2:** Oxidation state of O in OF₂: F is more electronegative, so F = −1 each → O = **+2**.

**Example 3:** Nature of oxides across period 3: Na₂O (basic), MgO (basic), Al₂O₃ (amphoteric), SiO₂ (weakly acidic), P₄O₁₀, SO₃, Cl₂O₇ (acidic) — acidity increases left to right.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying F has the most negative electron gain enthalpy.
- Confusing electronegativity (in a bond) with electron gain enthalpy (isolated atom).
- Treating Al₂O₃ as purely basic — it is amphoteric.

statements.s: Chlorine has a more negative electron gain enthalpy than fluorine.
Fluorine is the most electronegative element.
Noble gases have large negative electron gain enthalpies.
Al₂O₃ is amphoteric.
Electronegativity increases down a group.

quiz.why: Fluorine is the most electronegative element, with a value of 4.0 on the Pauling scale.
A diagonal relationship exists between Li and Mg, as they have a similar charge-to-size ratio. Be and Al, and B and Si, are other pairs.
Acidic character of oxides increases across a period. So Cl₂O₇ is the most acidic, while Na₂O and MgO are basic and Al₂O₃ is amphoteric.

quiz.q: Second electron gain enthalpy of oxygen is
quiz.why: The second electron gain enthalpy of oxygen is positive, because adding an electron to the O⁻ ion, which is already negative, needs energy to overcome repulsion.
Cs has the lowest ionisation enthalpy among these alkali metals, so it loses an electron most easily and is the most reactive.

sources: NCERT Chemistry Class 11 (topic: periodic trends)

questions.q: Number of periods in the modern periodic table
questions.why: The modern periodic table has 7 periods.

questions.q: Elements of group 17 are called
questions.why: Group 17 elements are called halogens, which means salt formers.

questions.q: Which is a noble gas?
questions.why: Argon (Ar) is a noble gas in group 18. Au is gold, Al is aluminium and As is arsenic.

questions.q: IUPAC symbol for Z = 119
questions.why: IUPAC symbols are the first letters of the digit roots. For 119: un-un-enn gives Uue (ununennium).

questions.q: Assertion: Atomic radius decreases across a period. Reason: Effective nuclear charge increases while electrons enter the same shell.
options: Both true, Reason does not explain
questions.why: Both are true and R explains A. Across a period, the nuclear charge rises while electrons add to the same shell, so the pull increases and the atom shrinks.

questions.q: Element with configuration [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s² 4p⁵ is in group
questions.why: [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s² 4p⁵ is bromine, with 7 valence electrons. Group = 10 + 7 = 17.

questions.q: Correct order of first ionisation enthalpy
questions.why: First IE order is B < Be < C < O < N. Be is above B because of its filled 2s, and N is above O because of its half-filled 2p.

questions.q: Case: An element X has ΔᵢH₁ = 738, ΔᵢH₂ = 1451, ΔᵢH₃ = 7733 kJ/mol. X most likely belongs to group
questions.why: The third ionisation enthalpy (7733) is far larger than the first two, so the element loses two electrons easily. So it has 2 valence electrons and is in group 2.

questions.q: Which species has the smallest radius?
questions.why: Al³⁺, Mg²⁺, Na⁺ and F⁻ are isoelectronic (10 electrons). The ion with the greatest nuclear charge, Al³⁺ (Z = 13), is the smallest.

questions.q: Correct order of electron gain enthalpy (most negative first)
questions.why: Chlorine has the most negative electron gain enthalpy, then fluorine (small size, crowded 2p), then Br, then I.

questions.q: Amphoteric oxide among these
questions.why: Al₂O₃ is amphoteric, as it reacts with both acids and bases. Na₂O and CaO are basic, and SO₃ is acidic.

questions.q: Which element was predicted by Mendeleev as eka-silicon?
questions.why: Eka-silicon, predicted by Mendeleev, was later discovered as germanium (Ge).

questions.q: The element with Z = 34 is in
questions.why: Z = 34 is selenium, [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s² 4p⁴. It is in period 4 and has 6 valence electrons, so group 16.

questions.q: Why does Ga have a smaller atomic radius than expected (≈ Al)?
questions.why: The filled 3d electrons in Ga shield the nuclear charge poorly, so the outer electrons feel a higher effective nuclear charge. So Ga is about the same size as Al.

questions.q: An element forms an oxide X₂O₅ and a hydride XH₃; its oxide is acidic. X is likely in group
questions.why: An acidic oxide X₂O₅ and a hydride XH₃ show valencies of 5 and 3, which is typical of group 15, such as P or N.

questions.q: Electronegativity on the Pauling scale is highest for
questions.why: Fluorine has the highest electronegativity on the Pauling scale (4.0), higher than O and Cl.

lessons.title: Octet rule, Lewis structures and formal charge

scenes.text: Noble gases barely react. Kössel and Lewis guessed why: eight electrons in the outer shell is a very stable arrangement.
Other atoms gain, lose or share electrons to reach it — that is chemical bonding.

steps.title: Kössel–Lewis approach
steps.body:
- Atoms combine to achieve an **octet** (duplet for H, Li, Be in some cases).
- **Ionic (electrovalent) bond:** transfer of electrons (Na → Na⁺ + e⁻; Cl + e⁻ → Cl⁻).
- **Covalent bond:** sharing of electron pairs (single, double, triple).
- **Lewis symbols** show valence electrons as dots.

steps.title: Drawing Lewis structures and formal charge
steps.body:
1. Count total valence electrons (add for anions, subtract for cations).
2. Place the least electronegative atom in the centre (never H).
3. Connect with single bonds, complete octets of outer atoms, then the centre; form multiple bonds if needed.

**Formal charge** = V − L − ½S (V = valence electrons, L = lone-pair electrons, S = shared electrons). The best structure has formal charges closest to zero, with negative charge on the more electronegative atom.

**Limitations of the octet rule:** incomplete octet (BeCl₂, BF₃), odd-electron molecules (NO, NO₂), expanded octet (PCl₅, SF₆, H₂SO₄); does not explain shape or stability of noble-gas compounds like XeF₂.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** Lewis structure of CO₂: 16 valence electrons → O=C=O, two lone pairs on each O; formal charges all **0**.

**Example 2:** Ozone O₃: O=O⁺–O⁻ (with resonance). Formal charge on central O = 6 − 2 − ½(6) = **+1**; on single-bonded O = 6 − 6 − 1 = **−1**; on double-bonded O = 6 − 4 − 2 = **0**.

**Example 3:** In NH₄⁺, valence electrons = 5 + 4 − 1 = 8; formal charge on N = 5 − 0 − 4 = **+1**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting to adjust the electron count for ion charge.
- Putting H in the centre.
- Treating formal charge as the real charge on an atom (it is bookkeeping).

activity.prompt: Which octet-rule exception does each molecule show?

quiz.why: CO₃²⁻ has 4 (C) + 3 × 6 (O) + 2 (charge) = 24 valence electrons.

quiz.q: Formal charge on N in NH₃
quiz.why: Formal charge = valence electrons − non-bonding electrons − half the bonding electrons. For N in NH₃: 5 − 2 − 3 = 0.
NO₂ has 5 + 12 = 17 valence electrons, an odd number, so it has one unpaired electron. CO₂, CH₄ and H₂O have even numbers.
In SF₆ sulphur has 6 bond pairs, which means 12 electrons around it. This is an expanded octet. BF₃ has an incomplete octet.

quiz.q: The best Lewis structure has formal charges
quiz.why: The best Lewis structure is the one with formal charges closest to zero, which means least charge separation.

sources: NCERT Chemistry Class 11 (topic: Lewis structures)

lessons.title: Ionic bond, bond parameters, resonance and polarity

story.title: Why water bends and CO₂ doesn't

scenes.text: A charged comb bends a thin stream of water from a tap.
Water molecules are polar because they are bent; CO₂ is linear, so its bond dipoles cancel.

steps.title: Ionic bond and lattice enthalpy
steps.body: Ionic bonds form easily when one atom has low ionisation enthalpy and the other has a large negative electron gain enthalpy. Stability comes from **lattice enthalpy** — energy needed to separate one mole of solid ionic compound into gaseous ions (e.g. NaCl ≈ 788 kJ/mol). Larger charges and smaller ions → higher lattice enthalpy.

steps.title: Bond parameters and resonance
steps.body:
- **Bond length:** distance between nuclei; triple < double < single.
- **Bond angle:** angle between bonds around a central atom.
- **Bond enthalpy:** energy to break one mole of bonds in the gas phase; higher bond order → stronger.
- **Bond order** (Lewis): number of shared pairs (N₂ = 3, O₂ = 2).
- **Resonance:** when one Lewis structure cannot describe a molecule, the real structure is a hybrid of canonical forms (O₃, CO₃²⁻, benzene). Resonance lowers energy; all bonds become equivalent (both O–O in O₃ ≈ 128 pm).

steps.title: Polarity and dipole moment
steps.body:
- Unequal sharing creates a **polar** bond. **Dipole moment** µ = charge × distance (unit debye, 1 D = 3.336 × 10⁻³⁰ C m).
- Net µ is the vector sum: CO₂, BF₃, CH₄, CCl₄ → **0** (symmetric); H₂O 1.85 D; NH₃ 1.47 D; NF₃ 0.23 D (lone-pair moment opposes the N–F moments).
- **Fajans' rules:** covalent character of an ionic bond increases with small, highly charged cation and large anion (polarisation). E.g. LiI is more covalent than NaCl.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** Bond order and length in CO₃²⁻: three resonance forms, each C–O bond has order 4/3; all three bonds are of equal length.

**Example 2:** Why is µ(NH₃) > µ(NF₃)? In NH₃ the lone-pair moment adds to the N–H bond moments; in NF₃ it opposes the N–F moments.

**Example 3:** Arrange by covalent character: NaCl, MgCl₂, AlCl₃ → **NaCl < MgCl₂ < AlCl₃** (cation charge increases, size decreases).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking resonance structures interconvert rapidly — the molecule is ONE hybrid.
- Saying molecules with polar bonds must be polar.
- Confusing bond enthalpy with lattice enthalpy.

quiz.why: CO₂ is linear and symmetrical, so the two C=O bond dipoles cancel and the net dipole moment is zero.
Dipole moment is measured in debye (D). 1 D = 3.336 × 10⁻³⁰ C m.
N₂ has a triple bond (N≡N), so its bond order is 3.

quiz.q: According to Fajans' rules, covalent character is greater for
quiz.why: By Fajans' rules, covalent character is greater when the cation is small and highly charged, since it polarises the anion more.

quiz.q: Both O–O bonds in O₃ are equal because of
quiz.why: The two O–O bonds in ozone are equal because of resonance. The real structure is a hybrid of two forms, so each bond is between single and double.

sources: NCERT Chemistry Class 11 (topic: bond parameters)

lessons.title: VSEPR theory and molecular shapes

scenes.text: Tie four balloons at their necks and they spread into a tetrahedron by themselves.
Electron pairs around an atom do the same — they repel and spread as far apart as possible.

steps.title: VSEPR rules
steps.body:
- Shape depends on the number of electron pairs (bond pairs + lone pairs) around the central atom.
- Pairs arrange to minimise repulsion.
- Repulsion order: **lone pair–lone pair > lone pair–bond pair > bond pair–bond pair**.
- Multiple bonds are treated as one super pair.

steps.title: Shapes to remember
steps.body:
- 2 pairs: linear (BeCl₂, 180°)
- 3 pairs: trigonal planar (BF₃, 120°); 2 bp + 1 lp: bent (SO₂)
- 4 pairs: tetrahedral (CH₄, 109.5°); 3 bp + 1 lp: trigonal pyramidal (NH₃, ≈ 107°); 2 bp + 2 lp: bent (H₂O, ≈ 104.5°)
- 5 pairs: trigonal bipyramidal (PCl₅); 4 bp + 1 lp: see-saw (SF₄); 3 bp + 2 lp: T-shaped (ClF₃); 2 bp + 3 lp: linear (XeF₂)
- 6 pairs: octahedral (SF₆); 5 bp + 1 lp: square pyramidal (BrF₅); 4 bp + 2 lp: square planar (XeF₄)

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** Shape of ClF₃: Cl has 7 valence electrons, 3 used in bonds → 2 lone pairs; total 5 pairs → **T-shaped** (lone pairs in equatorial positions).

**Example 2:** Why is the H–O–H angle (104.5°) less than H–N–H (107°)? Water has two lone pairs (stronger lp–lp and lp–bp repulsion) vs one in NH₃.

**Example 3:** XeF₄: Xe has 8 valence electrons, 4 bonds → 2 lone pairs; 6 pairs → **square planar**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Naming the shape by electron geometry instead of atom positions (NH₃ is pyramidal, not tetrahedral).
- Placing lone pairs axially in trigonal bipyramidal structures (they go equatorial).
- Counting a double bond as two pairs.

activity.prompt: Match the molecule to its shape

quiz.why: Water has 2 bond pairs and 2 lone pairs around oxygen, so its shape is bent (V-shaped).
CH₄ is tetrahedral with 4 bond pairs and no lone pairs, so the bond angle is 109.5°.
XeF₂ has 2 bond pairs and 3 lone pairs, with the lone pairs in the equatorial plane. This makes the molecule linear.
The repulsion order is lone pair–lone pair > lone pair–bond pair > bond pair–bond pair. A lone pair is closer to the nucleus and takes more space.
PCl₅ has 5 bond pairs and no lone pairs, so its shape is trigonal bipyramidal.

sources: NCERT Chemistry Class 11 (topic: VSEPR)

lessons.title: Valence bond theory and hybridisation

scenes.text: Mix one blue and three yellow paints and you get four identical green cups.
Carbon mixes one 2s and three 2p orbitals into four identical sp³ hybrids — that is hybridisation.

steps.title: Valence bond theory
steps.body:
A covalent bond forms when half-filled atomic orbitals **overlap**; greater overlap → stronger bond.
- **σ bond:** head-on (axial) overlap; s–s, s–p, p–p along the axis; free rotation possible.
- **π bond:** sideways overlap of parallel p orbitals; weaker; prevents rotation.
- A double bond = 1σ + 1π; a triple bond = 1σ + 2π.

steps.title: Hybridisation
steps.body:
Mixing of atomic orbitals of similar energy to form equivalent hybrid orbitals.
- **sp:** linear, 180° (BeCl₂, C₂H₂)
- **sp²:** trigonal planar, 120° (BF₃, C₂H₄)
- **sp³:** tetrahedral, 109.5° (CH₄, NH₃, H₂O)
- **sp³d:** trigonal bipyramidal (PCl₅)
- **sp³d²:** octahedral (SF₆)

Shortcut: steric number = bond pairs (σ) + lone pairs on the central atom → 2 sp, 3 sp², 4 sp³, 5 sp³d, 6 sp³d². In PCl₅, axial bonds are longer than equatorial bonds (more repulsion).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** Hybridisation of C atoms in CH₂=CH–C≡CH: **sp², sp², sp, sp**.

**Example 2:** σ and π bonds in ethyne C₂H₂: σ = 3 (two C–H, one C–C), π = **2**.

**Example 3:** Hybridisation of S in SF₆: 6 σ bonds, 0 lone pairs → **sp³d²**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Counting π bonds in the steric number.
- Thinking hybridisation happens in isolated atoms — it occurs during bond formation.
- Saying π bonds can exist without a σ bond between the same atoms.

activity.prompt: Match the species to the hybridisation of its central atom

quiz.why: Carbon in CO₂ forms 2 σ bonds and has no lone pair, so it is sp hybridised and the molecule is linear.
A triple bond is made of one σ bond and two π bonds. Only one σ bond can form between two atoms.
Oxygen in H₂O has 2 σ bonds and 2 lone pairs, so 4 electron pairs, and it is sp³ hybridised.
sp² hybrid orbitals point to the corners of a triangle in a plane, with a bond angle of 120°.

quiz.q: Number of σ bonds in ethene C₂H₄
quiz.why: Ethene has 4 C–H σ bonds and 1 C–C σ bond, so 5 σ bonds. The C=C has an extra π bond.

sources: NCERT Chemistry Class 11 (topic: hybridisation)

lessons.title: Molecular orbital theory and hydrogen bonding

story.title: Liquid oxygen sticks to a magnet

scenes.text: Pour liquid oxygen between the poles of a strong magnet and it clings there.
Lewis structures show no unpaired electrons in O₂ — only molecular orbital theory explains its paramagnetism.

steps.title: MO theory basics
steps.body:
- Atomic orbitals combine (LCAO) to form **bonding** (lower energy, σ, π) and **antibonding** (higher energy, σ*, π*) MOs; number of MOs = number of AOs combined.
- Conditions: similar energy, same symmetry, good overlap.
- **Bond order** = ½(N_b − N_a). Bond order 0 → molecule does not exist (He₂).
- Unpaired electrons → **paramagnetic**; all paired → **diamagnetic**.

steps.title: Energy order
steps.body:
- For Li₂ to N₂: σ1s < σ*1s < σ2s < σ*2s < (π2pₓ = π2p_y) < σ2p_z < (π*2pₓ = π*2p_y) < σ*2p_z
- For O₂ and F₂: σ2p_z lies BELOW the π2p orbitals.

Results: H₂ BO 1; He₂ 0; Li₂ 1; B₂ 1 (paramagnetic); C₂ 2 (diamagnetic); N₂ 3 (diamagnetic); O₂ 2 (paramagnetic, 2 unpaired in π*); F₂ 1.
O₂⁺ 2.5, O₂⁻ 1.5, O₂²⁻ 1: bond length O₂²⁻ > O₂⁻ > O₂ > O₂⁺.

steps.title: Hydrogen bonding
steps.body:
Attraction between H bonded to a highly electronegative atom (F, O, N) and a lone pair on another such atom.
- **Intermolecular** (between molecules): HF chains, water, alcohols → higher boiling points (H₂O is a liquid, H₂S a gas).
- **Intramolecular** (within a molecule): o-nitrophenol — lowers boiling point and solubility compared with p-nitrophenol.
- Ice's open hydrogen-bonded structure makes it less dense than water.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** N₂ has 14 electrons: N_b = 10, N_a = 4 → BO = **3**, diamagnetic.

**Example 2:** O₂ (16 electrons): N_b = 10, N_a = 6 → BO = **2**; two unpaired electrons in π*2p → paramagnetic.

**Example 3:** O₂⁻ (superoxide, 17 e⁻): BO = (10 − 7)/2 = **1.5**, one unpaired electron.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the O₂ ordering for N₂ (σ2p and π2p swap).
- Counting only valence electrons in one place and all electrons in another — be consistent.
- Thinking hydrogen bonds are as strong as covalent bonds (they are much weaker, ≈ 10–40 kJ/mol).

activity.prompt: Match each species to its bond order

quiz.why: O₂ is paramagnetic because it has two unpaired electrons in its π* antibonding orbitals. N₂, C₂ and F₂ have all electrons paired.
He₂ has 2 bonding and 2 antibonding electrons. Bond order = (2 − 2)/2 = 0, so the molecule does not exist.

quiz.q: Longest bond among O₂⁺, O₂, O₂⁻, O₂²⁻
quiz.why: O₂²⁻ has the lowest bond order (1), so it has the longest bond. O₂⁺ has bond order 2.5 and O₂ has 2.

quiz.q: H₂O is a liquid while H₂S is a gas at room temperature because of
quiz.why: Water molecules form strong hydrogen bonds with each other, so water is a liquid. H₂S has none, so it is a gas at room temperature.
In B₂ the valence electrons are σ2s², σ*2s², π2p¹, π2p¹. Bond order = (4 − 2)/2 = 1.

sources: NCERT Chemistry Class 11 (topic: MO theory, hydrogen bonding)

questions.q: Shape of BeCl₂
questions.why: BeCl₂ has 2 bond pairs and no lone pairs on Be, so it is linear.

questions.q: Hybridisation of C in CH₄
questions.why: Carbon in methane forms 4 σ bonds, so it is sp³ hybridised.

questions.q: Which bond is strongest?
questions.why: The triple bond C≡C is the strongest and shortest because it has the highest bond order, 3.

questions.q: Number of lone pairs on Xe in XeF₄
questions.why: Xe has 8 valence electrons. Four are used in bonds with F, leaving 4 electrons, which is 2 lone pairs.

questions.q: Assertion: BF₃ has zero dipole moment though B–F bonds are polar. Reason: BF₃ is trigonal planar and bond dipoles cancel.
options: Both true, Reason does not explain
questions.why: Both are true and R explains A. BF₃ is trigonal planar and symmetrical, so the three polar B–F dipoles cancel out and the net dipole moment is zero.

questions.q: Which has the largest bond angle?
questions.why: CH₄ has no lone pairs, so its angle is 109.5°. NH₃ (107°) and H₂O (104.5°) have lone pairs that squeeze the angle.

questions.q: σ and π bonds in CH₂=CH–CH=CH₂ (buta-1,3-diene)
questions.why: In buta-1,3-diene (C₄H₆) there are 6 C–H σ bonds and 3 C–C σ bonds, which is 9 σ bonds. The two C=C bonds give 2 π bonds.

questions.q: Case: A student finds a molecule AB₃ with zero dipole moment and bond angle 120°. Hybridisation of A:
questions.why: A molecule AB₃ with a bond angle of 120° and zero dipole moment is trigonal planar. The central atom is sp² hybridised.

questions.q: Shape of SF₄
questions.why: SF₄ has 4 bond pairs and 1 lone pair, so the electron geometry is trigonal bipyramidal and the shape is see-saw.

questions.q: Formal charge on S in SO₄²⁻ drawn with two S=O and two S–O⁻
questions.why: Formal charge on S = 6 − 0 − 12/2 = 0, when it has two S=O double bonds and two S–O single bonds (6 shared pairs, 12 bonding electrons).

questions.q: Correct order of bond length
questions.why: Bond order is O₂⁺ (2.5) > O₂ (2) > O₂⁻ (1.5) > O₂²⁻ (1). Bond length is inverse, so it is longest in O₂²⁻ and shortest in O₂⁺.

questions.q: Which species is diamagnetic?
questions.why: N₂ has all electrons paired in its molecular orbitals, so it is diamagnetic. O₂, O₂⁻ and B₂ have unpaired electrons.

questions.q: o-Nitrophenol is more volatile than p-nitrophenol because of
questions.why: o-Nitrophenol has intramolecular hydrogen bonding, so its molecules do not link to each other. p-Nitrophenol has intermolecular H-bonds. So the ortho isomer is more volatile.

questions.q: Which has the highest lattice enthalpy?
questions.why: MgO has Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ ions, with double charges and small sizes, so its lattice enthalpy is the highest. NaF, NaCl and KCl have single charges.

questions.q: Number of electrons in antibonding MOs of N₂⁺ (all electrons counted)
questions.why: N₂⁺ has 13 electrons. The antibonding ones are σ*1s² and σ*2s², which is 4. The electron removed from N₂ comes from the bonding σ2p orbital.

questions.q: In PCl₅, why are axial bonds longer than equatorial bonds?
options: Axial bonds experience more bond-pair repulsion
questions.why: In PCl₅ each axial bond has three equatorial bond pairs at 90°, whereas each equatorial bond has only two at 90°. So the axial bonds feel more repulsion and are longer.
