lessons.title: System, state functions, work, heat and the first law

story.title: The pressure cooker as a system

scenes.text: Think of the pressure cooker as the system and the kitchen as the surroundings.
Heat flows in from the flame; steam pushes the whistle up and does work. Energy is just being moved around.

steps.title: Basic terms
steps.body:
- **System** (part studied) and **surroundings** (rest). **Open** (matter + energy exchange), **closed** (energy only), **isolated** (neither, e.g. ideal thermos).
- **State functions** depend only on state: U, H, S, G, P, V, T. **Path functions:** q, w.
- **Extensive** properties depend on amount (mass, V, U, H); **intensive** do not (T, P, density, molar quantities).

steps.title: First law (chemistry sign convention)
steps.body:
**ΔU = q + w** — q positive when heat is ABSORBED by the system; w positive when work is done ON the system.
- Expansion against constant external pressure: **w = −p_ext ΔV**
- Reversible isothermal expansion of an ideal gas: **w = −2.303 nRT log(V_f/V_i)**
- Free expansion (into vacuum): w = 0; for an ideal gas also q = 0 and ΔU = 0.
- Isothermal ideal gas: ΔU = 0 → q = −w.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** A gas expands from 10 L to 20 L against a constant 1 atm.
- w = −1 × 10 = −10 L atm = −10 × 101.3 = **−1013 J**

**Example 2:** A system absorbs 400 J of heat and 150 J of work is done on it. ΔU = 400 + 150 = **+550 J**.

**Example 3:** 1 mol ideal gas expands reversibly and isothermally at 300 K from 1 L to 10 L. w = −2.303 × 8.314 × 300 × 1 ≈ **−5.74 kJ**; q = +5.74 kJ.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the physics sign convention (ΔQ = ΔU + ΔW) in chemistry problems — be consistent.
- Forgetting 1 L atm = 101.3 J.
- Treating q and w as state functions.

quiz.q: A thermos flask (ideal) is an example of
quiz.why: A perfect thermos flask exchanges neither matter nor energy with its surroundings, so it is an isolated system.

quiz.q: In chemistry convention, work done BY the system is
quiz.why: In the chemistry convention, work done by the system (as in expansion) is negative, because the system loses energy. w = −p_ext ΔV.

options: q + w for each path separately
quiz.why: Internal energy (U) is a state function, as it depends only on the state of the system. Heat (q) and work (w) depend on the path.

quiz.q: Free expansion of an ideal gas: w =
quiz.why: In free expansion into a vacuum the external pressure is zero, so w = −p_ext ΔV = 0.

quiz.q: System loses 100 J heat and does 50 J work. ΔU =
quiz.why: Heat lost, so q = −100 J. Work done by the system, so w = −50 J. ΔU = q + w = −100 − 50 = −150 J.

sources: NCERT Chemistry Class 11 (topic: first law)

lessons.title: Enthalpy, heat capacity and calorimetry

scenes.text: A food lab burns a biscuit in a sealed steel 'bomb' to measure energy at constant volume.
A student mixes acid and base in a foam cup open to air to measure heat at constant pressure.

steps.title: Enthalpy
steps.body:
**H = U + pV**; at constant pressure, **ΔH = q_p** (heat exchanged at constant pressure). At constant volume, **ΔU = q_v**.

For reactions involving gases: **ΔH = ΔU + Δn_g RT** where Δn_g = moles of gaseous products − moles of gaseous reactants.
- ΔH < 0: exothermic; ΔH > 0: endothermic.

steps.title: Heat capacity and calorimetry
steps.body:
- q = C ΔT = m c ΔT; molar heat capacity C_m.
- For an ideal gas: C_p − C_v = R.
- **Bomb calorimeter** (constant V) gives ΔU; **coffee-cup calorimeter** (constant p) gives ΔH.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) → 2NH₃(g) at 298 K. Δn_g = 2 − 4 = −2.
- ΔH − ΔU = −2 × 8.314 × 298 ≈ **−4.96 kJ/mol**

**Example 2:** 1 g graphite burns in a bomb calorimeter (heat capacity 20.7 kJ/K); temperature rises from 298 K to 299 K.
- q = −20.7 × 1 = −20.7 kJ per g → for 1 mol (12 g): ΔU ≈ **−248 kJ/mol** (Δn_g = 0 here, so ΔH ≈ ΔU)

**Example 3:** For H₂O(l) → H₂O(g) at 373 K with ΔH = 40.7 kJ/mol: ΔU = 40.7 − (1 × 8.314 × 373/1000) ≈ **37.6 kJ/mol**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Counting liquids and solids in Δn_g.
- Forgetting to convert R from J to kJ.
- Thinking ΔH = ΔU always (only when Δn_g = 0 or no gases).

activity.prompt: For C(s) + O₂(g) → CO₂(g), what is Δn_g?

quiz.q: At constant pressure, heat exchanged equals
quiz.why: At constant pressure, the heat exchanged equals the change in enthalpy (q_p = ΔH).
Only gases count. Reactants: 2 + 1 = 3 mol of gas. Products: water is a liquid, so 0. Δn_g = 0 − 3 = −3.
A bomb calorimeter works at constant volume, so the heat measured is ΔU (change in internal energy).
An exothermic reaction releases heat to the surroundings, so ΔH is negative.

quiz.q: C_p − C_v for an ideal gas
quiz.why: For an ideal gas, C_p − C_v = R (Mayer's relation).

sources: NCERT Chemistry Class 11 (topic: enthalpy)

lessons.title: Enthalpies of reaction, Hess's law and bond enthalpy

scenes.text: You cannot burn carbon to make only CO — some CO₂ always forms. So how do we know ΔH for C → CO?
Hess's law lets us add and subtract equations we CAN measure to get the one we can't.

steps.title: Standard enthalpies
steps.body:
Standard state: pure substance at 1 bar (and stated T, usually 298 K).
- **ΔfH°:** enthalpy change when 1 mol of compound forms from elements in their standard states (ΔfH° of elements in standard state = 0).
- **ΔcH°:** combustion of 1 mol completely in oxygen.
- **ΔaH°:** atomisation (break all bonds to gaseous atoms).
- Phase changes: ΔfusH°, ΔvapH°, ΔsubH° = ΔfusH° + ΔvapH°.
- **ΔrH° = Σ ΔfH°(products) − Σ ΔfH°(reactants)**.

steps.title: Hess's law and bond enthalpies
steps.body:
**Hess's law of constant heat summation:** ΔH of a reaction is the same whether it occurs in one step or many (H is a state function).

**Bond enthalpy method (gas phase):** ΔrH° = Σ bond enthalpies of reactants − Σ bond enthalpies of products.

**Lattice enthalpy** (Born–Haber cycle) and **enthalpy of solution** = lattice enthalpy + hydration enthalpy.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1 (Hess):** C + O₂ → CO₂, ΔH = −393.5 kJ; CO + ½O₂ → CO₂, ΔH = −283.0 kJ. Then C + ½O₂ → CO: ΔH = −393.5 − (−283.0) = **−110.5 kJ/mol**.

**Example 2 (formation):** CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O(l); ΔfH°: CH₄ −74.8, CO₂ −393.5, H₂O(l) −285.8 kJ/mol.
- ΔcH° = −393.5 + 2(−285.8) − (−74.8) = **−890.3 kJ/mol**

**Example 3 (bond enthalpy):** H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl with H–H 435, Cl–Cl 243, H–Cl 431 kJ/mol.
- ΔH = (435 + 243) − 2 × 431 = **−184 kJ**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Reversing a reaction without changing the sign of ΔH.
- Forgetting to multiply ΔH when multiplying an equation.
- Using the bond-enthalpy formula backwards (it is reactants minus products, the opposite of the formation formula).

activity.prompt: Using ΔfH° (kJ/mol): CO₂ = −393.5, H₂O(l) = −285.8, C₂H₅OH(l) = −277.7, find ΔcH° of ethanol: C₂H₅OH + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O(l). (kJ/mol)

quiz.q: ΔfH° of O₂(g) at 298 K is
quiz.why: The standard enthalpy of formation of an element in its standard state, such as O₂(g), is zero by definition.

quiz.q: Hess's law is a consequence of H being
quiz.why: Hess's law holds because enthalpy is a state function. It depends only on the initial and final states and not on the path.

quiz.q: If A → B has ΔH = −50 kJ, then 2B → 2A has ΔH =
quiz.why: Reversing a reaction changes the sign of ΔH, and doubling doubles it. So for 2B → 2A, ΔH = +2 × 50 = +100 kJ.
Going from solid to gas can be done as solid → liquid → gas, so ΔsubH° = ΔfusH° + ΔvapH°.
Energy is needed to break bonds in the reactants and is released when bonds form in the products. So ΔrH = Σ BE(reactants) − Σ BE(products).

sources: NCERT Chemistry Class 11 (topic: Hess's law)

lessons.title: Entropy, Gibbs energy and spontaneity

story.title: Ice melting on a summer day

scenes.text: Ice absorbs heat to melt — an endothermic change — yet it happens by itself on a warm day.
Spontaneity is not just about energy; disorder (entropy) and temperature decide it together.

steps.title: Entropy
steps.body:
- **Entropy S** measures molecular disorder (randomness). Gas > liquid > solid.
- For a reversible process: **ΔS = q_rev/T** (J K⁻¹).
- **Second law:** total entropy of system + surroundings increases in a spontaneous process (ΔS_total > 0).
- **Third law:** entropy of a perfectly crystalline substance is zero at 0 K.
- Example: ΔvapS of water = 40.7 kJ/373 K ≈ **109 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹**.

steps.title: Gibbs energy
steps.body:
**G = H − TS; ΔG = ΔH − TΔS** (constant T, p).
- ΔG < 0 spontaneous; ΔG > 0 non-spontaneous; ΔG = 0 equilibrium.
- ΔH −, ΔS +: spontaneous at all T
- ΔH +, ΔS −: never spontaneous
- ΔH −, ΔS −: spontaneous at low T
- ΔH +, ΔS +: spontaneous at high T (T > ΔH/ΔS)

**Link with equilibrium:** ΔG° = −RT ln K = −2.303 RT log K. Large K ↔ very negative ΔG°.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** ΔH = +40 kJ/mol, ΔS = +100 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. Spontaneous above T = 40000/100 = **400 K**.

**Example 2:** K = 10 at 298 K. ΔG° = −2.303 × 8.314 × 298 × log 10 ≈ **−5.71 kJ/mol**.

**Example 3:** For a reaction ΔH° = −92 kJ and ΔS° = −199 J/K at 298 K: ΔG° = −92 − 298 × (−0.199) = −92 + 59.3 = **−32.7 kJ** → spontaneous at 298 K.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing kJ (ΔH) and J (ΔS) — convert first.
- Thinking all exothermic reactions are spontaneous.
- Equating 'spontaneous' with 'fast' — ΔG says nothing about rate.

quiz.why: Entropy measures disorder. Steam, a gas, is the most disordered of the three, so it has the highest entropy.
At equilibrium there is no net driving force, so ΔG = 0.

quiz.q: ΔG° and K are related by
quiz.why: The standard free energy change and the equilibrium constant are related by ΔG° = −RT ln K.

quiz.q: ΔH = −10 kJ, ΔS = −20 J/K. Spontaneous below
quiz.why: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS = −10000 − T(−20) = −10000 + 20T. It is negative when T < 10000/20 = 500 K, so it is spontaneous below 500 K.

quiz.q: Third law: entropy of a perfect crystal at 0 K is
quiz.why: The third law of thermodynamics says the entropy of a perfect crystal at absolute zero (0 K) is zero, since it is perfectly ordered.

sources: NCERT Chemistry Class 11 (topic: Gibbs energy)

questions.q: Which is an intensive property?
questions.why: Temperature is an intensive property, because it does not depend on the amount of matter. Mass, volume and enthalpy depend on the amount.

questions.q: For an isolated system
questions.why: An isolated system exchanges no energy or matter, so its internal energy does not change: ΔU = 0.

questions.q: ΔfH° of an element in its standard state
questions.why: By convention the standard enthalpy of formation of an element in its standard state is zero.

questions.q: Unit of entropy
questions.why: Entropy change is q/T, so its unit is J K⁻¹ (joules per kelvin).

questions.q: Assertion: Melting of ice is spontaneous above 0 °C. Reason: TΔS exceeds ΔH above 273 K.
options: Both true, Reason does not explain
questions.why: Both are true and R explains A. ΔG = ΔH − TΔS. Above 273 K, TΔS is larger than ΔH for melting, so ΔG is negative and ice melts spontaneously.

questions.q: A gas expands against 2 atm from 5 L to 15 L. Work done (L atm):
questions.why: Work = −p_ext × ΔV = −2 atm × (15 − 5) L = −20 L atm. It is negative because the gas expands.

questions.q: For CaCO₃(s) → CaO(s) + CO₂(g), ΔH − ΔU at 1000 K is about
questions.why: ΔH − ΔU = Δn_g RT. Here Δn_g = 1 (one CO₂ gas formed). So 1 × 8.314 × 1000 J ≈ 8.3 kJ.

questions.q: Case: ΔfH° of NH₃(g) is −46 kJ/mol. ΔH for 2NH₃(g) → N₂(g) + 3H₂(g):
questions.why: Forming 2 mol of NH₃ from the elements has ΔH = 2 × (−46) = −92 kJ. The reverse reaction, decomposing 2 mol NH₃, has ΔH = +92 kJ.

questions.q: C(graphite) + O₂ → CO₂ (−393.5); H₂ + ½O₂ → H₂O(l) (−285.8); CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O(l) (−890.3). ΔfH° of CH₄:
Bond enthalpies: C–H 414, C=C 611, C–C 347, H–H 436 kJ/mol. ΔH for C₂H₄ + H₂ → C₂H₆:
questions.why: Bonds broken: C=C (611) and H–H (436) = 1047. Bonds formed: C–C (347) and 2 C–H (828) = 1175. ΔH = 1047 − 1175 = −128 kJ.

questions.q: ΔH = +30 kJ/mol and ΔS = +75 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. Minimum temperature for spontaneity:
questions.why: With ΔH positive and ΔS positive, the reaction is spontaneous when TΔS > ΔH. T > 30000/75 = 400 K.

questions.q: ΔG° = −5.7 kJ/mol at 298 K. K is about
Entropy change when 1 mol water freezes at 0 °C (ΔfusH = 6.0 kJ/mol):
questions.why: Freezing is the reverse of fusion, so ΔS = −ΔH_fus/T = −6000/273 ≈ −22 J/K. Entropy falls as the liquid becomes solid.

questions.q: 2 mol ideal gas expands reversibly and isothermally at 300 K to 10 times its volume. Work done (R = 8.314):
questions.why: For reversible isothermal expansion, w = −2.303 nRT log(V₂/V₁) = −2.303 × 2 × 8.314 × 300 × log 10 = −11,488 J ≈ −11.5 kJ.

questions.q: Lattice enthalpy of NaCl 788 kJ/mol; hydration enthalpy of ions −784 kJ/mol. Enthalpy of solution:
questions.why: Enthalpy of solution = lattice enthalpy + hydration enthalpy = 788 + (−784) = +4 kJ/mol.

questions.q: Which process has ΔS < 0?
questions.why: Forming liquid water from gases reduces the number of gas moles and the disorder, so ΔS is negative. Evaporation, melting and dissolving increase disorder.

lessons.title: Dynamic equilibrium and equilibrium constants

scenes.text: At a metro station, people go up one escalator and down another at the same rate. The crowd upstairs stays the same.
Chemical equilibrium is like that: forward and backward reactions continue at equal rates.

steps.title: Dynamic equilibrium
steps.body:
- Physical equilibria: ice ⇌ water at 0 °C; liquid ⇌ vapour in a closed vessel (vapour pressure); solid ⇌ solution (saturated solution); gas ⇌ solution (Henry's law).
- Chemical equilibrium: rate forward = rate backward; concentrations become constant (not equal!). Can be reached from either side.

steps.title: Law of mass action, K_c and K_p
steps.body:
For aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD: **K_c = [C]ᶜ[D]ᵈ / [A]ᵃ[B]ᵇ**.
- Pure solids and liquids are omitted.
- **K_p = K_c (RT)^Δn**, Δn = moles of gaseous products − reactants (R = 0.0831 bar L mol⁻¹ K⁻¹).
- Reversing the reaction → 1/K; multiplying by n → Kⁿ; adding reactions → multiply Ks.
- K depends only on temperature.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** For N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃: K_c = [NH₃]²/([N₂][H₂]³); Δn = −2 → K_p = K_c(RT)⁻².

**Example 2:** For CaCO₃(s) ⇌ CaO(s) + CO₂(g): K_p = p_CO₂ only.

**Example 3:** If K for A ⇌ B is 4, K for 2B ⇌ 2A is (1/4)² = **1/16**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Including solids or pure liquids in K.
- Thinking equilibrium means equal concentrations.
- Forgetting that a catalyst does not change K.

statements.s: At equilibrium, forward and backward reactions stop.
K changes with temperature.
Pure solids appear in the expression for K_c.
For Δn = 0, K_p = K_c.

quiz.q: For H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI, K_p and K_c are related by
quiz.why: K_p = K_c(RT)^Δn. For H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI, Δn = 2 − 2 = 0, so K_p = K_c.

quiz.q: K for the reverse of a reaction with K = 5 is
quiz.why: The equilibrium constant of the reverse reaction is the inverse of K. So 1/5 = 0.2.
Pure solids and liquids are left out of the expression for K. So K_c = [CO]²/[CO₂], without C(s).

quiz.q: Which changes the value of K?
quiz.why: Only a change in temperature changes the value of K. A catalyst, pressure and concentration change the position or rate but not K.

quiz.q: Vapour–liquid equilibrium in a closed bottle is an example of
quiz.why: Equilibrium between a liquid and its vapour in a closed bottle is a physical equilibrium, as only a change of phase occurs, with no chemical change.

sources: NCERT Chemistry Class 11 (topic: equilibrium constant)

lessons.title: Reaction quotient, calculations and Le Chatelier's principle

scenes.text: Fertiliser plants make ammonia from N₂ and H₂ at high pressure and moderate temperature.
Le Chatelier's principle explains why: high pressure pushes the equilibrium toward fewer gas molecules.

steps.title: Reaction quotient Q
steps.body:
Q has the same form as K but uses current (not equilibrium) concentrations.
- Q < K: reaction goes forward.
- Q > K: reaction goes backward.
- Q = K: at equilibrium.

**Size of K:** K > 10³ products dominate; K < 10⁻³ reactants dominate; in between, significant amounts of both.

steps.title: Le Chatelier's principle
steps.body:
If a system at equilibrium is disturbed, it shifts to oppose the change.
- **Add reactant/remove product:** shifts forward.
- **Increase pressure** (decrease volume): shifts toward fewer gas moles.
- **Temperature:** raising T favours the endothermic direction (K changes).
- **Catalyst:** reaches equilibrium faster; no shift.
- **Inert gas at constant volume:** no shift; at constant pressure: shifts toward more gas moles.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI, K_c = 64. Start with 1 mol each of H₂ and I₂ in 1 L.
- Let x react: (2x)²/(1 − x)² = 64 → 2x/(1 − x) = 8 → x = 0.8
- At equilibrium: [H₂] = [I₂] = **0.2 M**, [HI] = **1.6 M**

**Example 2:** For N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ (ΔH < 0): higher pressure → more NH₃; higher temperature → less NH₃ (but faster); so industry uses high pressure, moderate temperature and an iron catalyst.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Claiming a catalyst increases yield.
- Forgetting that temperature changes K whereas concentration and pressure changes do not.
- Mixing moles and molarity when the volume is not 1 L.

a.text: You run the reaction 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g), ΔH < 0. You want more SO₃. What do you change first?

choices.label: Increase the pressure
choices.feedback: Good: 3 gas moles → 2 gas moles, so higher pressure favours SO₃.

choices.label: Add a catalyst to increase yield
choices.feedback: A catalyst only speeds up reaching equilibrium; it does not change the yield.

b.text: Now: should you raise the temperature a lot?

choices.label: No — keep it moderate; high T shifts an exothermic reaction backward
choices.feedback: Correct balance of yield and rate.

choices.label: Yes — always heat more
choices.feedback: Higher T lowers K for an exothermic reaction.

c.text: Rethink using Le Chatelier's principle: pressure toward fewer moles, temperature toward the endothermic side.

end1.text: Optimal: high pressure, moderate temperature, catalyst for speed.

quiz.why: If Q is greater than K, there is too much product compared with equilibrium. So the net reaction goes backward to turn product into reactants.

quiz.q: Increasing pressure on N₂O₄(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g) shifts it
quiz.why: Higher pressure favours the side with fewer moles of gas. N₂O₄ ⇌ 2NO₂ has 1 mole on the left and 2 on the right, so the shift is backward toward N₂O₄.

quiz.q: For an endothermic reaction, raising temperature
quiz.why: For an endothermic reaction, heating shifts the equilibrium forward, so more product forms and K increases.
A catalyst lowers the activation energy of both the forward and backward reactions equally, so equilibrium is reached faster. It does not change K or the yield.

quiz.q: Adding inert gas at constant volume
quiz.why: Adding an inert gas at constant volume does not change the concentrations or partial pressures of the reacting gases, so the equilibrium does not shift.

sources: NCERT Chemistry Class 11 (topic: Le Chatelier's principle)

lessons.title: Acids, bases, pH and ionisation constants

scenes.text: Lemon juice, vinegar and stomach acid all taste sour, but their strengths differ enormously.
The pH scale compresses this huge range into simple numbers using logarithms.

steps.title: Acid–base concepts
steps.body:
- **Arrhenius:** acids give H⁺ (H₃O⁺) in water; bases give OH⁻.
- **Brønsted–Lowry:** acid = proton donor, base = proton acceptor. Conjugate pairs differ by one H⁺ (HCl/Cl⁻, NH₄⁺/NH₃). Strong acid → weak conjugate base.
- **Lewis:** acid = electron-pair acceptor (BF₃, AlCl₃, H⁺), base = electron-pair donor (NH₃, OH⁻).

steps.title: Water, pH and weak acids
steps.body:
- **K_w = [H₃O⁺][OH⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴** at 298 K → pH + pOH = 14. Neutral water pH 7 (at 298 K).
- **pH = −log[H₃O⁺]**.
- Weak acid HA (concentration c, degree α): **K_a = cα²/(1 − α) ≈ cα²**, [H⁺] = √(K_a c); pK_a = −log K_a.
- For conjugate pairs: **K_a × K_b = K_w**.
- Polyprotic acids ionise stepwise: K_a1 > K_a2 > K_a3.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Taking pH of 10⁻⁸ M HCl as 8 — water's own H⁺ (10⁻⁷) dominates, so pH is slightly below 7 (≈ 6.98).
- Using [H⁺] = c for weak acids.
- Forgetting K_w changes with temperature (neutral pH is not 7 at all T).

activity.prompt: What is the pH of a 0.0001 M solution of HCl?

quiz.why: The conjugate base is formed when the acid loses one H⁺. H₂SO₄ losing one H⁺ gives HSO₄⁻.
BF₃ has an empty orbital on boron and can accept an electron pair, so it is a Lewis acid. It has no H⁺ or OH⁻ to be an Arrhenius or Brønsted base.
At 298 K, K_w = 10⁻¹⁴, so pH + pOH = 14.
pH = −log[H⁺] = −log 10⁻⁵ = 5.

quiz.q: For a conjugate pair, K_a × K_b =
quiz.why: For a conjugate acid–base pair, K_a × K_b = K_w, which is 10⁻¹⁴ at 298 K.

sources: NCERT Chemistry Class 11 (topic: ionic equilibrium)

lessons.title: Common-ion effect, hydrolysis, buffers and solubility product

scenes.text: Even after a heavy meal or exercise, blood stays near pH 7.4.
Buffers — mixtures of a weak acid and its salt — soak up extra acid or base.

steps.title: Common-ion effect and hydrolysis
steps.body:
- **Common-ion effect:** adding an ion already present suppresses ionisation of a weak electrolyte (adding CH₃COONa to CH₃COOH lowers [H⁺]).
- **Salt hydrolysis:**
  - Strong acid + strong base salt (NaCl): neutral, pH 7
  - Weak acid + strong base (CH₃COONa): basic; pH = 7 + ½(pK_a + log c)
  - Strong acid + weak base (NH₄Cl): acidic; pH = 7 − ½(pK_b + log c)
  - Weak acid + weak base (CH₃COONH₄): pH = 7 + ½(pK_a − pK_b)

steps.title: Buffers and K_sp
steps.body:
- **Buffer:** resists pH change. Acidic buffer: weak acid + its salt; **pH = pK_a + log([salt]/[acid])** (Henderson–Hasselbalch). Basic buffer: pOH = pK_b + log([salt]/[base]).
- **Solubility product:** for MₓAᵧ(s) ⇌ xM^(y+) + yA^(x−), K_sp = [M]ˣ[A]ʸ. With molar solubility s: AB → K_sp = s²; AB₂ → 4s³; A₂B₃ → 108s⁵.
- Precipitation occurs when ionic product Q_sp > K_sp.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** Buffer of 0.1 M CH₃COOH + 0.1 M CH₃COONa (pK_a = 4.74): pH = **4.74**. With salt 0.2 M: pH = 4.74 + log 2 = **5.04**.

**Example 2:** K_sp(AgCl) = 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰ → s = √K_sp ≈ **1.34 × 10⁻⁵ M**.
- In 0.1 M NaCl: s = 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰/0.1 = **1.8 × 10⁻⁹ M** (common-ion effect)

**Example 3:** CaF₂ with s = 2 × 10⁻⁴ M: K_sp = 4s³ = 4 × 8 × 10⁻¹² = **3.2 × 10⁻¹¹**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing K_sp = s² for every salt (stoichiometry matters).
- Inverting the Henderson ratio (it is salt/acid for acidic buffers).
- Forgetting that a buffer works best when pH ≈ pK_a.

activity.prompt: Match the salt to the nature of its aqueous solution

quiz.why: NH₄Cl gives NH₄⁺, which is common to the NH₄OH equilibrium. By the common-ion effect, this pushes the ionisation of NH₄OH back, so it decreases.

quiz.q: K_sp of Ag₂CrO₄ in terms of solubility s
quiz.why: Ag₂CrO₄ ⇌ 2Ag⁺ + CrO₄²⁻. With solubility s, [Ag⁺] = 2s and [CrO₄²⁻] = s. K_sp = (2s)² × s = 4s³.
For a buffer, pH = pK_a + log([salt]/[acid]). When [salt] = [acid], log 1 = 0, so pH = pK_a.
NH₄Cl is a salt of a strong acid and a weak base. NH₄⁺ hydrolyses to give H⁺, so the solution is acidic.
A precipitate forms when the ionic product Q_sp is greater than K_sp, because the solution is supersaturated and the excess salt separates.

questions.why: Pure water at 298 K has [H⁺] = 10⁻⁷ M, so its pH is 7, which is neutral.

questions.why: K_c = [NH₃]²/([N₂][H₂]³. Units are (mol/L)²/(mol/L)⁴ = (mol/L)⁻² = mol⁻² L².

questions.q: pH of 0.005 M H₂SO₄ (complete ionisation)
questions.why: Each H₂SO₄ gives 2 H⁺. [H⁺] = 2 × 0.005 = 0.01 M, so pH = 2.

questions.q: Assertion: Adding a catalyst does not change the equilibrium composition. Reason: A catalyst lowers the activation energy of forward and backward reactions equally.
options: Both true, Reason does not explain
questions.why: Both are true and R explains A. A catalyst speeds the forward and backward reactions equally, so it does not change the equilibrium composition, only the time to reach it.

Case: In a closed flask, Q for a reaction is 0.5 while K is 2. What will happen?
questions.why: If Q (0.5) is less than K (2), the system has less product than at equilibrium. So the net reaction goes forward.

questions.q: Equal volumes of 0.2 M CH₃COOH and 0.1 M NaOH are mixed (pK_a = 4.74). pH:
questions.why: 0.2 M acid mixed with half as much NaOH leaves equal amounts of acid and its salt, so it is a buffer with [salt] = [acid]. So pH = pK_a = 4.74.

questions.q: For 2NO₂ ⇌ N₂O₄, ΔH < 0. Which favours N₂O₄?
questions.why: 2NO₂ ⇌ N₂O₄ is exothermic, so low temperature favours N₂O₄. It also reduces gas moles from 2 to 1, so high pressure favours it too.

questions.q: K_sp of Mg(OH)₂ is 1.2 × 10⁻¹¹. Its solubility in 0.1 M NaOH:
questions.why: In 0.1 M NaOH, [OH⁻] = 0.1 M. K_sp = s[OH⁻]², so s = 1.2 × 10⁻¹¹ ÷ (0.1)² = 1.2 × 10⁻⁹ M. The common ion cuts solubility.

questions.q: Degree of dissociation of a weak acid on 4-fold dilution
questions.why: By Ostwald's dilution law, α = √(K_a/C). If the concentration falls to a quarter, α rises by √4 = 2 times, so it doubles.

questions.q: Which pair forms a buffer?
questions.why: A buffer needs a weak acid and its salt (or a weak base and its salt). CH₃COOH with CH₃COONa fits. HCl and HNO₃ are strong acids.
